title: The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: Revival Begins When One Thought Is Turned Around
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to lesson ninety-nine of 321 Morning Devotion. The title is “A Change of Mindset,” and the subtitle is “The Starting Point of the Selfless Life.”

Let me begin with a morning many of us have had. The alarm goes off, you switch it off, and you say to yourself, “Today I am definitely not going to lose my temper. I am definitely going to be patient. I am definitely going to love my family.” You clench your fists and head out the door full of resolve. But before noon — one sentence on the phone, one look in the office, one piece of clothing not put away at home — and that temper you only just “made a decision” to deal with this morning comes surging up like a spring bursting out of the ground. By night you’re lying in bed, and a familiar sentence rises in your heart: “How did I end up doing that again?”

Many Christians have walked that cycle for ten, twenty years. It isn’t that we don’t love the Lord, don’t read the Bible, don’t pray. We have simply been using the wrong method. We have been using “redoubled effort” to deal with something that effort can never deal with.

The answer Scripture gives us is the exact opposite of human instinct. God does not want us to work harder at improving the old self; God declares that the old self has already been dealt with on the cross. Not “I must strive to die,” but “Jesus has already died for me.” Not “I must try harder to change,” but “I must see things a different way.”

This is the heart of this lesson: revival begins not with outward actions but with an inward change of mindset. If the mindset does not change, the life will not change; if the life does not change, behaviour cannot change. God wants to bring us into the selfless life, and the first thing he does is turn our thinking around, so that we no longer rely on our own efforts to become holy, but rely on the death and resurrection of Jesus, letting “the life of Christ” replace “the life of the old self.”

Someone once compared a person to a clock. If the hands on the clock face are keeping poor time, you can move them with your finger; each time you move them they are right, but a little later they drift again. The real problem is not in the hands but in the movement inside. Our behaviour is the hands; our mindset is the movement. God never merely moves our hands; he wants to repair our movement.

Brothers and sisters, what kind of “movement” have you brought before the Lord this morning? The “I must try harder” movement, or the “Christ has already accomplished it” movement? These two movements produce two completely different lives.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Written for the Purity of the Gospel
sections.html:
Our key verse today is Galatians 2:20. To grasp the real weight of this verse, we first need to get to know this letter.

First, the author and the date. The author of Galatians is the apostle Paul. At the very start of the letter he solemnly declares his apostleship: “Paul, an apostle — not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Galatians 1:1). The letter is generally regarded as one of Paul’s earliest, written sometime around AD 48 to 55, to the churches in the region of Galatia.

Second, the situation that prompted it. Paul had preached the gospel in Galatia and led many Gentiles to the Lord. But after he left, a group of teachers known as the “Judaizers” came in and told these Gentile believers: believing in Jesus alone is not enough; you must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses before you are truly saved. That sounds very devout, yet it is a fatal deviation, because it moves the foundation of salvation from “what Christ has already accomplished” to “what I still have to add.”

That is why Paul’s tone in this letter is unusually severe. He says, “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). He even says, “But even though we, or an angel from heaven, should preach to you any ‘good news’ other than that which we preached to you, let him be cursed” (Galatians 1:8).

Third, the flow of the context. Chapter 2 records how Paul publicly rebuked Peter in Antioch. Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but when certain men came from James, he drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles, and even Barnabas was carried away by the hypocrisy. Paul opposed him to his face, because on the surface this was a matter of table manners, but at its core it was the truth of the gospel: is a person justified by works of the law, or by faith in Jesus Christ?

Paul’s conclusion is this: “yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law” (Galatians 2:16).

And then, at the very height of this battle for the gospel, Paul speaks the words that have shaken the church in every generation: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Brothers and sisters, notice this: Galatians 2:20 is not a lyrical line of poetry; it is a heavy shell fired by Paul on the battlefield of the gospel. What it sets out to resolve is precisely our deepest predicament today — am I going to live by my own strength, or am I going to let Christ live in me?

This also tells us something: “a change of mindset” is never a small subject. In Paul’s eyes, if the mindset goes astray, the gospel goes astray; if the gospel goes astray, the life goes astray. That is why he did not hesitate to oppose Peter to his face in order to set this mindset straight.

sections.heading: 1. From the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness: The Key Is Denying of Self
sections.html:
1. We Are All Born into a Self-Centred World

Every one of us is born into a self-centred world. We are used to putting ourselves at the centre, judging good and bad, right and wrong, success and failure by our own standards. This isn’t learned later; we are born with it. No parent has to teach a child to be selfish; what we have to teach is how not to be.

Where does this self-centredness come from? Scripture points clearly to its source. In the Garden of Eden the serpent said to the woman, “for God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). “You will be like God” — that is the root of humanity’s fall. Man was not content to be man; man wanted to be God. Man was not content to be loved by God in his originally intended position; he wanted to leave that position and take God’s place.

From that moment on, the human heart has held an extra throne, and the one sitting on it is “I.” My feelings matter most, my face is what counts, my plans must not be disrupted. We spend a lifetime of strength defending this throne, and a lifetime of pain paying the price for it.

The 321 vision puts it precisely: the old self’s problem is the self-centred life; the self-centred life shows itself as pride; and pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. And once a person sits in a seat that doesn’t belong to him, he has to guard it every moment, because the seat was never his in the first place.

2. The Life of Jesus Is the Exact Opposite

But the life of Jesus is the exact opposite. He did not live for himself; he lived for the Father’s will. He said, “For I have come down from heaven, not to do my own will, but the will of him who sent me” (John 6:38).

Paul describes him like this: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

“Emptied himself” in Greek is κενόω (kenoō), meaning “to empty out,” like pouring a cup out completely. See how stark the contrast is: Adam was a man yet wanted to be God; Jesus was God yet willingly became a man. Adam reached out to grab; Jesus opened his hands to let go. Adam left his originally intended position; Jesus returned to his.

Brothers and sisters, this is what the 321 vision means: humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

3. Denying Ourselves Is a Decision, Not Self-Punishment

To turn from the self-centred life to selflessness, the key is denying of self. Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, and take up his cross, and follow me” (Matthew 16:24). Luke records it in more detail: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23) — where the Chinese Union Version reads “take up his cross daily.”

“Deny” in the original is ἀπαρνέομαι (aparneomai), meaning “to disown, to declare that one has nothing to do with someone.” This word appears in the New Testament in another famous scene. Jesus said to Peter, “Most certainly I tell you that tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times” (Matthew 26:34). The word “deny” there is exactly the same word.

That throws a bright light on what denying ourselves means. Peter said to people, “I don’t know the man.” Jesus wants us to say to the old self, “I don’t know the man.”

It is not hating ourselves, not tormenting ourselves, not running ourselves down until we are worth nothing. It is this: when that familiar old self comes along again saying, “This has to go my way,” we can stand up and say, “I don’t know you. You are not my lord. My Lord is Jesus.”

So denying ourselves is not self-punishment, nor is it rejecting who we are; it is being willing to lay down a self-centred life and turn to a Christ-centred one.

4. A Confirmation from Psychology: We Are Not as Noticed as We Think

Interestingly, psychological research also confirms, from the side, how illusory the self-centred life is. In a study published in 2000 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Thomas Gilovich of Cornell University and his colleagues described the “spotlight effect”: people markedly overestimate how much others notice them. In the experiment, participants put on an embarrassing T-shirt and walked into a room; afterwards they estimated that about half the people there would have noticed it. In reality, far fewer had.

We think the whole world is looking at that one stray hair, that slip of the tongue, that one mistake; in fact others are busy worrying about the stray hair on their own heads. How much anxiety have we spent on a “self” that nobody is actually staring at?

Scripture said it long ago: “You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence” (Isaiah 30:15). When the “self” steps down from centre stage and the light falls on Jesus, we find we can breathe a sigh of relief.

5. An Everyday Illustration: The Grafted Branch

In an orchard, when the farmer wants a wild fruit tree to bear good fruit, he does not give it more fertiliser or more pruning. He cuts off the wild branch and grafts on a branch of a good variety. Wound is pressed to wound, growing layer to growing layer; it is bound tight, and then he waits. After a while the new branch draws nourishment from the old root and bears fruit of the new variety.

Notice two things. First, there must be a “cut,” or the graft won’t take. Second, what bears the fruit is not the effort of the root but the nature of the branch grafted on.

Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Denying ourselves is that cut; “Christ lives in me” is that new branch grafted on.

6. Grace, Not Effort

The selfless life is not gained by effort; it comes from grace. When we are willing to choose to deny ourselves, God’s grace comes upon us and enables us to live out the reality of “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

“For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.” (Ephesians 2:8–9)

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: denying ourselves is not the price we pay in exchange for grace; it is the posture by which we open ourselves to grace. Opening the curtains can’t manufacture sunlight — but open the curtains, and the sunlight comes in.

7. Applying the 321 Vision

The 321 vision lines up with this perfectly: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. What Satan is best at dealing with is the “self” that wants to defend itself; when he comes up against a truly selfless person, he has nowhere to get a grip, because there is nothing on that person to take hold of.

And remember: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless. An emptied cup is not a discarded cup; it is a cup ready to be filled. When we pour ourselves out, Christ fills us with himself — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

sections.heading: 2. A Change of Mindset Means Identifying with the Death and Resurrection of Jesus
sections.html:
1. One Verse, Two Worlds

Paul says: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

This verse reveals the starting point of selflessness: it is not that I go and die, but that Jesus has already died for me. What I must do is not be crucified all over again, but “choose” to be crucified with him — letting his death become my death and his resurrection become my resurrection.

2. One Perfect Tense Settles a Lifetime’s Struggle

“I have been crucified with Christ” is a single word in Greek: συνεσταύρωμαι (synestaurōmai). It has two key grammatical features we must grasp.

First, it is a compound word, with σύν (syn) on the front, meaning “together with.” It is not that I go and get crucified on my own; I am crucified “together with Christ.”

Second, it is in the perfect tense. The Greek perfect expresses something completed in the past whose effect continues right up to the present. So Paul is not saying “I am trying hard to be crucified,” nor “I hope to be crucified one day,” but: this has already been done, and it is still in force today.

Brothers and sisters, this is the turning point of the whole lesson. This morning you are not being called to complete a construction project; you are being called to believe in a project that is already finished. The last word the Lord Jesus spoke on the cross was “It is finished” (John 19:30). In Greek that word is τετέλεσται (tetelestai), also a perfect tense, and in the commercial documents of the day it was used to mean “debt paid in full.”

If you don’t believe this has already been done, you will spend your whole life trying to complete it by your own effort; if you believe it has already been done, your effort changes from “striving” to “responding.”

3. Scripture Interpreting Scripture: How Paul Explains the Same Thing in Romans

Paul, afraid we might not understand, spends a whole chapter of Romans explaining it:

“knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin” (Romans 6:6)

“For if we have become united with him in the likeness of his death, we will also be part of his resurrection” (Romans 6:5)

Then he gives a very practical instruction: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11).

The word “consider” in the original is λογίζομαι (logizomai), an accounting term meaning “to calculate, to enter in the books, to reckon.” Accountants don’t create facts; accountants record facts. If your books say a million and there is a million in the bank, that is bookkeeping; if your books say a million and there is nothing in the bank, that is fraud.

So “considering ourselves dead” is not self-hypnosis or pretending; it is honestly entering into our own mindset the fact God has already declared. God says the old self has been crucified with Christ, so that is how I keep the books. I am not manufacturing a fact; I am acknowledging one.

4. He Did Not Only Die for Us; He Died in Our Place

On the cross, Jesus defeated the power of sin and death for us. Paul exults: “Death, where is your sting? Hades, where is your victory? The sting of death is sin, and the power of sin is the law. But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:55–57).

He did not only die for us; he died in our place. “In our place” is different from “for our sake.” If he died only “for my sake,” I would still have to die again myself; but since he died “in my place,” my death has been accomplished in his.

So we can declare, “I have already died!” That “I” who was so often self-centred, bound by sin and grasping for itself came to an end on the cross.

5. A Historical Illustration: The Proclamation Was Issued, but the Chains Stayed in the Mind

On 1 January 1863, the Emancipation Proclamation signed by President Lincoln took effect. From a legal standpoint, from that day on many people were already free. Yet history tells us the news travelled slowly; in some places slaves did not learn they had long been free until more than two years later. More heart-breaking still, even after they knew, some went back to their old masters’ fields, bending low as before, keeping their heads down as before, not daring to look anyone in the eye as before — because the law had changed, but the mindset had not.

Brothers and sisters, aren’t you and I just the same? The proclamation of the cross was issued long ago, but our mindset is still living on the old plantation. We still report to a master who has been deposed; we still obey a voice that no longer has any authority.

“If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)

Freedom is an accomplished fact; enjoying freedom takes the renewing of our mindset.

6. A Confirmation from Psychology: Thoughts Shape Emotions and Behaviour

In the 1960s, the psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck of the University of Pennsylvania, while treating patients with depression, found that their suffering came not simply from events themselves but from their automatic interpretations of those events. From this he developed Cognitive Therapy, which became the foundation of today’s cognitive behavioural therapy. His contemporary, the psychologist Albert Ellis, had proposed his well-known ABC model in the 1950s: A is the Activating event, B is the Belief, C is the Consequence — the emotional and behavioural consequence is not determined directly by the event but passes through the checkpoint of “belief.”

Notice that psychology, at the level of common grace, is only confirming a principle Scripture revealed long ago. Scripture said it earlier and more deeply — in the words of the Chinese Union Version, “For as he thinks in his heart, so is he” (Proverbs 23:7).

If even the learning of this world acknowledges that “changing beliefs is the way to change behaviour,” shouldn’t we value all the more the renewal of mindset revealed in God’s word? “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

7. Not by Willpower but by Faith

The selfless life is not changed by willpower but by faith accepting a fact: the old self has been crucified with Christ, and the new self has risen in him.

Paul goes on: “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Look at the structure of that sentence: not “I live by my love for the Son of God,” but “I live by faith in the Son of God.” The source of strength is not my love but my faith — and what my faith rests on is his love: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.”

The nineteenth-century missionary Hudson Taylor, after many years in China, at one point sank into deep misery from trying to keep up his spiritual condition by his own strength. In 1869 he went through a spiritual turning point and grasped the truth of “union with Christ” — what later came to be called “the exchanged life.” In a letter to his sister he wrote that the key was not to strive to produce faith but to look to the Faithful One. From then on his ministry was no longer a grim effort to hold on but an overflow.

8. Applying the 321 Vision: The Fivefold Change Begins with Mindset

The 321 vision says the fivefold change is in mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Notice that this order cannot be reversed. Many people try to start changing with “ministry,” and end up exhausted and miserable; many try to start with “daily living,” and end up merely trimming leaves. God’s order starts from the innermost place — replace the movement first, and the hands will naturally keep good time.

This is also the shift of perspective the 321 vision speaks of: from man’s point of view to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Galatians 2:20 is the hinge of this shift: I no longer see myself in terms of “how much more I still have to do,” but in terms of “what Christ has already done for me.”

sections.heading: 3. Between Death and Resurrection, Experiencing True Release and Victory
sections.html:
1. Romans 7: A Self-Portrait of Every Honest Person

In Romans 7 Paul says: “I find then the law that, to me, while I desire to do good, evil is present” (Romans 7:21).

He describes it even more nakedly: “For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice” (Romans 7:18–19).

This is the struggle of the self-centred life: I know what I ought to do, but I can’t do it. I want to forgive, but I keep getting tied up by the hurt; I want to be humble, but pride keeps knocking me down.

Brothers and sisters, notice something very important: Romans 7 is not the confession of a failure; it is the confession of an honest man. A person who never struggles has usually not already overcome — he simply hasn’t got serious yet. Only those who are truly serious about holiness run into that wall.

2. Why Relying on Ourselves Can Never Succeed

Relying on ourselves can never defeat the “self,” because the “self” is itself the root of sin.

The logic is simple yet often overlooked: you cannot use the “self” to deal with the “self.” Using my willpower to defeat my sinful desires is like grabbing my right hand with my left and announcing, “I’ve got myself under control” — both hands are still on the same body. More dangerous still, when we do manage a little success “by our own strength,” we immediately gain something even harder to deal with: spiritual pride.

So in the end Paul cries out: “What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death? I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” (Romans 7:24–25).

The answer is not “which method” but “which Person.” Not how, but who.

3. The Picture of the Lifeguard

Every trained lifeguard knows this: the most dangerous drowning person is the one who still has the strength to struggle. The moment he sees someone come near, he instinctively clutches at his rescuer and often drags them both under. So lifeguard training teaches people to wait, or to approach from behind, until the person stops struggling; only then can they truly bring him to shore.

Brothers and sisters, how much this picture resembles our spiritual life. The harder we struggle, the deeper we sink. God is not asking us to give up on being saved; he is asking us to give up on saving ourselves.

“You will be saved in returning and rest. Your strength will be in quietness and in confidence.” (Isaiah 30:15)

4. Walking Out of Chapter 7 into Chapter 8

Only when we let Jesus’ death take the place of our death, and let his resurrection become our life, can we truly be free.

The end of Romans 7 is the beginning of chapter 8: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus, who don’t walk according to the flesh, but according to the Spirit. For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death” (Romans 8:1–2).

Notice that what overcomes one law is not effort but another, higher law. An aeroplane can leave the ground not because it has abolished gravity, but because a higher law — aerodynamics — overcomes gravity. Switch off the engines and the plane falls at once; switch them on and it flies.

We overcome “the law of sin and of death” by “the law of the Spirit of life.” This is what the 321 vision means: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll have worry, rely on the heart and you’ll have joy.

5. One Declaration Breaks the Power of the Old Self

When we declare, “Lord, I have been crucified with you,” in that moment the power of the old self is broken.

This is not a magic spell; it is faith taking hold of a fact. It is like a verdict already handed down in court: what the person concerned must do is stand up and accept the verdict, not keep fretting over a case already closed.

We no longer live for ourselves but for the Lord who died for us and rose again. Paul says: “For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died. He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:14–15).

6. A Scientific Fact About the Brain: Old Roads and New Roads

The way the brain works also offers an interesting analogy. In his book Thinking, Fast and Slow, Daniel Kahneman, winner of the 2002 Nobel Prize in Economics, divides human thinking into “System 1” and “System 2.” System 1 is fast, automatic and effortless — the intuitive reactions built up over many years; System 2 is slow, needs concentration and takes effort. Under pressure, System 1 takes over almost every time.

That explains why, when we are calm, we decide to be gentle, yet the moment someone treads on our toes we explode — because in that moment the old road is doing the driving. So what God wants to do is not just stick a note on our System 2; he wants to open a new road within us, until “Christ lives in me” becomes our new automatic response.

And this new road is laid by the Holy Spirit, day by day, with the word of God.

7. An Inner Resurrection We Can Experience Every Day

The selfless life is really the life of “Christ living in me.” Such a life does not depend on struggling or on suppressing, but on faith that relies on Christ’s victory.

The resurrection of Jesus is not only a historical event; it is also an “inner resurrection” we can experience every day.

Paul prays for the church in Ephesus that God would let them know “what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead” (Ephesians 1:19–20). Notice: the power that raised Jesus from the dead is the very power at work in us today.

“If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth. For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” (Colossians 3:1–3)

8. Applying the 321 Vision: Jesus Is the Focal Point

The 321 vision says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

Stare at yourself when you fail, and you’ll be discouraged; stare at yourself when you succeed, and you’ll be proud. Stare at others, and you’ll envy or despise them; stare at your circumstances, and you’ll be afraid. Only by fixing your eyes on Jesus will you have peace.

“looking to Jesus, the author and perfecter of faith, who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame, and has sat down at the right hand of the throne of God.” (Hebrews 12:2)

Brothers and sisters, this morning, take your eyes off yourself and put them on Jesus. You will find that the “self” that has tormented you for so many years suddenly looks very small in his glory.

sections.heading: 4. The Three Stages of Growth in Selflessness
sections.html:
For selflessness to become the habit of our life, we need to pass through three stages.

First, a change of mindset: identifying with the death and resurrection of Jesus — this is the beginning of selflessness

Everything starts here. If a person still believes deep down that “holiness is something I have to work hard to achieve,” all his practices will turn into burdens. Once the mindset changes, the burden turns into delight.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

“Transformed” here is the Greek μεταμορφόω (metamorphoō), the word our “metamorphosis” comes from. Interestingly, the same word is used in the account of Jesus’ transfiguration on the mountain: “He was changed before them. His face shone like the sun, and his garments became as white as the light” (Matthew 17:2).

And the noun for “renewing,” ἀνακαίνωσις (anakainōsis), means “made completely new in nature” — not patched up, but renewed.

The natural world gives us a marvellous picture. When a caterpillar becomes a butterfly, it doesn’t grow wings and stick them on its body. Inside the chrysalis its tissues break down and are reassembled; almost its whole body is taken apart and rebuilt. It doesn’t “crawl harder”; it “changes its form of life.”

Brothers and sisters, God’s purpose for us is not to make us “caterpillars that are very good at crawling,” but to make us butterflies.

Second, a change of choices: establishing godly values and a godly way of deciding — this is the condition for selflessness

Once the mindset has changed, we must make different choices at the crossroads of every day.

Moses was like this: “choosing rather to share ill treatment with God’s people than to enjoy the pleasures of sin for a time, considering the reproach of Christ greater riches than the treasures of Egypt; for he looked to the reward” (Hebrews 11:25–26).

Notice the words “considering” and “looked to” — that is a value system, a point of view. Moses’ choice was different because his system of valuation was different.

Years of research by the psychologist Carol S. Dweck of Stanford University show that how people respond to difficulty is deeply shaped by their “mindset.” Those with a “fixed mindset” see failure as a verdict on their worth; those with a “growth mindset” see failure as information to learn from. The same event, because of a different inner framework, leads to completely different choices.

Scripture gives us a higher framework: not “Can I do it?” but “What does the Lord want?” When before every decision we ask, “Is this what I want, or what you want, Lord?” our system of choosing is reset.

“throwing down imaginations and every high thing that is exalted against the knowledge of God and bringing every thought into captivity to the obedience of Christ” (2 Corinthians 10:5)

Third, a change of habits: continually obeying the Holy Spirit and living out the likeness of Christ — this is selflessness taking shape

Choices repeated often enough become habits; habits that hold steady become character; once character takes shape, what others see in us is the likeness of Christ.

Research by Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London, published in 2009 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, found that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit takes on average about sixty-six days, with wide individual variation — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

That figure gives us two reminders. First, don’t imagine you can change a lifetime in three days. Second, don’t imagine you can’t change. What God gives us is a road to be walked every day — “take up his cross daily and follow me,” as the Chinese Union Version renders Luke 9:23.

The brain’s plasticity confirms this too. In a study published in 2000, Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London found that London taxi drivers, after years of memorising the city’s complex streets, had a greater volume of grey matter in the posterior hippocampus than a control group, and that this correlated with how long they had been driving. A road walked every day leaves real traces inside a person.

Brothers and sisters, which road do you walk every day? Walk the road back to the old self, and that road grows wider and wider; walk the road of obeying the Holy Spirit, and that road too grows wider and wider.

Why the First Step Matters Most

The first step — a change of mindset — is the starting point of the whole selfless life.

If our mindset is still centred on “me,” all spiritual practices are merely religious behaviour; but if our mindset changes and we see “not I, but Christ,” our life will naturally be turned around.

If the foundation of a tower block is off by a single degree, the higher you build, the further it leans. Mindset is the foundation. That is why God wants us to spend time on the innermost place — the least visible, yet the one that decides everything.

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

sections.heading: 5. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let us put this lesson back into the whole picture of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model — he existed in the form of God, yet emptied himself and was made in the likeness of men (Philippians 2:6–7). The supreme model of selflessness is Jesus himself.

The Bible is my standard — a change of mindset rests not on feelings but on the word of God. “I have hidden your word in my heart, that I might not sin against you” (Psalm 119:11).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the power to put the old self to death lies not in me but in the Holy Spirit. “If by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live” (Romans 8:13).

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). The throne of the heart has room for only one. The old self comes down; Jesus goes up.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — “But far be it from me to boast, except in the cross of our Lord Jesus Christ” (Galatians 6:14). The selfless don’t grab the credit, because they know the credit was never theirs to begin with.

The Goal

Establish God’s system — when one person becomes selfless, there is less strife in the family; when a group of people become selfless, the church has unity; and a united church becomes God’s system on earth, fulfilling what the Lord’s Prayer asks: “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven” (Matthew 6:10).

Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

This lesson has been about “life” from beginning to end. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things.

When the mindset changes, the first thing mended is my relationship with God — I no longer try to earn his acceptance by my behaviour. Next comes my relationship with myself — I no longer wrestle with an old self that has already been crucified. Only then come my relationships with others and with things.

The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

The 920 practice says: every person connected to us is our “2”; before them we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice that fruit is “borne,” not “made.” A branch doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce grapes; it only has to stay joined to the vine. This is the very heart of this lesson: not effort, but union.

The 235 relationships say: become a “2” — spiritual companions — with a selfless person; build a “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. If a change of mindset stays inside one person alone, the old environment easily drags it back; but with companions to remind each other, spiritual parents to provide covering and a team to move forward together, the new mindset can stand firm.

sections.heading: 6. Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us four practices. Let us take them deeper using the 321 vision’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication.

Practice One: A Daily Declaration

Every morning, declare: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live.”

Information: first read Galatians 2:20 carefully, and know that these are Paul’s own words.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to turn these words from ink on a page into light in your heart.

Conviction: don’t believe because you have felt it; believe because God has said it.

Implementation: declare it out loud once every day before you leave the house — aloud, not just in your head.

Evaluation: in the evening, look back: at what moment today did I forget these words?

Correction: write that moment down, and pray ahead of time tomorrow for that situation.

Repetition: for forty days in a row, let the declaration turn from an assignment into breathing.

Multiplication: teach this declaration to your “2” — a family member or a companion.

Practice Two: Meditating on the Cross

Spend five minutes every day reflecting on the death and resurrection of Jesus, giving thanks for his taking our place and for his victory.

Don’t rush to ask for anything; simply look at him. Look at his hands, his side, his empty tomb. When I see his death, my “self” shrinks; when I see his resurrection, my hope grows large.

“so that in him we might become the righteousness of God.” (2 Corinthians 5:21)

Practice Three: Renewing the Mindset

Whenever you want to rely on yourself, turn to the Lord at once and say, “Lord, not by me, but by you.”

This is an “on-the-spot” practice. Don’t wait for the evening prayer meeting; turn in that very second.

“‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

Practice Four: Obeying the Holy Spirit

Before every decision, ask: “Is this what I want, or what you want, Lord?”

Start practising with small things. You needn’t ask about what to have for lunch today, but whether to reply to that sharply worded message today — that you do need to ask about.

“A man’s heart plans his course, but Yahweh directs his steps.” (Proverbs 16:9)

sections.heading: 7. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
Selflessness is not “having no worth”; it is “letting Christ’s worth replace my worth.”

Denying ourselves is not “low self-esteem” or “repression”; it is “letting Jesus live out his glory.”

The cross is not an ending but an exchange — exchanging “my life” for “the life of Christ.”

Brothers and sisters, please tell these apart. Low self-esteem is still self-centred; it just thinks very little of itself. Selflessness moves the self out of the way and lets Christ have first place. Repression locks the old self in the basement, and it can come out at any moment; being crucified with Christ acknowledges that the old self has already been dealt with and no longer has any authority.

sections.heading: 8. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, “a change of mindset” is the starting point of the selfless life, and the beginning of spiritual revival.

When we no longer rely on our own efforts but live by the life of Christ, we will experience the transformation from death to life, from “self” to “Christ.”

True freedom is not being able to do whatever I please; it is letting Jesus do whatever he pleases in me. That is the selfless life.

So this morning I issue a call to you: let Jesus be King. Not your adviser, not your guest of honour — your King. An adviser is consulted, a guest of honour is entertained, but a King is obeyed.

And let Jesus receive all the glory. When someone praises the change in you, point to him; when someone sees your peace, introduce them to him. Because the line that follows “it is no longer I who live” is always “but Christ lives in me.”

Unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone; but if it dies, it bears much fruit (John 12:24). The grain willing to fall today will become a whole field of wheat tomorrow.

May the glory be to Jesus, from now and for evermore.

We thank you. Thank you that you do not tell us to strive to die, because you have already died for us; you do not tell us to raise ourselves, because your resurrection has become our life.

discussion: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). In your life at present, in which area are you still “relying on your own efforts” rather than “living by Christ”? Please name one specific thing.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). sections.heading: Introduction: A Cheque Paid In Long Ago
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to lesson one hundred of 321 Morning Devotion, and our title is “From ‘I Can’ to ‘I Already Am’”.

Let me begin with a scene that banks see more often than you might think.

There was an old man who had scrimped and saved all his life. His son worked overseas, and every month he sent a fixed sum into his father’s account. But the old man never checked the balance and never drew a cent. He still got up at four every morning to go scavenging for recyclables. When his clothes tore he couldn’t bear to replace them; when he fell ill he couldn’t bear to see a doctor. Then one day he collapsed. His son rushed home, took him to the bank and had the account checked — and the passbook showed a figure he would never have dared to dream of. The old man sat on a bench in the bank and wept like a child. He wasn’t weeping because he had no money. He was weeping because the money had been there all along — he had simply never believed it.

Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of the spiritual life of a great many Christians.

Our difficulty is usually not “Has Jesus accomplished it?” but “Do we believe he already has?”

On the cross the Lord Jesus spoke one word: “It is finished” (John 19:30). In Greek it is tetelestai, a verb in the perfect tense. Archaeologists have found this very word on ancient papyrus bills — it was what a merchant wrote across a debt once it was settled, meaning “paid in full, nothing more owing”. What the Lord Jesus declared before he breathed his last was not “I did my best”, not “I gave it everything I had”, but “paid in full”.

Yet we go on paying off the debt day after day. We go on struggling day after day. Day after day we tell ourselves, “I will be a little holier,” “I can try a little harder,” “Next time I’ll definitely overcome.”

In the last lesson we talked about a change of mindset, and we saw that the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. In this lesson we take one step further: since our old self has already been crucified with Christ, what kind of faith will it take for us truly to live out a life of selflessness?

The lesson’s introduction puts it very clearly: selflessness is not a merit earned by behaviour; it is a life lived out by faith. On the cross Jesus has already accomplished everything. He has already defeated the power of sin and death, and he has already given us new life. The question is not whether Jesus has accomplished it, but whether we believe that “I have already been crucified with him”. If we still start from “I will” or “I can”, we are still relying on ourselves; but when we make “I already am” the ground of our faith, our life moves naturally from “striving” into “victory”.

This morning we are going to change a mindset together. It is a change of only a few words, yet it is the distance between heaven and earth: trade “I will” for “I already am”, and trade “I can” for “He has done it”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Letter Written for Freedom
sections.html:
To grasp the weight of the words “I have been crucified with Christ”, we have to go back to the scene in which they were written.

The author of Galatians is the apostle Paul. He wrote in his own hand: “See with what large letters I write to you with my own hand” (Galatians 6:11). The letter was most likely written around AD 48 or 49, and it is the most urgent in tone of all Paul’s letters. In his other letters Paul always begins by giving thanks to God; in Galatians alone he skips the thanksgiving and says straight out: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6).

Why such urgency? Because the churches of Galatia had fallen into a deadly distortion. A group of people had followed in Paul’s footsteps, telling the Gentile believers: believing in Jesus is good, but it isn’t enough. You must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses; only then are you complete. Church history calls them the “Judaizers”.

Brothers and sisters, notice that phrase: “not enough”. In two thousand years Satan’s script has hardly been updated. To the Galatians he said, “Believing in Jesus isn’t enough.” To you and me today he says exactly the same thing: “You’re not enough yet. You need to try harder.”

How did Paul respond? In chapter 2 he recounts a deeply awkward episode. In Antioch, Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but later, afraid of the people who came from James, he drew back — and even Barnabas was carried away by the hypocrisy. Paul opposed Peter to his face (Galatians 2:11–13). Straight after that, he compresses the whole core of the gospel into a few sentences, and the summit of them is 2:20: “I have been crucified with Christ.”

Please notice: this sentence is not Paul’s devotional reflection. It is the trump card he laid on the table in a debate on which the very survival of the gospel hung. What he means is this: salvation is not “Jesus plus my effort”; it is “Jesus has already finished it, and I simply believe.”

The original verb is even more powerful. “I have been crucified with Christ” uses the Greek perfect tense (sunestauromai). The perfect tense expresses an action completed in the past that produces a result still in force right now. Paul is not saying, “Every day I try hard to nail myself up there.” He is saying, “I have been nailed there, and I remain in that state now.”

The second half of the verse is more precious still: “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” Here we meet the most central line of the 321 vision — the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. Selflessness is not reducing yourself to zero; it is letting Christ move in, letting the limited “me” enter into the limitless him.

And the ground of it all is that final phrase: “who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” Brothers and sisters, the reason we can be selfless is that someone first denied himself for us. He denied himself first; that is why we can be selfless.

sections.heading: 1. Choosing the Faith of “I Already Am”
sections.html:
The lesson’s first key point is a choice: which kind of faith will you choose?

Paul says, “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts” (Galatians 5:24).

Please circle the words “have crucified” — the Chinese Union Version makes it even plainer: “have already crucified”. This is a fact already accomplished, not a goal to be reached by future effort.

The verb in this verse, a Greek aorist, likewise points to something that has already happened. Paul did not say, “Those who belong to Christ Jesus ought to try hard to nail the flesh up there.” What he said was, they “have crucified the flesh …” In other words, in God’s ledger, this case is already closed.

The moment we believed in Jesus, his death and resurrection were applied to our lives. This is not our feeling; it is our standing.

Scripture also says: “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin” (Romans 6:6).

This verse has three levels, like three steps you climb one at a time.

Step one: “our old man was crucified with him.” The old man, in Greek ho palaios anthropos, does not refer to some bad habit of ours. It is the old “I” in Adam, the old life that has itself at the centre. What God deals with is not our branches and leaves but our root.

Step two: “that the body of sin might be done away with.” The Greek katargeo does not mean “wiped out of existence”; it means “rendered ineffective, put out of action, relieved of office”. Think of a managing director who has been dismissed. He may still be walking around the office building, but he can no longer sign anything. Brothers and sisters, sin will still come knocking at your door, but it no longer has the key.

Step three: “so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.” That is the result. From slave to free man, from being held under to being set loose.

This means that the power of sin has been abolished. We are no longer ruled by sin, no longer controlled by “self”. This is the starting point of selflessness — not suppressing ourselves, but receiving by faith that the old “I” has already died and the new “I” has already been raised in Christ.

Here I want to underline one thing in particular, because it is the lifelong predicament of so many people: suppression has never overcome sin.

In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published the famous “white bear experiment” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Researchers asked participants, for five minutes, “not to think of a white bear”, and to ring a bell every time they did. The group told to suppress the thought not only rang the bell again and again while suppressing it; afterwards, when they were allowed to think freely, they thought of the white bear even more often than people who had never been asked to suppress it. Wegner called this the “ironic rebound effect”.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever experienced this? The more you tell yourself, “I mustn’t lose my temper,” the worse your temper gets. The more you tell yourself, “I mustn’t be greedy,” the more your heart itches. That isn’t because you are especially weak; it is the principle of the law. Paul said it long ago: “I wouldn’t have known sin, except through the law. For I wouldn’t have known coveting, unless the law had said, ‘You shall not covet’” (Romans 7:7). The law can point out sin, but it cannot take sin away.

The gospel of the cross takes another road. It does not tell you to press down harder on that white bear. It tells you that the old master who kept the white bear is dead.

I often use this picture. The biggest obstacle for someone learning to swim is thrashing about. The harder you thrash, the more you sink. Often the coach’s first words are, “Relax. Give your body to the water.” That isn’t passivity; it is a surrender that fits the laws of physics. More than two thousand two hundred years ago Archimedes discovered the principle of buoyancy: the upward force on a body in a liquid equals the weight of the liquid it displaces. The water’s lift is there all the time, from the very first second you get in. The question is whether you believe it — whether you dare to give your whole self over.

Grace is like that. Christ’s lift is there all the time. The question is not whether he is enough, but whether we are willing to let go.

Going a step further, the lesson says: Jesus’ resurrection is not only his business; it is ours too.

“But if we died with Christ, we believe that we will also live with him” (Romans 6:8).

We died with Christ to be set free from sin; we live with him to display his life. The cross has two sides: one an ending, the other a beginning; one a burial, the other a resurrection. Preach the death without the life, and faith becomes asceticism; preach the life without the death, and faith becomes licence. The gospel brings both sides to fulfilment together.

So selflessness is not losing yourself; it is letting Christ replace the old “I”, letting his love, his thoughts and his power live in me.

This has to be made clear, so that no one misunderstands. When the 321 vision speaks of selflessness, it does not mean the Buddhist “non-self”; it is not dissolving a person into emptiness. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Put a drop of water in the palm of your hand and it soon dries up; drop it into the ocean and it never dries — the drop hasn’t disappeared; it has entered the vastness of the sea.

That is why, in the 321 view, the first foundation is this: Jesus is my role model. In the garden of Gethsemane he said, “not what I desire, but what you desire” (Matthew 26:39). The road he walked was the road from “I will” to “as you desire”. Today we walk the very same road.

And the way onto that road is not gritting your teeth. It is raising both hands in surrender.

sections.heading: 2. The Faith of “I Already Am” versus the Faith of “I Can” and “I Will”
sections.html:
The lesson’s second key point is a very sharp contrast. We need to look at ourselves honestly.

Many Christians think, “I will learn to be crucified with Christ,” or “I can overcome myself by the Lord’s strength.” It sounds spiritual, but it hides a trap — because the focus is still on “I”.

Notice the difference between these three statements:

“I will” means I haven’t done it yet; “I can” means I do it by my own strength; but what Paul declares is: “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20).

This is not self-confidence; it is faith. It is not “I am striving” but “Christ has already accomplished it”.

Self-confidence and faith sound almost alike, yet they point in completely opposite directions. Self-confidence starts with me and ends with me; faith starts with Christ and ends with Christ.

In psychology there is a highly influential theory called “self-efficacy”. In 1977 the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the idea in Psychological Review: a person’s belief that he is able to accomplish a given task significantly shapes his behaviour and his persistence. The theory has proved enormously valuable in education, sport and health behaviour, and we do not deny it.

But brothers and sisters, listen carefully: self-efficacy is a true insight of psychology, but it is not the foundation of the gospel. What self-efficacy strengthens is “I can”; what the gospel declares is “He has done it”. Psychology can help us push the stone a little higher up the hill; the gospel tells us the Lord has already rolled that stone away for us. The Bible is our highest standard; psychology can serve as a servant, never as the master.

Now let’s look at the most dangerous place of all. Satan’s favourite lie is: “You’re not enough yet. You need to try harder.”

Scripture calls Satan “the accuser of our brothers … who accuses them before our God day and night” (Revelation 12:10). Day and night — he never rests. His methods of accusation are very refined. He won’t tell you to worship idols; he’ll tell you to be more spiritual. He won’t tell you to abandon your faith; he’ll make you feel for ever that you’re not good enough.

The result is the picture the lesson paints: he traps us in a religious struggle, wanting on the one hand to “live for the Lord” and bound on the other by sin’s accusations. As a result, “self” is not put to death at all; it becomes even more active — “jumping up and down” on the cross, never finding rest.

What a vivid picture that is. A man nailed to a cross who is still jumping up and down on it — what do you call that? You call it “not dead yet”. Someone who has truly died is quiet.

Paul long ago cried out to the Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:3). Beginning by the Spirit and then trying to finish by the flesh is the most common spiritual mistake of all. It’s like someone who boards a high-speed train but refuses to sit down, insisting on running forward along the carriages in the belief that he will arrive sooner. He runs himself into a sweat, yet he doesn’t reach the station one second earlier than the people who sat down. All he does is wear himself out.

This also touches on one of the most fundamental insights of the 321 vision: pride is the root of the problem, and pride very often wears religious clothing.

Isaiah 14 records the inner voice of the fallen one: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14).

Brothers and sisters, count them. How many times does “I will” appear? Five whole times. Satan’s fall was five “I will”s piled one on top of another. His sin was not going out and doing some monstrous deed; his sin was “leaving his originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God”.

The way of the Lord Jesus runs in exactly the opposite direction: “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8). “Emptied himself” translates the Greek kenoo, which means to pour out, to empty out. The Lord Jesus poured himself out to such an extent that he poured out even his life.

So 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

The faith of “I will” and “I can” is, at heart, a contest of strength with Satan; the faith of “I already am” is standing on the ground of Christ’s finished victory. The first is pride provoking pride, and both sides lose; the second is humility drawing out humility, and both sides win.

The lesson goes on to say: but when we believe “I already am”, we enter the standing of grace — no longer fighting sin in our own strength, but resting in the victory Christ has already completed.

“For he who has died has been freed from sin” (Romans 6:7).

The sentence is shockingly short. Can someone who has already died still be offended? Can he still be tempted? Can a look on someone’s face still ruin his whole day?

You no longer need to struggle to die to sin, because in Jesus you have already died. You no longer need to strive to rise again, because he has already made you alive together with him.

That is why Paul says in Romans 6:11: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” The word “consider” is the Greek logizomai, a bookkeeping term meaning “to reckon, to enter in the account”. Paul is not telling us to hypnotise ourselves by repeating, “I’m dead, I’m dead.” He is telling us to acknowledge and reckon with the fact already entered in God’s ledger. The deposit is already in the bank. Your job is not to manufacture the money; it is to believe the money is there — and then write the cheque.

In 1869 James Hudson Taylor, a missionary in China, went through a profound spiritual turning point. According to his biography, for years he had agonised over his own weakness; the harder he tried to be holier, the more he felt he had failed. Then, in a letter from a fellow worker, he came across a sentence that made him see: it is “not striving after faith, but resting on the Faithful One”. From then on he no longer said, “I must draw more from the Lord,” but, “The Lord is already in me.” His biography calls this experience “the exchanged life”. Brothers and sisters, that year Hudson Taylor didn’t change his mission field or his post. He changed only a mindset. And when the mindset changed, the life changed.

This is exactly what 321’s fivefold change describes: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living. This morning, what the Lord wants to change is our mindset.

sections.heading: 3. The Transformation the Faith of “I Already Am” Brings
sections.html:
The lesson’s third key point sets out four areas of transformation. These four transformations correspond neatly to 321’s fivefold change, renewing us layer by layer, from the inside out.

First, a change of identity: from slave to child

The lesson says: you are no longer a slave of sin; you are a child of God. Sin cannot rule over you, because the Spirit who sets people free already lives in you.

The scriptural basis is very clear: “But as many as received him, to them he gave the right to become God’s children, to those who believe in his name” (John 1:12). “Right” is the Greek exousia: a lawful entitlement, an official status. It is not a figure of speech; it is a legal term.

Paul says too: “For you didn’t receive the spirit of bondage again to fear, but you received the Spirit of adoption, by whom we cry, ‘Abba! Father!’” (Romans 8:15). Abba is Aramaic, the most intimate word a child in Palestine at that time used for his father — like our “Dad”. Just think: God actually allows a pardoned sinner to call him by so intimate a name.

And again: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death” (Romans 8:2). There are two “laws” here. Gravity is a law: when you jump, you are bound to come down. But an aeroplane can fly — not because gravity has been cancelled, but because a higher law, the lift of aerodynamics, overcomes it. The law of sin and death is still there, but the law of the Spirit of life is higher and stronger.

One mistaken identity can bring a lifetime of hardship. In the Old Testament, King Saul lived all his life in the fear that people would look down on him. He even said to Samuel, “please honor me now before the elders of my people, and before Israel” (1 Samuel 15:30). He was the king, yet he lived like a beggar, begging people for respect. Brothers and sisters, you are a child of God. Don’t live like an orphan.

This is what 321 calls the priority of relationships: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Once our relationship with God is settled, our relationship with ourselves is healed; and only when we are at peace with ourselves can we truly be at peace with others.

Second, a change of focus: from what I can do to what the Lord has done

The lesson says: faith is no longer “what I can do for the Lord” but “what the Lord has already done for me”. We no longer strive to please the Lord; because of his love we naturally live a life that pleases him.

This is a great reversal of direction. Religion runs “from the bottom up”: if I do well enough, God will accept me. The gospel runs “from the top down”: God accepts me first, and then I can do well.

“for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. It is not “works, therefore grace” but “grace, therefore works”. Turn the order upside down and the whole gospel goes bad.

The Lord Jesus himself gave the most beautiful picture: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch bears fruit not by effort but by connection. Have you ever seen a grapevine branch on the vine, gritting its teeth and saying, “I will bear fruit”? It simply stays connected, and the sap flows through.

321’s first core value is: let Jesus be King. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. When the focus is right, everything is right; when the focus is wrong, the harder we try, the further off course we go.

There is a practical difference here too. People whose focus is on themselves grow proud when they succeed and despise themselves when they fail. People whose focus is on Jesus give thanks when they succeed and turn back when they fail. Paul is the finest example. He said: “But by the grace of God I am what I am. His grace which was given to me was not futile, but I worked more than all of them; yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me” (1 Corinthians 15:10). In one breath he admits he worked harder than all of them, and in the next he says, “yet not I”. That is selflessness.

Third, a change of power: from my effort to his working

The lesson says: “I” am no longer the source of strength; Jesus becomes the wellspring of life within me. When I let go, he works; when I rest, he wins the victory.

That may sound passive, but it is in fact the most active thing there is. Look at the scene of the Israelites at the Red Sea: “Moses said to the people, ‘Don’t be afraid. Stand still, and see the salvation of Yahweh, which he will work for you today … Yahweh will fight for you, and you shall be still’” (Exodus 14:13–14).

The Red Sea ahead, the pursuing army behind — and God’s command was to “stand still” and “be still”. The greatest work Israel did that day was to do no work.

The psalm says as well: “Be still, and know that I am God” (Psalm 46:10). The Hebrew word for “be still”, raphah, originally means to relax, to let go. Before we can know that he is God, we first have to unclench our hands. The tighter we grip, the less we can feel his hand.

Here is a scientific fact to consider. Medicine generally estimates that an adult heart beats about seventy times a minute — around a hundred thousand times a day — and that we breathe about twenty thousand times a day. Let me ask you: when you got up this morning, did you remind your heart, “Remember to beat”? Did you keep breathing by willpower? Not at all. The most vital workings of life are all grace, simply received. If even our physical life is not kept going by ourselves, how could our spiritual life be held up by our own strength?

“There remains therefore a Sabbath rest for the people of God. For he who has entered into his rest has himself also rested from his works, as God did from his” (Hebrews 4:9–10).

“Rested from his works” — that is the definition of rest. It is not doing nothing; it is ceasing to “do it by myself”. At the opening of his Confessions, Augustine wrote a line that has been quoted down the centuries: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). The Holy Spirit is my guide — that is the third foundation. Letting go is not giving up; letting go is handing the helm to someone else.

Fourth, a change of daily living: from “I must be strong” to “I have already overcome”

The lesson says: when I am weak, I no longer say, “I must be strong”; instead I declare, “I have been crucified with Christ.” When I am tempted, I no longer say, “I mustn’t sin”; instead I declare, “I have already died to sin.” Faith like this lets us experience the real power of the cross every single day.

Brothers and sisters, notice the difference between those two declarations. “I mustn’t sin” puts the focus on sin, and the more you look at it, the bigger it grows. “I have already died to sin” puts the focus on Christ, and the more you look at him, the brighter he shines.

Go back to the principle of the white bear experiment: the harder you try not to think about something, the more it takes over your mind. That is why Scripture never tells us simply “not to think”. Scripture tells us to set our minds on something: “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2). Not emptying, but changing clothes; not suppressing, but replacing.

When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, not once in three times did he argue with Satan about whether he could overcome. He said only one thing: “It is written …” (Matthew 4:4). He stood on the word already written. The Bible is my standard — that is the second foundation.

Here I want to add a word of balance: a declaration is not a magic spell. We declare, “I have been crucified with Christ,” not because saying it has magical power, but because it is true. The power of faith lies not in the volume of the declaration but in its content — in the Lord who has already accomplished it.

“For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace” (Romans 6:14).

“There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” (Romans 8:1).

Brothers and sisters, keep these two verses in your heart. When accusation comes, you don’t need to argue with it. Just produce the verdict. The court has already pronounced you not guilty; however loudly the plaintiff protests, the verdict cannot be changed.

A change in daily living often begins on a single morning. A sister once testified in our fellowship that every day, the first thought when she opened her eyes used to be, “Another day to get through.” Later she learned to make her first words on waking, “Lord, I have been crucified with you; today you live in me.” She said her tasks didn’t become fewer, and people didn’t become easier to get along with, but the string that had always been pulled taut inside her went slack. This is the “daily living” link in the fivefold change: the mindset changed, the life changed, and daily living changed along with them.

sections.heading: 4. Integrating the 321 Vision: The Complete Map from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
When we set today’s message within the whole map of 321, we see it more clearly still.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — on the cross he said, “It is finished,” and the road he walked to the end is the road I am to walk. The Bible is my standard — my faith is not built on feelings but on “It is written”. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is not I who make myself live out Christ; it is the Holy Spirit who makes real in me what Christ has accomplished.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — the faith of “I already am” is handing the throne back to him. Let Jesus receive all the glory — when I acknowledge that all of this is his doing, the glory naturally goes to him and not to me.

The Goal: establish God’s system — only people who no longer fight for themselves and no longer fear for themselves can be built together.

Notice this: the faith of “I will” and “I can” will never establish God’s system. When everyone is busy proving that they “can”, the church becomes an arena; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. Only when a company of “I already am” people come together does humility draw out humility, so that both sides win.

The fivefold change is precisely the road the four transformations of this lesson travel. A change of mindset (from “I will” to “I already am”) brings a change of life (from slave to child), which brings a change of daily living (from struggle to rest), which brings a change of relationships (no longer proving ourselves to others), and finally a change of ministry (no longer serving out of our own zeal, but letting Christ serve through us).

The order cannot be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry. So many people rush into work the moment they come to faith, and end up producing nothing but exhaustion and comparison. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

The shift of perspective is in here too. From man’s perspective to God’s — man looks at how much I have done; God looks at what Christ has accomplished. From the earthly to the heavenly — on earth, rewards follow merit; in heaven, all is of grace. From the temporary to the eternal — my efforts will pass away; his accomplishment endures for ever. From the worldly to the godly — the world says, “You must be stronger”; God says, “My grace is sufficient for you.”

We can also place it within the 920 practice. 920 says that everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; before them we are to live out the selfless “0” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Notice something very important: Scripture does not call these “the behaviour the Spirit demands”; it calls them “the fruit of the Spirit”. Fruit is not hung on; it grows. An apple tree doesn’t strain or take a vow; when the season comes, it bears apples. When we live in “I already am”, the nine graces are not results we squeeze out by desperate effort; they are the life the Holy Spirit naturally produces in us.

And this sits right before Galatians 5:24. First come verses 22 and 23, the fruit of the Spirit; then comes verse 24, “have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts”. The fruit and the cross have always been two sides of one thing.

Then there are the 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people — spiritual companions; build the “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, someone still living in “I can” finds it hard to have a true companion, because without realising it he treats his companions as rivals. Only “I already am” people can truly hold others up, because they no longer have anything to protect.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit guides me (Spirit); in Scripture I see “I already am” (Understanding); this truth becomes my life (Life); then I can let Jesus reign as King in my serving (Service); and in the end all the glory goes to him (God).

sections.heading: 5. Practice for Daily Living: Walking the Truth into Our Days
sections.html: The lesson gives us four practices. I want to take them deeper by following 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

sections.heading: 6. A Gentle Reminder: Telling Spiritual Counterfeits from the Real Thing
sections.html:
The lesson closes with a vital reminder, and I want to walk through it with you once more, word for word.

“I can” and “I will” look spiritual, but in reality they are pride — because the focus is still on “me”. “I already am” is true faith — the focus has turned to “Christ”. Faith is not achieving by effort; it is receiving what is already done. The heart of faith is not “I did it” but “He has done it”.

Brothers and sisters, it is said that when bank tellers are trained, they spend most of their time getting to know not counterfeit notes but genuine ones. Once you know the real note through and through, a fake gives itself away the moment it touches your hand. Spiritual discernment works the same way. When we know “He has done it” through and through, any spiritual language centred on “me” sounds wrong the moment it reaches our ears.

A word of balance is needed here too. When we say we do not rely on “I can”, we are not saying Christians may be lazy or stop pursuing God. Paul himself was the hardest worker of them all. The difference lies in the source of motivation: do we work “in order to be accepted”, or “because we are already accepted”? The first is the drudgery of a slave; the second is the joy of a child. Both break a sweat — but one sweats in despair, the other in sweetness.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words could not be clearer:

“I can” is struggle; “I already am” is rest. “I can” relies on my own strength; “I already am” relies on grace. True faith is believing that Jesus has already accomplished it on the cross, and living within that finished grace. Once the mindset changes, the life is set free; once the focus turns, Christ is glorified in me.

“For by one offering he has perfected forever those who are being sanctified” (Hebrews 10:14). Once — for ever. That is the gospel.

So this morning I want to issue three calls to you, brothers and sisters.

First, hand over your “I will”s. Is there a long list of “I will”s in your heart? I will get rid of this temper; I will become a better father; I will be fruitful in my service. These desires are not bad in themselves, but if they sit on the throne they will crush you. Lay them one by one at the Lord’s feet and say, “Lord, this is your work, not mine.”

Second, take home your “I already am”. You are already forgiven, already accepted, already a child of God, already raised together with Christ. This is not a prize handed to you once you perform well; it is an inheritance deposited in your account two thousand years ago. Today, open the passbook.

Third, let Jesus be King. We are selfless so that he may reign; we let him reign so that he may receive all the glory. When one day others see the change in us, we can honestly say, “Yet not I, but the grace of God which was with me.” In that moment the glory goes to Jesus.

Look to Jesus, the author and perfecter of our faith (Hebrews 12:2). He began it, and he will finish it. What we need to do is lift up our heads and look at him.

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
“Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.” (Galatians 5:24)
declarations: Each morning when you get up, declare: “I have been crucified with Christ!”
