This is the first step of “Implementation”, and the simplest one. Don’t wait until you’re in a good mood; don’t wait until it feels right. Before your feet touch the floor, let the words leave your mouth.

Here is a suggestion: write Galatians 2:20 on a card by your bed or on your phone’s lock screen. The first thing you do on waking is not check your messages but read this verse. Do it for thirty days in a row, and you’ll find that your day starts from a different place.
Whenever you find yourself relying on your own effort, pray at once: “Lord, this is already accomplished — not by me, but by you!”

This is “Evaluation” and “Correction”. The key is “at once”. The moment you notice yourself starting to grit your teeth, grow anxious or compare, turn around at once. Spiritual correction costs less the sooner it is made. It’s like a steering wheel: when you’re one degree off, a light touch puts you right; once you’re ten degrees off, it takes a great deal of effort.
Here is a simple self-check: today, how many times did “I” appear in my sentences? How many times did “He”?
Each day, write down one thing that Jesus has already accomplished for you, training eyes of thankfulness and faith.

This is the practice of “Repetition”, and the one with the strongest scientific backing. In 2003 the American psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They divided participants into groups: one group wrote down each week the things they were grateful for, another the things that annoyed them, and a third ordinary events. After ten weeks, the group that recorded gratitude rated their lives as a whole markedly higher, complained less of physical ailments, and exercised more often.

Brothers and sisters, notice the difference. An ordinary gratitude journal records “what good things happened to me today”; a grace journal records “what the Lord has already accomplished for me”. The first looks at circumstances; the second looks at the cross. Circumstances change; the cross does not.
When you write, you can use a fixed pattern: “Lord, you have already ______ for me, so today I don’t have to ______.”
Learn, in the midst of hardship, not to be anxious and not to struggle, but to rest in the promise that “he has already overcome the world”.
“I have told you these things, that in me you may have peace. In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world.” (John 16:33)

Notice the Lord’s choice of words: not “I will overcome the world”, but “I have overcome the world”. He said this on the eve of his arrest, before he had gone to the cross. In the darkest night, he spoke in the perfect tense.

The Lord also said: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:28–29). A yoke is borne by two oxen together. The Lord did not say, “Take the yoke off”; he said, “Take my yoke” — because the other end of the yoke is him.

A concrete practice: when anxiety rises, stop for thirty seconds and take a deep breath. Then hand the matter over in a single sentence: “Lord, you have already seen this. I am placing it in your hands.” This is not dodging responsibility; it is changing who carries the load.
Information: today you have heard this truth — Christ has already accomplished it.
Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to let this truth drop from your head into your heart and become your own seeing.
Conviction: not persuading yourself, but surrendering to the fact God has spoken.
Implementation: begin the first declaration tomorrow morning.
Evaluation: three minutes each evening, asking yourself: at what moment today did I slip back into “I can”?
Correction: admit it on the spot and turn at once — don’t leave it until tomorrow.
Repetition: at least thirty days. For truth to become life, it needs time to soak in.
Multiplication: find a brother or sister, pass this mindset on to them, and hold each other accountable. You learn most deeply when you are teaching someone else.
prayer: Lord, thank you!
Because you have already accomplished everything on the cross, I have been crucified with you; it is no longer I who live, but you who live in me.
I no longer rely on “I will” or “I can”; by faith I receive “I already am”.

Lord, forgive me for these years of struggle and self-righteousness. I thought I had to try harder to deserve your love; I treated the work you have already finished as homework I still had to complete. Today I lay all of it down.
Make me live in this faith every day. Let your life replace my life, and let your victory become my victory.
Let the Holy Spirit remind me: whenever I reach once more to seize sovereignty, let me hear that word — It is finished.
May my family have peace because I am at rest; may my church be built up because we are humble towards one another; may Jesus reign as King among us and receive all the glory.
In the victorious name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). In your life right now, which phrase comes up most often — “I will”, “I can” or “I already am”? Give one concrete example and talk about the different outcomes these three ways of speaking would lead to.

The Lord Jesus says, “In the world you have trouble; but cheer up! I have overcome the world” (John 16:33). What trouble or struggle are you facing right now? If “He has already overcome” is true, where could you begin this week to learn to let go and enter into rest?
l100.title: From “I Can” to “I Already Am”
l100.subtitle: A Change of Mindset (Part 2): Living in the Grace Christ Has Already Accomplished
l100.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: A Lifetime of Striving, and Never Once a Victory
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Early this morning I want to begin by asking you to be quiet for thirty seconds and answer one question honestly: over this past year, what has been your most common feeling in your faith? Lightness, or weariness? Freedom, or a heavy burden?

I know a sister who has been a believer for twenty-two years. Every day she gets up at five in the morning to read the Bible, pray and copy out verses by hand. She has served in her church for more than ten years — from welcome team to choir, from small-group leader to Sunday school teacher. She has done it all, and done it all wholeheartedly. Yet one day, in a counselling conversation, she suddenly burst into tears and said, “Pastor, I’m so tired. I feel as if I’ve been climbing a mountain that never ends. The harder I try, the more I feel I’m not good enough; the more I serve, the further away God feels.”

Brothers and sisters, this is not one person’s story. It is the shared predicament of many who sincerely love the Lord. It isn’t that we haven’t tried hard; we have tried too hard. It isn’t that we don’t love the Lord; we have been loving him the wrong way. The problem isn’t our diligence. The problem is our mindset.

This is the very heart of what the series “A Change of Mindset” must face as it reaches its third lesson: many people get stuck in their spiritual lives not because they don’t try hard, but because their mindset has not changed. When the mindset is wrong, any amount of effort becomes a burden; when the mindset is right, life moves naturally into lightness and victory.

Let me begin with a true story from history. Hiroo Onoda, a second lieutenant in the Japanese army, was sent at the end of 1944 to Lubang Island in the Philippines on a guerrilla mission. In August 1945 the Second World War ended. Japan surrendered; the war was over. But Onoda didn’t believe it. He thought it was enemy propaganda. So he hid in the jungle and kept fighting a war that had long since ended. He hid for ten years, then twenty; his comrades died one by one, and still he fought on. Only in March 1974, when his former commanding officer flew to the island in person and relieved him of his mission face to face, did he finally walk out of the jungle and hand over his rusted sword. Twenty-nine years.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this: the war had long been over, but because he didn’t believe it, he fought on for another twenty-nine years.

That is a picture of a great many Christians. Two thousand years ago the Lord Jesus cried out on the cross, “It is finished” (John 19:30). That cry declared that the power of sin had been shattered, that the old self had been put to death, that the enemy had been disarmed. The war is over. Yet we are still in the jungle, day after day fighting an already condemned enemy in a battle that has already been won; day after day wrestling, in a bout we no longer need to fight, with an old self that has already been crucified. We sweat, we weep, we grit our teeth, we use up every ounce of willpower — and we still have no peace.

Why? Because our mindset is still stuck at “I can” and “I will”, and has not yet moved on to “I already am”.

God never wanted us to become good by our own strength. He wants us to believe that he has already done it. So the real breakthrough does not begin with “I’ll try harder”; it begins by turning from “I try” to “I believe”. In this lesson today we are going to make a complete turn of mindset together: from “I can” to “I already am”.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Urgent Letter Written for Freedom
sections.html:
Today’s theme verse comes from Galatians. To grasp the weight of Galatians 2:20, we first need to know the circumstances in which Paul wrote it.

The author is the apostle Paul. Right at the start of Galatians he says: “Paul, an apostle — not from men, nor through man, but through Jesus Christ, and God the Father, who raised him from the dead” (Galatians 1:1). An introduction like that is urgent in tone and carries authority, because he is dealing with a matter on which the very survival of the gospel depends.

The date and the recipients. Most evangelical scholars hold that Galatians may well be Paul’s earliest letter, written around AD 48 or 49 — after Paul’s first missionary journey, around the time of the Jerusalem Council (Acts 15). It went to the churches of the Galatian region, including Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe — places Paul and Barnabas had pioneered at the risk of their lives, where at Lystra Paul was even stoned (Acts 14:19). These churches were spiritual children Paul had brought to birth with blood and sweat.

The historical and cultural setting. After Paul left, a group known as the “Judaizers” came into the churches. They said: it’s good that you believe in Jesus, but it isn’t enough. You must be circumcised and keep the law of Moses; only then are you truly saved. That sounds very devout, even “ambitious for God” — but it is deadly. It quietly swaps the foundation of the gospel from “Christ has already accomplished it” to “I still have to do something more”. Paul was outraged. He wrote: “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6).

The surrounding context. The climax of Galatians 2 is a deeply awkward episode: in Antioch Paul publicly opposed the apostle Peter. Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but when people came from James, he drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles, afraid of the circumcision party. Paul says: “I said to Peter before them all, ‘If you, being a Jew, live as the Gentiles do, and not as the Jews do, why do you compel the Gentiles to live as the Jews do?’” (Galatians 2:14). What follows, from 2:15 to 2:21, is the theological summing-up of Paul’s words. In a single breath he explains that justification is not by the works of the law but by faith in Jesus Christ — and the substance of that faith is condensed into the earth-shaking declaration of 2:20.

So Galatians 2:20 is not a devotional nugget, nor a piece of comforting poetic sentiment. It is a boundary stone Paul set up on the very edge of the gospel’s cliff, to guard the freedom of the whole church. It answers precisely our question today: what does a person saved by grace actually live by? By “I can” — or by “I already am”?

sections.heading: 1. Where Faith Begins: Not Works, but Believing
sections.html:
“yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law” (Galatians 2:16).

In this one short sentence Paul says “not by the works of the law” three times, and three times he points to faith. The repetition isn’t wordiness; it is emphasis — he is driving in a stake. He wants to hammer one pillar deep into our mindset: our relationship with God is not built on “how much I have done” but on “whether I believe in Jesus”.

The meaning of the original words helps us see more clearly. “Justify” is the Greek δικαιόω (dikaioō), a courtroom term meaning “to declare righteous”, not “to make better”. When a judge bangs the gavel and declares someone not guilty, that is justification. He doesn’t first reform the person and then pronounce the verdict; on the basis of Christ’s atonement, the verdict comes first and the renewal follows. So justification is God’s verdict, not our report card. And “the works of the law” is ἔργων νόμου (erga nomou) in the original — literally “works of law” — meaning trying to earn God’s acceptance by keeping rules.

Paul goes on: “because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.” That blocks every way of retreat. It doesn’t say most people can’t manage it; it says not a single person can. Ephesians puts the same truth even more directly: “for by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast” (Ephesians 2:8–9).

Letting Scripture interpret Scripture, we find Paul using even fiercer words in Galatians 3: “Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified? I just want to learn this from you: Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith? Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” (Galatians 3:1–3). Brothers and sisters, hidden here is a vitally important spiritual principle: the way you came in is the way you must walk on. You weren’t saved by works, and you cannot grow by works either. The entrance is grace, and the completion is grace; the starting point is faith, and the journey is still faith.

Someone will ask: so do works not matter? Of course they matter. James says, “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (James 2:17). But notice the order: works are the fruit of faith, not its root. Fruit grows on the tree; the tree does not grow on the fruit. It isn’t “I do, therefore I am”; it is “I am, therefore I do”. Reverse that order, and the whole of life is turned upside down.

Let me use a picture from everyday life. A child adopted into a family doesn’t have to wash the dishes every day to earn his place on the family register. He washes the dishes because he already is a child of the family; he doesn’t wash them in order to become one. Yet many Christians live like a child who is afraid every day of being sent back: today I had my quiet time, so I feel God loves me; today I lost my temper, so I suppose God doesn’t want me any more. People like this aren’t ungodly. They have simply turned “son” into “hired hand”.

Psychology offers a supporting witness here. The American clinical psychologist Albert Ellis founded Rational Emotive Behaviour Therapy (REBT) in 1955. Over many years he observed that much of people’s anxiety and depression comes not from events themselves but from the absolute commands they lay on themselves — “I must succeed,” “I should be better,” “I mustn’t fail.” Ellis described this way of thinking as people whipping themselves with “musts”. Mark this: that is only a human observation. Scripture diagnosed the root of the disease more thoroughly two thousand years ago: the problem is not that the demands are too high, but that the direction is wrong altogether. Human research can only describe the symptoms; only the gospel can heal the root. Paul had already pointed out that as many as are of the works of the law are under a curse (Galatians 3:10).

The same principle applies to the practice of selflessness. The core message of 321 tells us: the problem of the old self is the self-centred life; the way out for the new self is selflessness. But the moment many people hear “selflessness”, they roll up their sleeves and say, “Right — I will work hard at denying myself; I will crucify my old self every day.” Brothers and sisters, if selflessness also has to be achieved with the strength of the self-centred life, it is nothing but legalism with a new religious programme.

The truth is this: Jesus has already accomplished this for us on the cross. We do not go and “achieve” it; we go and “receive” it. Selflessness is not a project to be completed but a fact to be believed. It isn’t me working hard to hollow myself out; it is me believing that Christ has already moved in and filled me. That is what 321 means: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living out that fullness. “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

The second of the Three Foundations is: the Bible is my standard. And here the standard does its work. When my feelings say, “You’re not enough yet,” the Bible says, “a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ.” Which will I choose to believe? Brothers and sisters, this morning let us together move the starting point of faith back where it belongs — not my works, but his accomplishment.

sections.heading: 2. The Faith of “I Already Am”: Where Selflessness Begins
sections.html:
“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Notice the verb Paul uses. He did not say, “I will be crucified with Christ,” nor “I can be crucified with Christ.” What he said is “I have been” — I already am.

This is especially clear in the Greek. “I have been crucified with Christ” is συνεσταύρωμαι (synestaurōmai): perfect tense, passive voice, first person singular. In Greek the perfect tense means an action completed in the past whose effect continues right up to the present. The passive voice means this was not something I did; it was done for me by someone else. So, rendered literally, this one word carries a double release: first, it is already done; second, it was not I who did it.

Brothers and sisters, both points matter enormously. Had it been the active voice, the responsibility would rest on me; I would have to find a way every day to nail myself up there — an endless self-torment. But it is passive: the old self was not crucified by me; Jesus has already crucified it on my behalf. Romans states this truth just as plainly: “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin” (Romans 6:6). Notice the word “knowing”. In the original it is γινώσκοντες (ginōskontes), meaning to recognise clearly, to know for certain. The first step to victory is not “doing” but “knowing”.

So the starting point for living out selflessness is not effort but a choice of faith. That choice has three sentences:

The first: I have been crucified with Christ.

The second: It is no longer I who live.

The third: But Christ lives in me.

These three sentences are the turning of the mindset. It isn’t that I must die, but that I have already died; it isn’t that I must live out Christ, but that Christ will live in me. The first is a burden; the second is rest.

Here a common misunderstanding needs clearing up. Someone asks: if the old self has already been crucified, why do I still lose my temper, still get jealous, still feel greedy? Brothers and sisters, Scripture does not say we no longer have “the flesh”. What Scripture says is that the identity of the “old self” has come to an end and the power of sin has been broken. Romans goes on: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11). The Greek word for “consider” is λογίζεσθε (logizesthe), an accounting term meaning “reckon the account this way”. God has already entered it this way in his ledger; what we must do is bring our ledger into line with his. When the books are right, daily living will come right.

Further on, Romans 6:14 gives a conclusion: “For sin will not have dominion over you. For you are not under law, but under grace.” Notice: sin will still come knocking, but sin is no longer the master. It may shout; it cannot give orders.

There is a phenomenon in psychology that, from the opposite direction, helps us feel the release of “already finished”. In 1927 the Russian-born psychologist Bluma Zeigarnik published research at the University of Berlin showing that people remember “unfinished” tasks especially well: incomplete business keeps occupying the mind and creates tension, and once the task is completed, that tension lets go. It came to be known as the Zeigarnik effect. Brothers and sisters, think about it: what must the heart of someone be like who thinks salvation isn’t finished yet? It is a tension that can never be switched off. But when we truly believe “It is finished”, that tension lets go. This is not the power of suggestion; it is the effect a fact produces — because on the cross it really has been finished.

Go back to Hiroo Onoda. He spent twenty-nine years in the jungle not because he lacked courage. Quite the opposite: he was too brave, too loyal, too hard-working. What he lacked was not willpower but a piece of news; not the drive to act but the act of believing. Brothers and sisters, this morning what you lack may not be more resolve either, but one moment of truly believing.

Seen from 321, “I already am” is exactly where selflessness begins. 321 says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Have you noticed that behind “I can” and “I will” there actually hides a very deep pride? Isaiah records the words in the heart of the fallen one: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Brothers and sisters, count them: five “I will”s. The grammar of pride is “I will”; the grammar of humility is “I already am” — I am already redeemed, already crucified, already loved, and none of it did I earn.

So 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. “I already am” is not passivity; it is the highest humility and the strongest posture for battle. For when I say “I already am”, I hand the throne back to God — let man be man and let God be God. I return to my originally intended position, and the enemy loses the only foothold he had.

sections.heading: 3. How a Mindset Changes: From Knowing to Living It Out
sections.html:
“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

A change of mindset doesn’t happen in an instant; it is a process. The lesson gives us four stages: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation. 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset carry it further, adding Evaluation, Correction, Repetition and Multiplication — eight steps in all. Today let us walk through them one at a time.

Step one: Information. When we first hear “I already am”, it is only information. It is like an unopened letter lying on the desk of the heart. Information is necessary, because “faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17). But information by itself cannot change people — otherwise libraries would long ago have become temples.

Step two: Revelation. When the Holy Spirit shines his light, information becomes revelation. Paul prayed for the church in Ephesus “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him” (Ephesians 1:17). The mark of revelation is this: the same verse that read in black and white yesterday reads in colour today; yesterday it was someone else’s story, today it is mine. Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the third of 321’s Three Foundations — the Holy Spirit is my guide. Without the Holy Spirit, reading the Bible is just reading data; with the Holy Spirit, the Bible becomes a living standard.

Step three: Conviction. When we accept it inwardly, we enter conviction. The Greek background of the word is related to “being persuaded” — a state of glad, wholehearted assent in which we no longer argue. It isn’t that I grudgingly concede; it is that something inside me has truly yielded. That was Abraham’s faith: “being fully assured that what he had promised, he was also able to perform” (Romans 4:21).

Step four: Implementation. Once convinced, we must put it into practice in daily living. James is right: faith without works is dead. But remember, implementation here is not doing it “by my ‘I can’”; it is living “because I already am”. Two people both get up early to pray: one does it to earn God’s pleasure, the other because God is already pleased with him. On the outside they look the same; on the inside they are utterly different.

Step five: Evaluation. After implementation there is always a gap, and the gap calls for honest evaluation. David prayed: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24). Evaluation is not accusing yourself; it is inviting God to search you. Accusation comes from the enemy; searching comes from the Holy Spirit. Accusation makes people hide; searching draws them near.

Step six: Correction. When you find you have drifted, turn back. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness” (1 John 1:9). In putting this into practice we may stumble and fail, but don’t be afraid. Every time you find yourself back at “I can” or “I will”, repent again and choose “I already am” afresh. The Greek word for repentance, μετάνοια (metanoia), has at its root “a change of mind” — the very essence of repentance is a change of mindset.

Step seven: Repetition. Once is not enough; it must be again and again. Here there is a supporting witness from science. In 1949 the Canadian neuropsychologist Donald Hebb proposed, in his book The Organization of Behavior, that when neurons are repeatedly activated together, the connections between them grow stronger — later summed up as “neurons that fire together wire together”. It is a cornerstone of research on the brain’s plasticity. Brothers and sisters, this shows one thing: repeated practice really does carve a new path inside us. When God made us, he placed the grace of “repetition” in our brains. An old mindset is an old road walked for decades, wide and smooth; a new mindset begins as a narrow track through the long grass. But every time you walk it, it becomes a little clearer; walk it long enough, and the old road falls into disuse.

Step eight: Multiplication. When “I already am” becomes your life, you will pass it on to others. This is exactly what 321 calls the 235 relationships: become a “2” with selfless people, build the “3” — a heritage of spiritual parents and spiritual children — and finally become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. If a mindset stays only with you, it is a single lamp; if it multiplies, it becomes a whole dawn.

Let me give an illustration. Over many years of research, the Stanford psychologist Carol Dweck found that the view people hold of their own abilities — what she calls a “mindset” — significantly affects how they respond to setbacks: those with a fixed mindset tend to give up after failure, while those with a growth mindset treat failure as learning. Her conclusion is simple: the mindset changes first, and only then does behaviour change. Brothers and sisters, if even the world’s scholarship can see this order, how much more heavenly truth? 321 said it long ago: the fivefold change — mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change your daily living.

So don’t underestimate this hour and a half this morning. You may think we have only swapped one way of speaking for another, but in fact we are swapping a neural pathway, swapping the default setting of a life. As we keep practising, “I already am” will no longer be merely a mindset; it will become our life.

sections.heading: 4. Measuring Our Faith: “I Can”? “I Will”? Or “I Already Am”?
sections.html:
“No temptation has taken you except what is common to man. God is faithful, who will not allow you to be tempted above what you are able, but will with the temptation also make the way of escape, that you may be able to endure it” (1 Corinthians 10:13).

Our faith shows in our reactions. Ordinarily you can’t see it; the moment temptation comes, it is exposed. Faith is not measured amid the sound of praise; it is measured under pressure.

When we face the lure of sin, the faith of “I can” and “I will” has three marks: first, we struggle, strive and suppress; second, we find it exhausting; third, we are still swayed by the world. You clench your teeth so as not to look at that image; you clench your fists so as not to say that word; inside, you are playing tug-of-war with yourself. On the surface you win a round, but inside you are already worn out. And you will find that the more you suppress it, the bigger the thing grows in your heart.

A psychological experiment can serve as a supporting witness here. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published the famous “white bear experiment”. Researchers asked participants, for five minutes, “not to think of a white bear” — and the participants ended up thinking of the white bear even more often. What is more, once the ban was lifted, they thought about the white bear more frequently than people who had never been asked to suppress it. The phenomenon came to be called the “rebound effect of thought suppression”. Brothers and sisters, this shows one thing clearly: fighting sin with willpower is not only useless; it often rebounds.

Scripture pointed this out long ago. Paul says: “These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh” (Colossians 2:23). Those words — “not of any value” — pass a death sentence, once and for all, on every religious effort that relies on punishing the body.

But the faith of “I already am” reacts entirely differently: first, it no longer wrestles with sin; second, it turns straight to Jesus; third, it lives in the identity of one who has already overcome.

Notice the key here: it is not “refusing sin” but turning to the salvation Jesus has already completed. What is the difference? With “refusing sin”, the focus is still on sin; your eyes are still fixed on it, and you are still grappling with it. With “turning to Jesus”, the focus is on Christ; you don’t push sin away — you walk away. When Joseph faced his master’s wife’s seduction, Scripture records: “He left his garment in her hand, and ran outside” (Genesis 39:12). He didn’t stand his ground and debate with desire; he ran. 321 puts it exactly: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances.

Let me tell another true story from history. It helps us see how deadly the gap between “already” and “knowing” can be. On 1 January 1863, President Lincoln’s Emancipation Proclamation took effect; in law, those slaves were already free. But in far-off Texas, the news was slow to arrive. Not until 19 June 1865, when General Granger led his troops into Galveston and publicly read out the order, did the slaves of Texas learn that they had long been free. For two and a half years they were free men in law and still slaves in daily living — only because they didn’t know. That day later became America’s “Juneteenth”.

Brothers and sisters, do you hear it? The proclamation of freedom has been issued, but those who don’t know it are still living as slaves. Galatians says: “Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage” (Galatians 5:1). Your freedom isn’t waiting to be handed out at the next special conference; your freedom was signed two thousand years ago on the cross.

In 1967 the psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier, at the University of Pennsylvania, put forward the theory of “learned helplessness”: if laboratory animals repeatedly experience pain they cannot control, then even when a way out is later opened, they no longer try to escape. They have learned a false lesson — “It’s no use anyway.” Brothers and sisters, how many Christians have learned that lesson too? After defeat upon defeat they quietly concede in their hearts: I’ll never change this temper; this weakness of mine will be with me for life. The door is plainly open, yet they lie flat where they are. This morning the Lord Jesus himself comes to us — like that officer walking into the jungle on Lubang Island — and says to us: child, the war is over. The door is open.

When we choose “I already am”, the world’s influence on us loses its power, because “self” has already been crucified with Christ. This is not psychological hypnosis; it is the renewal of an identity. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

In 321 terms, this is exactly the shift of perspective: from man’s to God’s; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective sees “I haven’t managed it yet”; God’s perspective declares “My Son has already done it”. 321 also reminds us: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you worry, rely on the heart and you rejoice. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). “I can” and “I will” rely on the brain; “I already am” relies on the heart.

sections.heading: 5. The Key to Victory: Not Striving, but Believing
sections.html:
“For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith” (1 John 5:4).

Look closely at the apostle John’s words. He did not say, “The victory that has overcome the world is your effort,” nor “your perseverance, your integrity, your service”. He says: “your faith”.

“Has overcome” is the Greek νικήσασα (nikēsasa), the aorist participle of the verb νικάω (nikaō), whose root νίκη (nikē) simply means “victory”. John uses the past tense, implying that this victory has already been settled in time. In the next verse he names the answer outright: “Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” (1 John 5:5). The list of overcomers is not ranked by merit; it is drawn up by faith.

So victory does not come from our trying harder but from our believing more.

When we believe that I am already in Christ, that I have already died with him and risen with him, that I have already received his life — then we naturally live out victory. Notice the word “naturally”. A truly spiritual life is not squeezed out by force; it flows out. The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). A branch never has to grit its teeth in order to bear fruit. It only has to stay connected.

There is a very apt picture from physics here. When someone falls into water and thrashes about desperately, the body actually sinks; if they relax and lie back, trusting the water’s buoyancy, they float. The reason is quite simple: the average density of an adult body is roughly 0.95 to 0.99 grams per cubic centimetre, slightly less than fresh water’s one gram, so with the lungs full of air and the body relaxed, a person can float. But the moment they struggle, their breathing quickens and their limbs flail, and the balance is broken. Brothers and sisters, the water is holding you up all the time; the question is whether you are willing to lie back. Grace too is holding you up all the time; the question is whether you are willing to believe.

What has God already done? Scripture says he is the one “who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1:13). Notice the tense of these two verbs: “delivered” and “translated” are both things already completed. It isn’t that he will deliver us; he has delivered us. It isn’t that he will transfer us once we perform well; he has already transferred us. Your citizenship now is not in the kingdom of darkness but in the kingdom of light.

Second Peter says too: “his divine power has granted to us all things that pertain to life and godliness, through the knowledge of him who called us by his own glory and virtue” (2 Peter 1:3). “Has granted to us all things” — notice: all things, and already granted. Brothers and sisters, we are often like someone who owns a fully stocked warehouse yet stands outside picking up breadcrumbs. What we need is to receive it by faith.

That is why Paul, at the very start of Romans, sets out the theme of the whole letter: “For in it is revealed God’s righteousness from faith to faith. As it is written, ‘But the righteous shall live by faith’” (Romans 1:17). From beginning to continuing, it is all “from faith to faith”. On the first day it is by faith, and on the ten-thousandth day it is still by faith; we are saved by faith, and we overcome by faith.

This verse once lit a great fire in the history of the church. In 1545, in the preface he wrote to the complete edition of his Latin works, Martin Luther recalled that as a young man he had hated the words “the righteousness of God”, because he thought they meant the standard by which God would judge him. Later the Holy Spirit enlightened him, and he understood that this is the righteousness God gives to people, received by faith. He said that at that moment he felt himself altogether born again, as though he had entered paradise itself through open gates. Brothers and sisters, the Reformation did not begin with a movement; it began with one man’s mindset being turned around.

A missionary of more recent times had a similar experience. In a letter to his sister in 1869, Hudson Taylor wrote that for years he had agonised and struggled over his lack of faith, until one day he understood: the key was not his straining to “exercise” faith but looking to the Faithful One; it was not that he had to lay hold of Christ, but that Christ had already laid hold of him. From then on his ministry moved from anxiety into rest. Later generations called this experience “the exchanged life”.

Seen from 321, this is the practical content of “let Jesus be King”. Letting Jesus be King is not inviting him in as a consultant; it is my stepping down from the throne and his taking it. I am no longer the one straining with all my might; he is the Lord who has accomplished it. And when we no longer rely on ourselves, all the glory goes naturally to him — which is the second of the Two Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory. If victory came through my effort, I would have a share in the credit; if victory is his accomplishment, the glory belongs wholly to him.

Brothers and sisters, take this sentence home with you: the key to victory is not how hard you try, but how much you believe.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road from the Self-Centred Life to Selflessness
sections.html:
Let us take what we have read today and look at it once more within the framework of 321. You will find that this lesson is really the heart of the whole 321 message.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — on the cross he said, “It is finished.” For us he lived out a life of complete obedience and complete self-denial; Philippians says he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7), and that is the very prototype of selflessness. The Bible is my standard — when my feelings say, “You can’t do it yet,” the Bible says, “I have been crucified with Christ,” and I choose to stand on the Bible’s side. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is the Holy Spirit who turns “Information” into “Revelation”, the Holy Spirit who reminds us in our weakness: you are one who has already overcome.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King: in someone who still says “I can” and “I will”, the one sitting on the throne is really himself; when I say “I already am”, I hand the throne back to the Lord. Let Jesus receive all the glory: if the victory were something I earned, I would have a share of the applause; since the victory is his accomplishment, the glory belongs wholly to him.

The Goal: establish God’s system. God’s system is not propped up by a group of very hard-working people; it is built by a group of people who truly believe. A system built on “I can” will collapse from exhaustion; a system built on “I already am” will multiply.

The self-centred life and selflessness. 321 says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Go back to Eden, where the serpent said, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). Humanity’s first fall was wanting to take the place of God. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take the place of God; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. Brothers and sisters, “I can” and “I will” are that ancient temptation in a devout new coat: I will sanctify myself by my own strength; I can overcome by my own strength. “I already am” hands the power back and returns to our originally intended position as creatures and as recipients of grace.

So 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When two people in a family both say “I can” and “I will”, that home becomes a battlefield; when one of them begins to say “I already am”, he no longer needs to win, and that home begins to know peace.

Selflessness is not having nothing. This is the most important sentence of all. Selflessness is not erasing yourself and becoming someone with no feelings and no aspirations. Selflessness is “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me — the limited “me” making way for the limitless him. An empty cup is not empty for the sake of being empty; it is empty in order to be filled.

The fivefold change. The lesson’s closing words put it beautifully: when the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes. 321 maps out the whole road: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Notice that this order cannot be reversed. Many people start changing at “ministry”, and so they are very busy outwardly while nothing has changed inwardly. 321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. And relationships have their own order: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. This lesson today is working at the very headwaters — if the mindset upstream runs clear, the whole river downstream will run clear.

The shift of perspective. “I can” is man’s perspective, an earthly perspective, a temporary perspective, a worldly perspective; “I already am” is God’s perspective, a heavenly perspective, an eternal perspective, a godly perspective. The same difficulty, seen from man’s perspective, is a dead end; seen from God’s perspective, it is a stage.

The 920 practice. The 321 vision is not theory; it has to touch the ground every day. The 920 practice is this: everyone we are in relationship with is our “2”; as I live out the selfless (0) life before them, I bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, notice that this is “the fruit of the Spirit”, not “results I squeeze out by effort”. Patience produced by gritted teeth will explode in the end; patience produced by the Holy Spirit grows from within. That difficult person you will face today is your “2”. You don’t need to change him first; you only need to live out “I already am” before him.

The 235 relationships. Become a “2” with selfless people — find a spiritual companion and remind each other of “I already am”. Build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children — pass this mindset on and let it multiply. Become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — only a company of people who no longer rely on themselves can establish God’s system.

Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves. Rely on the brain and you worry; rely on the heart and you rejoice. “I can” is the language of the brain: it calculates, compares and tenses up. “I already am” is the language of the heart: it rests, trusts and rejoices. “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Training “I Already Am” into Life
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper, step by step, using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: discern the state of your faith. Today, when you face difficulty or temptation, notice your reaction — is it “I can”, “I will” or “I already am”? Face the true condition of your faith honestly.

Information: first, memorise these three phrases — I can, I will, I already am. Write them on a sticky note and put it somewhere you will see it every day. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit, in some real situation today, to show you on the spot which box you are standing in. Conviction: when you see it, don’t make excuses and don’t condemn yourself; simply admit, “Lord, I’ve slipped back into ‘I can’ again.” Implementation: set three reminders today — morning, noon and bedtime — and each time ask yourself: in what just happened, which phrase was I living by? Evaluation: in the evening, write one sentence recording the most obvious instance. Correction: rewrite that “I can” as “I already am”, and declare it afresh. Repetition: keep it up for seven days in a row, and you will begin to see your own habits. Multiplication: find a brother or sister, tell them these three phrases, and invite them to discern alongside you.

Practice two: replace “I must try harder” with “I already am”. When you find yourself struggling, don’t fight with willpower any more; instead declare, “I have been crucified with Christ,” and turn to the salvation Jesus has already completed.

Information: learn Galatians 2:20 by heart. Not roughly — word for word, because in the three seconds when temptation strikes, you won’t have time to look it up on your phone. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to make this verse “light up” in the very area where you are weakest. Conviction: say one honest thing to yourself — for how many years have I fought with willpower? Has it worked? Implementation: the next time a struggle comes, don’t grapple with it first; do three things at once — stop, declare, turn. Stop; declare, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live”; then turn your eyes to Jesus — with a sentence of prayer, or with a hymn. Evaluation: note which situations most easily push you back into wrestling mode. Correction: for those situations, have a verse ready in advance. Repetition: don’t give up because of one failure; when you fall, turn back at once and choose “I already am” again. Multiplication: share your experience in your small group, so that others can gain from it too.

Practice three: practise the choice of faith every day. In everyday life, deliberately practise the faith of “I already am”. Even when you fall, turn back at once, so that this faith becomes habit and life.

Information: recognise a fact — habits are the product of repetition, and spiritual habits are no exception. Revelation: ask God to show you which mindset of yours most needs to be turned around. Conviction: make up your mind to stop living in the cycle of “quiet time yesterday, condemnation today”. Implementation: every morning when you get up, before you look at your phone, meditate on and declare the lesson’s declaration of faith. Evaluation: set a fixed time each week to look back. Correction: when you find yourself trying to earn God’s love again, change it at once into receiving God’s love. Repetition: practise in forty-day cycles, and keep going. Multiplication: after forty days, take someone else through the same forty days.

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to steps five, six and seven: Evaluation, Correction, Repetition. Most people who fail don’t fail because they refuse to put things into practice; they fail because after they fall, they never come back. May the Lord help us to turn back at once whenever we fall. Turning back is not starting to earn all over again; it is coming back again to “I already am”.

The lesson ends with a gentle reminder, and I ask you to keep it in your heart: the key to victory is not how hard you try, but how much you believe.

And here is the lesson’s declaration of faith. Let us begin each new day with it: Lord, I no longer rely on my own effort. I choose to believe in the salvation you have already completed. I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: Let Jesus Be King, and Let the Glory Go to Jesus
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we are nearly at the end. This lesson today has really said only one thing: exchange “I can” and “I will” for “I already am”.

When the mindset changes, the life changes; when the life changes, daily living changes. This is not a motivational slogan; it is a spiritual law. For your life will never rise above your mindset, and your daily living will never rise above your life.

So from today, lay down “I can” and “I will”, enter into the faith of “I already am”, and live out the victorious life of Christ.

Let me ask you one last time: in your jungle, is there a war that should have ended long ago? Is there a past that has already been forgiven, yet you still blame yourself for it every day? Is there an old self that has already been crucified, yet you still feed it every day? Is there a door that has already been opened, yet you refuse to walk out through it?

This morning the Lord Jesus himself walks into your jungle and says to you: child, it is finished. The war is over. You can come out now.

This Lord who gave himself up for you is worthy to be King. He doesn’t want to be your life’s consultant; he wants to be your life’s King. Letting Jesus be King means I step down and he takes the throne; it means I no longer prove myself but only display him. When we no longer rely on ourselves, all the glory goes naturally to him.

“But thanks be to God, who gives us the victory through our Lord Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 15:57). Brothers and sisters, he has already fought this battle to the end. All we need to do today is believe, then walk out, and hand over that rusted sword.

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“yet knowing that a man is not justified by the works of the law but through faith in Jesus Christ, even we believed in Christ Jesus, that we might be justified by faith in Christ, and not by the works of the law, because no flesh will be justified by the works of the law.” (Galatians 2:16)
“For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith.” (1 John 5:4)
practices: Discern the state of your faith
Replace “I must try harder” with “I already am”
Practise the choice of faith every day
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

We confess that we have lived by “I can” for too long, and held ourselves up with “I will” for too long. We thought loving you meant trying harder, and the harder we tried, the further we got from rest. Lord, forgive us for turning your grace into our project, and your cross into our treadmill.

This morning, by faith, we receive what you have already accomplished: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. Lord, may your Holy Spirit carry these words from our heads into our hearts — from information into revelation, from revelation into conviction, and from conviction into our daily living.

Help us, before everyone we meet today, to live out a selfless life and bear the fruit of the Spirit. Help us no longer to wrestle with sin, but simply to turn to you; no longer to prove ourselves, but only to display you.
Reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory go to you.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Read Galatians 2:20. This verse says “I have been” — “I already am” — not “I will” and not “I can”. Share: over the past week, in what matter did you discover that you were actually living by “I can”? If you switched to “I already am”, how would your reaction be different?

Read 1 John 5:4–5: “For whatever is born of God overcomes the world. This is the victory that has overcome the world: your faith. Who is he who overcomes the world, but he who believes that Jesus is the Son of God?” Share: what is the one area in which you most want to overcome right now? How will you practise the three actions of “stop, declare, turn” this week? Please also pray for one another.
l101.title: From “I Can” to “I Already Am”
l101.subtitle: A Change of Mindset (Part 3) — Faith Turned Around
l101.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: One Sentence Can Turn a Whole Life Around
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we begin this morning’s reading, I want to ask you to be still for thirty seconds and answer one question in your heart: over this past year, what is the sentence you have said to yourself most often?

Some people say most often, “How have I failed again?” Some say, “I have to try harder.” Some say, “I can’t do it.” And some say, “I’ll deal with it once I’m a bit better.” These sentences sound very honest, very humble. But look closely and you’ll find they all share one subject — I. I fail, I try, I can’t, I get better. In the whole script of our life, the lead role is always played by “I.”

I once walked alongside a brother. He had believed in the Lord for more than ten years. He knew his Bible well and served faithfully, yet he was living in deep weariness. He told me, “Pastor, every morning when I get up, I first have to fight a battle with myself. I have to deal with my temper, my greed, my laziness, my envy. I’m like a man with a broom, sweeping every day in a house that will never be clean.” When I’d heard him out, I asked him one thing: “Brother, have you ever considered that the Lord Jesus finished this battle for you two thousand years ago?” He froze. “I know that,” he said. “Of course I know Jesus died for me.” I said, “You know it, but you don’t live this way. Your knowledge has stopped in your head. It hasn’t yet become your mindset.”

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly what we are going to talk about today. This is the fourth session in our series on the change of mindset. In the three sessions before it, we saw one thing again and again: change the mindset and you change the life, and change the life and you change the daily living. Today we want to follow that road to its deepest point — when the mindset changes, what changes is not only our thinking; the whole way our life operates is turned upside down.

The lesson puts it beautifully: “I have been crucified with Christ” is not a slogan but a truth that brings real change. There is a key word here, and I want you to remember it, because it is today’s key — “already.” Not “I will be,” not “I hope to be,” not “I’m trying hard to become,” but “I already have been.” Scripture speaks in the language of something completed, because this was accomplished on the cross. We are not striving for an identity we don’t yet have; we are believing a fact that is already ours.

When we truly choose to believe “I already have been,” life no longer stays stuck in struggle and effort; it enters a completely new way of living — no longer I, but Christ. This is the beginning of selflessness, and the starting point of a victorious life.

I love one illustration. A man bought a brand-new car, but he kept pushing it. He pushed until he was drenched in sweat, until his back ached. Every day he pushed it three kilometres to work, and he told people, “Driving is exhausting.” One day someone beside him asked, “Why don’t you start the engine?” He said, “The engine? I thought that was just for decoration.” Brothers and sisters, many Christians are just like that. The greatest power in the universe lives within us — the risen Christ — yet we are still pushing our life along with the strength of our own flesh. This morning, let’s learn together how to start the engine.

In the 321 vision there is a saying that captures this vividly: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of every problem. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Today’s lesson is the entrance to the road of selflessness.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: How Galatians 2:20 Came to Be Written
sections.html:
To truly understand “no longer I,” we first have to go back to the scene where these words were spoken.

The author of Galatians is the apostle Paul. As to when it was written, evangelical scholars generally hold one of two views. If “Galatia” refers to the churches of South Galatia (Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra and Derbe — the churches Paul founded on his first missionary journey), it was written around AD 48–49, possibly Paul’s earliest letter, before the Jerusalem Council. If it refers to North Galatia, it dates to around AD 53–55. Whichever view we take, one thing is clear: this letter was written in great haste and with great weight, because the very foundation of the gospel was being shaken.

What was happening? A group of people known as the “Judaizers” had come into the Galatian churches, teaching: believing in Jesus is good, but it isn’t enough; if Gentiles are to become God’s people for real, they must be circumcised and must keep the law of Moses. In other words, on top of “justification by faith” they added “plus works.” It sounds very devout, but it is deadly. Because the moment you add anything at all to the gospel, the focus shifts from Christ back to ourselves — Have I done it? Am I good enough? Am I keeping it well?

Paul was furious. In this letter he doesn’t begin, as he usually does, by commending the church he is writing to. He says straight out, “I marvel that you are so quickly deserting him who called you in the grace of Christ to a different ‘good news’” (Galatians 1:6). Then he spends two chapters on his own testimony: his gospel was not received from man but came by revelation from Jesus Christ. He also tells how, in Antioch, he opposed Cephas (that is, Peter) to his face, because Peter, afraid of the circumcision party, had drawn back and separated himself from the Gentile believers.

Galatians 2:20 is the concluding sentence of that whole argument. Paul first says, “For I, through the law, died to the law, that I might live to God” (Galatians 2:19). Then comes the declaration that has shaken the church through every age: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Notice that these words were not originally a quiet devotional meditation; they were a banner raised in the middle of a theological war. Paul is saying: you want me to become a child of God by relying on the law, on circumcision, on my own effort? No need. The “I” that wanted to rely on itself is already dead — it has already been nailed to the cross. The one who lives now is Christ.

Let’s also look at the force of the original. “I have been crucified with Christ” — the Greek uses the perfect tense (συνεσταύρωμαι). The perfect tense means an action completed in the past that brings an effect continuing into the present. It is like someone who has had a heart transplant: the operation was completed in the past, but the new heart is still beating today. So Paul isn’t saying, “Every day I try hard to nail myself up there.” He is saying, “I have already been nailed there, and that is still in effect today.”

Another key word is “live.” “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” — here “in me” (ἐν ἐμοί) tells us that the life of Christ is at work inside this person that I am. He isn’t standing beside me cheering me on; he has moved in and become the source of my life.

The third key word is in the second half of the verse: “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God.” The original’s “by faith” shows that the one and only channel by which we draw on this life is faith. Christ has already moved in, but whether we live by that fact each day depends on whether we believe it.

So the whole verse has three layers. The first is the fact — I have been crucified with Christ. The second is the identity — it is no longer I who live. The third is the method — I live by faith in the Son of God. Today’s five key points unfold step by step along these three layers.

One more piece of background is worth mentioning. In Roman times the cross was no ornament. It was the most shameful, most brutal instrument of execution, reserved for slaves, rebels and the lowest criminals. Roman citizens were, in principle, exempt from it. So when Paul said, “I have been crucified with Christ,” it would have grated on first-century ears — it was the same as saying: by the world’s system of values, I have been sentenced to death; I am out of the game. And the paradox is this: it was precisely this sentence of being “out” that opened up the freest, most powerful life of all.

sections.heading: 3. Choose “I Already Have Been,” and Life Changes Naturally
sections.html:
The lesson’s first key point says this: when we choose to believe “I have been crucified with Christ,” the standard by which we live changes.

No longer “How do I get better?” or “How do I overcome?” but “It is no longer I who live” and “Christ lives in me.” This is a change of identity, and it is also a change in the way we live. We no longer strain to be justified by the law; we live in grace by faith.

As Scripture says, “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord” (Romans 6:11).

Brothers and sisters, notice the most important word in this verse: “consider.” In the original it is a bookkeeping term (λογίζεσθε), meaning “to enter it in the account,” “to reckon it at this figure.” This is the language of accounting. An accountant doesn’t keep the books by feel; he records the facts. On the cross God has already settled the account, and now he says to us: keep your books according to this fact — reckon yourself dead to sin and alive to God.

There is an order here, and it’s crucial — don’t get it backwards. It isn’t that I first feel I’m dead and then believe it. It’s that I first believe this is the fact, and then my feelings slowly catch up. Fact first, faith in the middle, feelings last. So much of the chaos in life comes from turning that order upside down: we let our feelings decide whether we believe, and let our feelings decide whether God loves us.

There’s a very fitting example. After a war had ended, the defeated nation had signed its surrender, and the war was legally over. But deep in the jungle there were soldiers who didn’t know. They went on fighting, went on hiding, went on with the battle for years. Their suffering was real, but their war no longer existed. What they lacked was not courage but information. Brothers and sisters, Satan’s greatest trick is to make people who have already overcome go on living by the identity of the defeated. He cannot change the fact of the cross; all he can do is deceive you into not keeping your books by the facts.

Psychology offers us good corroborating evidence here. In the 1960s Aaron T. Beck (1921–2021), a psychiatrist at the University of Pennsylvania, developed cognitive behavioural therapy. His central discovery was that our emotions and behaviour are not determined directly by events, but by our “cognitions” of those events and our “automatic thoughts.” Change the core beliefs, and emotions and behaviour change with them. This echoes Scripture exactly: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind” (Romans 12:2). Only Scripture goes further than psychology — psychology helps us replace mistaken thoughts, but the gospel replaces the whole “I.”

Brain science encourages us too. The research of Eric Kandel, winner of the 2000 Nobel Prize in Physiology or Medicine, showed that learning and memory change the synaptic connections between neurons — in other words, the brain is plastic. Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London published a study in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, finding that London taxi drivers, after years of memorising a complex road network, had greater grey-matter volume in the posterior hippocampus than a control group. Brothers and sisters, if even memorising roads can change the structure of a person’s brain, how could the life of someone who keeps his books every day by “I have been crucified with Christ” possibly stay unchanged?

In the 321 vision, this is the starting point of the five-fold change: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Mindset is the first domino. Many people try to start changing from “daily living,” so they draw up a pile of plans and make a pile of resolutions, and they can’t keep them going for even three months. They pushed the wrong domino. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living. If you take away only one thing this morning, take this: stop asking, “How do I get better?” and start saying, “I already have been.”

When the mindset changes, our feelings, attitudes and reactions all begin to change. This isn’t self-hypnosis; it’s living according to the facts God has spoken.

sections.heading: 4. Gaining Christ: Finding Your True Self
sections.html:
The lesson’s second key point says: “No longer I, but Christ” is not losing yourself; it is finding your true self.

We need to pay special attention to this, because many people are frightened when they hear the word selflessness. They think Christianity wants to wipe out our personality and turn us into soulless tools. Not at all. The 321 vision says it plainly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless.

Let me use an illustration. Leave a drop of water on a table, and within an hour it has dried up. Put that same drop into the ocean, and it will never dry up. What did it lose? It lost the fragility of existing on its own. What did it gain? It gained the vastness of the whole ocean. That is selflessness. Not being swallowed up, but being enlarged.

When we are selfless, Christ becomes our everything: his life becomes my life; his wisdom becomes my wisdom; his power becomes my power.

This is what Ephesians says: “and what is the exceeding greatness of his power toward us who believe, according to that working of the strength of his might which he worked in Christ, when he raised him from the dead and made him to sit at his right hand in the heavenly places” (Ephesians 1:19–20).

Brothers and sisters, look carefully at what Paul uses to measure the size of this power. He doesn’t say “as great as a mighty wind,” or “as great as the ocean waves.” He says: the measure of this power is the very might and strength that raised Jesus from the dead and seated him at God’s right hand in the heavens. In other words, the power God measures out to us who believe is “resurrection-grade” power. This is one of the boldest sentences in the whole Bible. Here Paul piles up four words for power one after another (δύναμις power, ἐνέργεια working, κράτος might, ἰσχύς strength), as though language were no longer enough and he had to heap every word he had on top of each other.

Why, then, do we so often not feel it? Because we are still living on the budget of “I.” If a man has ten million in the bank but thinks he only has a thousand, he’ll still live like a poor man. What we lack is not power; what we lack is the right mindset about that power.

We are no longer limited by our own limitations, because the “self” has been crucified. When we face weakness, we no longer say, “I can’t do it.” Instead we declare: I have been crucified with Christ; the one who lives now is Christ.

Someone may ask, “So am I allowed to admit I’m weak?” Of course — and you should. Paul himself says, “He has said to me, ‘My grace is sufficient for you, for my power is made perfect in weakness.’ Most gladly therefore I will rather glory in my weaknesses, that the power of Christ may rest on me” (2 Corinthians 12:9). Brothers and sisters, where is the difference? “I can’t do it” is a full stop: once you’ve said it, you stay right there. “I can’t, but Christ in me can” is a comma: once you’ve said it, you keep going. The first makes us smaller; the second lets us be filled.

In the nineteenth century Hudson Taylor (1832–1905), founder of the China Inland Mission, went through a season of deep spiritual dryness in mid-life. He found that the harder he pursued holiness, the more he felt himself failing. In 1869, in a letter to his sister, he described the light he had received: he had finally seen that it was not for him to strive harder to lay hold of Christ, but that Christ already lived in him, united with him. His son and daughter-in-law later called this “the exchanged life” in their book Hudson Taylor’s Spiritual Secret. From then on his service was no longer a matter of grimly holding on, but of overflowing. Brothers and sisters, what we need today is exactly this discovery.

Self-determination theory in psychology offers further corroboration. Research put forward since the 1980s by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan of the University of Rochester shows that a person’s truly lasting motivation comes from intrinsic motivation, not from outside pressure, rewards and punishments. Whatever we force ourselves through with “I absolutely must get this done” won’t last; only what wells up naturally from within can go the distance. The gospel moves our motivation from the outside to the inside — from law to life.

This is what 321 means when it says Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When the focus is right, we stop asking, “How much do I have?” and start asking, “How much does he have?” That brings tremendous release and hope.

sections.heading: 5. True Satisfaction: Not Living for Ourselves
sections.html:
The lesson’s third key point says: when it is “no longer I,” the focus of our daily living changes as well. We no longer live for ourselves; we live for Christ.

We no longer ask, “What do I want?” but “What is the Lord’s heart in this?” A life like that may look as though it has lost its freedom, but in fact it has entered true freedom.

Why? Because if we live for ourselves, we will end up in nothing but emptiness: “‘Vanity of vanities,’ says the Preacher; ‘Vanity of vanities, all is vanity’” (Ecclesiastes 1:2).

Brothers and sisters, the Hebrew word for “vanity” in this verse is הֶבֶל (hevel), whose root meaning is “breath, vapour, mist.” Breathe out on a cold morning and you can see a little white cloud; reach out to grab it and there is nothing to hold. When Solomon uses this word, he isn’t saying life has no value. He’s saying: apart from God, nothing under the sun can be held on to. He goes on: “I have seen all the works that are done under the sun; and behold, all is vanity and a chasing after wind” (Ecclesiastes 1:14). “Chasing after wind” — what a vivid picture. Someone who lives for himself spends his whole life chasing a gust of wind.

Solomon is the person best qualified to say this. He had wisdom, wealth, great building works, parks and gardens, men and women singers, every kind of pleasure. In Ecclesiastes 2 he tried them all one by one, and his conclusion was: chasing wind. Very few people in this world have ever taken “living for yourself” as far as he did, and very few have told us the outcome as honestly as he did.

What alternative does Scripture give us? “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again” (2 Corinthians 5:15). Notice the logic of this verse: Christ died for me, therefore I no longer live for myself. It is a response of love, not moral blackmail.

Here I need to draw a very important distinction. “Not living for yourself” does not mean “not taking care of yourself,” and it doesn’t mean becoming someone with no boundaries who lets others use them up. Jesus himself withdrew into the wilderness to pray, and went up the mountain to rest. “Not living for yourself” means this: my life no longer has me at its centre. Change the centre of the circle, and every radius changes with it.

On this point, modern psychology has, surprisingly, come down on the Bible’s side. In 2008 Elizabeth Dunn, Lara Aknin and Michael Norton published a study in Science, finding that people who spent money on others felt happier than people who spent the same money on themselves. The Harvard Study of Adult Development, which began following its participants in 1938, is one of the longest studies of adult life ever conducted. Its current director, Robert Waldinger, points out that over the long run, the biggest factor in keeping people healthy and happy is not wealth, not fame, but good relationships.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order 321 teaches: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. And the priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Someone who lives for himself will always turn that order upside down — he chases things first, then people, and only last of all thinks of God. The result: the task gets done, the people are lost, and God is far away.

At the opening of his Confessions, the church father Augustine wrote a line that has been repeated for over a thousand years: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” This is not a deduction of psychology; it is the personal confession of a prodigal who has come home.

So what does a person who lives for the Lord gain? The lesson puts it well: the Lord’s satisfaction is my satisfaction; the Lord’s joy is my joy. Jesus himself lived this way: “Jesus said to them, ‘My food is to do the will of him who sent me and to accomplish his work’” (John 4:34). Brothers and sisters, have you noticed that Jesus calls doing the Father’s will his “food”? Not his job, not his duty — his nourishment. When someone truly reaches this place, obedience is no longer pressure; it is delight.

The psalmist says too: “You will show me the path of life. In your presence is fullness of joy. In your right hand there are pleasures forever more” (Psalm 16:11). True satisfaction is not found in “getting what I want,” but in being “in his presence.” This is the true meaning of life.

This is also the shift of perspective that 321 talks about: from the human to the divine; from the earthly to the heavenly; from the temporary to the eternal; from the worldly to the godly. Once our perspective shifts, our whole definition of what is “worth it” shifts too. We used to ask, “What will I get out of doing this?” Now we ask, “What glory will the Lord’s name receive if I do this?”

sections.heading: 6. Living Out Christ: The Most Powerful Witness
sections.html:
The lesson’s fourth key point says: when Christ lives himself out through us, people will see Jesus. This doesn’t depend on eloquence; it depends on life.

Jesus said, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself” (John 12:32).

The context of this verse is precious. Some Greeks had come up to the feast, and they said to Philip, “Sir, we want to see Jesus” (John 12:21). Philip went and told Andrew, and the two of them went together and told Jesus. Jesus’ answer was unusual. He didn’t go straight out to meet them. Instead he said, “The time has come for the Son of Man to be glorified.” Then he spoke these words: “Most certainly I tell you, unless a grain of wheat falls into the earth and dies, it remains by itself alone. But if it dies, it bears much fruit” (John 12:24). Only then did he say, “And I, if I am lifted up from the earth, will draw all people to myself.” And John adds an explanation: “But he said this, signifying by what kind of death he should die” (John 12:33).

Brothers and sisters, look at the sequence: someone wants to see Jesus → a grain of wheat must die → if I am lifted up, I will draw all people. So the key to people seeing Jesus is “dying” and “being lifted up.” And this sequence is our sequence too. When the “I” falls into the ground and dies, Christ is lifted up in me; when Christ is lifted up, people are drawn.

We so often get the direction wrong. We work hard to lift up the “I” — to lift up my eloquence, my knowledge, my achievements, how dramatic my testimony is — and what people end up seeing is us, not Jesus. John the Baptist had the right attitude: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

The lesson gives a wonderful example: Peter and John in the early church were unschooled men, yet when people saw them, they recognised that they had been with Jesus.
