This is how Scripture records it: “Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus” (Acts 4:13).

Notice that act of “recognising.” The members of the Council weren’t listening to how many verses they could recite; they “recognised” the likeness of Jesus in them. What did that look like? It was the boldness and composure of men who, even under threat, could still say, “for we can’t help telling the things which we saw and heard” (Acts 4:20). Brothers and sisters, people may doubt your arguments, but it’s very hard for them to doubt your life.

Brain science offers an interesting piece of corroboration. In the 1990s Giacomo Rizzolatti’s team at the University of Parma discovered mirror neurons in the brains of macaque monkeys — when a monkey watches another perform an action, the neurons in its own brain responsible for that action fire as well. Later research has linked this to imitation and empathy in human beings. In 1977 Albert Bandura (1925–2021) of Stanford University put forward social learning theory, showing that a great deal of human behaviour is learned by observing role models, not by being lectured. Brothers and sisters, when God made us, he placed “seeing, then learning” inside us. So the most effective way the gospel has ever been passed on is not by debate, but through a life that can be seen.

This is the first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. And when Christ lives himself out through us, we too become role models others can see — not in our own likeness, but in the likeness of Christ. This is also the spirit of the 920 practice: everyone connected to us is our “2,” and before them we practise living out the selfless “0,” bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Brothers and sisters, your colleague doesn’t read the Bible every day, but he reads you every day. That is the most powerful gospel there is.

sections.heading: 7. Faith Plus Obedience: Letting the Light Shine Out
sections.html:
The lesson’s fifth key point says: with faith alone and no action, people cannot see Jesus; but when faith is joined with obedience, life begins to shine.

Jesus said, “Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 5:16).

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to the second half of this verse. When it’s quoted, people often stop at “good works,” but the Chinese Union Version goes on with the most crucial line of all: “and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” The purpose of shining is not to make people see us, but to make people give the glory to God. This is the second of 321’s Two Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory. If people see our good works and end up praising us, the light is shining in the wrong direction.

James says, “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself” (James 2:17). Faith and obedience are not two things; they are two sides of one thing. Real faith always walks out into action. A faith that never walks out isn’t faith — it’s an opinion.

The lesson reminds us: many people work hard at fighting the darkness, and the more they fight it, the more exhausted they become. In fact the way is very simple — you don’t need to chase the darkness away; you only need to shine.

That statement holds up completely in physics. Darkness is not a substance; darkness is the absence of light. You can’t carry a bucket of darkness and pour it into a bright room, but you can carry a candle into a dark room. The speed of light is 299,792,458 metres per second — the fixed value by which the International System of Units defines it. The instant you switch on a lamp, the darkness in the room has no “time to escape.” It simply ceases to exist.

Scripture begins exactly this way: “God said, ‘Let there be light,’ and there was light” (Genesis 1:3). God didn’t deal with the darkness first; he simply said, Let there be light. John says too: “This is the message which we have heard from him and announce to you, that God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5). Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life” (John 8:12). And to us he says, “You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden” (Matthew 5:14).

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to this order: Jesus is the light, and we are the light. Our light is reflected light, like the moon’s. The moon gives off no light of its own; it simply doesn’t block the sun. So the secret of our shining is not burning ourselves brighter, but not standing in Christ’s way.

Nature gives us another wonderful example. A firefly’s bioluminescence is a “cold light” that gives off almost no heat, and it converts energy with remarkable efficiency, far beyond a traditional incandescent bulb. One tiny firefly needs no blazing fire to be seen on a summer night. Brothers and sisters, you don’t need to become a sun. You only need to glow quietly in the corner where you are.

So how do we actually do it? The key lies in the word “obedience.” Obedience is the step that puts faith into action. In the 321 vision this is called “Implementation” — the fourth of the eight stages of changing our mindset. Many people get stuck at the third stage, “Conviction,” and go no further; they feel they already understand it all. But understanding the truth doesn’t mean the life has changed.

Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London published a study in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, finding that for a new behaviour to become an automatic habit, participants needed sixty-six days on average, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. That gives us two reminders. First, don’t assume that if you’ve obeyed for three days and felt nothing, you’ve failed. Second, don’t assume that once you’ve heard a message, your life will change automatically. You have to repeat it, and keep at it.

When we live out Christ, darkness naturally retreats. It isn’t that we drive the darkness away; it’s that the light of Christ shines out from within us.

sections.heading: 8. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s set today’s five key points back into the 321 framework and look at them once more.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, taking the form of a servant (Philippians 2:7); this is the most perfect demonstration of “no longer I.” The Bible is my standard — we keep our books according to Romans 6:11, not according to our feelings. The Holy Spirit is my guide — Christ living in me is accomplished through the Holy Spirit who dwells within us.

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — the positive way of saying “no longer I” is “let Christ reign as King.” There is only one throne: if he isn’t sitting on it, I am. Let Jesus receive all the glory — which is why the purpose of our shining is that people may give the glory to the Father in heaven (Matthew 5:16).

The Goal: establish God’s system. Only a selfless person can work together with others; only a company of selfless people together can establish God’s system. When self-centred people gather, all they do is compete with one another: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Here I want to say a little more clearly what the “self” is. 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. So “no longer I” is not self-belittling; it is returning to our originally intended position. A soldier returning to his post hasn’t failed; everyone is simply in their proper place. Once a person is willing to let God be God, he can at last be at peace being human. What a tremendous release that is.

Look again at the five-fold change: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Today’s first key point is “mindset”; the second is “life” — Christ becomes my life; the third is “daily living” — no longer living for ourselves; the fourth is “relationships” — people recognise Jesus in us; the fifth is “ministry” — faith plus obedience, and the light shines out. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The five key points of this lesson are precisely 321’s five-fold change, in exactly the same order. That’s no coincidence; it is the order Scripture itself has always had.

Then there are the 235 relationships. Become a “2” with a selfless person — do you have a spiritual companion beside you, someone with whom you can speak the truth to each other? Build your “3” — do you have spiritual parents, and are you walking alongside spiritual children? Become part of a “5” — are you working together with brothers and sisters of the fivefold ministry, as a team of spiritual comrades? Brothers and sisters, if “no longer I” stays only in private meditation, it will slowly dry up; put it into relationships, and it comes alive.

Finally, the Path of Serving: Spirit → Understanding → Life → Service → God. The Holy Spirit is my guide (Spirit), the Bible is my standard (Understanding), Jesus is my role model (Life), let Jesus be King (Service), let Jesus receive all the glory (God). Today’s lesson is really a walk through all five steps.

And there’s one more 321 reminder that fits today perfectly: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

sections.heading: 9. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. We’ll keep all three, and deepen them with the eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — so that they truly take root.

Practice 1: Live by your new identity

Remind yourself every day, “It is no longer I who live,” and in every decision learn to respond from the standpoint of “Christ lives in me.”

Information: Copy Galatians 2:20 and Romans 6:11 onto a card and put it somewhere you’re sure to see it every day — beside the mirror, in the car, as your phone wallpaper.

Revelation: Be still for three minutes each morning and ask the Holy Spirit to turn this verse from knowledge into sight. Pray, “Lord, let me truly see today that the ‘I’ who wanted to rely on myself is already dead.”

Conviction: Say it out loud to yourself. Not self-hypnosis, but keeping the books according to God’s word: “I have been crucified with Christ. This is a fact, not a feeling.”

Implementation: Choose one very concrete situation. For example, the moment today when someone makes you angry, pause for three seconds and say in your heart, “It is no longer I who live.” Only then open your mouth.

Evaluation: In the evening, take thirty seconds to look back — how many times today did I react out of “I”? How many times did I let Christ react?

Correction: Identify the time of day, or the kind of person, where you are most likely to give ground, and prepare especially for it tomorrow.

Repetition: Keep it up for at least sixty-six days. Remember, forming a habit takes sixty-six days on average.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister, share your experience with them, and invite them to practise with you.

Practice 2: Turn from satisfying yourself to satisfying the Lord

In everyday choices, deliberately ask, “Is this what I want, or what pleases the Lord?” Practise finding your satisfaction in the Lord’s heart.

Information: Memorise 2 Corinthians 5:15 and John 4:34.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you where the centre of your life’s circle is right now. Be honest with this one; don’t rush to give a spiritual answer.

Conviction: Admit that “living for myself is chasing wind.” This isn’t low self-esteem; it’s waking up.

Implementation: Each day, pick one small decision and deliberately ask that question: “Is this what I want, or what pleases the Lord?” Start with small things — how will I use my time today? Should I say this or not? How will I spend this money?

Evaluation: At the end of the week, notice which kinds of things you find hardest to let go of: is it time? Money? Face?

Correction: Take the hardest of these on its own before the Lord in prayer, and ask him to reign as King in that very thing.

Repetition: Let this question become a reflex.

Multiplication: Share your week’s practice with one another in your small group, and let this question become the common language of the fellowship.

Practice 3: Bear witness to Jesus with your life

Don’t only share the gospel with your mouth; live out Christ in your daily living, so that people see Jesus in your reactions, your attitudes and your love.

Information: Memorise the whole of Matthew 5:16, especially its last line: and glorify your Father who is in heaven.

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you which fruit of Christ the three people around you who don’t yet believe most need to see in you.

Conviction: Believe that the witness of a life is more powerful than eloquence; believe the law of “the grain of wheat.”

Implementation: This week, do one practical thing for each of those three people — a phone call, a meal, a helping hand, an apology.

Evaluation: Did they come to know a little more of Jesus because of it? When I did it, was my heart set on my own image, or on the Lord’s name?

Correction: If your motives weren’t pure, there’s no need to condemn yourself. Simply return to your originally intended position and set your focus right again.

Repetition: Put these three people on your prayer list and keep bringing them before the Lord over the long haul.

Multiplication: When one day they come to believe in the Lord, take them along to do the same for three others. That is spiritual multiplication.

A Gentle Reminder

It isn’t about trying hard to shine; it’s about letting Christ live himself out through you.

sections.heading: 10. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we are nearly at the end. Let’s walk today’s road once more.

Once the mindset changes, life begins to turn around. From “I’m trying hard” into “the Lord is alive”; from “living for myself” into “living for the Lord.” When we live like this, the light shines out naturally, and revival begins with us.

I want to say one thing in particular: revival does not begin with a meeting; revival begins with a person — one person who truly believes “I already have been.” It has been this way in every generation. When one person gives up the throne, God’s power has a channel.

So this morning I want to invite you to make a decision that is very simple, yet very deep. Not a decision to try harder, but a decision to believe. Not a decision to do more, but a decision to step aside.

Please answer three questions in your heart:

First, in what area am I still saying, “How do I get better?” Exchange it for “I already have been.”

Second, who is at the centre of my life’s circle right now? Give that place back to the Lord.

Third, who around me is waiting to see Jesus in me? Hold his or her name in your heart.

May we enter together into this kind of daily living: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. May we no longer be the one who sweeps every day and never gets the house clean, but the one who switches on the light. For the one we believe in is Jesus, “who for the joy that was set before him endured the cross, despising its shame” (Hebrews 12:2). He has already walked this road to the end for us.

No longer I, but Christ. May these words today be not just our slogan, but our daily living.

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
declarations: Lord, I choose to believe: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me! Let my life be your witness, so that people see you in me!
practices: Turn from satisfying yourself to satisfying the Lord
Bear witness to Jesus with your life
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Thank you that on the cross you have already put to death the old self that wanted to rely on itself. Lord, I confess that I still often live by my old identity, struggling every day in my own strength. This morning I choose to believe the fact you have spoken: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.

Lord, please take back the throne. One by one I place into your hands my plans, my wants, my face, my fears. Holy Spirit, guide me, so that I rely on the heart and on you, not on the brain and on myself. Let your resurrection power work within me, so that I no longer say, “I can’t do it,” but say, “Christ in me can.”

And make my life a lamp — not so that people will see me, but so that they will give the glory to you. Let the people around me recognise, from my reactions, my attitudes and my love, that I have been with Jesus.
Reign as King in my home, reign as King in my workplace, reign as King in my heart. May all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) In your life right now, what specific situation makes it hardest for you to “consider yourself dead”? If you kept your books today by “I already have been,” how would your reactions be different?

“Even so, let your light shine before men; that they may see your good works, and glorify your Father who is in heaven.” (Matthew 5:16) Name one person who is watching your daily living. What one concrete thing could you do this week so that what he or she sees in you is not you, but Jesus?
l102.title: No Longer I
l102.subtitle: A Change of Mindset (Part 4)
l102.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: Between Knowing and Doing Lies a Choice
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning.

On our journey through 321 Morning Devotion, we have already walked through “the change of mindset.” We have learned that the old self’s problem is the self-centred life, and the new self’s blessing is selflessness. We have learned that pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place, while humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. These truths have shone into our hearts like one beam of light after another.

And yet let’s ask ourselves honestly: why is it that some people hear a great many sermons, yet their lives don’t change?

There’s something every one of us has experienced. At the start of the year, many people make resolutions: this year I’m definitely going to read through the Bible, definitely going to get up early to pray, definitely going to stop losing my temper with my family. The resolutions are fine, and the intention is sincere. But at the end of the year you look back, and the Bible is still stuck in Genesis, the alarm still gets switched off, and the temper still flares as before. It isn’t that we don’t know what to do, and it isn’t that we don’t want to. Where we get stuck is not in “knowing,” but in that stretch of road between “knowing” and “doing.”

That stretch of road is called “choice.”

The lesson points to this key right at the start: once the mindset has changed, the next step is a “change of choices.” Many people stay at “knowing” and never enter into “doing,” and so their lives don’t change.

What does Scripture say? James 2:17 says, “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” Brothers and sisters, notice that James doesn’t say, “Faith without works is weak.” He uses a very heavy word — “dead.” In the original it is νεκρά (nekra), the “dead” of a corpse. A faith without works is not a faith with a frail constitution; it’s a corpse with no breath — outwardly whole, every feature in place, yet unable to walk, unable to breathe, unable to bear fruit.

James 2:26 says, “For as the body apart from the spirit is dead, even so faith apart from works is dead.” Works are the breathing of faith.

So the lesson says: real change doesn’t begin with understanding; it begins with “choice.” When we make the right choices, our life begins to run on the right track — that is, it enters God’s system.

There’s a truth here we often overlook. We think we’re only making lots of scattered little decisions every day, but in fact every choice is building an invisible structure around us. Thirty minutes scrolling short videos, or ten minutes reading the Bible; venting our resentment, or first kneeling to pray — these choices add up until they form a wall, a room, an environment. And that environment, in turn, shapes you.

In 1943, in the debate on rebuilding the House of Commons, the British Prime Minister Winston Churchill said these famous words: “We shape our buildings, and afterwards our buildings shape us.” He was talking about how the shape of the debating chamber influenced Britain’s political culture. The saying is just as accurate when applied to the spiritual life: by our choices we shape a system, and then the system shapes our life.

Brothers and sisters, in today’s lesson we’ll look at five things: from mindset to choice — faith must be lived out; life needs a system — without the right environment there is no growth; two systems determine two kinds of life; the purpose of new birth is to enter a new system; and establishing God’s system begins with the choices of each day.

May the Holy Spirit shine on us this morning, so that we don’t just know a little more, but from today on, in every choice, let Jesus be King.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Letters, One Shared Concern
sections.html: Before we come to the key points, let’s first understand the background of this lesson’s two theme passages. One comes from Paul and one from James; the two apostles, from different angles, point to the same truth.

sections.heading: (1) The Background of Galatians 2:20
sections.html:
Galatians was written by the apostle Paul, generally thought to be somewhere between AD 48 and 55, and it is one of Paul’s earliest letters. It was addressed to the churches in the region of Galatia — the believers in Pisidian Antioch, Iconium, Lystra, Derbe and other places, whose churches Paul had founded on his first missionary journey.

The church was facing a serious crisis at the time. A group of Judaizing teachers had followed on Paul’s heels, telling the Gentile believers: simply believing in Jesus is not enough; you must also be circumcised and keep the law of Moses before you can count as saved. This was not only a theological dispute but a dispute between systems — they wanted to drag the Gentile believers out of the system of grace and back into the system of the law.

In Galatians 2, Paul records how he publicly rebuked Peter in Antioch. Peter had been eating with the Gentile believers, but when people came from James, he drew back and separated himself from the Gentiles, because he was afraid of the circumcision party. Paul says that they “didn’t walk uprightly according to the truth of the Good News” (Galatians 2:14). You see, Peter’s theology was right; there was nothing wrong with his mindset. What was wrong was his “choice” in that moment. That is precisely the theme of this lesson: the mindset can be right, and the choice can still be wrong.

Then Paul makes his great declaration: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

“I have been crucified with Christ” — in the Greek, “crucified with” is συνεσταύρωμαι (synestaurōmai), a perfect passive. In Greek, the perfect tense means something completed in the past whose effect continues right into the present. So the sentence doesn’t mean, “I’m trying hard to nail myself up there,” but, “I have already been nailed there, and I am still in that state now.”

This is what 321 means: this is a faith of “I already have been,” not a religion of “I must try harder.” The cross is not a mountain we have to climb; it is the place we have already been brought to. What we are to do today is to acknowledge this “I already have been” in every choice, and live it out.

sections.heading: (2) The Background of James 2:17
sections.html:
The author of the letter of James is generally thought to be James, the brother of the Lord Jesus according to the flesh, the leader of the church in Jerusalem (Acts 15:13; Galatians 1:19). It was addressed “to the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — that is, to Jewish Christians scattered abroad.

The style of this book is distinctive. Rather than reasoning step by step like Paul, it is more like the Old Testament Proverbs: short sentences fired off one after another, each one piercing the heart. James has only 108 verses, yet more than fifty verbs in the imperative mood. Why? Because what concerns James is whether faith actually touches the ground.

James 2:14–17 says, “What good is it, my brothers, if a man says he has faith, but has no works? Can faith save him?” Then he gives an example: someone says to a brother who is naked and lacking food, “Go in peace,” but doesn’t give him what his body needs. And then he concludes: “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.”

Notice that James is not opposing Paul’s “justification by faith.” Paul is talking about how we are saved — not by works, but by grace. James is talking about how those who are saved are shown to be genuine — true faith inevitably bears the fruit of works. The root can’t be seen, but the fruit can; and a tree with no fruit makes people wonder whether it has any root at all.

So Galatians 2:20 tells us our position — “I already have been” — and James 2:17 tells us how it must show — “I must.” Put the two together and you have the heart of this lesson: living out, in the choices of each day, the position that has already been accomplished.

sections.heading: 1. From Mindset to Choice: Faith Must Be Lived Out
sections.html:
1. “I already have been” is not a slogan but a fact to be lived out

The lesson says: we already know that “I have been crucified with Christ,” but this isn’t just a mindset; it is a faith that must be lived out.

Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

Notice the two kinds of “living” in this verse. The first is “Christ lives in me” — this is our position, the work the Holy Spirit already completed when we were born again. The second is “That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God” — this is our experience, which we draw on by faith every day, in one small matter after another.

Romans 6:6 says, “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.” Paul first says “knowing” — that is mindset. Then Romans 6:11 says, “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” To “consider” is to choose, every day, in our thoughts and intentions, to reckon it so. And Romans 6:13 goes on: “but present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.” To “present” — that is action; that is choice.

Knowing, reckoning, presenting — these three steps are the road from mindset to choice. If we stop at the first step, all we have is a correct set of spiritual knowledge. The lesson puts it very bluntly: if we only “believe” and never “choose,” our life remains stuck in the self-centred life.

2. The practical expression of denying of self is living out “no longer I” in every choice

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me” (Luke 9:23).

Brothers and sisters, notice the word the Lord adds here, which the Chinese Union Version (like many English versions) keeps: “daily” — take up his cross daily. The cross is not an anniversary; it’s a daily schedule. Denying of self is not a once-in-a-lifetime decision; it is a choice made many times a day.

The lesson gives two very practical scenes.

The first scene: when facing conflict, do you choose yourself, or choose Christ?

A husband and wife fall into an argument over something small. You know perfectly well you’re partly in the wrong, yet a voice inside says, “If I apologise first, doesn’t that mean I’ve lost?” In that moment, the part of you that’s “afraid of losing” is the “self.” 321 puts it well: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When you choose to bow your head first, you’re not losing to the other person; you’re letting Christ win in you.

The second scene: when facing your own interests, do you choose yourself, or choose God’s will?

An opportunity comes up at work. All you have to do is gloss over one sentence and the contract is yours — no one will ever know. What you choose in that moment is not just a sales figure, but which system you are going to live in.

3. Choosing is hard because of the power of habit

Here a piece of psychological research can help us understand ourselves. In a study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues found that about 43 per cent of people’s everyday behaviour consists of habits repeated in the same settings, rather than decisions freshly thought through each time.

That finding cuts deep. It tells us that we think we’re “choosing” every day, but most of the time we’re actually “replaying.” This is exactly why changing the mindset alone isn’t enough — because the mindset lives in the head, but habits live in situations. Unless we make new choices in those situations, the old tracks will keep carrying us back to the old places.

In a paper published in 1999 in the journal American Psychologist, the psychologist Peter Gollwitzer put forward the idea of “implementation intentions.” He showed that merely setting a vague goal gives a low rate of success, whereas turning the goal into a concrete “If …, then I will …” form raises the success rate markedly.

Brothers and sisters, this echoes the message of this lesson exactly. Spiritual growth can’t stay at a vague wish like “I want to love the Lord more”; it has to become concrete choices: if my spouse says something cutting, then I will keep my mouth shut for three seconds and pray in my heart; if I want to prove I’m right yet again, then I will choose to let Jesus receive the glory.

4. Applying the 321 Vision

321 says the five-fold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living.

But notice: between mindset and life there is a door, and that door is choice. Truth doesn’t change us automatically because we know it; truth changes us because we obey it.

321 also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When in conflict we choose to stop proving ourselves, and in the face of our own interests we choose to stop grasping, our focus shifts from the “self” to Jesus. Every shift of focus is an exercise in selflessness.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the limitless and living out the limitless — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Brothers and sisters, this morning, is there a choice you’ve never dared to make?

sections.heading: 2. Life Needs a System: Without the Right Environment, There Is No Growth
sections.html:
1. Fish need water, birds need sky

The lesson uses a beautiful illustration: the growth of life always needs a suitable environment. Just as fish need water and birds need sky — if a fish leaves the water, no amount of effort will keep it alive.

There’s a very important spiritual truth in this illustration: the problem is not how much effort we make, but whether we’re in the right environment or the wrong one. A fish washed up on the shore isn’t lacking in effort. It leaps with all its might, struggles with all its might, and the harder it tries, the faster it dries out and dies. What it needs is not willpower; it’s water.

This is also why so many Christians are weary: it isn’t that we don’t love the Lord, but that we’re loving him in the wrong environment, so loving him is a hard slog.

From a scientific angle, the illustration becomes even more remarkable. Oxygen makes up about 21 per cent of the air by volume, whereas ordinary fresh water at 20°C holds only 8 to 9 milligrams of dissolved oxygen per litre. The oxygen in water is far thinner than in air, yet fish glide through it at ease by means of their gills, because God has prepared for them the right structure and also the right environment. Only when structure and environment match can life function.

The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5). “Remain” in Greek is μένω (menō), meaning to settle, to stay, to go on dwelling. The Lord didn’t say the secret of bearing much fruit is doubling your effort; he said, “remain in me.” The branch doesn’t have to strive to bear fruit; it only has to stay on the vine.

2. What is a system? A system is an environment that keeps on shaping you

The lesson gives a very clear definition: a system is “an environment that keeps on shaping you.” It has three dimensions — your thought environment, your relational environment and your way of life. All of them are shaping your life.

In fact, the Bible spoke of these three dimensions long ago.

On the thought environment, Paul says, “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2). “This world” literally means “this age” in the original — the values and patterns of thought an era holds in common; in other words, a system of thought.

On the relational environment, Proverbs says, “One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm” (Proverbs 13:20). Paul says too, “Don’t be deceived! ‘Evil companionships corrupt good morals’” (1 Corinthians 15:33).

On our way of life, Paul says, “whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:7–8).

3. A scientific example: trees without wind fall over

In the 1990s there was a famous experiment in Arizona called “Biosphere 2.” Scientists built a vast sealed glass structure containing a rainforest, an ocean and a desert, trying to simulate a self-sustaining ecosystem. One unexpected finding was that the trees inside grew fast and tall, yet often toppled over before they reached maturity — and one of the reasons was that there was no wind in that environment. In the natural world, trees swaying in the wind year after year grow tougher wood where the stress falls, and their roots go down deeper. A tree without wind looks as though it’s growing well, but in fact it can’t bear its own weight.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us two reminders. First, an environment doesn’t only provide nourishment; it also provides training. A spiritual environment with no challenges, where no one has to rub along with anyone else, produces lives that grow fast but can’t stand. Second, if a tree is growing in salty, alkaline ground or in deep shade, no amount of wind will save it. So the first priority of an environment is the right soil — that is, God’s word and the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

Psalm 1 puts these two things together: “Blessed is the man who doesn’t walk in the counsel of the wicked, nor stand on the path of sinners, nor sit in the seat of scoffers; but his delight is in Yahweh’s law. On his law he meditates day and night. He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither. Whatever he does shall prosper” (Psalm 1:1–3).

Look: the psalmist first speaks of not walking, not standing, not sitting — that is the choice to leave the old system. Then he speaks of delighting and meditating day and night — that is the choice to enter the new system. Only last does he speak of the tree planted by the streams of water — that is the result the system brings. When the position is right, bearing fruit becomes the natural thing.

4. Applying the 321 Vision

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things.

Why does 321 place such weight on relationships? Because relationships are the main material a system is built from. Your relationship with God determines your thought environment; your relationship with yourself determines your inner environment; your relationships with others determine your environment of support.

This is the meaning of 321’s “235 relationships”: become a “2” with a selfless person, build your “3,” and go on to become part of a “5.” Brothers and sisters, if you have no “2” beside you — someone who can tell you the truth and who will also kneel and pray for you — your life is like a tree with no windbreak.

The writer of Hebrews reminded us long ago: “Let’s consider how to provoke one another to love and good works, not forsaking our own assembling together, as the custom of some is, but exhorting one another, and so much the more as you see the Day approaching” (Hebrews 10:24–25).

sections.heading: 3. Two Systems Determine Two Kinds of Life
sections.html:
1. There are only two systems in the world

The lesson puts it very bluntly: there are only two systems in the world.

The first is the Worldly system, and its essence is the self-centred life. Its marks are these: it puts self at the centre, lives for self, relies on its own effort and pursues its own glory. Its outcome is struggle, pressure, emptiness and corruption.

The second is God’s system, and its essence is selflessness. Its marks are these: it lets Jesus be King, lives for God, relies on the Holy Spirit and gives the glory to God. Its outcome is peace, joy, victory and growth.

The Lord Jesus put this with absolute finality: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon” (Matthew 6:24).

The word “serve” in Greek is δουλεύω (douleuō), meaning to be a slave. The Lord Jesus isn’t talking about “liking” two masters, but about “being a slave to two masters.” A slave can belong to only one master’s household and live under only one household’s rules. You cannot live in two systems at the same time.

The apostle John says too: “Don’t love the world or the things that are in the world. If anyone loves the world, the Father’s love isn’t in him. For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:15–16).

Notice that John is not telling us not to love the people of the world — God loves the world, and we too should love people. The “world” he speaks of is κόσμος (kosmos), a system of values set against God: the lust of the flesh (I want to enjoy), the lust of the eyes (I want to possess), the pride of life (I want to be seen). These three are precisely the three faces of the self-centred life.

2. The fruit of the two systems always shows in the end

There was a brother whose career was a great success and whose diary was packed full. One day he said to his pastor, “I’ve got everything, but every morning when I wake up, the first thing I feel is tired.” That is where the Worldly system ends up: it gives you a great many things, but it takes you away. Because there, your worth has to be kept up by constant performance, and the moment you stop, you start to fall.

In God’s system, worth isn’t earned; it’s given. “For we are his workmanship, created in Christ Jesus for good works, which God prepared before that we would walk in them” (Ephesians 2:10). We don’t trade work for an identity; we first have an identity, and then we have work.

Augustine’s prayer in Book One of his Confessions expresses the reality deep in the human heart: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” The human heart comes in only one size — God’s size. Try to fill it with the world, and it will never be full.

3. An observation from social science: systems are contagious

In a study published in 2007 in the New England Journal of Medicine, Nicholas Christakis and James Fowler of Harvard University analysed social-network data on more than twelve thousand people spanning thirty-two years. They found that if a person’s friend became obese during a given period, that person’s own chance of becoming obese rose by about 57 per cent.

The researchers’ explanation was this: the people around us change, without our noticing, what we take to be “normal.”

Brothers and sisters, this is both what makes systems so frightening and what makes them so precious. Spend time with people who complain, and you’ll feel complaining is normal; spend time with people who fear God, and you’ll feel getting up early to pray is normal.

A system isn’t imposed by shouting; it soaks in. Whatever you steep in, that’s the flavour you’ll take on.

4. The key is not whether you believe in the Lord, but which system you live in

Here the lesson makes a very important statement: the key is not whether you believe in the Lord, but which system you live in. Many Christians have “received life,” yet still live in the Worldly system, and so they live a very hard life. This statement isn’t saying that whether we are saved doesn’t matter; it is saying that salvation is an accomplished fact, but victory is a daily choice.

It took the Israelites only one night to get out of Egypt; but it took forty years to get Egypt out of their hearts. Their feet had left Egypt, but their tastes and ways of thinking stayed behind. So whenever they met hardship, they said, “when we sat by the meat pots, when we ate our fill of bread” (Exodus 16:3).

Brothers and sisters, could it be that we’ve been baptised for years, yet we’re still sitting by the meat pots of Egypt as we think about our lives?

5. Applying the 321 Vision

321 says the shift of perspective is from the human to the divine, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

These four shifts are exactly the dividing line between the two systems. The Worldly system sees only earthly gain and loss; God’s system sees the reward in heaven. The Worldly system wears itself out for what is temporary; God’s system offers itself for what is eternal.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. For out of the heart is the wellspring of life (Proverbs 4:23). The driving force of the Worldly system is the brain — analysing, calculating, controlling. The driving force of God’s system is the heart — trusting, obeying, resting. Brothers and sisters, could it be that what’s troubling you today comes from relying on the brain and on yourself?

sections.heading: 4. The Purpose of New Birth: Entering a New System
sections.html:
1. New birth is not only being saved; it is moving house

The lesson quotes from 1 Peter. The full verse reads: “Blessed be the God and Father of our Lord Jesus Christ, who according to his great mercy caused us to be born again to a living hope through the resurrection of Jesus Christ from the dead” (1 Peter 1:3).

“Born again” in Greek is ἀναγεννάω (anagennaō), literally “to be begotten once more,” and here it stands in the passive — new birth is not the product of our effort; it is God who “caused us to be born again.” The Lord Jesus said to Nicodemus, “Most certainly, I tell you, unless one is born anew, he can’t see God’s Kingdom” (John 3:3).

Where the Chinese Union Version speaks of a “lively hope,” the original literally says “a living hope.” The world’s hopes are so often dead, because they are built on things that perish; the Christian’s hope is alive, because it is built on a Lord who rose from the dead and lives today.

The lesson says: new birth is not only being saved; it is entering a new life and a new system. You no longer belong to the world; you belong to God.

This is exactly what Paul says in Colossians: “who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love” (Colossians 1:13).

The word “translated” is wonderfully chosen. In the original it is μεθίστημι (methistēmi), a word commonly used in that day for an empire relocating a whole population from one kingdom to another. When God saves us, he doesn’t just let us out of prison and leave us to fend for ourselves at the gate; he moves us into a new kingdom, a new household register, a new system.

“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new” (2 Corinthians 5:17).

2. New life needs a new environment — this is the Creator’s law

There is something in nature that can help us understand this truth. After a caterpillar becomes a chrysalis, its body undergoes a drastic reorganisation, and at last it breaks out of the chrysalis in the form of a butterfly. It is the same life, yet with an entirely new structure — it no longer crawls on its prolegs, but flies on wings.

What would happen if a newly emerged butterfly insisted on going back under the leaf and living like a caterpillar? It wouldn’t die, but it would never know it was made to fly. Brothers and sisters, that is a picture of many Christians: we have wings, but we’re still crawling.

Paul says, “For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20). Peter says too: “But you are a chosen race, a royal priesthood, a holy nation, a people for God’s own possession, that you may proclaim the excellence of him who called you out of darkness into his marvelous light” (1 Peter 2:9).

Your identity has already changed. Only one question remains: has your living environment caught up with your identity?

3. If we stay in the Worldly system, our spiritual life will wither

The lesson gives two warnings: if you stay in the Worldly system, you will keep on struggling, and your spiritual life may even wither.

“Wither” is a very precise word. It isn’t dying overnight; it’s losing moisture little by little: first prayer grows shorter, then Bible reading becomes a chore, then meetings become a habit, and finally even sin no longer stings.

The book of Jeremiah sets two kinds of people side by side. One “will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land”; the other “will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit” (Jeremiah 17:6–8).

Notice that both trees face the same weather: the heat comes to both, the drought comes to both. The difference isn’t whether conditions are favourable or harsh, but where the roots go down. God’s system doesn’t guarantee you’ll never meet drought, but it does guarantee you won’t be concerned in the year of drought.

4. Applying the 321 Vision

321 says the Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

These Three Foundations are the three pillars of God’s system, and they correspond to the three environments the lesson describes.

The Bible is my standard — this is the foundation of the thought environment. If you don’t feed your thoughts with God’s word, the world will feed you with its information.

Jesus is my role model — this is the pattern for the relational environment. How he treated people, how he forgave, how he served, is the pattern for all our relationships.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — this is the driving force of our way of life. “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God” (Romans 8:14).

And what 321 calls “life first, then relationships, then ministry” is also the order of growth after new birth. Many people rush into work the moment they are born again, and before their life has put down roots, the ministry has crushed them. God’s order is always: first he makes you live, then he makes you love, and only last does he have you work.

sections.heading: 5. Establishing God’s System Begins with Choice
sections.html:
1. Not a one-time decision, but a daily choice

The lesson says: establishing God’s system is not a one-time decision, but a daily choice. Every time you choose Jesus, every time you lay yourself down, every time you obey the Holy Spirit, you are establishing God’s system.

At the end of his life, Joshua gathered all Israel at Shechem and said to them: “If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15).

Notice the word “today.” Joshua didn’t tell them to remember the Red Sea, nor to dream about the future; he wanted them to make their decision today. Moses said the same thing: “I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants” (Deuteronomy 30:19).

God never forces anyone. He sets life and death, blessing and curse before us, and then says: choose life. Brothers and sisters, God’s system is not a house God builds for us so we can just move in; it is a temple for which God supplies the materials and we build together with him, brick by brick and tile by tile.

2. A study on habits: new tracks take time

In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London followed ninety-six participants as they formed new habits. They found that the median time for a behaviour to become automatic was about sixty-six days, with wide individual differences, ranging from eighteen days to over two hundred.

This study gives us two comforts. First, slow is normal. Don’t conclude you’re not growing just because a practice still feels hard after three days — the new track is still being laid. Second, if you keep going, it really will become natural.

The study also found that occasionally missing a day did not significantly derail habit formation. Brothers and sisters, that’s a picture of grace. The day you fall is not a day when everything goes back to zero. “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again” (Proverbs 24:16).

But we must also be clear: habit formation is a natural law that God has established, but the growth of spiritual life is the work of the Holy Spirit. We practise not in order to build a good religious habit by our own strength, but in order to place ourselves, again and again, where the Holy Spirit can work. Paul puts it with perfect balance: “work out your own salvation with fear and trembling. For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:12–13).

3. This is the very heart of 321

Here the lesson sets out 321 in full.

The Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model; the Bible is my standard; the Holy Spirit is my guide.

The Two Core Values: let Jesus be King; let Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal: establish God’s system.

The Three Foundations are the basis of our daily choices. When I don’t know what to do, I ask three questions: What would Jesus do? What does the Bible say? Is there peace from the Holy Spirit in my heart?

The Two Core Values are the direction of our daily choices. Every choice answers two questions: Who is King in this? Who receives the glory in this?

The Goal is the outcome of our daily choices. When the foundation is right and the direction is right, the system is established quite naturally.

The Lord Jesus said, “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock” (Matthew 7:24). Hearing is mindset; doing is choice; the house is the system. And the rock is Christ himself.

4. An example from daily living: the power of morning devotion

Those of us who do 321 Morning Devotion are actually doing something every day that establishes a system. When you open your eyes in the morning, you have two choices: reach for your phone and let the world’s information in first, or open your Bible and let God’s word in first. The two choices seem only thirty centimetres apart, yet they decide whose is the “first voice” of your whole day. Over one day, the difference is small; over three hundred and sixty-five days, the difference is a whole life.

One sister shared that she used to start scrolling on her phone the moment she woke up, and her mood would already be half sunk. Later she started charging her phone in the living room and kept only her Bible by the bed. She said, “I didn’t become more spiritual. I just changed who gets to speak to me first.” Brothers and sisters, that is a system — a system isn’t a grand plan; it’s a small arrangement kept up steadily.

5. Applying the 321 Vision: the 920 practice

321 has a very practical exercise called “the 920 practice”: everyone connected to us is our “2”; before each “2,” we practise living out a selfless life — that is the “0”; and when we live like this, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit are borne.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). Paul uses the singular, “fruit.” These nine are not nine separate items to be picked up one by one, but a single cluster of fruit growing from a single life.

The “0” is the key. Unless the “self” in the middle is brought down to zero, the nine graces cannot grow; for what blocks patience is “I can’t stand it,” what blocks kindness is “he doesn’t deserve it,” and what blocks gentleness is “I’m right.” So the 920 practice is very simple, yet very deep: today, before every person I meet, I choose to let Christ live, not to let myself win.

When you live like this, the lesson’s final sentence comes true: selflessness is no longer theory; it becomes your daily living.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: A Road from the Heart to the System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s place what we’ve learned today into the complete picture of 321.

1. The self-centred life and selflessness: the watershed between systems

321 says: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

In the Garden of Eden the serpent said, “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). This is the foundation of every Worldly system — man wanting to take God’s place. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

When all is said and done, the difference between the two systems comes down to one thing: who is sitting on the throne. In the Worldly system it is the “self”; in God’s system it is Jesus.

Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan has never been able to overcome a truly selfless person, because he has nothing to get a grip on. The Lord Jesus said, “the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me” (John 14:30).

2. The five-fold change: this lesson stands at the second stop

321 says the five-fold change is mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry.

In the previous lesson we talked about “the change of mindset”; in this lesson we’re talking about “the change of choices.” Choice is the very bridge that leads from mindset to life.

Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change the daily living. But if there is no choice in between, change stays on paper. A person’s daily living today is the sum of yesterday’s choices; Scripture said it long ago — whatever a man sows, that he will also reap (Galatians 6:7).

3. The shift of perspective: retuning in four directions

From the human to the divine: no longer asking, “What do others think of me?” but, “How does God see this?”

From the earthly to the heavenly: no longer reckoning only this season’s harvest, but seeing the reward stored up in heaven.

From the temporary to the eternal: “For our light affliction, which is for the moment, works for us more and more exceedingly an eternal weight of glory” (2 Corinthians 4:17).

From the worldly to the godly: no longer using the world’s methods to achieve God’s purposes.

Brothers and sisters, every choice is a retuning. Whatever channel you tune to, that’s the voice you’ll hear.

4. The 235 relationships and the fivefold ministry: a system needs companions

No one can establish a system on their own. 321’s “235 relationships” tell us: first become a “2” with a selfless person — a spiritual companion, each holding the other up; then build your “3” — spiritual parents and spiritual children, so that life can be both received and passed on; and finally become part of a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

“Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up” (Ecclesiastes 4:9–10).

5. The Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God

321 describes the order of serving as a road: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God — first the Holy Spirit’s guidance, then an understanding of the truth; with understanding comes choice; with choice comes service; and the destination of all service is to let Jesus receive all the glory. “Whether therefore you eat, or drink, or whatever you do, do all to the glory of God” (1 Corinthians 10:31).

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Turning Choices into a System
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices for daily living. We’ll put them into effect one by one, and deepen them with 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Examine the system of my daily living

Ask yourself honestly: is my daily living right now centred on myself, or am I letting Jesus be King?

Information: First, gather the real data. Take stock of the past seven days: What do you do in the first hour after you wake up? Who are the three people you talk with most in a week? Where do your three largest expenses in a month go? Don’t evaluate; just record. Time and money never lie; they faithfully show who is sitting on our throne.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts” (Psalm 139:23). Being shown the truth is not condemnation; it is the first step towards healing.

Conviction: Sincerely acknowledge what God points out. Not the vague self-reproach of “I know I’m not good enough,” but saying specifically: Lord, I see that in this matter I am the one reigning as king.

Implementation: From your stocktaking, choose the smallest, most concrete thing and adjust it today.

Evaluation: After a week, look back to see whether you made that adjustment, and in what situations you gave ground.

Correction: Don’t swap it for a bigger goal; remove the obstacle instead — if your phone is what’s in the way, move it out of the bedroom.

Repetition: Take stock once a month, the way you’d check your blood pressure.

Multiplication: Take this practice to your “2.” Ask each other how it’s going and pray for each other, and the practice grows from private self-examination into a system shared by a pair of spiritual companions.

Practice 2: Live out faith in your choices

Every day, deliberately choose to obey God in small things, living out the faith of “I already have been” through your actions.

Information: Understand what the faith of “I already have been” is. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20). We don’t nail ourselves to death by effort; by faith we acknowledge that we have already died and risen with Christ.

Revelation: Ask God to show you which situation today is your cross. Usually it isn’t anything big; it’s the retort you badly want to make but shouldn’t.

Conviction: Say “yes” to God in your heart, and surrender before you act.

Implementation: Make three concrete “If …, then I will …” commitments —

If I’ve just opened my eyes, then I will first say, “Lord Jesus, today you are King.”

If someone embarrasses me, then I will first bless them in my heart, and only then speak.

If I want to argue my own case, then I will choose to be quiet and hand the matter over to God.

Evaluation: Every evening, take three minutes to look back: When did I choose Christ today? When did I choose myself?

Correction: When you fail, confess at once; don’t let it run on overnight. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins” (1 John 1:9).

Repetition: Keep it up for at least sixty-six days. Remember, missing the occasional day doesn’t send you back to zero.

Multiplication: When you overcome in small things, someone will ask you, “Why are you so different from before?” That is your moment to bear witness.

Practice 3: Establish a godly environment

Adjust your circle, your thoughts and your habits, so that you remain continually in God’s word and under the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

Information: First admit one thing — we cannot cultivate spiritual life in an environment that feeds the flesh.

Revelation: Ask God to show you which environment in your life most needs adjusting. Is it the first hour of the morning? The two hours after you switch off the computer? Or a relationship that keeps dragging you down?

Conviction: Accept a fact — adjusting your environment will cost something. You may have to watch one less series, turn down one more get-together, be a little less liked.

Implementation: Tackle all three environments at once. Thought environment — a fixed time of morning devotion every day, letting God’s word in first. Relational environment — find your “2,” and share and pray for each other at least once a week. Way of life — settle on one thing you will “not do” and one thing you “must do.”

Evaluation: After a month, check: has your heart become quieter, or more agitated?

Correction: If you set the bar too high, lower it to a level you can sustain. A small practice you can keep up beats a grand plan you can’t carry out.

Repetition: Let it become a rhythm. Life doesn’t grow by effort; it is cultivated by environment.

Multiplication: Open your morning devotion time to one other person and invite them to join you. In this way you go from being “someone cultivated by an environment” to being “someone who prepares an environment for others.” That is exactly how God’s system spreads.

A Gentle Reminder

The lesson leaves us with one beautifully concise sentence: life doesn’t grow by effort; it is cultivated by environment.

Brothers and sisters, this doesn’t mean we shouldn’t make an effort; it means putting our effort in the right place. Our effort isn’t for “growing up” — no child can grow taller by willpower. Our effort is for “staying in the right environment.”

A farmer can’t make a seed sprout, but a farmer can loosen the soil, water it and pull the weeds. The Lord Jesus said, “the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how” (Mark 4:27).

We are responsible for choosing and offering; God is responsible for growth and maturity.

sections.heading: Closing and Call: The Mindset Is the Starting Point; the Choice Is the Key
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing words are beautiful: a change of mindset is the starting point; a change of choices is the key. When you begin to choose Jesus, you begin to enter a new system; and that system will lead you into a life of victory, abundance and revival.

Let’s gather up today’s message in three sentences.

First: every choice you make is a vote. Today, are you voting for the “self,” or for Jesus? There is no abstaining — not choosing is itself a choice.

Second: the system you establish will one day shape you. The house you build with your choices today is the house you’ll live in tomorrow.

Third: Jesus is to reign as King in this system. 321’s Two Core Values are: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory. We establish God’s system not so that life will go smoothly for us, but so that the Lord who is worthy may truly sit on the throne in our families, our workplaces and our fellowship.

One day, “The kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15). What will be fulfilled on that day can begin, even now, in your daily living and mine.

So let us respond together with the lesson’s declaration of faith: Lord, I am willing to choose you. I will no longer live in the Worldly system. I will let Jesus be King and live in God’s system, so that my life can grow into the shape of selflessness.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, may you leave not with a new piece of knowledge, but with a new choice. A change of mindset is the starting point; a change of choices is the key.

Glory to Jesus.

keyVerses: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
“Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” (James 2:17)
practices: Examine the system of my daily living
Live out faith in your choices
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you that you have accomplished everything for us; we have been crucified with you, and it is no longer we who live, but you who live in us. Lord, forgive us. So often we know, yet do not do; we understand so much truth, yet we still go round in circles in our own system, living weary and living parched.
Lord, today we choose you.

Let your Holy Spirit shine on us, so that we see our true condition. Give us courage, in every small choice, to lay ourselves down and let you be King. Help us adjust our thought environment, our relational environment and our way of life, so that our roots go down by the streams of water and we will not be concerned in the year of drought.
Give us spiritual companions, so that we can consider one another and provoke one another to love and good works; and use us to pass this system of God on to others.
May every choice of our lives point to one thing: let Jesus be King, let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: James 2:17 says, “Even so faith, if it has no works, is dead in itself.” Share: what is one thing recently that you have “known” but never “done”? Is what’s holding you back not knowing how, or not being willing to let go of yourself? What is the first concrete choice you could make today?

Joshua 24:15 says, “but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” Look at your current thought environment, relational environment and way of life: which one helps you most to draw near to God? Which one most drags you back into the Worldly system? Which one are you willing to adjust first this month, and how would you like your small group to pray for you and follow up with you?
l103.title: Changed Choices Establish God’s System
l103.subtitle: Every Choice Is Establishing a System
l103.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: Which Tree Are You Eating From Today?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we step into God’s word together, I’d like to ask you a question that is very ordinary, and yet cuts very deep: across the whole of yesterday, how many choices did you make?

Wendy Wood, a psychologist at the University of Southern California, published a tracking study with her colleagues in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. They found that about forty-three per cent of our daily behaviour is habit — repeated in the same settings, almost without a thought. In other words, you think you are “choosing,” but most of the time you are really “replaying.” However you answered that remark yesterday, you will probably answer it the same way today.

And that raises a deeper question: where do these almost thoughtless reactions actually grow from?

Let me describe an early-morning scene that plenty of families know well. The alarm has gone off for the third time, and your child is still lying in bed. You’ve called twice; on the third call your voice changes. Your child fires back a cheeky reply, the blood rushes to your head, and a harsher word is already on the tip of your tongue. In that one second, brothers and sisters, you are actually standing between two trees.

One path says: I’m going to crush this right now, I’m going to prove I’m right, I’m going to let him know who’s in charge. The moment that word leaves your mouth, the breakfast table falls dead silent. You’ve won on volume, but you’ve lost the relationship, and your heart stays heavy all day. The other path says: Lord, I need you this second; give me words, not volume. You take a deep breath, crouch down, look your child in the eye and say, “I know you’re tired. Let’s work this out together.” The same thirty seconds — two kinds of fruit, two different endings.

Many people think life is made of a thousand different choices, but from God’s point of view there are only two roads in life: God’s system and the Worldly system. These two systems aren’t a classification some scholar of religion invented later on. They have been lying there since Genesis chapter 2, on the very first page of human history — in the middle of the garden stand two trees, one the tree of life, the other the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.

From that day to this, the human race has never stepped out of the shadow of those two trees. Your thoughts, your choices and your reactions every day are all settling one thing: which tree you are eating from.

Someone will say, “But I don’t worship idols — how could I be living in the Worldly system?” Brothers and sisters, the most frightening thing about the Worldly system isn’t that it openly opposes God. It’s that, without your even noticing, it gets you to “be your own god.” It doesn’t need you to burn incense. All it needs is for you to say, about every single thing: I can handle this one myself.

So today’s lesson isn’t a class for gaining knowledge; it’s a health check. May the Holy Spirit, in the time ahead, shine his light on every one of us: did my reactions today grow from the tree of life, or from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Trees at the Starting Line of Human History
1. The Author, Date and First Readers of Genesis
sections.html:
Genesis is the first book of the five books of Moses. The long-standing consensus of the evangelical church — and the testimony of the Lord Jesus himself (John 5:46–47) — is that the body of these five books came from the hand of Moses. They were written in the wilderness period, after Israel came out of Egypt and before they entered Canaan, somewhere between the fifteenth and thirteenth centuries BC.

Notice who the first readers were: a people who had just left four hundred years of slavery in Egypt and had not yet entered the promised land. They carried Egypt’s way of thinking with them, and ahead of them lay Canaan’s Baal and Asherah. All around them was a culture of many gods, of idol worship, of human desire at the centre.

Why did Moses begin his writing with “In the beginning, God created the heavens and the earth”? Because what these people needed most was not a route map for the wilderness but a fundamental answer: Whose is the world? Who am I? Whom should I listen to? The first three chapters of Genesis answer exactly those three questions — God is the Creator, man is the creature, and man’s originally intended position is to live in dependence on God.

sections.heading: 2. The Historical and Cultural Setting of Eden
sections.html:
“Eden” in Hebrew is עֵדֶן (eden), meaning “delight, abundance, exquisite enjoyment.” “Garden” is גַּן (gan), a walled, bounded, carefully tended garden, much like the royal gardens of the kings of the ancient Near East. God placed man in it — not to lock him up, but to entrust him with it: “Yahweh God took the man, and put him into the garden of Eden to cultivate and keep it.” (Genesis 2:15)

There are two key trees in the garden, and Scripture takes particular care to stress where they stand — “in the middle of the garden.” Not in a corner, not outside the wall, but right in the centre, in the place you’d walk past and see every day. God did not hide the temptation away, because love without the possibility of choice is not love, and obedience without the possibility of disobedience is not obedience.

Then comes the first commandment in the whole Bible: “Yahweh God commanded the man, saying, ‘You may freely eat of every tree of the garden; but you shall not eat of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil; for in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die.’” (Genesis 2:16–17) Count up the proportions: what may be eaten is “every tree of the garden”; what may not be eaten is a single tree. God’s heart has never been to restrict but to protect. He gave a whole expanse of abundance and fenced off only one boundary.

sections.heading: 3. Key Word: What Does “Knowing Good and Evil” Mean?
sections.html:
The Chinese name, “the tree that distinguishes good and evil,” easily misleads people into thinking that God doesn’t like us having knowledge, or doesn’t want us to tell right from wrong. But the Hebrew עֵץ הַדַּעַת טוֹב וָרָע, translated literally, is “the tree of knowing good and evil.” The key lies in the verb “to know,” יָדַע (yada).

In Hebrew, yada goes far beyond head knowledge. It means experiencing something first-hand, entering into it, taking hold of it and deciding it. So “knowing good and evil” doesn’t mean “being able to tell right from wrong”; it means “I will decide for myself what is right and what is wrong.” This is a seizure of power: the authority to define good and evil is moved out of God’s hands and into man’s.

Once you see this clearly, the whole story becomes clear. That tree is not a “tree of knowledge”; it is a “tree of setting my own standard.” The tragedy of the human race is not that we know too much, but that we want to be the standard ourselves.

sections.heading: 4. The Background of Our Theme Verse: Romans Chapter 8
sections.html:
Our theme verse comes from Romans 8:6. The apostle Paul wrote this letter around AD 57, near the end of his third missionary journey, while he was staying in Corinth. He wrote it to the church in Rome, which he had never yet visited in person. Rome was the capital of the empire, a city brimming with power, wealth, class and lust — a model city of the Worldly system through and through.

Romans chapters 6 to 8 form the main trunk of the letter’s teaching on sanctification, and chapter 8 is the summit of that section. In 8:5–8 Paul draws an utterly clear contrast that sets the whole human race under two principles of life: “For those who live according to the flesh set their minds on the things of the flesh, but those who live according to the Spirit, the things of the Spirit. For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace; because the mind of the flesh is hostile toward God; for it is not subject to God’s law, neither indeed can it be. Those who are in the flesh can’t please God.” (Romans 8:5–8)

The word translated “mind” here is the Greek φρόνημα (phronēma). It refers to the orientation of the mind, a pattern of thinking — the direction in which a whole person cares, calculates and leans. It isn’t a thought that pops up now and then; it’s where your “default setting” as a person is fixed.

Brothers and sisters, do you see it? What Moses tells in Genesis with two trees, Paul tells in Romans with two kinds of mind — and it is the same thing: two systems, two sources of life, two endings. The Old Testament uses a picture, the New Testament uses teaching, but the message of the Holy Spirit has never changed.

sections.heading: 1. Two Trees: Two Sources of Life
sections.html:
“Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” (Genesis 2:9)

There were many trees in the garden of Eden, but Scripture gives names to only two of them. That’s because these two trees are not a botanical category; they are pictures of two systems.

The Tree of Life: God’s System

“Tree of life” in Hebrew is עֵץ הַחַיִּים (ets hachayyim). Notice that the word for “life,” חַיִּים (chayyim), is plural in Hebrew. What it expresses is not a bare breath that barely keeps you alive, but life overflowing, abundant, many-layered. That is exactly what the Lord Jesus said: “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

The system the tree of life stands for has four marks: it is centred on God, it depends on God, it submits to God’s standard, and it receives life from God.

Pay special attention to the last of these — receiving life from God. This is the lifeline of the whole of God’s system. Man was never created as a self-powered unit, but as a creature that must stay connected to its source. Adam became a living soul only when God himself breathed the breath of life into his nostrils (Genesis 2:7); from the very first second, his life was “received.”

And what does this tree produce? Life, peace, and connection with God.

The Tree of the Knowledge of Good and Evil: the Worldly System
