The system the other tree stands for also has four marks, and they are the exact opposite: it is centred on self, it judges right and wrong for itself, it is its own master, and it no longer depends on God.

Its outcome is recorded plainly in Scripture: fear, shame and death. After Adam and Eve ate, their first reaction was to discover they were naked (shame); their second was to hide among the trees (fear); and their final end was to be driven out of Eden and to return to the dust (death).

Satan’s Words: You Can Be Your Own God

What did Satan say to Eve? “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

Put into plain words, the heart of that sentence comes down to four: you can be God.

And that is where “self” began. The root of every human problem is not ignorance, not weakness, not circumstances — it is this one swallowed lie: I can be my own god. From that moment on, this thing called “self” climbed onto the throne of the human heart, and it still hasn’t come down today.

Scripture Interpreting Scripture: The Tree of Life Runs Through the Whole Bible

The tree of life doesn’t appear only in Genesis. Proverbs says: “She is a tree of life to those who lay hold of her. Happy is everyone who retains her.” (Proverbs 3:18) The “she” here is wisdom, and the wisdom Scripture speaks of begins with the fear of Yahweh.

And in the very last chapter of the Bible, the tree of life appears again: “On this side of the river and on that was the tree of life, bearing twelve kinds of fruits, yielding its fruit every month. The leaves of the tree were for the healing of the nations.” (Revelation 22:2) “Blessed are those who do his commandments, that they may have the right to the tree of life, and may enter in by the gates into the city.” (Revelation 22:14)

Brothers and sisters, the beginning and the end of the Bible form an arch: at the start, man lost the tree of life; at the close, God gives the tree of life back again beside the throne of the Lamb. The long road in between is called the cross.

An Everyday Illustration: Two Pots of Plants

Two pots of plants stand on the same table in a living room, and from a distance they look equally bright. One is an artificial plant; the other is an ivy just brought in from the balcony. You can’t tell them apart right now, because both are “performing life.” Three months later you can: the artificial plant looks exactly the same — it doesn’t wither, but it doesn’t grow either — while the ivy has put out new shoots and climbed along a whole row of the bookshelf.

The difference isn’t in how they look; it’s whether there are roots. A life lived in the Worldly system is often a very well-made artificial plant: an impressive CV, efficient in everything, never a mistake — but never growing, and never bearing a single fruit. The Lord Jesus could not have said it more clearly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: Autonomy Is Not Independence

The loudest slogan of modern culture is “be yourself.” Interestingly, psychology itself offers a caution. Beginning in the 1980s, Edward Deci and Richard Ryan of the University of Rochester developed “self-determination theory,” which holds that people have three basic psychological needs: autonomy, competence and relatedness. But they have clarified again and again that autonomy is not the same as independence. Truly healthy autonomy isn’t cutting yourself off from all authority; it’s wholeheartedly embracing and internalising the values you belong to. A person can submit entirely willingly and still be highly autonomous; another can decide everything for himself and yet be driven by desire within, with no freedom at all.

Brothers and sisters, this is just what Scripture told us long ago: every “freedom” that walks away from God ends up as another kind of slavery. “If therefore the Son makes you free, you will be free indeed.” (John 8:36)

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The system of the tree of life, in the language of 321, is the Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Look — every one of these three pillars points to that tree in the middle of the garden: my role model isn’t someone I imagine for myself, my standard isn’t one I set myself, my guidance isn’t something I grope my way to on my own. Turn it around, and the system of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil has three pillars too: I am my own role model, my feelings are my standard, my judgement is my guide.

Brothers and sisters, this morning please ask yourself honestly: under which tree are my three pillars standing right now?

sections.heading: 2. The Nature of Sin: Putting Self in God’s Place
sections.html:
When people sin, they don’t just do the wrong thing; they take the wrong “position.”

The New Testament Greek word for “sin” is ἁμαρτία (hamartia), which originally meant an arrow that misses the centre of the target, that strays from the mark. What is the target man was made for? To let God be God and man be man. Sin is leaving that originally intended position: God should have been allowed to be God, but man wanted to be God himself.

The Anatomy of Pride: Five “I Will”s

The passage where Scripture lays this “replacing God” attitude most bare is in Isaiah: “You said in your heart, ‘I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!’” (Isaiah 14:13–14)

Five “I will”s, climbing all the way up, and the last one shows the hand: I will make myself like the Most High. Evangelical interpreters have long held that this lament over the king of Babylon reflects, behind it, the pattern of Satan’s own fall. And the words Satan spoke to man in Eden were precisely his own virus planted in the human race: he didn’t tell people to go and murder or burn; he simply handed them a thought — you can rise up, you can be the one who decides.

After Eating, Man Began Doing Two Things

Once man had eaten the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, he immediately began doing two things: setting his own standards, and solving his own problems.

Scripture records it in remarkable detail: “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.” (Genesis 3:7)

Look at those words, “for themselves.” This was the first home-made garment in human history, and humanity’s first self-rescue project. A problem appeared, and man’s first reaction was not to come back before God but to set to work covering it up. This is the most typical mark of the Worldly system: using my own methods to solve the problems I caused myself.

Fig leaves have one fatal flaw — they wither. However tightly you sew them today, three days later they curl and crumble. Every human covering is like that: an image can hold up for a while, an excuse can be argued for a while, busyness can numb you for a while, but none of them lasts.

God’s Response: Garments of Skin

Then Scripture records a verse that is profoundly tender and profoundly heavy: “Yahweh God made garments of animal skins for Adam and for his wife, and clothed them.” (Genesis 3:21)

Where did the skins come from? From an animal that was killed. This is the first time in Scripture that blood is shed — and it was shed to cover human shame. From this verse on, a scarlet thread runs all the way to the Passover lamb, to the altar of the tabernacle, to the cross at Golgotha. Hebrews puts it in a single sentence: “According to the law, nearly everything is cleansed with blood, and apart from shedding of blood there is no remission.” (Hebrews 9:22)

Brothers and sisters, here is a contrast that never changes: man’s covering is leaves, God’s covering is skins; man’s covering costs nothing, God’s covering requires someone to die in our place; man’s covering withers, God’s covering lasts for ever. True covering has never come from your effort; it comes from God’s grace.

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: The First Self-Justification

After the fruit was eaten, God came looking for Adam. How did Adam answer? “The man said, ‘The woman whom you gave to be with me, she gave me fruit from the tree, and I ate it.’” (Genesis 3:12)

In one sentence he shifts the blame first to his wife, then to God. This is the first self-justification in human history.

In 1957 the social psychologist Leon Festinger put forward the theory of cognitive dissonance: when our behaviour clashes with our view of ourselves, we very seldom change the behaviour; mostly we rework the explanation. In their 2007 book “Mistakes Were Made (But Not by Me),” Carol Tavris and Elliot Aronson use a wealth of research to show that the most natural instinct after we do wrong is not to admit it but to find ourselves a story that holds together — and the more we tell it, the more we really believe it.

Brothers and sisters, nobody has to learn how to justify themselves, because this is the fruit of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil at work in our blood. And the reason repentance is so hard is not that we don’t understand the teaching; it’s that we have to take off the fig-leaf skirt we’ve worn for decades.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 puts it with great precision: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

So the core movement of repentance is not doubling our effort but “returning to our place.” It isn’t that I’ll do a better job of being God; it’s that I stop being God. The old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

This morning, if you are sewing a fig-leaf skirt inside — wanting to prove something, to cover something, to explain something away for yourself — please lay it down, and let God make you that garment of skin.

sections.heading: 3. The Two Systems Cannot Coexist
sections.html:
“Yahweh God said, ‘Behold, the man has become like one of us, knowing good and evil. Now, lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever—’ Therefore Yahweh God sent him out from the garden of Eden, to till the ground from which he was taken. So he drove out the man; and he placed cherubim at the east of the garden of Eden, and a flaming sword which turned every way, to guard the way to the tree of life.” (Genesis 3:22–24)

On the surface, God driving man out of Eden looks like judgement, but hidden inside it is immense mercy — and it also lays down a spiritual principle.

Driven Out So That Sin Would Not Be Fixed for Ever

Notice the reason God gives: “lest he reach out his hand, and also take of the tree of life, and eat, and live forever.” If man, already fallen and already cut off from God, had then eaten from the tree of life, what would have happened? That broken condition would have been frozen in place for ever. That would not have been grace; it would have been eternal punishment.

So God set man apart in order to keep the possibility of redemption open. He placed cherubim and a flaming sword to guard the way to the tree of life. From then on, the road to the tree of life was sealed.

Interestingly, when God later instructed Moses to make the tabernacle, its curtains were to be made “with cherubim … the work of a skillful workman” (Exodus 26:1, 31). That veil embroidered with cherubim hung in front of the Most Holy Place, still declaring the same thing: no one can come before God by his own effort.

Until that day — “Behold, the veil of the temple was torn in two from the top to the bottom.” (Matthew 27:51) Brothers and sisters, at the moment the Lord Jesus breathed his last, the sword that barred the way fell upon him, and the road to the tree of life was opened again.

A Spiritual Principle: You Cannot Eat from Both Trees

From the moment Eden was sealed, God laid down a clear principle: the tree of life and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil cannot both be eaten from.

You cannot depend on God while also depending on yourself. You cannot let Jesus be King while also being your own master. These two systems are completely opposed; there is no middle ground, and no mix-and-match option.

The Lord Jesus said it with absolute finality: “No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24) On Mount Carmel, Elijah put the same question to the people: “How long will you waver between the two sides? If Yahweh is God, follow him; but if Baal, then follow him.” (1 Kings 18:21)

An Everyday Illustration: One Branch Can’t Be Grafted onto Two Trees

Anyone who grafts fruit trees knows one thing: a branch can be grafted onto only one rootstock. You can’t graft one end of a branch onto one tree and the other end onto another and let it draw nourishment from both sides. If you force it, you don’t get a double harvest — the whole branch dies.

This is exactly where many Christians’ weariness comes from. On Sunday they are grafted onto the tree of life; Monday to Saturday they graft themselves back onto the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. When they pray, they hand things over; once they hang up, they take it all back and carry it themselves. It isn’t that they don’t love the Lord; they’re grafted onto the wrong place, the nourishment pulls in two directions, and in the end both sides lose.

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: The White Bear Experiment

In 1987 the psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published the famous “white bear experiment” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. Participants were asked, for five minutes, to try as hard as they could not to think of a white bear, and to ring a bell whenever they did. The group told “don’t think of it” actually rang the bell far more often than the control group — and once the ban was lifted, there was a marked rebound as well.

Wegner called this the “rebound effect of thought suppression.” Brothers and sisters, this is precisely the self-rescue trap of the Worldly system: you try to use the power of “self” to deal with “self,” and “self” only grows louder.

The way out Scripture gives has never been suppression but turning; not hiding the old tree’s fruit, but having your whole person grafted onto the new tree. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

There is only one throne. When Jesus sits on it, I come down; if I stay seated, Jesus can only stand outside the door. This isn’t a matter of feelings; it’s a matter of position. So every day’s devotion is really an exercise in “giving up the seat”: Jesus is the focal point — not myself, not other people, not my circumstances.

sections.heading: 4. “Self” Is Satan’s Best-Hidden Deception
sections.html:
“For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

Many people imagine there’s a third road in life: not God, and not Satan, but “being yourself.” It sounds so neutral, so healthy, so modern. But Scripture tells us that this road simply doesn’t exist.

“Self” is Satan’s best-hidden trap. His greatest cunning isn’t forcing you to worship him; it’s persuading you to worship yourself — because the result is the same: God is not on the throne.

Four Baits

The things Satan uses to lure people come down, again and again, to four: fame, money, status and the gratification of lust.

And the apostle John long ago grouped them into three: the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes and the pride of life. You’ll find that the three temptations the Lord Jesus faced in the wilderness are the very same set: turning stones into bread is the lust of the flesh; seeing the splendour of all the kingdoms is the lust of the eyes; throwing himself down from the pinnacle of the temple for all to see is the pride of life.

All three of the Lord Jesus’ answers begin the same way: “It is written” (Matthew 4:4, 7, 10). Brothers and sisters, this is what “the Bible is my standard” means. When “self” speaks up inside you, the only thing that can overpower it is not your willpower but God’s word.

The Bait’s Sales Pitch: You’re Fulfilling Yourself

All four baits are wrapped in the same sugar coating, so that people feel: I’m “fulfilling myself.”

You work late into the night and say it’s for your family, but really you’re afraid of losing to others. You send that message and say it’s for the sake of the truth, but really you want people to see you standing on the right side. Even ministry can become a way of proving yourself — the more you serve, the more afraid you are to stop, because if you stop, nobody will see you any more.

But in reality, people are bound by “self.” And in the end it brings three things: emptiness, bondage and pain.

Solomon was the man in all the land best qualified to draw the conclusion. He wrote: “Then I looked at all the works that my hands had worked, and at the labor that I had labored to do; and behold, all was vanity and a chasing after wind, and there was no profit under the sun.” (Ecclesiastes 2:11) The man who had everything is telling you: it’s empty in there.

An Everyday Illustration: The Hand That Won’t Let Go

There’s a long-told parable: a monkey hunter fixes a narrow-necked jar to the ground and puts a few peanuts inside. The monkey reaches in, grabs the peanuts, makes a fist — and can’t pull its hand out. If it would only let go, it could escape at any moment; but it won’t, and so what traps it is not the jar but its own clinging.

Brothers and sisters, what binds us is often not our circumstances, but the hand we refuse to open.

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: The Cost of Chasing External Goals

In 1993 the psychologists Tim Kasser and Richard Ryan published a study in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology entitled “A Dark Side of the American Dream.” They found that people who make wealth, fame and appearance the core goals of their lives show significantly higher levels of anxiety and depression and significantly lower well-being, while those whose core goals are personal growth, close relationships and contributing to their community are clearly healthier. This finding has been replicated again and again in cross-cultural studies over the decades since.

Science has gone the long way round to confirm the sentence Augustine wrote in the fourth century AD at the opening of the first book of his Confessions: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.”

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

This is exactly Paul’s testimony: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, laying down “self” doesn’t make you smaller; it connects you to the infinite. When the monkey lets go of the peanuts, what it gains is the whole forest.

sections.heading: 5. Two Choices: Two Endings
sections.html:
“For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)

This verse is the theme verse of this lesson, and it is the final balance sheet of the two systems. Earlier we spoke of where the two trees come from; here we speak of their fruit.

The Worldly System: The Mind of the Flesh Ends in Death

Relying on yourself, living in “self” — the outcome is death.

But this “death” usually isn’t immediate. On the day Adam ate the fruit, his heart did not stop beating. When God said, “in the day that you eat of it, you will surely die” (Genesis 2:17), he meant first of all the spiritual death of being cut off from God. It is something that happens slowly: drifting away from God, losing peace, living in fear.

Scripture captures the process vividly: “They heard Yahweh God’s voice walking in the garden in the cool of the day, and the man and his wife hid themselves from the presence of Yahweh God among the trees of the garden.” (Genesis 3:8) Once, the cool of the day had been the moment they looked forward to most; now the same cool breeze made them tremble.

God called, “Where are you?” Adam answered, “I heard your voice in the garden, and I was afraid, because I was naked; so I hid myself.” (Genesis 3:10) Brothers and sisters, the first symptom of sin is not doing evil; it is hiding. God hadn’t changed; it was man’s way of seeing that had changed.

An Everyday Illustration: A Cut Rose

A rose freshly cut and put in a vase is a vivid red, its fragrance still there; it may look even lovelier than the ones in the garden. But it is already dead — it just hasn’t shown it yet. The moment it was separated from its root, its end was settled; the few days that remain merely play out slowly what has already happened.

A life lived by our own strength is often just like that: on the outside it looks wonderful, but on the inside it has already been cut off from its source.

God’s System: The Mind of the Spirit Brings Life and Peace

Depending on God and obeying the Holy Spirit, the outcome is life and peace — closeness to God, a settled heart, life lived in the light.

Jeremiah paints these two kinds of people as two trees, echoing the two trees of this lesson perfectly: “Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land. Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.’” (Jeremiah 17:5–8)

Notice: both trees meet the heat, and both run into drought. God’s system doesn’t mean having no difficulties; it means having roots. When the heat comes, it doesn’t fear, because its roots aren’t in the weather; its roots are by the water.

Supporting Evidence from Science and Research: The Strongest Predictor

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development, begun in 1938, has followed several hundred men from youth into old age; it is one of the longest-running longitudinal studies in history, and its current director is the psychiatrist Robert Waldinger. Its conclusion is quoted again and again: the strongest predictor of whether a person will be healthy and happy in later life is not wealth, not fame, but the quality of their relationships.

This is exactly the order 321 stresses: life first, then relationships, then ministry; people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The Worldly system frantically piles up things; God’s system invests the heart in relationships — first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
The parting of the two endings is really a parting of viewpoints. 321 says: turn from man’s viewpoint to God’s viewpoint, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

The very same redundancy notice, seen from an earthly viewpoint, is a disaster; seen from a heavenly one, it may be God turning a corner for you. The very same season of waiting, seen from a temporary viewpoint, is a waste; seen from an eternal one, it is putting down roots. “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.” (2 Corinthians 4:16)

sections.heading: 6. Choosing a System Every Day
sections.html:
“I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants.” (Deuteronomy 30:19)

This isn’t a once-for-all choice; it’s a choice made every day.

The Lord Jesus said: “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23) The Chinese Union Version, following the Greek text it translates, has one more word here: take up his cross “daily.” Notice that word — daily. In the original it is καθ' ἡμέραν, day by day. The cross isn’t a decoration hanging on the wall; it is something to be picked up afresh every morning.

Three Questions to Face Every Day

The lesson distils each day’s choices into three questions. Please hold them honestly in your heart right now:

First, today, will I rely on myself, or depend on God?

Second, will I hold on to “self,” or lay myself down?

Third, will I control, or entrust?

Every choice is deciding which system you live in. At the end of his life, Joshua said to the whole assembly: “as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15) That was the conclusion an old man had built up after a lifetime of choosing, day after day.

An Everyday Illustration: A Course One Degree Off

Pilots all know a practical rule of thumb called the “one-in-sixty rule”: for every degree your heading is off, for every sixty nautical miles you fly you’ll drift one nautical mile from your target. One degree is almost invisible on the instruments; but if you fly from Taipei to Los Angeles, that one degree will put you more than a hundred kilometres off course, nowhere near the runway.

The spiritual life is the same. No one leaves God suddenly one day; everyone drifts away one degree at a time: today I’ll just decide this small thing myself, tomorrow I can skip that prayer, the day after I’ll put that prompting to one side. And the reverse is true as well — coming back also happens one degree at a time.

Supporting Evidence from Psychology: New Habits Take Time

Phillippa Lally and her colleagues at University College London published a study in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology showing that forming a new daily habit takes on average about sixty-six days, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days; and that missing the odd day along the way does not ruin the whole process.

Brothers and sisters, this gives us two reminders. First, don’t expect to be completely transformed in a single morning; turning towards the tree of life takes daily practice. Second, falling once doesn’t mean losing everything — just get up, confess, and keep walking. “For a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again.” (Proverbs 24:16)

sections.heading: Applying the 321 Vision
sections.html:
321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Because “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

And each day’s choices bring a fivefold change: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes. What today’s lesson sets out to move is the very first square — the mindset. The mindset is the root; the other four are the branches.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: Putting the Two Trees on the 321 Map
sections.html:
Gather up the six points of this lesson and you’ll see that what 321 teaches is precisely the system of the two trees.

The Three Foundations are the roots of the tree of life: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. The system of the tree of the knowledge of good and evil has three foundations too, only the subject has been switched to “I”: I am my own role model, my feelings are my standard, my judgement is my guide.

The Two Core Values are the trunk of the tree of life: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. In the garden there has only ever been one question — who sits on the throne.

The Goal is the fruit of the tree of life: establish God’s system. Brothers and sisters, that is the very title of this lesson. God has been doing this since Genesis, and he will keep doing it all the way to the city in Revelation where the tree of life stands.

And the key to the change from the old self to the new self lies in one word: “self.” The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. So humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

Selflessness isn’t erasing yourself; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

In relationships, this lesson can be worked out concretely in the 920 practice: every person I’m in relationship with is my “2”; as I practise living out a selfless (0) life before them, the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit will grow — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice, it’s “fruit,” not “product”; fruit can only grow on a tree — it can’t be manufactured by willpower. The way you reacted today to your spouse, to your colleague, to the person you find hardest to get along with, is the lab report on the fruit that shows which tree you’re grafted onto.

One step further is the 235 relationships: find someone else who is also willing to be selfless and become each other’s “2,” spiritual companions; then go on to build the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing it on from generation to generation; and finally become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. It’s hard for one person to stand under the tree of life every day, but a group of people can hold one another up.

And the order of the Path of Serving is here too: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide), Understanding (the Bible is my standard), Life (Jesus is my role model), Service (let Jesus be King), God (let Jesus receive all the glory). Life first, then relationships, then ministry — not a single step can be reversed.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Walking Three Exercises Through the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives three exercises. Let’s walk through them thoroughly using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Exercise 1: Identify the Source System of My Reactions

In every reaction, ask yourself: is this coming from me, or from God?

Information: today you have received this lesson’s information — there are only two systems in the world, and every reaction of yours has a source. Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to carry this truth from your head into your heart, and to shine his light on the one scene where “coming from me” shows up most often. Conviction: stop making excuses, and admit that this really is fruit from the tree of the knowledge of good and evil. Implementation: today, choose three moments (for example 10 a.m., after lunch and before bed), stop for thirty seconds, and ask yourself this question. Evaluation: in the evening, note down how many times today your reactions came from yourself. Correction: confess one of those times specifically, and think through how you will respond next time. Repetition: keep it up for seven days in a row. Multiplication: share this exercise with a “2” and invite them to do it with you.

Exercise 2: Deliberately Turn Towards the Tree of Life

When you want to rely on yourself, pray at once, choose to depend on God, and return to God’s system.

Information: turning isn’t a feeling; it’s an action. Revelation: let the Holy Spirit remind you that the moment the thought “I’ll just do it myself” appears, that’s the alarm bell. Conviction: admit that I have no power to save myself. Implementation: prepare a short prayer, such as “Lord, I hand this over to you — please reign as King,” and the moment the thought arises, pray it out loud. Evaluation: after a week, look back — which times did you manage to turn, and which times not? Correction: identify the times of day or the people where you most easily give ground, and prepare ahead. Repetition: let this short prayer become a reflex. Multiplication: write your short prayer down and give it to a brother or sister who is going through anxiety.

Exercise 3: Refuse the Deception of “Self”

When “I must be in control” or “I must prove myself” rises up within you, be on your guard at once and turn to Jesus.

Information: “I must be in control” and “I must prove myself” are the two lines “self” uses most often. Revelation: ask God to let you hear these two lines at the very moment they sound within you. Conviction: admit that this is Satan’s trap, not just my personality. Implementation: declare on the spot, “I don’t need to prove myself; in Christ I am already accepted,” and break its hold with one concrete action — delete the message you were about to send, hand that task to someone else, or be the first to say, “I was wrong.” Evaluation: which bait works best on you — fame, money, status, or the gratification of lust? Correction: set a concrete boundary against that one. Repetition: every morning, hand over your sovereignty first; don’t wait until you’ve lost control to pray. Multiplication: open up about your weakness to a spiritual companion, and ask them to keep watch for you in prayer.

A Gentle Reminder

The problem isn’t the situation; it’s which system you are responding from.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the key to life isn’t how much you’ve done, but — which tree you are living under.

Some people do a great deal in their lifetime, but they do it under the tree of the knowledge of good and evil, and the fruit is fear, shame and exhaustion. Others look quite ordinary, yet they are trees planted by the waters, never ceasing to bear fruit in the year of drought. This morning God isn’t asking you to become a better person first; he is simply inviting you to change trees. When you choose the tree of life, you choose life; when you choose Jesus, you step onto the true road of revival.

So let us together hand the throne back to him. Not I as King, but let Jesus be King; not glory for me, but let Jesus receive all the glory.

“Oh taste and see that Yahweh is good. Blessed is the man who takes refuge in him.” (Psalm 34:8)

keyVerses: “For the mind of the flesh is death, but the mind of the Spirit is life and peace.” (Romans 8:6)

“Out of the ground Yahweh God made every tree to grow that is pleasant to the sight, and good for food, including the tree of life in the middle of the garden and the tree of the knowledge of good and evil.” (Genesis 2:9)
declarations: Lord, I choose the tree of life! I will no longer live in the system of the knowledge of good and evil. I don’t want to be my own master — I want to let Jesus be King, so that I live in life and peace!
practices: Identify the source system of my reactions
Deliberately turn towards the tree of life
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we are quiet before you. Thank you for setting two trees in the middle of the garden and giving us the freedom to choose; and thank you even more that, after we chose wrongly, you still prepared garments of skin for us and gave up your only beloved Son for us.

Lord, forgive us for so often praying while being our own masters, for saying we entrust things to you while gripping them tightly. Today we are willing to let go. Holy Spirit, shine your light on every reaction of ours that comes from ourselves, and give us courage to take off the fig-leaf skirts we have sewn for ourselves.

Let our roots go down by the waters, let our minds be set on the Spirit, and in every choice we make today, let us choose the tree of life. Let Jesus reign as King in our homes, reign as King in our work, reign as King in our thoughts and intentions. May all the glory go to Jesus. In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Looking back over the past week, what is one thing you solved “your own way”? How did it turn out? If you could do it again, what would doing it in dependence on God look like? “Their eyes were opened, and they both knew that they were naked. They sewed fig leaves together, and made coverings for themselves.” (Genesis 3:7)

Of the four baits — fame, money, status and the gratification of lust — which one attracts you most? What concrete boundary do you plan to set? “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)
l104.title: Two Trees, Two Systems
l104.subtitle: A Change of Choices (Part 2)
l104.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: It Isn’t Ability That Decides Your Life, but Whom You Choose to Depend On
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. This morning I’d like to start with a question: if you spread out every difficulty of your whole life and looked at them all, what is it that really decides how things end?

Many people’s first answer is “ability”: if I were a bit cleverer, a bit more gifted, my life would be different. The second answer is “circumstances”: if I’d been born into another family, or had a different boss, my fate would be different. The third answer is “luck”: if only the traffic hadn’t been jammed that day, everything would have turned out differently.

But brothers and sisters, from Genesis to Revelation the Bible keeps repeating one simple yet crucial principle: whichever system a person lives in, that is the kind of outcome he lives out.

It isn’t ability that decides your life — Solomon had wisdom, wealth and a kingdom at peace, yet in his old age his heart turned away from God and the nation was torn apart. It isn’t circumstances that decide the outcome — Joseph was sold, falsely accused and thrown into prison, yet in an Egyptian jail he lived out blessing. It isn’t luck that decides your destiny — the word “God” does not appear even once in the whole book of Esther, yet behind every “coincidence” the hidden God is on the throne.

Then what does decide it? “Whom you choose to depend on.”

The same desk lamp shines when it’s plugged into a live socket; unplug it and set it on the most beautiful desk, and it is still dark. The problem has never been the quality of the bulb, but which power source it’s connected to. We often polish the bulb furiously, buy a more expensive lampshade, and forget to ask the most important question of all: what power source am I actually plugged into?

The Bible uses a deeper word to describe these two power sources: “two systems.” At the heart of God’s system is “God as King,” and it runs on “depending on God”; at the heart of the Worldly system is “me as king,” and it runs on “depending on myself.” These aren’t two styles but two tracks running in opposite directions; not two options but two endings.

When people return to God’s system, they enter blessing; when people leave God’s system, they enter the curse. This isn’t a scare tactic; it’s a law, like gravity — it doesn’t stop working on you just because you don’t believe in it.

Today’s lesson is the third in the series “A Change in Our Choices.” In the first two lessons we saw that behind our choices lies our mindset, and behind our mindset lies the self-centred old self within. Today we pull the camera back: history has already run the experiment for us. God has let generation after generation walk both systems through before our eyes, and the results are written in black and white in Scripture. What we need to do today is not take the risk one more time, but return to the road that has already been proven.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Last Lesson on the Plains of Moab
sections.html:
To understand the “two systems,” we first need to understand the setting in which our theme verse was spoken.

The author of Deuteronomy is Moses. The book is made up of three sermons he preached to a new generation of Israelites in the last days of his life. The time is around 1406 BC; the place is the plains of Moab, on the east bank of the Jordan, looking across to the land of Canaan.

Pay special attention to who was standing in front of Moses. The generation that came out of Egypt had already fallen dead in the wilderness; before him stood their children — a generation that had not seen the ten plagues with their own eyes, had not walked through the Red Sea themselves; what they had seen was their parents wandering for forty years. Moses knew he would not cross the Jordan; this was the last time he would preach. What does a man preach in his last sermon? Surely the thing he considers most important of all.

And the most important thing Moses preached was “choice.”

In its form, Deuteronomy closely resembles the “suzerain–vassal treaties” of the ancient Near East. These covenants had a fixed structure, and one of its elements was blessings and curses. Deuteronomy chapters 27 and 28 are exactly that part; and in chapter 30 Moses gathers the whole covenant up into one sentence and sets it before them: life and death, blessing and curse — you must choose.

“I call heaven and earth to witness against you today” — an ancient covenant needed witnesses, and Moses could find no witnesses more enduring than heaven and earth, so he called on them: this is no small matter; heaven and earth must keep the record.

“I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse” — “set before you” means laid out, spread open in front of your eyes, nothing hidden, nothing blurred. God never plays guessing games. He draws the map of both roads clearly — the route, the road conditions, the destination — and then says: look for yourself.

“Therefore choose life” — the Hebrew for “choose” is bachar (בָּחַר). It doesn’t mean grabbing something at random; it means a decisive choice made after examining and comparing. God doesn’t want us to shut our eyes and take a gamble; he wants us to open our eyes, see clearly, and then choose.

“To love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him” — notice these three verbs: love, obey, cling. These are exactly the three ways God’s system operates. Love is relationship; obeying is submission; clinging is dependence. And the opposite of these three verbs is how the Worldly system operates: love yourself, listen to yourself, rely on yourself.

“For he is your life” — Moses didn’t say “he gives you life”; he said “he is your life.” In God’s system, God is not one item in your life, not one slot in your calendar; God is life itself. Leaving him isn’t losing one thing; it’s losing the very source of life.

There’s another detail that’s often overlooked: the “you” here is singular in Hebrew. Moses stood before hundreds of thousands of people, yet he used the singular to say to each one: you must choose. Brothers and sisters, no one can choose for you — this is a decision you make standing alone before God.

Next, let’s walk through the history of Scripture and see how God has confirmed this spiritual law through one real life after another.

sections.heading: 3. The Witness of History: Return to God and Be Blessed
sections.html:
The history in Scripture isn’t just stories; it is spiritual law. When we read the biographies of Bible characters, if all we take away is “how wonderful he was,” we gain only inspiration; when we see “why he was blessed,” we gain a road to walk.

(1) Noah’s Choice: Plugging into God’s System in a Corrupt Generation

The generation Noah lived in is one of the darkest the Bible describes.

“Yahweh saw that the wickedness of man was great in the earth, and that every imagination of the thoughts of man’s heart was continually only evil.” (Genesis 6:5)

The Bible doesn’t say evil “some of the time,” but “continually”; it doesn’t say “partly” evil, but “only evil.” This was a generation completely occupied by the Worldly system. In such a generation, could a person still live in God’s system? Noah gives us the answer.

“Thus Noah did. He did all that God commanded him.” (Genesis 6:22)

God told him to build a huge ship on dry land with no sea in sight. He built it for many years, enduring ridicule every day — and Scripture’s verdict on his whole life is just this one sentence. And the outcome?

“Yahweh said to Noah, ‘Come with all of your household into the ship, for I have seen your righteousness before me in this generation.’” (Genesis 7:1)

“God blessed Noah and his sons, and said to them, ‘Be fruitful, multiply, and replenish the earth.’” (Genesis 9:1)

First, he was saved in the midst of judgement; second, he received blessing. And the content of that blessing is exactly what God had said to Adam at the beginning (Genesis 1:28). As soon as Noah returned to God’s system, God handed the original blessing back to the human race.

The New Testament gives us the best commentary, Scripture interpreting Scripture:

“By faith, Noah, being warned about things not yet seen, moved with godly fear, prepared a ship for the saving of his house.” (Hebrews 11:7)

The key is “things not yet seen.” When Noah started work, there wasn’t a single dark cloud in the sky; what he depended on was not data his eyes could see, but what God had said. The Worldly system says, “I’ll believe it when I see it”; God’s system says, “God has said it, so I believe it.”

In 2013, Nathan Putman and his colleagues at Oregon State University published a study in the journal Current Biology showing that sockeye salmon can find the river mouth of home across thousands of kilometres of ocean by remembering the magnetic signature of the place where they were born. The salmon has no map; it simply responds to the sense of direction placed inside it when it was made. Augustine put it well in his Confessions: you made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. Noah wasn’t stronger than everyone else; he simply swam back along the way home.

From a 321 point of view, Noah lived out the most solid of the Three Foundations: the Bible is my standard. As soon as God’s word came, he didn’t debate it or discount it; there was only one action — he did it. Today we need to ask ourselves: when God’s word clashes with my own ideas, which is the standard? If God’s word only counts once it has passed my inspection, then the standard is really me, not the Bible.

(2) Abraham’s Choice: Leaving the Old System, Entering the New

If Noah represents “standing firm in the midst of corruption,” Abraham represents “walking out of the old system.”

“Now Yahweh said to Abram, ‘Leave your country, and your relatives, and your father’s house, and go to the land that I will show you.’” (Genesis 12:1)

Your country is culture, your relatives are your network, your father’s house is your security; moving from the outside in, each layer is harder to cut loose than the last. God’s call is for a person to detach, layer by layer, from what the old system supplies, and to be connected to God instead.

“By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went.” (Hebrews 11:8)

“Not knowing where he went” — this is the hardest and also the most precious thing about God’s system. The Worldly system insists on seeing the whole route clearly before it will move; God’s system takes the first step first, and the light shines before its feet one step at a time.

Abraham didn’t learn this all at once. He went down to Egypt in a famine; to save his own skin he said Sarah was his sister. He fell, he strayed — but each time he came back into God’s system. By the time he reached Mount Moriah, God’s response was the greatest oath in the Old Testament:

“‘I have sworn by myself,’ says Yahweh, ‘because you have done this thing, and have not withheld your son, your only son, that I will bless you greatly, and I will multiply your offspring greatly like the stars of the heavens, and like the sand which is on the seashore. Your offspring will possess the gate of his enemies. All the nations of the earth will be blessed by your offspring, because you have obeyed my voice.’” (Genesis 22:16–18)

There is no one greater than God by whom he could swear, so he swore by himself; this is the highest guarantee God can give. And what triggered that guarantee was not Abraham’s talent or success, but just one phrase: “because you have obeyed my voice.”

“He believed in Yahweh, who credited it to him for righteousness.” (Genesis 15:6)

The Hebrew for “bless,” barak (בָּרַךְ), shares a root with “knee” (berek), and carries the image of kneeling. In Hebrew, blessing and kneeling belong to the same family. This expresses a truth: we receive blessing in a kneeling posture. A hand held standing up is a clenched fist; only a kneeling hand is open.

In 1966 the American psychologist Julian Rotter put forward the theory of “locus of control”: people with an internal locus believe outcomes are mainly determined by their own actions, while those with an external locus believe outcomes are decided by luck or fate; research shows that people with an internal locus are generally more proactive and more resilient than those with an external one. Brothers and sisters, handing your life over to luck is the most passive thing of all; but the Bible gives us a third way — hand your sovereignty over to the true and living God who loves us to the end. This isn’t an external locus, because he isn’t blind fate; nor is it an internal one, because I am no longer the centre. This is what it means to “let Jesus be King.”

Abraham’s lesson corresponds exactly to what 321 calls “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” God didn’t give him a ministry plan first; God gave him an altar first. The problem with many weary servants today isn’t a lack of gifts but a reversed order — they run the ministry first and patch up their life afterwards; and once the order is reversed, a person slides into the Worldly system without even noticing.

Brothers and sisters, these people weren’t especially impressive; they made one crucial choice — to return to God’s system. Noah was a farmer, not a shipbuilder; Abraham was a herdsman, not a military strategist. God has never been looking for impressive people; God is looking for people who are willing to come back.

sections.heading: 4. Israel’s Cycle: The Two Systems Side by Side
sections.html:
If Noah and Abraham are personal testimonies, Israel is a controlled experiment on a national scale: God uses the history of an entire people to plot the results of the two systems on the same chart.

(1) Deuteronomy 28: The List of Blessings and Curses

Through Moses, God told the Israelites plainly: obey God and you will be blessed; disobey and you will be cursed.

“It shall happen, if you shall listen diligently to Yahweh your God’s voice, to observe to do all his commandments which I command you today, that Yahweh your God will set you high above all the nations of the earth.” (Deuteronomy 28:1)

“All these blessings will come upon you, and overtake you, if you listen to Yahweh your God’s voice.” (Deuteronomy 28:2)

“But it shall come to pass, if you will not listen to Yahweh your God’s voice, to observe to do all his commandments and his statutes which I command you today, that all these curses will come on you and overtake you.” (Deuteronomy 28:15)

Notice that both sides use the same verbs: “come on you and overtake you.” Blessing chases after people, and so does the curse; we aren’t choosing between “an outcome or no outcome,” but between “which outcome will catch up with me.”

This isn’t God’s mood; it’s a spiritual law. Fire burns your hand, not because fire hates you. God made the universe this way: life can only come from the source of life, and whatever leaves the source naturally withers.

The Hebrew for “curse,” qelalah (קְלָלָה), comes from the root qalal, which originally means “to make light of, to regard as trivial”; while the Hebrew for “glory,” kabod (כָּבוֹד), originally means “heaviness.” Brothers and sisters, treat God as weighty, and your life will have weight; treat God lightly, and your life will be as light as chaff.

Jeremiah describes these two systems with great vividness:

“Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.’” (Jeremiah 17:5)

“Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.” (Jeremiah 17:7–8)

God hasn’t promised that his people will never meet heat and drought. Both trees face the drought; the only difference is where the roots go down. The Worldly system puts its roots down in circumstances, and when circumstances change, people wither; God’s system puts its roots down by the river, and however much circumstances change, the supply never stops.

(2) The Cycle of Judges: Departure, Oppression, Crying Out, Deliverance

The period of the judges covers roughly 1375 to 1050 BC. The book of Judges has a cycle that turns like a wheel: leave God and be oppressed; cry out to God and be delivered; the judge dies, and they turn back to evil again.

“Yahweh raised up judges, who saved them out of the hand of those who plundered them.” (Judges 2:16)

“But when the judge was dead, they turned back, and dealt more corruptly than their fathers in following other gods to serve them and to bow down to them. They didn’t cease what they were doing, or give up their stubborn ways.” (Judges 2:19)

This cycle went round more than seven times, and the conclusion of the whole book is a heartbreaking sentence:

“In those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes.” (Judges 21:25)

Listen carefully to the logic: there was no king, so everyone did what was right in his own eyes. This is the very essence of the Worldly system — not that there is no God, but that God is not allowed to be King; not that people don’t believe in God, but that they sit on the throne themselves.

This shows something extremely important: the problem isn’t the enemy; it’s the system. Every time the Israelites were oppressed, they fixed their focus on the Midianites or the Philistines, thinking that defeating them would set them free. But God’s diagnosis was different: the enemy was only the symptom; leaving God was the disease. Drive out the Midianites without changing the system, and twenty years later the Philistines will come.

This is exactly what 321 says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. How many of our prayers are really asking God to adjust our circumstances or change other people? We ask God to drive out the Midianites, but God wants us to come back to him.

In experiments in 1967, the psychologists Martin Seligman and Steven Maier described “learned helplessness”: after animals repeatedly experience electric shocks they cannot escape, they no longer try even when they later have the chance to get away. The Israelites in Judges were like a case of spiritual learned helplessness — oppressed for so long that they assumed this was simply their fate.

Brothers and sisters, if someone here has been going round in the same weakness for many years and feels, “I suppose this is just how I am,” I want to tell you: the door isn’t locked. The sentence repeated most often in Judges is “the children of Israel cried to Yahweh,” and not once did God turn a deaf ear. Even the time he said, “I will save you no more” (Judges 10:13), when they put away their foreign gods and served him again, “his soul was grieved for the misery of Israel” (Judges 10:16).

sections.heading: 5. Even in Hardship, You Can Still Live in God’s System
sections.html:
Someone might say: those were all spiritual giants; I go to work in an environment that has nothing to do with God, my family don’t believe in the Lord, I even have to hide to pray. Can someone like me still live in God’s system?

The story of Esther was written precisely for people like that.

Esther was a descendant of the exiled Jews. King Ahasuerus in the book is generally identified with the historical Xerxes I, who reigned from 486 to 465 BC. She was an orphan, brought up by her cousin Mordecai; in a foreign palace her identity had to be hidden and her faith could not be made public. The word “God” does not appear anywhere in the whole book. On the surface, this is the setting furthest from God — and yet it is right here that God’s hand is clearest.

“For if you remain silent now, then relief and deliverance will come to the Jews from another place, but you and your father’s house will perish. Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14)

There are two core mindsets in Mordecai’s words. First, God’s plan doesn’t depend on me — this cures pride. Second, my position is for God’s time — this cures self-pity. My job, my connections, my situation are not for my own sake.

Then comes Esther’s response:

“Go, gather together all the Jews who are present in Susa, and fast for me, and neither eat nor drink three days, night or day. I and my maidens will also fast the same way. Then I will go in to the king, which is against the law; and if I perish, I perish.” (Esther 4:16)

“If I perish, I perish” — these four words are the turning point of the whole book of Esther. This isn’t passive resignation but active entrusting: I no longer treat my life as something that must be preserved; I place my life in God’s hands.

This is exactly what 321 calls “selflessness.” Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite. Had she saved herself, she would have saved only one person; when she laid herself down, God used her to save a whole nation.

Notice her order: fast first, then go in. The Worldly system says, do everything humanly possible first and leave the rest to God; God’s system says, go before God first, and then act boldly. Those three days weren’t a delay; those three days were where the battle was won.

In 2002, research by the American psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues showed that more than forty per cent of people’s daily behaviour is habit repeated in the same settings, not a deliberate decision made in the moment. Most of our “choices” are really the automatic replay of past choices. So the real choice is mostly not made at the moment of crisis; the crisis merely reveals the choice you had already made.

So even in a foreign land, even in a crisis, you can still choose God’s system. Your environment may not belong to God, but your heart can. A system isn’t a geographical location; a system is whom you depend on.

sections.heading: 6. Jesus’ Example: Living Fully in God’s System
sections.html:
All the people we’ve looked at so far were imperfect: Noah got drunk after leaving the ark, Abraham told lies, the Israelites fell again and again. Only one lived entirely in God’s system from birth to death, without straying a single step — our Lord Jesus Christ.

(1) The Son Can Do Nothing of Himself

“Jesus therefore answered them, ‘Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.’” (John 5:19)

Who is saying this? The one who created heaven and earth, the one who raises the dead. He has the power, and yet he says: I can do nothing of myself.

“Of himself” in Greek is ap’ heautou (ἀφ' ἑαυτοῦ), literally “out from himself.” What Jesus means is: I don’t act out of myself; all my actions come out of the Father.

This is selflessness at its fullest. Jesus’ selflessness wasn’t a lack of power — he had complete divinity and power. Selflessness is this: I have it, but I don’t act of myself. Selflessness isn’t turning yourself into a zero; it’s placing that zero after God, and so entering into the infinite.

This also lets us see the root of humanity’s fall. What did the serpent say in the garden of Eden?

“For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5)

“You will be like God” — this was the birth of the self-centred life, the first day of the Worldly system. Satan didn’t tell people to worship idols; he simply invited them to sit on the throne themselves. From that moment the human race switched systems: no longer depending on God, but on its own judgement.

Jesus walked the opposite road. What the second Adam did was exactly what the first Adam refused: return to his originally intended position, and let God be God.

(2) Not What I Desire, but What You Desire

The touchstone of God’s system isn’t found in the good times, but in the garden of Gethsemane.

“He went forward a little, fell on his face, and prayed, saying, ‘My Father, if it is possible, let this cup pass away from me; nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.’” (Matthew 26:39)

Notice that Jesus didn’t pretend. He said honestly: let this cup pass away from me. God’s system isn’t about suppressing your emotions and pretending to be strong; true obedience carries a real struggle and still says that one sentence: nevertheless, not what I desire.

That one word, “nevertheless,” is the most powerful turning point in the whole universe. Before that “nevertheless” lay human fear; after that “nevertheless” came the salvation of all humanity.

The Greek word for obey, hupakouō (ὑπακούω), is made up of hupo (under) and akouō (to hear); literally it means “to listen from underneath.” The Worldly system puts itself on top and speaks; God’s system puts itself underneath and listens.

Paul wrote this road of the Lord’s into one of the church’s earliest hymns:

“And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name.” (Philippians 2:8–9)

Look at those words: “Therefore God.” He went down to the very lowest, therefore God raised him to the very highest. The Worldly system says, “I will go up,” and ends up thrown down; God’s system says, “I am willing to come down,” and ends up raised up by God. This is exactly what 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan; pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

This one choice of Jesus brought salvation and eternal life to all humanity. Brothers and sisters, the greatest blessing in human history began with one sentence: “not what I desire.”

In 2001, the French researcher Henri Weimerskirch and his colleagues published a study in the journal Nature showing that when great white pelicans fly in a V formation, their heart rates are markedly lower than when they fly alone. They aren’t working harder; they have entered a system where each borrows strength from the others. People who live in God’s system are the same: very often they aren’t working harder — they are carrying a lighter load.

sections.heading: 7. The Lives of the Apostles: Bringing Out God’s Power
sections.html:
After the Lord ascended, this road did not come to an end. The apostles of the early church lived in God’s system in the same way, and carried that system into the whole Roman world.

“But Peter and the apostles answered, ‘We must obey God rather than men.’” (Acts 5:29)

The background to these words is that the Jewish council had strictly forbidden them to teach in the name of Jesus; the council held religious and social authority, and crossing them came at a high price.

The Greek word for “obey” here, peitharcheō (πειθαρχέω), is made up of peithō (to be persuaded) and archē (ruler), meaning “to obey the one in authority because you are persuaded.” True obedience comes from conviction, not from pressure. The apostles weren’t gritting their teeth and holding on; in their hearts they were truly persuaded by the Lord who reigns, and so human threats carried no weight.

Notice the order too: Scripture teaches us to submit to those in authority, but when a human command directly conflicts with God’s command, God comes first. God’s system isn’t anarchy; it has order — and God is at the very top.

What marked these apostles?

First, they didn’t rely on their own cleverness.

“Now when they saw the boldness of Peter and John, and had perceived that they were unlearned and ignorant men, they marveled. They recognized that they had been with Jesus.” (Acts 4:13)

In the Worldly system, “unlearned and ignorant men” is a fatal flaw on a CV. Yet what amazed people wasn’t their learning but their boldness, and “they recognized that they had been with Jesus.” When people live in God’s system, what others see isn’t their credentials, but whom they have been with.

Second, they didn’t rely on human methods: they didn’t curry favour with the council, didn’t cultivate political connections, didn’t adjust the message to suit the market.

Third, they depended on the Holy Spirit alone.

“But you will receive power when the Holy Spirit has come upon you. You will be witnesses to me in Jerusalem, in all Judea and Samaria, and to the uttermost parts of the earth.” (Acts 1:8)

Before he ascended, the Lord didn’t give them a strategy; he gave them a promise: wait for the Holy Spirit. This is exactly the third of 321’s foundations: the Holy Spirit is my guide.

And the result? The gospel spread far and wide, lives were turned around, and even their opponents said:

“These who have turned the world upside down have come here also.” (Acts 17:6)

This was originally an accusation against Paul in Thessalonica, but it became the highest praise of the early church. A group of unlearned, ordinary people, with no army and no funds, shook their generation. Why? Because they weren’t straining within their own system; they were plugged into the source of power. However good a vacuum cleaner’s motor is, pull the plug and it stops dead; some ministry is full of effort yet bears no fruit — not because the machine is bad, but because the power isn’t connected.

The Lord himself put it most clearly:

“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The Greek for “remain,” menō (μένω), carries the sense of settling down, living somewhere for good, not visiting now and then. God’s system isn’t a Sunday visitor’s status; it’s an everyday resident’s status.

sections.heading: 8. Key Summary: The System Decides the Outcome
sections.html:
From the whole of Scripture we see one clear conclusion: return to God’s system, and you enter life, blessing and victory; live in the Worldly system, and you enter chaos, pain and destruction.

The Lord Jesus said this very directly:

“No one can serve two masters, for either he will hate the one and love the other; or else he will be devoted to one and despise the other. You can’t serve both God and Mammon.” (Matthew 6:24)

The Lord didn’t say “shouldn’t”; he said “can’t.” This isn’t moral exhortation; it’s a statement of fact: the two systems cannot coexist, just as one plug can’t be plugged into two power sockets at once.

John also draws a clear line between the two systems:

“For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s. The world is passing away with its lusts, but he who does God’s will remains forever.” (1 John 2:16–17)

The Greek word for “world” here is kosmos (κόσμος). It doesn’t mean the planet or the human race, but the system that turns its back on God and runs by itself.

So the question isn’t “have you believed in the Lord?” but “are you living in God’s system?”

Brothers and sisters, that is a weighty statement, but it is an honest one. A person can have made a decision for Christ, been baptised and attended every Sunday, and yet in every real decision still depend on himself. That kind of faith is like someone who has bought a plane ticket and got a boarding pass, but stays sitting in the departure lounge — the ticket is real, but he never gets on the plane.

The Lord Jesus told a very famous parable:

“Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock.” (Matthew 7:24–25)

Both houses went through the rain, the floods and the wind. God hasn’t promised that his people will never meet storms; what God has promised is that the house will not fall. The difference between the two systems isn’t the weather but the foundation.

From a 321 point of view, this is exactly the “shift of viewpoint”: turn from man’s viewpoint to God’s viewpoint, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly.

“While we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal.” (2 Corinthians 4:18)

In his 2011 book “Thinking, Fast and Slow,” the psychologist Daniel Kahneman distinguishes two kinds of thinking: System 1 is fast, intuitive and automatic; System 2 is slow, effortful and requires deliberate attention. Most of our everyday reactions belong to System 1. This explains why “switching systems” is so hard — the old reactions are automatic. The spiritual battle is often not fought over big things but in that half-second of automatic reaction. So what we need isn’t more resolve, but a renewed mindset.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

The original word for “be conformed” carries the sense of “being pressed into the same mould as ….” The Worldly system is like a mould, pressing us into shape every day; but God’s word and the Holy Spirit renew us from the inside. If you are not actively being renewed, you will automatically be shaped.

sections.heading: 9. Us Today: The Same Choice
sections.html:
Someone may feel: these things all happened thousands of years ago. No, brothers and sisters — what we face today is exactly what the Israelites faced on the plains of Moab. Their three questions are our questions this morning too:

Will I obey God? Will I depend on God? Will I let Jesus be King?

These three questions aren’t asked once in a lifetime; they are asked every day, in every matter.

When the alarm goes off in the morning, do you reach for your phone first, or your Bible? That’s a choice.

When a colleague shifts the blame onto you, do you hit back at once to protect yourself, or do you first come back before God? That’s a choice.

Late at night, when all is quiet and no one can see, with the phone screen glowing, do you follow the lust of the eyes, or follow the Holy Spirit? That’s a choice.

Brothers and sisters, life isn’t made up of a few major decisions; it is built up from tens of thousands of tiny choices. At the end of his life Joshua said to the people:

“If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15)

Notice that word, “today.” Moses said “today,” and Joshua said “today.” God’s choice is never scheduled for tomorrow. Tomorrow is another name for putting things off; today is the tense of faith.

In his 2019 book “Tiny Habits,” B. J. Fogg of the Behavior Design Lab at Stanford University argues that lasting change doesn’t come from great willpower but from shrinking a behaviour down to something tiny and attaching it to a behaviour that already exists. This fits perfectly with the biblical principle of “being faithful in little things.” We don’t need to decide this morning never to be weak again for the rest of our lives; we only need to return to God in the very first choice.

“Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

321 puts it well: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. What we need to tend this morning isn’t those hundred things, but that one heart.

sections.heading: 10. Integrating the 321 Vision: What God’s System Looks Like
sections.html:
What exactly does God’s system look like? The 321 vision draws it as a single picture.

(1) The Three Foundations: The Groundwork of the System

Jesus is my role model — so I don’t act of myself, just as he said, “the Son can do nothing of himself” (John 5:19).

The Bible is my standard — so when God speaks, I act, like Noah, who “did all that God commanded him” (Genesis 6:22).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — so I don’t rely on my own cleverness, like the apostles waiting for the Holy Spirit to come (Acts 1:8).

These Three Foundations are a portrait of the three groups of people in this lesson: Noah and Abraham are the testimony of taking the Bible as the standard, Jesus is the role model himself, and the apostles are the fruit of the Holy Spirit’s guidance. The Three Foundations aren’t slogans; they are the three piles driven under the system.

(2) The Two Core Values: Let Jesus Be King, Let Jesus Receive All the Glory

The tragedy of Judges is that “in those days there was no king in Israel. Everyone did that which was right in his own eyes” (Judges 21:25); the ending of Revelation is that “the kingdom of the world has become the Kingdom of our Lord, and of his Christ. He will reign forever and ever!” (Revelation 11:15) From no king to his reign — that is the direction of the whole Bible.

“Let Jesus be King” isn’t a line from a worship song; it’s a concrete change of position: I step down from the throne and let him go up. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

“Let Jesus receive all the glory” is the destination. Esther saved a nation, but the glory wasn’t hers; the apostles shook a generation, but the glory wasn’t theirs. God’s system bears one mark: the work is done, the people disappear, and only the Lord is seen.

(3) The Goal: Establish God’s System

The title of this lesson is precisely 321’s Goal. God wants to establish on earth a system that runs according to his heart — what the Lord’s Prayer calls:

“Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

How does heaven run? In heaven no creature competes for the throne; there is only one who sits on it. If earth runs the same way, it becomes an extension of the kingdom of heaven.

(4) The Old Self Is Self-Centred; the New Self Is Selfless

From beginning to end, this lesson is really about just one thing: the self-centred life and selflessness.

The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall. The serpent said, “you will be like God” (Genesis 3:5), and from then on man has been his own master. Pride is the root of the problem, because pride is moving God’s seat over for yourself to sit in.

Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Esther said, “if I perish, I perish”; the Lord Jesus said, “not what I desire”; the apostles said, “we must obey God rather than men” — the structure is the same every time: put the “I” down, lift “him” up, and God’s power is revealed.

Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Satan cannot defeat a person who “isn’t preoccupied with himself,” because every one of his hooks hangs on the human self.

“Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) Notice the order: first submit to God, and only then can you resist the devil.

(5) The Fivefold Change and Its Order

321 speaks of mindset, life, daily living, relationships and ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

The mindset this lesson sets out to change is this: it isn’t ability that decides your life, and it isn’t circumstances that decide the outcome; it is whom you depend on that decides the ending. Once the mindset changes, the life changes; once the life changes, the choices change; once the choices change, relationships change; and when relationships change, ministry naturally bears fruit.

Nor can the order be reversed: life first, then relationships, then ministry; and the priority of relationships is first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things.

Harvard’s Study of Adult Development has, since 1938, followed several hundred participants through their whole lives. Its director, Robert Waldinger, points out that the clearest finding of the study is that good relationships predict a person’s health and happiness better than wealth and fame do. This confirms the order Scripture sets out.

(6) The 920 Practice and the 235 Relationships

This lesson lends itself especially well to the 920 practice: every person we’re in relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out a selfless (0) life before them, the nine (9) graces of the fruit of the Spirit will grow.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23)

Scripture speaks of “fruit,” not “product.” Fruit isn’t manufactured; it grows. It doesn’t depend on my straining, but on the branch staying joined to the tree. This is a question of system, not of effort.
