Practise 235 at the same time: become a “2,” spiritual companions, with someone who is selfless; build the “3” relationship of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and go on to become the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Esther didn’t step forward alone; behind her stood Mordecai and the Jews of the whole city fasting. God’s system isn’t a lone fight; it is a body joined together.

sections.heading: 11. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three exercises. Let’s take them one at a time and deepen them using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Exercise 1: In Decisions, Choose God’s Will

When you face a choice, don’t ask first, “Which option benefits me?” but “What is God’s will?”

Information: first understand that there are two systems, and copy out the theme verse somewhere you’ll see it every day.

Revelation: ask God to show you, in one concrete matter, that you have actually been making decisions by yourself all along.

Conviction: admit that God’s will is more reliable than my own interests. “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” (Proverbs 3:5–6)

Implementation: for anything that takes more than three minutes’ thought to decide, stop first and ask: Lord, what is your will?

Evaluation: in the evening, take three minutes to look back — how many decisions today did I ask God about, and how many did I just charge into on my own?

Correction: identify the times of day when you’re most likely to leave God out, and set a reminder ahead of time.

Repetition: practise for twenty-one days in a row. Once doesn’t count as practice; only repetition does.

Multiplication: teach this exercise to your “2,” and do it together.

Watch out for one trap: turning “seeking God’s will” into an excuse for procrastination. God’s guidance usually comes through his word, inner peace, confirming circumstances and spiritual companions; seek what is clear first, then wait for what is not yet clear.

Exercise 2: In Hardship, Return to God

When the pressure of circumstances comes, don’t rely on yourself to solve it; first come back before God and seek him.

Information: when pressure comes, a person’s first reaction is instinct, not faith.

Revelation: ask God to show you your “default escape hatch”: losing your temper, scrolling your phone, working yourself into the ground, or withdrawing into silence.

Conviction: coming back to God first doesn’t waste time; it saves time. Esther fasted for three days first, and only then went in to see the king.

Implementation: set yourself a “ninety-second rule” — the moment pressure hits, don’t reply to messages, don’t make decisions, don’t speak; quietly call on the Lord’s name.

Evaluation: this week, how many times did I truly come back to God first? How many times did I rush back to my old escape hatch?

Correction: for the situations where you fail most often, put a verse on your phone’s home screen in advance.

Repetition: let “coming back to God first” change from a decision into a reflex.

Multiplication: when someone under pressure comes to you, don’t rush to give advice; first lead them in prayer together.

“Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

This verse doesn’t tell people not to labour; it simply points out that the same labour, in different systems, is called “in vain” in one and “building” in the other.

Exercise 3: Practise Obeying the Holy Spirit’s Guidance

Pay attention every day to the Holy Spirit’s promptings, obey in small things, and build the habit of living in God’s system.

Information: know that the Holy Spirit still speaks today, and that his guidance never contradicts Scripture.

Revelation: think back over this week — was there one very gentle prompting that you let slip by?

Conviction: believe that “as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God” (Romans 8:14). Being guided isn’t a privilege for a few; it belongs to being his child.

Implementation: every day, obey at least one small prompting — make that phone call, say that apology, switch off that screen.

Evaluation: “Don’t quench the Spirit.” (1 Thessalonians 5:19) Which prompting did I quench today?

Correction: if a prompting got pushed down, act on it today.

Repetition: one a day makes three hundred and sixty-five acts of obedience in a year.

Multiplication: share your experiences of obedience in your small group, so that your brothers and sisters can be encouraged together.

Obeying the Holy Spirit is like learning to check the rear-view mirror when you learn to drive: at first you have to remind yourself deliberately; over time it becomes instinct. God’s system is meant, in the end, to become instinct.

A Gentle Reminder

You don’t need to change your whole life; you only need to change “whom you depend on.”

Many people are frightened off by the word “change,” thinking they have to tear their whole life down and start again — so they don’t move at all. Not so. God isn’t asking you to change your job, your spouse or your personality; God is only asking you to change whom you depend on. Change that, and everything else will change along with it. To turn a ship, you don’t have to take the whole ship apart; you only turn that very small rudder.

sections.heading: 12. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, history has proven it: those who depend on God will not fail, and those who leave God will fall in the end.

But “will not fail” doesn’t mean “will not suffer.” Noah was mocked, Abraham walked through the wilderness, Esther risked death, the apostles were thrown into prison, and the Lord Jesus went to the cross. God’s system doesn’t guarantee plain sailing all the way; what it guarantees is the ending — the house won’t fall, the fruit won’t cease, and life will endure for ever.

“‘For my thoughts are not your thoughts, and your ways are not my ways,’ says Yahweh. ‘For as the heavens are higher than the earth, so are my ways higher than your ways, and my thoughts than your thoughts.’” (Isaiah 55:8–9)

Today the choice is in your hands. Moses set life and death, blessing and curse, before the people and then said: choose life. This morning God sets the same two roads before us too.

When you choose God, you enter blessing; when you let Jesus be King, your life begins to move onto the track of victory.

Perhaps someone says: I’ve walked in the Worldly system for too long; I can’t go back. The good news is this: every time the Israelites in Judges cried out, God raised up deliverance; when the prodigal son came to his senses in the pigsty, his father was still waiting at the roadside day after day. The road home has never been closed, because the Lord Jesus has already opened it with his own body.

Perhaps someone says: I don’t know where to begin. Begin with the first decision of today — the next message you reply to, the next thing you say, the next decision you make: let Jesus be King right there.

May all the glory go to Jesus. He is worthy, he is King, and he will reign for ever and ever.

keyVerses: Deuteronomy 30:19–20

“I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants, to love Yahweh your God, to obey his voice, and to cling to him; for he is your life, and the length of your days, that you may dwell in the land which Yahweh swore to your fathers, to Abraham, to Isaac, and to Jacob, to give them.” (Deuteronomy 30:19–20)
declarations: Brothers and sisters, let us declare together:
Lord, I choose to return to God’s system! I will no longer depend on myself. I will obey your will and let Jesus be King, so that my life becomes a blessing to others!
practices: Practise obeying the Holy Spirit’s guidance
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you. This morning you have once again set life and death, blessing and curse, before us.

Lord, forgive us. With our mouths we confess that you are Lord, yet in so many things we still depend on our own cleverness and methods; we often ask you to change our circumstances and change other people, but we are unwilling to change the one we depend on.
Lord Jesus, you are our role model. You said the Son can do nothing of himself; in the garden of Gethsemane you said, not what I desire, but what you desire. Please give us that same heart.

Holy Spirit, please guide us. Teach us to obey in the small things of every day, and let our roots go down deep by the river of living water, so that we do not fear when the heat comes, are not anxious in the year of drought, and never cease to bear fruit.

Lord, today we make a choice: we choose to return to God’s system, we choose to let Jesus be King, we choose to let you receive all the glory. Make our lives a blessing to others, and make our homes, our workplaces and our churches all part of your system.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh.” “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh.” (Jeremiah 17:5, 7) What is one thing this week that you were really handling in your own strength? If you could do it again, how would you hand it back to God?

“Who knows if you haven’t come to the kingdom for such a time as this?” (Esther 4:14) In what position has God placed you today — at home, at work, at school or at church? If this position is not for your own sake but for God’s present purpose, what one concrete step will you take this week?
l105.title: Returning to God’s System
l105.subtitle: A Change of Choices (Part 3): Two Systems
l105.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: What Sets the Course of a Life Is Not the Size of the Matter
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning.

Let me begin with a morning many people have lived through. It isn’t light yet, and a sister lies awake in bed. Last night her husband said only one sentence: “You really haven’t thought this through.” It was no big thing, but that sentence was like a small thorn lodged in her heart, and all night long she couldn’t pull it out. Dawn comes, and she is more tired than when she went to bed.

We often think it’s the “thing” that makes us suffer. It isn’t. If that very same sentence had come from an older person she deeply respected, she might simply have smiled and said, “Thank you for the reminder.” The same sentence, falling into different hearts, bears completely different fruit. So what truly sets the course of our lives has never been the size of the matter. It is the “system” we use to face the matter.

Here’s another picture. Two cars meet in a narrow lane. Neither can go forward, and one of them would only have to back up thirty metres. Neither driver budges. They lean on their horns and glare at each other, a long line of cars builds up behind them, and everyone ends up late together. If just one of them were willing to reverse first, it would all be sorted in thirty seconds. But to the self-centred, those thirty metres feel longer than three kilometres — because it isn’t a question of distance. It’s a question of who bows his head first.

Brothers and sisters, we make choices every day: what to eat for breakfast, what time to leave the house. Most of them won’t change a lifetime. But there is one choice we make every single day that decides the direction of our lives:

Will I live in the system of the self-centred life, or in the system of selflessness?

Will I choose pride, or will I choose humility?

This isn’t merely a matter of whether we have a good temper or enough self-discipline. It is the key to whether our life can grow at all. For God’s principle has never changed: “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (1 Peter 5:5)

Notice how serious that is. It doesn’t say, “God dislikes the proud.” It says, “God resists the proud.” Those whom God resists find that the harder they push, the less they move; those to whom God gives grace grow stronger the further they walk. Both are walking — but one walks into the wind and the other walks with it. The difference isn’t in the strength of their legs. It’s in the direction they face.

Today we’ll look at five things together: judging the system by its results, the nature of humility and pride, how our environment shapes our life, three practices of humility, and the cycle of grace that humility brings.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: A Servant’s Apron
sections.html:
This letter was written by the apostle Peter (1 Peter 1:1), with Silvanus as his scribe (1 Peter 5:12). It is generally dated between AD 62 and 64 — right around the time the Roman emperor Nero turned on the church.

It was addressed “to the chosen ones who are living as foreigners in the Dispersion in Pontus, Galatia, Cappadocia, Asia, and Bithynia” (1 Peter 1:1), all in what is now Turkey. Those words “living as foreigners” are the key: in Roman society these believers had no roots, no standing, no one to back them — and in that culture a person’s worth was built up out of birth, wealth and rank. In a situation like that, Peter did not teach them to fight for status. Instead he told them to gird themselves with humility.

The Greek word for “gird” (WEB: “clothe yourselves”) is ἐγκομβόομαι (engkomboomai), and it appears only this once in the entire New Testament. It means to tie on a servant’s apron and fasten it tight. In that day, slaves at work would tie an apron over their outer clothing, and that apron was the badge of a slave. Peter isn’t saying, “Have a slightly better attitude.” He is saying: tie on the slave’s apron, fasten it, and don’t take it off.

What was in Peter’s mind when he wrote that line? John’s Gospel records that Jesus “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet” (John 13:4–5). Peter was there that night. He was the one who said, “You will never wash my feet!” (John 13:8). Thirty years had passed, and that towel was still in his memory. In effect he is saying: the towel the Lord tied around his waist that night — tie it around your own.

The Greek word for “humility” is ταπεινοφροσύνη (tapeinophrosynē), which literally means “lowliness of mind”. In Greco-Roman culture it was originally a term of contempt: base, mean, lacking ambition. Yet Scripture turned it on its head and made it the highest of Christian virtues. How could it be turned around? Because the Son of God himself walked that road first.

There’s another word here with real force. The Greek for “resists” is ἀντιτάσσομαι (antitassomai), a military term meaning “to draw up in battle array against”. Hear this clearly: when someone chooses pride, he hasn’t just run into a little trouble. He has placed God on the opposite side and caused God to draw up his ranks against him.

Peter is quoting Proverbs 3:34: “Surely he mocks the mockers, but he gives grace to the humble.” James quotes the same verse (James 4:6). Two apostles, writing separate letters, both reach for the same Old Testament verse — this isn’t one apostle’s personal preference. It is an iron law the Holy Spirit wants to press on the church of every generation.

Peter goes on: “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you” (1 Peter 5:7). And: “Be sober and self-controlled. Be watchful. Your adversary, the devil, walks around like a roaring lion, seeking whom he may devour” (1 Peter 5:8). Notice the order: humility, casting off our worries, and then keeping watch against the enemy. Why are they linked? Because the proud can’t cast off their worries — they insist on carrying them themselves. And the weary person staggering under a load is exactly the one that lion finds easiest to devour. This is what the 321 vision says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.

sections.heading: 1. Judging the System by Its Results: Your Life Is Speaking
sections.html:
The lesson opens by giving us a very practical test. It doesn’t ask how many years we’ve been reading the Bible. It asks only two questions:

Is my life growing more joyful, or more painful?

Is my service growing lighter, or more exhausting?

These two questions are short, but they are honest, because results speak. The Lord Jesus said, “Every good tree produces good fruit; but the corrupt tree produces evil fruit” (Matthew 7:17). Get the system right and the fruit comes right of its own accord; get the system wrong and no amount of effort will produce good fruit.

The lesson sets the two outcomes side by side. If we live in the Worldly system — the system of the self-centred life — then the more we serve, the more tired we get; the more we do, the more we compare; and we grow ever drier. If we live in God’s system — the system of selflessness — then the more we serve, the more joyful we become; the more we live, the freer we are; and our life grows ever richer.

Take first “the more we serve, the more tired we get.” Service itself doesn’t dry a person out. The Lord said, “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. … For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28, 30). The yoke the Lord gives is light — so who put that heavy yoke on our shoulders? “I can’t let people down.” “What will others think of me?” These aren’t the Lord’s yoke; they are the yoke of “self”. Of course we get tired when we serve carrying “self”, because we’re doing two jobs at once: serving others with one hand and protecting ourselves with the other.

Next, “the more we do, the more we compare.” Comparison is pride’s most honest thermometer. Paul says, “But they themselves, measuring themselves by themselves, and comparing themselves with themselves, are without understanding” (2 Corinthians 10:12). Comparison has a cruel streak: win, and you grow proud and then live in fear of being overtaken; lose, and you grow envious and then live in fear of being seen. Win or lose, you aren’t free. This is what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose.

Third, “we grow ever drier.” The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea are both fed by the Jordan River — the same water. But the Sea of Galilee has an outlet; its water flows on downstream, so it has fish, fishing boats and life. The Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out. With no outlet, its salt content runs above thirty per cent, and almost nothing can live in it. Brothers and sisters, that is geography — and it is also a portrait of the spiritual life. A life that only takes in and never gives out, that only wants to be loved and won’t go and love, will in the end become a Dead Sea, however much truth it soaks up.

On the other hand, the system of selflessness bears entirely different fruit. The more we serve, the more joyful we become, because when the focus is no longer on ourselves, service stops being an exam and becomes grace. Paul says, “For though I was free from all, I brought myself under bondage to all, that I might gain the more” (1 Corinthians 9:19). The more we live, the freer we are — because freedom isn’t having no one over me; it’s no longer being tied up by myself. The hardest master we’ll ever serve in this life is, in fact, ourselves.

In a paper published in 2000 in the Journal of Social and Clinical Psychology, the American psychologist June Price Tangney drew together several elements of humility: an accurate assessment of oneself, the ability to acknowledge one’s mistakes and limitations, openness to new ideas, and no longer being overly focused on the self. She stressed in particular that humility is not low self-esteem but “a relative lack of focus on the self”. That is very close to Scripture. The Bible has never told us to run ourselves down; it tells us to move the focus off ourselves and onto the Lord.

The lesson’s final line puts it superbly: this isn’t an outward problem; it’s the system inside. Solomon says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23). In 321 we often say: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. This morning, let’s honestly examine the system inside us. Your life is speaking — what is it saying?

sections.heading: 2. The Two Core Values: Humility and Pride
sections.html:
The lesson puts it plainly: the most direct expressions of selflessness and the self-centred life are humility and pride. The system of selflessness is humility; the system of the self-centred life is pride.

Look first at the nature of pride. The lesson uses a very precise verb: clinging to self — clinging to our rights, clinging to face, clinging to our own ideas.

Notice that pride isn’t necessarily swaggering. Very often pride is quiet. It’s the insistence that “I can’t give way here”, the injured “Why should I be the one to apologise first?”, the righteous certainty that “this is a matter of principle”. What pride does best is dress itself up as principle.

Where does pride come from? Isaiah records the inner voice of the fallen one: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! I will sit on the mountain of assembly, in the far north! I will ascend above the heights of the clouds! I will make myself like the Most High!” (Isaiah 14:13–14). Count them: in just two verses there are five “I will”s. The core grammar of pride is “I will”.

In the Garden of Eden the serpent said the same thing to the woman: “For God knows that in the day you eat it, your eyes will be opened, and you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5). “Like God” — that is the very nature of pride: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. In 321 we say: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

The lesson says that the result of clinging to self is strained relationships, inner pressure and a life gone dry.

Strained relationships. For decades the American psychologist John Gottman observed couples interacting in his laboratory, and he identified what he calls the “Four Horsemen”: criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling. Of these, the strongest predictor of a marriage breaking down is contempt. Contempt is the face pride wears in a relationship — I am above you, I look down on you. It bears out the proverb: “Pride only breeds quarrels, but wisdom is with people who take advice” (Proverbs 13:10).

Inner pressure. Holding on to something takes effort. Try clenching your fist tightly for ten minutes and your hand will ache. Clinging to face and clinging to rights ache just the same — only the ache is in the heart. And the tighter you cling, the more you fear losing it; the more you fear losing it, the tighter you cling. It’s a cycle with no way out.

A life gone dry. In the chapter of Mere Christianity called “The Great Sin”, C. S. Lewis says that pride is “the complete anti-God state of mind”, and he points out that pride is essentially competitive — pride gets no pleasure out of having something, only out of having more of it than the next person. Someone who can only be happy by having more than others will never be truly happy in this life, because there will always be someone who has more.

Now look at the nature of humility. Once again the lesson uses a precise verb: letting go of self — letting go of our rights, letting go of face, letting go of control. These three are exactly the three things pride clings to most tightly. Humility isn’t putting yourself down. Humility is unclenching your hand.

Scripture’s fullest definition of humility is the Lord Jesus himself. “Have this in your mind, which was also in Christ Jesus, who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:5–8).

“Emptied himself” is the Greek κενόω (kenoō), which means to pour out until empty. What did the Lord Jesus empty himself of? He did not give up his divinity. What he laid aside were the rights, the glory and the honour that were his by right. He was entitled to them, yet he did not cling to them. Brothers and sisters, this is humility at its deepest: being entitled, and not clinging.

Some people think humility is weakness. Not so. Real humility is something only a person with power can do. When someone who has nothing lets go, that’s having no choice; when someone who has everything lets go, that is humility. That is why John takes care to record: “Jesus, knowing that the Father had given all things into his hands … arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist” (John 13:3–4). It was precisely because he knew all things were his that he bent down.

The lesson says that the result of letting go of self is restored relationships, a heart set free and a life that grows.

Restored relationships, because humility draws out humility. In 321 we say: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. In that narrow lane, if just one car is willing to back up, the whole road comes alive.

A heart set free. The Lord Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29). Notice that the Lord didn’t say “learn my power”; he said “learn from me”. Nor did he tell us to learn his miracles; he told us to learn his gentleness and humility. And the result of learning that one thing is rest for our souls.

A life that grows. In Good to Great, Jim Collins analysed companies that leapt from mediocre to excellent and found that every one had what he calls a “Level 5 leader”, marked by a paradoxical blend of personal humility and professional will: giving the credit to others and shouldering the responsibility themselves. Even management research that never speaks of faith has stumbled on this principle — how much more we, who believe in the God who gives grace to the humble.

sections.heading: 3. Environment Shapes Life: What Culture Are You In?
sections.html:
The lesson goes on to remind us of something we often overlook: our life is shaped not only by us as individuals but also by the culture around us.

We tend to think spiritual growth is entirely a personal matter. That is certainly true — but Scripture also tells us clearly that environment shapes people: “One who walks with wise men grows wise, but a companion of fools suffers harm” (Proverbs 13:20). How a seed grows depends not only on the seed but on the soil. The same seed sown along the path, on rocky ground with shallow soil, among thorns, and on good soil comes to entirely different ends (Matthew 13:3–8). Brothers and sisters, the family is soil, the small group is soil, the workplace is soil, and the church is soil too.

1. A Proud Environment: The System of the Self-Centred Life

This kind of environment has three marks: it stresses performance, it stresses comparison, and it stresses being seen.

None of these is bad in itself. Work should bear results; learning from one another is good; everyone needs to be affirmed. The problem lies in the word “stresses”. When what a group values most is performance, comparison and exposure, the very air of that group changes. In that air, the lesson says, people want to make a name for themselves, people want to prove themselves, and people won’t let go.

Scripture gives us a real example. After the Lord Jesus foretold for the second time that he would be killed and rise on the third day, what were the disciples doing behind him? “But they were silent, for they had disputed with one another on the way about who was the greatest” (Mark 9:34). See how stark the contrast is: the Lord out in front speaking of the cross, the disciples behind him arguing about who was greatest. Why? Because the system inside them had not yet been exchanged. They had simply carried the ranking habits of the Jewish culture of their day, untouched, into the company that followed Jesus. And how did the Lord respond? “If any man wants to be first, he shall be last of all, and servant of all” (Mark 9:35). The Lord didn’t rebuke them for being ambitious. He turned the whole ranking table upside down.

What is the most frightening result of an environment like this? The lesson says it very soberly: the selfless life is choked to death.

Picture a sapling that has just broken through the soil, tender and green. If it’s surrounded by tall, dense trees, the light can’t get in and it won’t grow. A selfless life is like that sapling: it needs room and sunlight. But in an environment where everyone has to be seen, the one willing to stay hidden is treated as useless, the one willing to give way is treated as spineless, and the one willing to help others succeed is treated as lacking drive. Over time, the heart that was willing to be humble shrinks back.

In The Narcissism Epidemic, published in 2009, the psychologists Jean M. Twenge and W. Keith Campbell report that the average scores of American college students on the Narcissistic Personality Inventory have shown a marked upward trend since the 1980s, one cause being a change in the cultural environment — a culture that keeps urging, “You must be special; you must be seen.” Scholars still debate the details, but at the very least it reminds us that culture really does shape a person’s sense of self.

The Lord Jesus warned us long ago: “Be careful that you don’t do your charitable giving before men, to be seen by them, or else you have no reward from your Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 6:1).

2. A Humble Environment: The System of Selflessness

This kind of environment also has three marks: it stresses hiddenness, it stresses helping one another succeed, and it stresses letting Jesus be seen.

“Stressing hiddenness” doesn’t mean being passive or withdrawn. Hiddenness means this: what I do is seen, but I myself am not — better still, the Lord is seen. John the Baptist spoke words that every servant of God should engrave on the tablet of the heart: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30). And the Lord said, “But when you do merciful deeds, don’t let your left hand know what your right hand does” (Matthew 6:3).

“Stressing helping one another succeed.” Paul says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others” (Philippians 2:3–4). And again: “In love of the brothers be tenderly affectionate to one another; in honor preferring one another” (Romans 12:10). “Preferring one another” — in a generation where everyone competes with everyone, what a beautiful picture that is.

Nature offers a fitting example. The coast redwoods of North America are the tallest trees on earth, able to grow beyond a hundred metres, yet their roots are shallow, often only two or three metres deep. How do they stay standing? Because redwoods grow in groves, and underground their roots intertwine and lock into one another. A lone redwood topples easily, but a grove of redwoods can stand for a thousand years. That is the picture of helping one another succeed: we don’t stand by our own strength; we stand within relationships that hold on to one another. This is exactly what 321 calls the “235 relationships” — becoming a “2”, a spiritual companion, with a selfless person; establishing the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and going on to become a “5”, a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

“Stressing letting Jesus be seen.” These are the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The measure of a healthy fellowship isn’t “Who spoke best today?” but “Did anyone see more of Jesus today?”

In an environment like this, the lesson says, people are willing to let go, people hold each other up, people make Jesus their focal point — and the result is that selflessness grows naturally. Notice that word “naturally”. In the right soil, a seed doesn’t have to strain; it simply grows. “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase” (1 Corinthians 3:6). Our responsibility is to provide the soil; the growing is God’s work.

That gives us a very practical lesson: it isn’t enough for you to choose humility yourself; you also need to create an environment where the people around you can be humble. In your home, do your children dare to admit their mistakes? In your small group, if someone says, “I failed this week,” will they be accepted?

In 321 we say: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. An environment that treats people as tools belongs to the Worldly system, however big it grows; an environment that treats people as treasures belongs to God’s system, however small it is.

sections.heading: 4. Three Practical Exercises in Humility
sections.html:
Next the lesson brings humility down from heaven to earth. In daily life, it says, humility isn’t abstract; it is a very concrete choice. The lesson gives us three sentences — short enough to memorise, practical enough to use this very morning.

1. I Will Listen to You

Set aside your own opinion and be willing to listen to others. The lesson reminds us: this isn’t having no mind of your own; it is letting God speak to you through people.

Many people don’t listen — not because they didn’t hear, but because “I already know the answer.” Solomon says, “He who answers before he hears, that is folly and shame to him” (Proverbs 18:13). James says, “Let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19). Notice the order: swift to hear, slow to speak, slow to anger. Human nature runs exactly the other way.

In communication research there is a widely known idea called “active listening”, put forward in 1957 by the American psychologists Carl Rogers and Richard Farson. They argued that real listening isn’t waiting for the other person to finish; it is entering the other person’s frame of reference and reflecting their meaning back, so that they know, “You really understand me.” When someone is truly understood, their defences come down of their own accord, and only then does change become possible. Many family quarrels aren’t really disagreements at all; they’re “You’re not even listening to me.” One sentence — “I will listen to you” — can defuse a whole war.

Going deeper, the lesson says: let God speak to you through people. God often doesn’t speak in thunder. He speaks through the very person we least want to hear — through a spouse, a child, a co-worker. If we’ve already decided in our hearts, “What does he know?”, we have shut God’s word outside the door.

This is the 920 practice of 321: every person who is in relationship with us is our “2”, and with each “2” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life — and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23). “I will listen to you” is what patience, gentleness and self-control look like in that moment.

2. I Will Take Care of You

Stop waiting for others to meet my needs, and reach out to care for others. The lesson puts it powerfully: move from “You must love me” to “I will love you.”

That one sentence could heal more than half of our relationship problems, because the vast majority of the pain in relationships comes from the same sentence pattern: “You should love me, and you don’t.”

“You must love me” is a demand. The one who demands is never satisfied, because no person can fill the bottomless pit in another person’s heart — that pit was never meant to be filled by a person; it is God’s place. When we lay “You must love me” on a person, we do two wrong things at once: we seat that person in God’s place, and then we resent them for failing to do what only God can do. “I will love you”, on the other hand, is giving. How can the giver keep on giving? Because his supply doesn’t come from people; it comes from the Lord. “We love him, because he first loved us” (1 John 4:19).

The Lord Jesus said, “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them” (Luke 6:31). Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “Treat people the way they treat you” — that’s retaliation. He said you take the first step. Scripture’s most beautiful example is still that night. The one who would betray him sat at the table; the one who would deny him sat at the table too. He had every reason to say, “You love me first.” Instead he got up, tied on the towel, washed their feet and said, “If I then, the Lord and the Teacher, have washed your feet, you also ought to wash one another’s feet” (John 13:14).

In a study published in 2003 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, the American psychologists Robert Emmons and Michael McCullough asked one group of participants to write down, each week, five things they were grateful for. After ten weeks, this group’s sense of well-being was clearly higher than that of the group who recorded their hassles, and they were also more willing to help others. That is a telling clue: only those who see how much they have received have something to give. Paul goes straight to the heart of it: “For who makes you different? And what do you have that you didn’t receive?” (1 Corinthians 4:7).

3. I Will Change Myself to Fit You

Stop demanding that others change, and adjust yourself first. The lesson says: this is the most practical expression of selflessness.

Of the three sentences, this is the hardest. “I will listen to you” can still be endured; “I will take care of you” can still be done; but “I will change myself to fit you” — that touches who I am. Our inborn logic says: the problem is the other person, so the other person is the one who has to change. The sentence most often heard in marriage counselling is, “Pastor, please talk some sense into him.” Very few walk in the door and say, “Please tell me how I should change.”

What did Paul do? “I have become all things to all men, that I may by all means save some” (1 Corinthians 9:22). He was an apostle — he had theology, vision and authority — yet he chose to change himself to fit people, all so that he might “by all means save some”.

Someone will ask: then won’t I lose myself? Yes — and that is exactly the point. “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me” (Galatians 2:20).

In 321 we say it very clearly: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. Letting go of self isn’t wiping yourself out. It is exchanging that small, tight “I” — so concerned with face and so afraid of being hurt — for the infinite, abundant, never-failing Christ. That is no losing bargain. It is the best exchange under heaven.

In Mindset, published in 2006, the psychologist Carol S. Dweck distinguishes between a “fixed mindset” and a “growth mindset”. People with a fixed mindset believe ability is fixed, so every criticism is a verdict on them personally, and they must defend themselves. People with a growth mindset believe ability can be developed, so every criticism is information, and they can learn. The fixed mindset is protecting “me”; the growth mindset is concerned with growth. Pride locks people in place; humility lets them grow. This is just what 321 calls the fivefold change: change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes.

Put these three sentences together and you have the very road the Lord Jesus walked in Philippians 2: he listened to the Father’s word, he took care of us, and he changed his own form to fit us, being made in human likeness. Humility isn’t a concept. Humility is a road the Lord himself has walked.

sections.heading: 5. Humility Brings a Cycle of Grace
sections.html:
The lesson closes by giving us a vitally important insight: when we choose humility, we enter a spiritual cycle — we humble ourselves, and God gives grace; with grace we have more strength; and the stronger we become, the more we know that strength isn’t our own, so we grow humbler still. On the other hand, when we choose pride, God resists us; being resisted, we struggle all the more; the more we struggle, the less we’re willing to yield, and so we grow prouder still.

Both cycles gather speed. That is why some people find life growing lighter the longer they live, while for others it grows harder and harder. The lesson puts it well: the difference isn’t ability; it is “choice”.

Look first at the cycle of grace. “But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). Notice “more grace” — God’s grace isn’t rationed out in fixed portions; it is “more”. Why do the humble receive grace? Because grace is like water, and water flows to the lowest place. A person who exalts himself is like a cup set upside down in the rain: however hard it pours, the cup stays empty. It isn’t that there’s too little rain; the mouth of the cup is facing the wrong way. Physics works the same way: air always flows from high pressure to low pressure, and that is how wind is formed. The lower the pressure in your heart, the more grace blows your way.

Now look at the cycle of pride. “Pride goes before destruction, and an arrogant spirit before a fall” (Proverbs 16:18). “When pride comes, then comes shame, but with humility comes wisdom” (Proverbs 11:2).

The most vivid example in Scripture is Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon. Walking on the roof of his royal palace, he said, “Is not this great Babylon, which I have built for the royal dwelling place, by the might of my power and for the glory of my majesty?” (Daniel 4:30). The words were still in his mouth when judgement fell. After he had passed through seven periods of discipline, he lifted his eyes to heaven, his reason returned, and his conclusion was this: “Those who walk in pride he is able to abase” (Daniel 4:37). Herod in the New Testament was no different. The people shouted, “The voice of a god, and not of a man!”, and Luke goes on to record: “Immediately an angel of the Lord struck him, because he didn’t give God the glory. Then he was eaten by worms and died” (Acts 12:23). The problem wasn’t that others praised him; the problem was that he kept the glory for himself to enjoy. This is the exact opposite of the second of 321’s Core Values: let Jesus receive all the glory. If glory lingers in our hands, it rots; if we pass it on and give it to the Lord, it turns into grace and flows back to us.

The Lord Jesus put this cycle into one short sentence: “For everyone who exalts himself will be humbled, and whoever humbles himself will be exalted” (Luke 14:11). Peter says too: “Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time” (1 Peter 5:6).

Notice “in due time”. The humble don’t need to arrange their own promotion; God has his timing. Joseph waited in prison for years; David, after he was anointed, went on tending sheep and then fled for years. They didn’t grab a position for themselves; God himself set them in place. A position you grab for yourself, you have to strain to hold on to, and holding on is exhausting. A position God sets you in, God himself will hold you up in.

Philippians sets this cycle down in the most beautiful passage in the universe: “He humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross. Therefore God also highly exalted him, and gave to him the name which is above every name” (Philippians 2:8–9). Look at that “Therefore”. The Lord Jesus himself walked this whole cycle through — he humbled himself, and God exalted him to the highest place. He isn’t asking us to walk a road he hasn’t walked; he is asking us to follow in his footsteps. This is exactly the first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model.

sections.heading: 6. Integrating the 321 Vision: Humility Is the Doorway to the Whole System
sections.html:
When we set what we’ve seen today back into the whole picture of 321, it becomes even clearer.

The Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — the road in Philippians 2, from the throne to the manger and from the manger to the cross, is the road of humility. The Bible is my standard — when we quarrel with someone, the standard we pull out in our hearts is often “I feel”, not “It is written”. The Holy Spirit is my guide — humility isn’t something we grit our teeth and force out; it is the Holy Spirit at work within us. “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure” (Philippians 2:13).

The Two Core Values. Let Jesus be King — a kingdom can have only one king. The essence of pride is that I want to sit on the throne; the essence of humility is that I step down from the throne and give the seat back to the Lord. Let Jesus receive all the glory — Herod’s end reminds us that glory is something that can only be passed on, never stored away.

The Goal: establish God’s system. The Worldly system is the self-centred life, and its shopfront is pride; God’s system is selflessness, and its shopfront is humility. We aren’t talking today about a slightly better temperament. We’re talking about two entirely different kingdoms.

The old self and the new self. “That you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man … and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind” (Ephesians 4:22–23). The old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem.

In 321 we say: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Why? Because every work of Satan has to plug into the socket called “self”. Temptation always begins with “You deserve more” or “Why should you be treated like this?” But if that “self” has already been crucified with Christ, Satan has nothing to get a grip on. James links the two together: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you” (James 4:7). Notice the order: first be subject to God, and only then can you resist the devil.

The fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The most crucial step today is the first — mindset. If our mindset is still stuck at “humility means being taken advantage of”, we will never choose humility. When our mindset changes to “humility is the posture for receiving grace”, everything is different.

The order: life first, then relationships, then ministry. What the lesson calls “the more we serve, the more tired we get” is usually a case of the order being reversed. The priority of relationships is the same: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things. That driver in the narrow lane who wouldn’t back up — his problem isn’t his relationship with the other driver but his relationship with God. He has forgotten that everything he has, he received.

The shift in perspective. From man’s view to God’s: in man’s eyes, the one who bows first has lost; in God’s eyes, the one who bows first receives grace. From the earthly to the heavenly: earthly rankings keep shifting, but the books of heaven do not change. From the temporary to the eternal: swallowing your pride is a moment’s discomfort, and what it buys is eternal fruit. From the worldly to the godly: the Worldly system runs on grasping; God’s system runs on entrusting. “Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth” (Colossians 3:2).

The 920 practice. Every person in relationship with us is our “2”: your spouse is a 2, your children are a 2, your parents are a 2, your co-workers are a 2, and that person who makes you most uncomfortable is a 2 as well. The lesson’s three sentences — “I will listen to you”, “I will take care of you”, “I will change myself to fit you” — are the most concrete operating manual for 920.

The 235 relationships. It is very hard to hold on to humility alone, because pride is stirred up in relationships and must also be healed in relationships. So we need a “2” — a spiritual companion who can tell me the truth and whom I’m willing to hear; we need a “3” — someone ahead of me leading me and someone behind me following; and we need a “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. This is what the lesson calls “a humble environment”.

Brothers and sisters, Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not others, not our circumstances. This morning, if your heart is wound tight because of some person or some matter, please shift your focus a little.

sections.heading: 7. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three exercises. Let’s put them into practice using the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Exercise 1: Examine How I React

The lesson says: today, in conflict or under pressure, am I clinging to self, or choosing to let go of self?

Information: put the truth into your heart. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble” (1 Peter 5:5). Copy it out and stick it somewhere you’ll see it.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to show you your own pattern of reacting. We are all very good at seeing other people’s pride and very poor at seeing our own. “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts” (Psalm 139:23).

Conviction: settle it in your heart — I admit that most of my pain doesn’t come from the situation; it comes from my clinging to self.

Implementation: today, pick the situation where you’re most likely to react. Before you react, count three seconds silently and ask yourself, “What am I clinging to right now?”

Evaluation: before bed, spend three minutes looking back. How many times did I cling today? How many times did I let go? After I let go, how did my heart feel?

Correction: write down the thing you cling to most often — is it face? Your rights? Your own ideas? Pray specifically about it.

Repetition: keep it up for a full seven days. A change of mindset isn’t a single flash of insight; it is formed through repeated practice.

Multiplication: find a spiritual companion, tell them what you’ve discovered, and invite them to practise with you.

Exercise 2: Deliberately Practise the Three Sentences

The lesson says: in daily life, practise “I will listen to you”, “I will take care of you” and “I will change myself.”

Information: learn these three sentences by heart, and the verses behind them too — “swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger” (James 1:19); “As you would like people to do to you, do exactly so to them” (Luke 6:31); “I have become all things to all men” (1 Corinthians 9:22).

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you whom you should say these three sentences to today. Usually the one the Holy Spirit brings to mind is the name you least want to mention.

Conviction: tell yourself — these three sentences aren’t about losing out; they are my doorway into grace.

Implementation: do it at least once today. No need to announce it, no need to explain it — just do it. Hear someone out without interrupting; take the initiative to ask, “Are you all right today?”; do one small thing their way.

Evaluation: in that moment, how did the other person’s expression change? How did the feeling in your own heart change?

Correction: which of the three sentences is hardest for you? That hardest one is exactly where God most wants to work in you today.

Repetition: one sentence a day, taking them in turn, for a full three weeks.

Multiplication: share the story of your practice once in your small group. One true story is worth more than ten sermons.

Exercise 3: Build a Humble Environment

The lesson says: in your family, small group and church, deliberately cultivate a culture of “letting Jesus be seen” rather than making people famous.

Information: read Philippians 2:3–4 until you know it well: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.”

Revelation: ask the Lord to show you what the air is like right now in the group you belong to. Does it let people dare to admit weakness, or do they only dare to share good news?

Conviction: believe that an environment can be changed by one person. The temperature of a room changes as soon as one person opens a window.

Implementation: this week, do three things in your family or small group. First, publicly give the glory to the Lord — change “what I did” into “what the Lord did”. Second, publicly praise someone who has gone unnoticed. Third, publicly admit one weakness or mistake of your own.

Evaluation: afterwards, how is the atmosphere of the group different? Has anyone else become willing to speak the truth as a result?

Correction: if no one responds, don’t be discouraged, and don’t push hard. Changing the soil takes time.

Repetition: let these three things become your settled habit within the group.

Multiplication: invite one or two co-workers to guard this kind of culture with you. Air guarded by two people is far steadier than air guarded by one.

sections.heading: 8. A Gentle Reminder
sections.html:
The lesson leaves us with a reminder that is very short but cuts to the heart:

It isn’t the situation that makes you suffer; it’s that you are facing the situation with “the system of pride”.

Brothers and sisters, please take this sentence home with you. The next time your heart is churning, don’t rush to analyse the situation. First ask yourself one question: which system am I in right now?

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing words say it beautifully: humility is not just a virtue; it is the way of life.

A virtue is something we bring out now and then to show; a way is the road we must walk every day. Humility isn’t something we take out only on special occasions. Humility is the road we must choose to step onto the moment we get up each morning.

When you choose humility, you are choosing three things.

You are choosing grace, because God gives grace to the humble.

You are choosing growth, because only those who lower their defences can learn anything.

You are choosing revival, because revival has never begun with a big rally. Revival begins with a group of people willing to bow their heads. “If my people, who are called by my name, will humble themselves, pray, seek my face, and turn from their wicked ways; then I will hear from heaven, will forgive their sin, and will heal their land” (2 Chronicles 7:14). Notice that the very first condition God gives for revival is “humble themselves”.

And when you let go of yourself, Jesus begins to live himself out in you. That is today’s greatest promise. Letting go of self doesn’t turn you into an empty person. Letting go of self makes room for the infinite Lord to live within you. “It is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

So let me call each one of us.

This morning, is there a name in your heart? A name that makes you tense up the moment you think of it. Perhaps a spouse, perhaps a child, perhaps a co-worker, perhaps someone who once hurt you. Today the Lord says to you: let Jesus be King. Not so that you win — so that Jesus reigns as King.

This morning, is there something in your heart you can’t let go of? Something where you feel, “Why should I be the one to give way?” Today the Lord says to you: lay down your rights and return to your originally intended position. Let man be man and let God be God.

This morning, is your service so exhausted that it is close to running dry? The Lord says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls” (Matthew 11:29).

Brothers and sisters, we aren’t humble in order to become better people; we are humble so that Jesus may receive all the glory. May all of us together become a redwood grove whose roots hold fast to one another. May every family, every small group and every church we belong to become good soil where selflessness can grow naturally.

Let Jesus be King. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

keyVerses: 1 Peter 5:5–6: “Likewise, you younger ones, be subject to the elder. Yes, all of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’ Humble yourselves therefore under the mighty hand of God, that he may exalt you in due time.”
declarations: Lord, I choose humility,
letting go of myself and returning to my originally intended position,
letting Jesus be King,
so that my life is lived in your grace,
and others see you in me!
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,
We thank you that, though you existed in the form of God, you emptied yourself, took the form of a servant, and walked the road of the cross for us. Lord, you are our role model.
Lord, we confess that there is much “self” within us. We cling to our rights, cling to face, cling to our own ideas — and then dress it all up as principle. Have mercy on us, and forgive our pride.

Lord, give us a humble heart. Let us be able, this very day, to say those three sentences: I will listen to you, I will take care of you, I will change myself to fit you. Holy Spirit, remind us and hold us up in every moment, for we cannot do it on our own.
Lord, use us to build an environment in our families, small groups and churches where Jesus is seen. May we help one another succeed and prefer one another in honour, so that your name is glorified.

Lord, we are willing to humble ourselves under your mighty hand and cast all our worries on you, because you care for us. Bring us into the cycle of grace — the humbler we are, the more grace we receive; the more grace we receive, the humbler we become — until you live yourself out in us.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: 1 Peter 5:5: “All of you clothe yourselves with humility, to subject yourselves to one another; for ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.’” Examine yourself honestly: in the most recent situation that left you upset, what were you clinging to — your rights, face, or your own ideas? If you had chosen to let go in that moment, how might things have turned out differently?

Philippians 2:3–4: “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself; each of you not just looking to his own things, but each of you also to the things of others.” In your family, small group or workplace, is the air right now closer to “a proud environment” or “a humble environment”? What one concrete thing could you do this week to bring a little more of a culture of “letting Jesus be seen” there?
l106.title: Choose Humility
l106.subtitle: A Change of Choices (Part 4): Humility and Pride
l106.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: The Same on the Outside, Utterly Different Within
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you this morning. Let’s begin by asking you to picture a scene in your heart: two people, on the same morning, doing the same thing.

The first gets up at six, opens the Bible, reads three chapters, writes some notes, prays for ten minutes and heads off to work. The whole thing takes twenty-five minutes — not a minute more, not a minute less.

The second also gets up at six and reads the same three chapters. But when he comes to one sentence he stops, reads it again, bows his head and says, “Lord, are these words for me?” He is quiet for a while, and his eyes grow wet. When he leaves the house, he is seven minutes later than he planned.

From the outside, these two people are doing the same thing — their devotions. Same time, same passage, same posture. And yet, brothers and sisters, the lives those two mornings produce are completely different.

Why? Because the first person is “completing” his devotions, while the second is “meeting” God. The first relies on his own discipline; the second relies on the guidance of the Holy Spirit.

That is the question this lesson takes up today. We often think the key to the spiritual life lies in “how well we do” — did we finish our Bible reading, did we pray enough, did our service go off well? But Scripture wants to tell us something more fundamental: the real key isn’t what you do, but whom you rely on to do it.

The same sermon can be preached relying on the manuscript, or relying on the Holy Spirit. The same decision can be made relying on experience, or relying on the Holy Spirit. On the outside they look exactly alike, but the outcome in a person’s life is worlds apart.

This is the watershed between the self-centred life and selflessness. Self-centred people put themselves at the centre and rely in everything on their own cleverness, experience, ability and methods. Selfless people put Jesus on the throne, and in everything they seek the Holy Spirit’s guidance, obey the Holy Spirit’s promptings and rely on the Holy Spirit’s power.

On the 321 road, what trips us up most easily is often not some obvious sin but a kind of “relying on ourselves” that looks very devout. We go on serving, go on reading the Bible, go on attending meetings — but the Holy Spirit has already been ushered off to one side.

Brothers and sisters, this morning let’s honestly ask ourselves one question together: the things I did this week — whom did I actually rely on to do them?

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Three Books, One Shared Cry
sections.html: Today’s three key passages come from three entirely different eras, three different authors and three different situations. Yet they all raise the same cry.

sections.heading: 1. Proverbs 3: A Father’s First Lesson to His Son
sections.html:
The bulk of Proverbs comes from the hand of King Solomon. Solomon reigned over Israel from roughly 970 to 930 BC and is the king Scripture renowned for his wisdom. Proverbs 25:1 also tells us that some of these proverbs were later the ones “which the men of Hezekiah king of Judah copied out” — which shows that Proverbs is a collection of wisdom gathered and edited over a long period.

Chapters 1 to 9 of Proverbs have a very distinctive form: they are a father’s long exhortation to his son, with the call “My son, listen” sounding again and again. So Proverbs 3:5–6 is not an abstract maxim. It is an old father with his hands on his child’s shoulders, saying: you’ll learn a great many skills in life, but remember this — don’t lean on your own understanding.

It’s worth pondering that these words come from Solomon, the man with the best claim of anyone to lean on his own understanding. And the failure of his later years became a witness from the other side: 1 Kings 11 records that when he was old, his heart turned away from Yahweh. Having wisdom is not the same as having a refuge; gifts are not the same as life.

A few key words in the original are worth noting. “Trust” is the Hebrew בָּטַח (batach), whose basic meaning is “to lie down at ease, to put your whole weight on something, to entrust yourself without any guard”. It doesn’t picture lightly steadying yourself on a railing with two fingers; it pictures lying full length on a bed. “Lean” is a different word, שָׁעַן (sha’an), meaning “to rest your body against something, to prop yourself on it” — it too puts the weight down, only in the wrong place. “Understanding” is בִּינָה (binah), meaning “discernment, insight, seeing how things work”. So what this verse really says is: my child, put the whole weight of who you are on Yahweh, not on your own skill at reading situations.

sections.heading: 2. Galatians 3: A Heartbreaking Question
sections.html:
Galatians was written by the apostle Paul. As to its date, scholars who hold the “South Galatian” view place it after the first missionary journey and before the Jerusalem Council, around AD 48–49; those who hold the “North Galatian” view put it at around AD 53–57. Whichever date you take, the situation is clear: a group of Judaising teachers had come into the churches of Galatia and were telling these Gentile believers that simply believing in Jesus wasn’t enough — they also had to be circumcised and keep the law of Moses in order to be complete.

Paul wrote this letter in a state of deep agitation; of all his letters to churches, it is the only one that doesn’t open by giving thanks to God. In 3:1 he says, “Foolish Galatians, who has bewitched you not to obey the truth, before whose eyes Jesus Christ was openly portrayed among you as crucified?” Then in 3:2 he asks, “Did you receive the Spirit by the works of the law, or by hearing of faith?” And only then comes today’s key verse, 3:3: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”

The word for “begun” is ἐνάρχομαι (enarchomai), meaning “to start, to make a beginning”; “completed” is ἐπιτελέω (epiteleō), meaning “to finish, to reach the end”. Paul’s question paints a deeply ironic picture: your spiritual life was begun by the Holy Spirit — do you now mean to finish it off in your own flesh? It’s like someone flying across the Pacific who, halfway over, says, “I’ll swim the rest of the way myself.”

Notice this: the Galatians hadn’t left the church, hadn’t gone off to worship idols, hadn’t fallen into gross moral sin. They simply wanted to be “a bit more complete”, to add a little of their own effort on top of grace. Yet Paul calls this “foolish”, and in 5:4 he even says they have “fallen away from grace”. That reminds us that relying on ourselves doesn’t necessarily wear the face of self-indulgence. More often it wears the face of “pursuing spiritual growth”.

sections.heading: 3. Romans 8: The Charter of the Holy Spirit
sections.html:
Romans was written around AD 57, while Paul was in Corinth. Many commentators call Romans 8 one of the summits of the whole Bible. It moves from the struggle of chapter 7 — “desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good” — to the release of chapter 8 — “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus” — and the turning point in between is the Holy Spirit. In this one chapter alone, the word “Spirit” appears around twenty times.

Romans 8:13 says, “For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” Notice that Paul doesn’t say, “Try a little harder and put your evil deeds to death.” He says to put them to death “by the Spirit”. In putting evil deeds to death, we have to act, but the power doesn’t come from us. Verse 14 follows straight on: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.” The word for “led”, ἄγω (agō), is in the passive voice here, describing a person who is being led, being drawn along. The mark of a child of God isn’t “I’m good at walking” but “I’m willing to be led.”

Three books, three eras, one shared cry: don’t rely on yourself; rely on the Spirit of God.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: Two Kinds of Reliance, Two Kinds of Outcome
sections.html:
Right at the outset the lesson spreads out the whole map: when you trace every choice in life back to its root, there are only two kinds of reliance, and these two lead to two entirely different outcomes.

Relying on Self: The System of the Self-Centred Life

People who rely on themselves lean on four things: experience, ability, methods and control.

None of these four is bad in itself. Experience is a gift from God; ability is a gift from God; methods are the distilled fruit of wisdom. The problem isn’t in “having” them but in “relying” on them. When I put my whole weight on them, they turn from tools into idols.

Jeremiah 17:5–6 speaks very severely: “Yahweh says: ‘Cursed is the man who trusts in man, relies on strength of flesh, and whose heart departs from Yahweh. For he will be like a bush in the desert, and will not see when good comes, but will inhabit the parched places in the wilderness, an uninhabited salt land.’” Notice the image — a bush in the desert. It isn’t dead. It’s still alive, still green; but it lives on salt land, so it never grows tall and never bears fruit. How many Christians are in just that condition: not dead, but not growing either.

The lesson lists the four results of relying on ourselves with great precision: pressure, exhaustion, dryness and finally spiritual death.

These four are a downhill road. First comes pressure — because I have to carry every outcome myself. Then exhaustion — because my strength is limited and the needs are limitless. Then dryness — not just a lack of strength, but a heart that has lost its savour. Finally, spiritual death — not the loss of salvation, but the loss of living fellowship with God; the person is still there, but the spirit has gone stiff.

Psychology describes this downhill road precisely. From 1981 onwards, the social psychologist Christina Maslach of the University of California, Berkeley developed the Maslach Burnout Inventory, which identifies three core dimensions of burnout: emotional exhaustion, depersonalisation (coldness and cynicism towards people) and a reduced sense of personal accomplishment. In 2019 the World Health Organization formally listed burnout in the eleventh revision of the International Classification of Diseases as an occupational phenomenon resulting from chronic workplace stress that has not been successfully managed. Brothers and sisters, these three dimensions follow almost the same track as the exhaustion, dryness and spiritual death the lesson describes. Scripture simply traces it deeper: the root of burnout is often a heart that has moved God out of the way and is carrying everything alone.

Relying on the Holy Spirit: The System of Selflessness

People who rely on the Holy Spirit do four things: they seek his guidance, obey his promptings, rely on his power and entrust him with sovereignty.

These four correspond exactly to the Three Foundations and the Two Core Values of 321: seeking guidance — the Holy Spirit is my guide; obeying promptings — the Bible is my standard; relying on power — Jesus is my role model; entrusting sovereignty — let Jesus be King.

Jesus himself is the perfect demonstration. John 5:19: “Most certainly, I tell you, the Son can do nothing of himself, but what he sees the Father doing. For whatever things he does, these the Son also does likewise.” Brothers and sisters, the Son of God on earth said, “I can do nothing of myself.” If even the Lord Jesus chose not to rely on himself, what makes us think we can?

The four results of relying on the Holy Spirit: peace, joy, lightness and a life that grows.

Galatians 5:22–23: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” Notice that Paul speaks of “fruit”, not “products”. Products have to be manufactured; fruit only needs connection. A branch doesn’t have to grit its teeth to produce grapes; it only has to stay on the vine.

In Matthew 11:29–30 Jesus says, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” The word for “easy” is χρηστός (chrēstos), meaning “well-suited, well-fitting”. Carpenters in those days would measure an ox’s neck to make its yoke, so that it wouldn’t chafe. The Lord’s yoke is light not because there’s no work, but because that yoke has been made to measure for you — and a yoke is made for two: at the other end, the Lord carries it with you.

A Real-Life Contrast: The Sea of Galilee and the Dead Sea

Israel has two lakes that drink from the same river, the Jordan. In the north, the Sea of Galilee has water flowing in and flowing out; there are fish in it, and the disciples cast their nets there. In the south, the Dead Sea only takes in and never gives out, so its salt keeps concentrating. Today its salinity is around thirty per cent, nearly ten times that of ordinary seawater, and apart from a few salt-loving microbes, no fish can survive in it — which is why it is called the “Dead” Sea. The same source of water — so why is one alive and the other dead? There’s only one difference: whether or not the water flows on.

People who rely on themselves are like the Dead Sea — only interested in absorbing, accumulating and controlling, wanting to grip everything in their hands, so the more they hoard, the saltier and deader they become. People who rely on the Holy Spirit are like the Sea of Galilee — grace flows in from God and flows out again through me, so within there is always life.

Applying the 321 Vision: The Key Isn’t What You Do, but Whom You Rely On

The lesson sums up this point in one sentence: “The key isn’t what you do, but whom you rely on.”

That sentence is the very starting point of the fivefold change. 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. What this lesson sets out to change is the mindset at the very headwaters — turning “I must get this done well” into “I will let the Holy Spirit do it.”

Our perspective must shift along with it. From man’s perspective, the most capable person wins; from God’s perspective, the one willing to rely on him wins. From an earthly perspective, busyness is fruitfulness; from a heavenly perspective, being connected to the Lord is what counts as fruitfulness.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Greatest Danger — Once We Can Do It, We Stop Relying
sections.html:
The lesson says something very sharp: “The most dangerous thing isn’t not knowing how — it’s ‘knowing how’.” Brothers and sisters, that sentence deserves to be copied onto the flyleaf of your Bible.

A Curve Everyone Has Travelled

The lesson traces the path very clearly: at first we don’t know how, so we rely on God; once we become skilled, we start relying on ourselves.

Do you remember the first time you led a small group? You couldn’t sleep the night before, and you prayed over and over: Lord, I don’t know how to do this; please help me. And that time it went with surprising power. Three years later, with the same small group, you spend five minutes thinking through the plan in the car on the way, walk in and get started — and you speak far more smoothly than you did three years ago. But that prayer, “Lord, I don’t know how,” has disappeared.

The curve of rising skill and the curve of falling reliance often cross. That is exactly the situation of Galatians 3:3.

Why the Brain Works This Way

Science offers a fascinating piece of corroboration. The MIT neuroscientist Ann Graybiel and her team have long studied the role of the brain’s basal ganglia in forming habits. They found that a sequence of actions that at first requires step-by-step thought is, after repeated practice, “packaged” by the brain into a single chunk: once triggered, it runs to completion automatically, with almost no conscious monitoring. Research by the psychologists Sian Beilock and Thomas Carr (2001) also shows that highly skilled people, after performing the actions they are best at, often can’t say what steps they just went through — what is called “expertise-induced amnesia”.

This is a wonderful part of how God made us — otherwise just walking and driving every day would wear us out. But once this design is carried over into the spiritual life, a danger appears: prayer, Bible reading and service can also be “packaged” into automatic routines. The hands are moving, the mouth is speaking, and the heart can be entirely absent.

Isaiah 29:13 pointed this out long ago: “Because this people draws near with their mouth and honors me with their lips, but they have removed their heart far from me.” Brothers and sisters, what the spiritual life should fear most isn’t being out of practice; it’s being “too familiar”. Too familiar, and you don’t have to think; no need to think, no need to ask; no need to ask, no need to rely.

Three Places Where Things Most Easily Go Wrong

The lesson singles out three conditions: when we’ve served a long time, when we’ve gained a lot of experience, and when our skills have become second nature.

Then we begin to say three things: it’s fine without praying; it’s fine without seeking; it’s fine without waiting.

No one would ever say these sentences out loud, yet they are an honest record of our diaries. When you find the time spent doing growing longer and the time spent waiting growing shorter; when you find yourself saying “I don’t know” less and less; when your first thought in a difficulty is “I’ll find a way” rather than “Lord, how do you see this?” — brothers and sisters, the alarm bell is already ringing.

Scripture has a heartbreaking example. In Joshua 9, the Gibeonites came with mouldy bread and split wineskins to deceive Israel. Joshua 9:14 records the reason for Israel’s failure: “The men sampled their provisions, and didn’t ask counsel from Yahweh’s mouth.” It wasn’t that their judgement was poor; it was that, that one time, they didn’t ask. Fresh from the great victory at Jericho, that was precisely when they least felt the need to ask.

The Result: The More We Do, the More Tired and Empty We Become

The lesson says: the more we do, the more tired we get, the emptier we become, the less life there is.

That is the very portrait of the church in Ephesus. The Lord commended their toil, their perseverance and their ability to discern false teaching, and then said, “But I have this against you, that you left your first love” (Revelation 2:4). Full marks for ministry; a failing grade for love.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. When ministry runs ahead of life, ministry begins to devour people. It isn’t ministry that crushes you; it’s “doing ministry by relying on yourself” that crushes you.

Applying the 321 Vision: Selflessness Overcomes Satan

Why is “once we can do it, we stop relying” so dangerous? Because its root is pride.

321 puts it penetratingly: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place.
