When I stop relying on the Holy Spirit because “I know how now”, I am doing God’s work while sitting in God’s seat. Isaiah 14:13–14 records what Satan said in his heart: “I will ascend into heaven! I will exalt my throne above the stars of God! … I will make myself like the Most High!” Those “I will”s are the template of the self-centred life.

That is why 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. The way to deal with “once we can do it, we stop relying” isn’t to do a little less. It is, in every single thing “I’m best at”, to deliberately return to our originally intended position and say once again, “Lord, without you I can do nothing.”

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Real Cause of Spiritual Dryness
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if I asked you, “Why have you been so dry spiritually lately?”, the lesson has already listed the three answers we most often give: too busy, too tired, bad circumstances.

All three answers sound reasonable, and they’re often true. But the lesson tells us that none of them is the real cause. There is only one real cause: we have left the system of relying on the Holy Spirit.

The Difference Between the Disease and the Symptoms

Too busy, too tired, bad circumstances — these are symptoms, not the disease.

When a person relies on the Holy Spirit, he can be busy and still have peace; when a person relies on himself, he can be idle and still dry up. On Mount Carmel, in a single day, Elijah took on four hundred and fifty prophets of Baal and then ran ahead of Ahab’s chariot — busy to the utmost, yet full of power. But one threatening message from Jezebel, and he fled into the wilderness, sat down under a broom tree and asked to die. The same man, the same God — what changed was where his eyes were fixed.

Jeremiah 2:13 says, “For my people have committed two evils: they have forsaken me, the spring of living waters, and cut out cisterns for themselves: broken cisterns that can’t hold water.” Look carefully at the order: first they forsook the spring, and then they went to cut out cisterns. A spring takes no effort; it wells up on its own. A cistern takes effort, and it cracks. People who rely on themselves are forever cutting out cisterns, and the harder they dig, the more it proves how far they are from the spring.

Symptom 1: Devotions Become a Duty

The lesson’s first example pierces many hearts: Bible reading becomes a task, prayer becomes a formality, and the result is that the more devotions we do, the less we want to do them.

That is a vitally important observation. If our devotions are an encounter with God, how could anyone want to see him less the more they meet him? Unless it isn’t an encounter at all, but just getting the job done.

Psychology offers some corroboration here. Self-determination theory, developed from the 1980s by the University of Rochester psychologists Edward Deci and Richard Ryan, distinguishes between autonomous motivation and controlled motivation. When an activity springs from inner meaning and free choice, people show lasting engagement and vitality; once it is taken over by external rules, evaluation or pressure, intrinsic motivation is eroded and engagement actually drops. Turning “I want to” into “I have to” is the quickest way to put out a fire.

Brothers and sisters, this is the double edge of a Bible-reading plan. The plan itself is good; it is a tool. But when the plan becomes the master, Bible reading shifts from “What does the Lord want to say to me today?” to “How many chapters am I behind today?” How many chapters you’re behind can be counted; what the Lord says cannot. And our nature always prefers what can be counted — because that is what I can control.

In 1 Samuel 15:22, Samuel says to Saul, “To obey is better than sacrifice, and to listen than the fat of rams.” Saul’s sacrifice was real, the sheep were real, the outward show of piety was real; the problem was that he hadn’t listened. In sacrifice, I bring something to God; in obedience, I hand myself over to God. The first I can do by relying on myself; the second is impossible without relying on the Holy Spirit.

So the way to restore our devotions isn’t to step up the reading plan; it is to return to encounter. Psalm 46:10 says, “Be still, and know that I am God.” First be still, and then you will know. People who cannot stop will never meet God.

Symptom 2: Service Loses Its Joy — a Fish Out of Water

The lesson’s second example uses a wonderfully vivid image: doing a great deal without any life is like a fish out of water. The best fish food in the world won’t help, because the environment is wrong.

Scientifically, the image is spot on. A fish out of water dies, not because there’s no oxygen in the air — the air actually holds far more oxygen than water does. It dies because in water its gill filaments are held open by buoyancy, keeping up an enormous surface for exchange; once out of the water, the filaments stick together and collapse, the surface area plummets, and even surrounded by oxygen-rich air it can’t get oxygen into its blood. The oxygen is right there beside it, yet it suffocates.

Brothers and sisters, a servant of God who has left the Holy Spirit doesn’t dry up for lack of resources. He is surrounded by sermons, courses, materials and applause — resources galore. He dries up because he has left the environment in which grace can be absorbed.

Jesus said the same thing even more directly. John 15:5: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” The word for “remains” is μένω (menō), meaning “to settle down, to stay, not to move out”. The Lord doesn’t ask the branches to strive to bear fruit; he only asks them to stay on the vine. Take a branch that has been cut off from the vine, plant it in the richest soil, tie the loveliest grapes onto it — it is still withered. Brothers and sisters, have you ever tried “tying on grapes” in your service? Fruit on the outside, no sap within.

Jeremiah 17:7–8 gives us the positive picture: “Blessed is the man who trusts in Yahweh, and whose confidence is in Yahweh. For he will be as a tree planted by the waters, who spreads out its roots by the river, and will not fear when heat comes, but its leaf will be green, and will not be concerned in the year of drought. It won’t cease from yielding fruit.” This tree meets the same heat and the same year of drought; the difference is that its roots are set down beside the water. In the same drought year, the bush on the salt land withers, while the tree by the water never stops bearing fruit.

So, brothers and sisters, let’s stop blaming our dryness on our circumstances. The problem isn’t the drought year; the problem is where the roots are set.

Applying the 321 Vision: Life First, Then Relationships, Then Ministry

Here the 321 order shows how wise it is: life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is just as clear: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last of all with things.

Spiritual dryness is almost always the result of the order being turned upside down — things running ahead of people, and people running ahead of God. When the day comes that you find there’s no sap left in your heart, it’s usually not because you’ve done too much, but because you’ve given the first-place seat to what belongs fourth.

321 also says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Proverbs 4:23 says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” When all that’s left of our service is the brain, troubles pile up; when our service returns to the heart, joy comes back.

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Key to Preaching and Serving
sections.html:
Here the lesson turns its lens on the most spiritual arena of all — preaching. For the place Satan most loves to hide is often the holiest place.

Materials Aren’t the Problem; Reliance Is

The lesson is very balanced: “The materials themselves aren’t the problem. The key is this — are you relying on the materials, or letting the Holy Spirit use them?”

We need to hear this clearly: 321 never tells anyone to despise preparation. The Bible is my standard, and that requires us to study it diligently. Getting up to speak without preparing isn’t spiritual; it’s lazy. And calling laziness “leaving it to the Holy Spirit” is an affront to the Holy Spirit.

The real difference isn’t whether there’s a sermon manuscript, but in whose hands the manuscript lies. The rod in Moses’ hand was an ordinary shepherd’s staff. Held in a man’s hand, it was only wood; stretched out at God’s command, it parted the Red Sea. The rod didn’t change; whose command it obeyed was the key.

Relying on the Manuscript: Content, but No Life

We’ve all heard that kind of message: neatly structured, richly referenced, perfectly timed — and when it’s over, nothing has happened. We’ve all heard the other kind too: the speaker may even stumble over his words, but one sentence flies into your heart like an arrow, and you weep all the way home.

1 Corinthians 2:4–5: “My speech and my preaching were not in persuasive words of human wisdom, but in demonstration of the Spirit and of power, that your faith wouldn’t stand in the wisdom of men, but in the power of God.” Paul didn’t want people to admire him; he wanted their faith “not to stand in the wisdom of men”. A message that relies on self, even when it succeeds, only brings people to the preacher; a message that relies on the Holy Spirit brings people to God.

This is exactly the Two Core Values of 321: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The deepest battle in the pulpit has never been over content; it has always been over who gets the glory.

The nineteenth-century missionary Hudson Taylor is generally credited with saying, “God’s work done in God’s way will never lack God’s supply.” The weight falls on the middle phrase — in God’s way. The same work of God, done in man’s way, has to be propped up by man’s strength; only when it’s done in God’s way does it have God’s supply.

Relying on the Holy Spirit: Life, Power, and Hearts Touched

The lesson says the results of relying on the Holy Spirit are three: life, power, and the ability to touch people’s hearts. And the reason comes down to one sentence: “because the Holy Spirit knows what people really need.”

When we prepare, we are facing “a general congregation”. The Holy Spirit is facing the sister who had a row with her husband just this morning, the brother who got his medical results yesterday, the young person who has already decided this will be the last time he comes. However good our materials, they can only reach “people in general”; the Holy Spirit can reach “that one”.

1 Corinthians 2:10 says, “But to us, God revealed them through the Spirit. For the Spirit searches all things, yes, the deep things of God.”

And in 2 Corinthians 3:5 Paul says, “Not that we are sufficient of ourselves, to account anything as from ourselves; but our sufficiency is from God.”

Brothers and sisters, this section isn’t only for preachers. An email you write at work, a sentence you say to your child at home, a message you reply to in a group chat — each one can be done relying on your materials or relying on the Holy Spirit. You can rely on your arguments to win against your child, or you can rely on the Holy Spirit to speak into your child’s heart. With the first you’ll win, but both of you will lose; only the second brings life.

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. That holds true in the pulpit, and it holds just as true at the dinner table.

Applying the 321 Vision: Let the Holy Spirit Use the Five Loaves and Two Fish in Your Hands

The five loaves and two fish in a boy’s hands could never have fed five thousand people. But placed in Jesus’ hands — given thanks for and broken — there was more than enough.

Your sermon notes, your professional expertise, your experience — these are your five loaves and two fish. 321 doesn’t tell you to throw them away; it tells you to hand them over. Handing them over is letting Jesus be King; being broken is selflessness; and when twelve baskets are left over, giving the glory to the Lord is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: Relying on the Holy Spirit as a Practical Way of Life
sections.html:
Someone may say: relying on the Holy Spirit sounds beautiful, but it’s too abstract. What exactly am I supposed to do?

The lesson answers without hesitation: “Relying on the Holy Spirit isn’t abstract; it is a concrete way of living.” Then it gives us five very workable sentences.

Three “Firsts”: Pray First, Seek First, Wait First

One: before making a decision, pray first.

Two: before acting, seek first.

Three: before speaking, wait first.

Brothers and sisters, notice what these three sentences have in common: each contains the word “first”. The line between relying on the Holy Spirit and relying on ourselves is often only a few seconds wide — those few seconds before you press “send”, those few seconds before you open your mouth.

James 1:19 says, “So, then, my beloved brothers, let every man be swift to hear, slow to speak, and slow to anger.” The order of swift and slow is the spiritual order.

In 2 Samuel 5, David twice faced the same Philistine army. The first time he inquired of Yahweh, God said, “Go up,” and he won. The second time — same enemy, same place — he inquired again, but God’s answer was different: “You shall not go up. Circle around behind them, and attack them in front of the mulberry trees” (2 Samuel 5:23). Had David relied the second time on his experience from the first, he would not have won. God’s leading is living; it can’t be copied and pasted.

Two “Don’ts”: Don’t Rush to React, Don’t Rely on Feelings

Four: don’t rush to react; ask the Holy Spirit first.

Five: don’t rely on feelings; rely on guidance.

The first “don’t” deals with impulse; the second deals with emotion. The old advice to “count to ten before you speak” has something to it. But, brothers and sisters, a Christian’s “wait a moment” isn’t just waiting for the emotion to pass; it is waiting for the Holy Spirit to speak. The world counts to ten; we ask the Lord.

“Don’t rely on feelings; rely on guidance” is a vitally important balance. Some people take “relying on the Holy Spirit” to mean “going by feelings” — if I feel moved, I do it; if I don’t, I don’t. That is dangerous. The Three Foundations of 321 settle this once and for all: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide — and the three never fight one another. Any prompting that goes against the teaching of Scripture is not the Holy Spirit.

John 16:13 says, “However when he, the Spirit of truth, has come, he will guide you into all truth, for he will not speak from himself; but whatever he hears, he will speak.” See — even the Holy Spirit “will not speak from himself”. Selflessness is, in fact, the very nature of God himself.

The Result: Life Grows Lighter, Work Grows More Joyful

The lesson says a life like this brings a change: the more we live, the lighter it grows; the more we do, the more joyful we become; and more and more, we have God’s presence.

Notice that the lesson uses “the more … the more” — this is a rising curve, the exact opposite of the falling curve of relying on ourselves: “the more we do, the more tired and empty we become”.

The “broaden-and-build theory” put forward by the University of North Carolina psychologist Barbara Fredrickson holds that positive emotions broaden a person’s attention and range of thought and action, and over time build up physical, intellectual, social and psychological resources, while negative emotions narrow our attention. Joyful people see more widely and think further ahead; anxious people find their field of vision growing narrower and their road running into a dead end.

Isaiah 40:31 says it more beautifully still: “But those who wait for Yahweh will renew their strength. They will mount up with wings like eagles. They will run, and not be weary. They will walk, and not faint.”

Brothers and sisters, the eagle isn’t the bird best at flapping its wings. What makes the eagle remarkable is that it can find a rising current of air, spread its wings and let the wind lift it up. When it flies highest is exactly when it is working least.

In both Hebrew and Greek, the word for “spirit” (רוּחַ ruach / πνεῦμα pneuma) also means “wind”. Jesus says in John 3:8, “The wind blows where it wants to, and you hear its sound, but don’t know where it comes from and where it is going. So is everyone who is born of the Spirit.”

Brothers and sisters, our lives can be like a rowing boat or like a sailing boat. A rower goes only as far as his strength will take him; a sailor does just one thing — he raises the sail and sets it to the wind. This morning, are you rowing, or are you sailing?

Applying the 321 Vision: The 920 Practice

321 has a very concrete practice called 920: every person who is in relationship with us is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless (0) life before them, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions.

The fruit of the Spirit isn’t grown in the prayer closet; it’s grown in relationships. Patience only comes out when someone provokes you; gentleness only shows when someone talks back to you. That’s why God has placed your spouse, your colleagues and that relative you find hardest to get on with right beside you — they are your “2”.

And the key to the fruit of the Spirit is the “0” in the middle. In relationships, the self-centred bear temper; the selfless, in exactly the same relationships, bear fruit. That is the theme of this whole lesson from beginning to end.

sections.heading: Key Point 6: The Crucial Spiritual Shifts
sections.html:
Finally the lesson distils everything into two shifts. They’re short enough to write on a sticky note, yet powerful enough to turn a whole life around.

The first shift: from “I’ll do it” to “Lord, you do it”

This isn’t doing nothing; it’s changing who does it.

The classic contrast in Scripture is Peter. In Luke 5:5 he says to Jesus, “Master, we worked all night, and took nothing; but at your word I will let down the net.” “We worked all night” is the limit of relying on himself — he was a professional fisherman, he had spent the longest possible time at the thing he was best at, and he had caught nothing. “But at your word” is the moment of the shift. The result: they “caught a great multitude of fish, and their net was breaking” (Luke 5:6).

Notice this: Jesus didn’t let down the net for Peter. Peter still let down the net; the boat was still Peter’s; the effort was still Peter’s. Only one thing changed — this time he let it down at the Lord’s word.

That is the true meaning of “Lord, you do it.” It isn’t me lying still and doing nothing; it is my doing beginning from his word.

The second shift: from “I know how to do it” to “Holy Spirit, guide me”

This shift is harder than the first.

“I’ll do it” still carries some toil; people get tired, and when they’re tired they’re willing to turn back. But “I know how to do it” carries a sense of satisfaction — it’s ability, it’s confidence, it’s other people’s approval. Getting someone to put down a heavy load isn’t hard; getting someone to put down their self-confidence is very hard.

In Revelation 3:17 the Lord says to the church in Laodicea, “Because you say, ‘I am rich, and have gotten riches, and have need of nothing;’ and don’t know that you are the wretched one, miserable, poor, blind, and naked.” It isn’t that they were poor and didn’t know it; it’s that they thought themselves rich and so didn’t know they were poor. Those words “need of nothing” are the death certificate of the spiritual life — because a person who lacks nothing will never reach out a hand.

So this second shift needs, not an increase of knowledge, but a lowering of the heart.

This Is the Heart of Selflessness

The lesson closes this point with one sentence: this is the heart of selflessness.

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Galatians 2:20 is the root of that saying: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.”

Brothers and sisters, hear this clearly: selflessness doesn’t turn you into zero; it connects you to the infinite. A drop of water in the palm of your hand evaporates in a few minutes; pour the same drop into the ocean, and it becomes as vast as the ocean. Selflessness isn’t disappearing; it’s returning to your rightful place. John the Baptist put it most simply: “He must increase, but I must decrease” (John 3:30).

From beginning to end, this lesson is really about one thing: let God be God. Those who rely on themselves are doing God’s work but not letting God be God; those who rely on the Holy Spirit return to man’s originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Let’s set today’s message into the whole picture of 321 and look at it once more.

The Three Foundations Are the Three Rails of Relying on the Holy Spirit

Jesus is my role model — at the Lord’s baptism the Holy Spirit came down on him; when he was tempted, he was led by the Spirit into the wilderness; when he began to preach, he said, “The Spirit of the Lord is on me” (Luke 4:18). If even the Lord relied on the Holy Spirit, how can we rely on ourselves?

The Bible is my standard — this keeps “relying on the Holy Spirit” from sliding into “going by feelings”. The Holy Spirit inspired Scripture and never contradicts it; the better you know the Bible, the better you can discern what is the Holy Spirit’s voice.

The Holy Spirit is my guide — Romans 8:14: “For as many as are led by the Spirit of God, these are children of God.”

The Three Foundations are one whole: take away Scripture, and relying on the Spirit becomes doing as we please; take away the Spirit, and reading Scripture becomes mere knowledge of the letter.

The Two Core Values Decide Whom I Really Rely On

Let Jesus be King — when I say, “Lord, you do it,” I am handing the throne back to him in that one small matter. The throne isn’t handed over once and for all; it’s handed over a hundred times a day.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — this is the most honest measuring stick for testing whom we rely on. When something has gone well, what is your first thought? If it’s “Good thing I had the experience,” you know whom you relied on just now; if it’s “Lord, you did this,” then you’ve got it right. Those who rely on themselves are most exhausted after success, because they have to keep that image propped up; those who rely on the Holy Spirit are lightest after success, because the glory was never theirs in the first place.

The Goal: Establish God’s System

From the very start the lesson used the word “system” — relying on self is the system of the self-centred life; relying on the Holy Spirit is the system of selflessness. This is the core concern of 321.

The Babylonian system relies on man, on self, on ability, on control; God’s system relies on God, on the Holy Spirit, on grace, on entrusting. A person can be sitting in church and still be living in the Babylonian system — that is the most sobering reminder of this lesson. Relying on the Holy Spirit isn’t a one-off decision; it is the exchange of an entire system.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

Mindset: from “I must get this done well” to “I will let the Holy Spirit do it.”

Life: from pressure, exhaustion and dryness to peace, joy and lightness.

Daily living: from rushing to react to praying first, seeking first and waiting first.

Relationships: from relying on arguments to win people over to relying on the Holy Spirit to speak into their hearts.

Ministry: from content without life to life, power and hearts touched.

This order can’t be reversed. Many people want to change their ministry directly — new methods, new materials, new venues — but refuse to change their mindset, and so they simply carry on relying on themselves in a new place. If the headwaters aren’t clear, the river downstream will be muddy.

The Shift in Perspective

From man’s view to God’s: man looks and says, “How capable he is!”; God looks to see whether he is willing to rely on him.

From the earthly to the heavenly: earth counts output; heaven counts connection.

From the temporary to the eternal: relying on ourselves may get us through this one round; only relying on the Holy Spirit will carry us through the whole of life.

From the worldly to the godly: the law of the world is “the stronger the better”; the law of God is, “For when I am weak, then am I strong” (2 Corinthians 12:10).

The 235 Relationships

A life of relying on the Holy Spirit isn’t something you practise hidden away on your own. The 235 relationships of 321 give us a concrete path:

The “2” — find a spiritual companion who is equally willing to be selfless, and ask each other the question others don’t dare to ask: “That thing you did — did you do it relying on yourself, or relying on the Holy Spirit?”

The “3” — establish spiritual parents and spiritual children. The most important lesson spiritual parents pass on isn’t their methods but their reliance. If you pass on only methods, you’ll multiply a crowd of people who are even better at relying on themselves.

The “5” — work alongside spiritual comrades in a fivefold-ministry team. God never puts anyone in the position of fighting alone, because those who fight alone will always end up relying on themselves.

The order of the Path of Serving is: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). The very first step is “Spirit”. Relying on the Holy Spirit isn’t one link among many in serving; it is the first step of serving. Get the first step wrong, and every step after it will veer off course.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three exercises. Let’s use the eight stages of changing our mindset in 321 — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take these three exercises deep.

Exercise 1: Turn to the Holy Spirit First in Everything

The lesson says: before making a decision, stop and pray first; learn to rely on the Holy Spirit rather than immediately using your own judgement.

Information: Proverbs 3:5–6: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.” Underline “In all your ways” — all of them, not just the few big ones.

Revelation and Conviction: be still and ask the Lord: which matter this week did it never even occur to me to ask you about? And admit: my judgement is limited, and the more sure of myself I am, the less I ask.

Implementation and Evaluation: set an action so small it can’t fail — for the next seven days, every time you’re about to reply to a message that stirs your emotions, close your eyes first and pray one line: “Lord, how do you want me to reply?” Each evening spend two minutes writing two lines: Which matter did I ask the Lord about first today? Which did I forget to ask about?

Correction and Repetition: if you forget two days running, find the time of day when you’re most likely to slip and set a reminder there. If a week isn’t enough, do it for a full forty days. Habits aren’t formed by resolve; they’re formed by repetition.

Multiplication: pass this exercise on to a brother or sister, and check in with each other once a week. As you pass it on, you’ll do it more genuinely yourself.

Exercise 2: Rely on God Even in What Is Familiar

The lesson says: especially in the things you’re “best at”, deliberately practise seeking the Holy Spirit’s guidance.

Information: Galatians 3:3: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”

Revelation and Conviction: quietly ask the Lord — what have I become “too good at”, so good that I no longer need to ask you? My profession? My ministry? The way I bring up my children? Then admit it: skill is grace, not entitlement.

Implementation and Evaluation: this week, choose the one thing you’re “best at”, and before you do it, add thirty seconds of prayer: “Lord, I know this well, but I don’t want to do it out of familiarity. Please come and do it yourself today.” Afterwards ask yourself: how was this time different from usual?

Correction and Repetition: if after praying you still slip into the old groove, deliberately change one small thing so you can’t run on autopilot; and make those thirty seconds a fixture until they are more familiar to you than your routine.

Multiplication: raise it with your team of co-workers: before we start serving, shall we first ask the Lord one question together?

Exercise 3: Restore Living Devotions

The lesson says: don’t just complete your devotions; meet God, and ask the Holy Spirit to speak to you.

Information: Psalm 46:10: “Be still, and know that I am God.” John 15:5: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit.”

Revelation and Conviction: let the Holy Spirit show you when your devotions shifted from “encounter” to “getting the job done”; and believe that what God wants is you yourself, not your reading schedule.

Implementation and Evaluation: this week, cut three chapters down to three verses. When you’ve read them, don’t hurry on; stay there and ask: what kind of God are you in this verse? What is this verse saying to me today? How should I respond to you? Then be quiet for two minutes. After a week, ask honestly: do I want to meet the Lord more now, or less?

Correction and Repetition: if it’s still dry, try a different approach — pray through a psalm, or sing a hymn first, or change the time or the place; the form exists for the sake of the encounter. And make “meeting God” the one measure of success for your devotions.

Multiplication: pass on to someone, that same day, one sentence you received; the sentence you share will live longer in you.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s closing word says two beautiful things:

When you rely on yourself, even the simplest thing becomes a burden;

when you rely on the Holy Spirit, even the hardest thing becomes light.

We often think the difference between light and heavy lies in the size of the task. It doesn’t. The same task is heavy when we rely on ourselves and light when we rely on the Holy Spirit, because the weight was never in the task; it is in the person carrying it.

At the very end the lesson sets the choice before us: rely on yourself, and you head towards weariness; rely on the Holy Spirit, and you head towards victory. And the lesson’s gentle reminder is like a needle that goes in at exactly the right spot: “The question isn’t how much you do, but whether you are still relying on yourself.”

This morning I want to invite you to make a choice. Not a choice to try harder — you’ve tried hard enough. Not a choice to do more — you’ve done more than enough. It is the choice to hand the steering wheel you’ve been gripping all this time back to the Holy Spirit.

Let Jesus be King again over your schedule, King over the very thing you’re most skilled at, King over your pulpit, your kitchen and your office.

Let’s say the lesson’s declaration of faith together:

Lord, I will no longer lean on my own understanding;

I will trust in you with all my heart,

and rely in everything on the guidance of the Holy Spirit,

so that my life is no longer dry,

but lives out your life and your power.

Today, let’s choose afresh — to return to the Holy Spirit’s leading. May all the glory go to Jesus.

keyVerses: Proverbs 3:5–6: “Trust in Yahweh with all your heart, and don’t lean on your own understanding. In all your ways acknowledge him, and he will make your paths straight.”
Galatians 3:3: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?”
Romans 8:13: “For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.”
practices: Turn to the Holy Spirit first in everything
Rely on God even in what is familiar
prayer: Dear Heavenly Father, we thank you for shining your word on us this morning.

Lord, we confess that we often do your work in our own strength. Once we’re skilled, we stop asking; once we know how, we stop waiting. We have put experience in place of your guidance and busyness in place of fellowship with you. Please forgive us.
Lord Jesus, on earth you said, “The Son can do nothing of himself.” Remove the stubborn “self” within us, so that it is no longer we who live, but Christ who lives in us.

Holy Spirit, come and guide us afresh: remind us to pray before we make decisions, lead us to seek before we act, and teach us to wait before we speak. Make our devotions once again an encounter with you, and make our homes, our workplaces and our fellowship places where God’s system is established. Make us like a tree planted by the waters, unconcerned in the year of drought and never ceasing to bear fruit.
Reign as King in our lives, and may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Galatians 3:3: “Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” Share: what is one area of your life that you “began in the Spirit” but have gradually been trying to complete by relying on yourself? How did you rely on God at the start? And when did you stop relying on him?

John 15:5: “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” Share: this week, in which thing you’re “best at” will you concretely practise praying first, seeking first and waiting first? Name one question the members of your group can ask you next time.
