sections.heading: Introduction: You Don’t Live in Your Circumstances — You Live in Your Choices
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, peace be with you. Today we come together to Lesson 108 of 321 Morning Devotion, and our theme is “A Change in Our Choices (6): By Faith or by Sight, Love or Hate.”

First, I’d like you to think about something. From the moment you opened your eyes this morning until now, how many choices have you already made?

What time to get up — that was a choice. Whether to pray first or check your phone first — that was a choice. When you saw that message that left you uneasy inside, whether to reply to it straight away — that was a choice too. Most of these choices are so small we don’t even notice them, yet one after another, day after day, they slowly pile up into our character, and pile up into our destiny.

We think we live in our circumstances, but in fact we live in our choices. Circumstances are only the stage; our choices are the script.

And among the thousands upon thousands of choices we make, two are the most decisive — so decisive that they can set the course of our whole life.

The first choice is this: will I live by faith, or by sight?

The second choice is this: will I choose love, or will I choose hate?

Brothers and sisters, these two choices sound simple, yet the difference between them is not merely a difference in behaviour; it is the difference between two systems of life.

Living by sight and hate belong to the system of the self-centred life; living by faith and love belong to the system of selflessness.

The self-centred system has self at the centre: what I see, what I feel, whether my rights have been infringed, whether I’m getting the short end of the stick.

The selfless system has God at the centre: what God has said, what God wants to do, how God’s love can flow out through me.

However you choose, that is the life you will live in.

This lesson is not about gritting our teeth and becoming better people. It is about seeing that every single day, God sets “life and death, the blessing and the curse” before us and lets us choose. On the east side of the Jordan, Moses said to the Israelites: “I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants” (Deuteronomy 30:19).

God never forces us. He respects our choices, yet he longs deeply for us to choose rightly.

This morning, let’s learn together about these two life-changing choices.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: An Apostle Who Still Lifted His Head in Affliction
sections.html:
Let’s begin with the background of our key passages.

“For we walk by faith, not by sight.” These words come from 2 Corinthians 5:7. The author is the apostle Paul, writing somewhere between AD 55 and 57, probably from Macedonia, to the church in Corinth.

Corinth was then the capital of the province of Achaia, an international trading port on an isthmus — fabulously wealthy and equally notorious. It was a city of the “seen”: you could see the wealth, you could see the lust, you could see the eloquence of the philosophers. The Corinthians were used to sizing up everything with their eyes, and they sized up Paul with their eyes too. They sneered that “his bodily presence is weak, and his speech is despised” (2 Corinthians 10:10), because to their eyes Paul simply didn’t look like a successful man.

And when Paul wrote 2 Corinthians, he was in the middle of very deep affliction. He says so himself: “our affliction which happened to us in Asia, that we were weighed down exceedingly, beyond our power, so much that we despaired even of life” (2 Corinthians 1:8).

Please notice: the man who says “by faith, not by sight” is not someone for whom life has been plain sailing, someone floating above the troubles of this world. He is a man who has been stoned, beaten with rods, shipwrecked three times, and has spent a night and a day in the deep (see 2 Corinthians 11:25).

It was in exactly that situation that Paul wrote, in chapter 4, the key to the whole letter: “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day” (2 Corinthians 4:16). And then he says: “while we don’t look at the things which are seen, but at the things which are not seen. For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

As for our second key passage, 1 John 3:18, it was written by the apostle John in his old age, sometime between AD 85 and 95, to the churches around Asia Minor. In those days the church was under the influence of early Gnosticism: some people talked grandly about spiritual knowledge yet looked down on what was done in the body; with their mouths they said they loved God, while in practice they hated their own brothers. So John tied “truth” and “deeds” tightly together: “My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth” (1 John 3:18).

One is about “faith,” the other about “love”; one concerns how we see, the other how we live. Put these two verses together and you have the two main threads of today’s lesson.

sections.heading: 1. By Faith: Seeing What Cannot Be Seen
sections.html:
“For we walk by faith, not by sight.” (2 Corinthians 5:7)

What does it mean to live by faith?

Brothers and sisters, I want first to clear up a very common misunderstanding. Living by faith does not mean “not seeing,” nor does it mean shutting your eyes and pretending the problem isn’t there.

Living by faith means “seeing what God has said.”

The original language is fascinating here. “By faith” in Greek is dia pisteos, and the word pistis means both “faith” and “faithfulness.” In other words, my faith stands firm not because my faith is big enough, but because the God I trust is faithful enough. The weight of faith never rests in faith itself; it rests in the one faith is placed in.

That is why Hebrews gives faith this definition: “Now faith is assurance of things hoped for, proof of things not seen” (Hebrews 11:1).

The Greek word behind “assurance” is hypostasis, meaning “what stands underneath and supports,” a “foundation”; in the business documents of the day it was also used for a “title deed.” The Greek word behind “proof” is elegchos, the “conclusive evidence” presented in a court of law.

Brothers and sisters, what a wonderful way to put it. Faith is not an optimistic mood; faith is a title deed. I don’t yet hold the thing itself in my hand, but I already hold the deed to it — because the signature on it is God’s own.

So then, does what cannot be seen simply not exist?

Brothers and sisters, our physical eyes are limited to begin with. What human beings can see is only a tiny sliver of visible light within the electromagnetic spectrum. To use eyes as limited as these to pass judgement on an infinite God is itself the deepest pride of the self-centred life.

Let’s look at a scientific fact. In December 1995 the Hubble Space Telescope was pointed at a patch of sky in Ursa Major that seemed completely empty — a patch so small it was only about one twenty-four-millionth of the whole sky — less than a hundredth of the apparent area of the moon. The telescope kept exposing that spot for ten days. When the image was processed, astronomers were stunned: in that tiny bit of darkness where there was “nothing,” more than three thousand galaxies were packed together. This is the famous Hubble Deep Field.

Not being able to see has never meant that nothing is there. It only means we haven’t kept the shutter open long enough.

Brothers and sisters, faith is that act of keeping the shutter open. You set your heart toward God’s promises and gaze at them, quietly and steadily, and the unseen glory will come into view little by little.

The lesson uses a very homely yet very precise picture: a hen sitting on her eggs.

Day after day the hen sits in the nest. What does she see with her eyes? Eggs. Cold, hard, motionless eggs. From beginning to end, all she ever sees are eggs.

But what does she believe in? Chicks.

So she is willing to pay the price. How long does a hen sit on her eggs? A full twenty-one days. Through those twenty-one days she hardly leaves the nest, getting off only briefly each day to drink and eat, and she has to turn the eggs with her beak at regular intervals so that every side is evenly warmed. She is not waiting for a miracle; she is taking part in a process.

For twenty-one days, what she sees is still eggs. Until, on the twenty-first day, the first tap comes from inside a shell.

Brothers and sisters, do you have an “egg” you have been sitting on in prayer for a long, long time? What you see is still an egg, you can’t hear a sound, and you have even begun to wonder whether the egg is empty after all.

Here are the three movements of faith: seeing the promise, trusting God, and waiting steadfastly.

Every one of the heroes of faith in Hebrews was like this. “By faith, Abraham, when he was called, obeyed to go out to the place which he was to receive for an inheritance. He went out, not knowing where he went” (Hebrews 11:8). As for Moses, “By faith, he left Egypt, not fearing the wrath of the king; for he endured, as seeing him who is invisible” (Hebrews 11:27).

“As seeing him who is invisible” — brothers and sisters, please treasure these words in your heart. This is what it means to live by faith.

Psychology, too, confirms from another angle the principle that what we believe determines what we do. In 1977 the Stanford psychologist Albert Bandura put forward the theory of “self-efficacy,” showing that a person’s belief about whether they “can do it” directly affects whether they are willing to try, how long they persevere when they hit difficulties, and how they finally perform. People who believe they can do it hold on longer; people who don’t often give up before they have truly failed.

Of course, brothers and sisters, a Christian’s faith rises far above “self-efficacy.” Self-efficacy is believing in yourself; our faith is believing in God. If even “believing in yourself” can produce such great power, how much greater the power that comes from “believing in the God who created heaven and earth”?

Seen through the 321 vision, living by faith is the concrete practice of the foundation “the Bible is my standard.” For those who live by sight, the standard is their circumstances; for those who live by faith, the standard is God’s word. Living by faith is also a great shift of perspective: from a human perspective to God’s perspective; from an earthly perspective to a heavenly one; from a temporary perspective to an eternal one; from a worldly perspective to a godly one.

Martin Luther King Jr. is generally credited with saying: “Faith is taking the first step even when you don’t see the whole staircase.”

Brothers and sisters, God usually won’t light up the whole staircase for you. He lights only the next step. And as you step onto it, the second step lights up.

sections.heading: 2. By Sight: Living Within Our Own Judgement
sections.html:
Then what does it mean to live by sight?

The lesson puts it very clearly: living by sight means three things — looking at our circumstances, looking at our resources, and looking at our feelings.

Looking at our circumstances — is the present situation in my favour?

Looking at our resources — do I have the money, the connections, the certainty?

Looking at our feelings — am I in a good mood today? Do I feel at peace?

Brothers and sisters, please notice that none of these three is a sin in itself. God gave us eyes so that we would observe; God gave us reason so that we would judge. The problem is not the “looking”; the problem is making what we see our final standard.

What does living by sight lead to? The lesson lists three things: we become anxious easily, afraid easily, and quick to retreat.

Why? Because circumstances change every day, our resources are often lacking, and our feelings are even less dependable. Build the foundation of your life on something that changes every day, and of course you will be anxious.

Neuroscience makes the mechanism clear. When the brain’s amygdala detects a threat signal, within a fraction of a second it triggers the “fight-or-flight” response: the heart races, breathing quickens, the muscles tense, and at the same time the prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for rational thought, is temporarily suppressed. That is why people in a panic say things they later regret and make decisions they later can hardly believe they made.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 says: rely on the brain and ourselves, and we worry; rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, and we rejoice.

The sharpest contrast in the Bible is between Abraham and Lot. The two of them started from exactly the same place: they came out of Ur together, walked the same road together, saw the land of Canaan together. They were uncle and nephew — family.

The turning point comes in Genesis 13. Their herdsmen quarrelled, and Abram said to Lot: “Please, let there be no strife between you and me, and between your herdsmen and my herdsmen; for we are relatives. Isn’t the whole land before you? Please separate yourself from me. If you go to the left hand, then I will go to the right. Or if you go to the right hand, then I will go to the left” (Genesis 13:8–9).

Look — Abram was the elder, and by the customs of the time the right to choose first was his. Yet he laid that right down. Brothers and sisters, this is what 321 means by “humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position.”

Then the Bible says: “Lot lifted up his eyes, and saw all the plain of the Jordan, that it was well-watered everywhere, before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah, like the garden of Yahweh, like the land of Egypt, as you go to Zoar. So Lot chose the Plain of the Jordan for himself. Lot traveled east, and they separated themselves from one other” (Genesis 13:10–11).

“Lifted up his eyes, and saw” — Lot used his eyes. What he saw was lushness, prosperity, gain he could cash in right away. The text adds a pointed aside: “before Yahweh destroyed Sodom and Gomorrah.” This is the Holy Spirit reminding us that everything Lot saw had an expiry date.

Then the text says: “Yahweh said to Abram, after Lot was separated from him, ‘Now, lift up your eyes, and look from the place where you are, northward and southward and eastward and westward, for I will give all the land which you see to you and to your offspring forever’” (Genesis 13:14–15).

Brothers and sisters, did you notice? Both men “lifted up their eyes and looked” — but one lifted his eyes by himself, and the other lifted his eyes because God told him to.

And how did Lot end up? First he “moved his tent as far as Sodom” (Genesis 13:12); later he was living in the city; and in the end he was sitting in the city gate — which in the ancient world meant he had entered the city’s ruling class. He was no longer just passing through Babylon; he had become part of Babylon.

By Genesis 19, the angels have come: “When the morning came, then the angels hurried Lot, saying, ‘Get up! Take your wife and your two daughters who are here, lest you be consumed in the iniquity of the city.’ But he lingered; and the men grabbed his hand, his wife’s hand, and his two daughters’ hands, Yahweh being merciful to him; and they took him out, and set him outside of the city” (Genesis 19:15–16).

“But he lingered.” Brothers and sisters, those few words are chilling to read. Fire was about to fall, and still he couldn’t bear to let go. What you gain by living by sight will, in the end, wrap itself tightly around your feet.

And Abraham? He became the father of faith. God said to him: “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you” (Genesis 12:3).

The same starting point, different choices, utterly different endings.

Seen through the 321 vision, living by sight is the classic self-centred life: I look, I judge, I decide, I control. And the self-centred life is the very root of humanity’s fall. What did Eve do in the Garden of Eden? “When the woman saw that the tree was good for food, and that it was a delight to the eyes, and that the tree was to be desired to make one wise, she took some of its fruit, and ate” (Genesis 3:6). “Saw,” “a delight to the eyes.” Humanity’s very first failure was living by sight.

So, brothers and sisters, living by sight is no small matter. It is the oldest habit of all, the one the serpent in Eden left us.

sections.heading: 3. Moments of Crisis Reveal Which System You Live In
sections.html:
When things are going smoothly, living by faith and living by sight look the same.

But as the lesson says: when things go smoothly, you can’t tell the difference.

What truly reveals which system we live in are three kinds of moments: crisis, pressure and uncertainty.

Crisis — the doctor clips the scan onto the light box, and his face doesn’t look good.

Pressure — the company announces layoffs, and your name is on the edge of the list.

Uncertainty — your child hasn’t set foot in church for three years, doesn’t answer your messages, and you don’t know what the next step is.

In that moment, you discover: oh, so this is what I really believe deep down.

Brothers and sisters, it’s like a tea bag. Sitting on a dry table, a tea bag doesn’t tell you what kind of tea it is. But drop it into boiling water, and whatever is inside comes steeping out at once.

Affliction is the same. Affliction doesn’t form character; affliction reveals character — and then God uses the choices we make in affliction to form our character.

In “The Problem of Pain” (1940), C. S. Lewis wrote that God whispers to us in our pleasures, speaks in our conscience, but shouts in our pains: pain is his megaphone to rouse a deaf world.

Brothers and sisters, a crisis is not God making things hard for you; a crisis is God waking you up.

The lesson lays out the responses of two kinds of people side by side.

Those who live by sight: they worry, they fear, they want to take control.

Those who live by faith: they look to the Lord, they wait on the Lord, they lean on the Lord.

Have you noticed that “wanting to take control” is the inevitable end point of living by sight? Because when all I can see is my circumstances, and my circumstances are unreliable, my only way out is to grab hold of them myself. So I start manipulating, I start applying pressure, I start arranging for God how he ought to act.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly what 321 calls pride: leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place.

The response of faith is just the opposite: looking up, waiting, leaning. All three are movements of “unclenching the hand.” This is humility: laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God.

Peter walking on the water is the most vivid lesson on faith in the whole Bible.

“But when he saw that the wind was strong, he was afraid, and beginning to sink, he cried out, saying, ‘Lord, save me!’ Immediately Jesus stretched out his hand, took hold of him, and said to him, ‘You of little faith, why did you doubt?’” (Matthew 14:30–31)

Brothers and sisters, please note: the wind didn’t only rise at that moment. When Peter climbed out of the boat, the wind was already strong. What changed was not the wind but Peter’s eyes. At first he was looking at Jesus; later he was looking at the wind.

Faith is usually lost not because the circumstances get worse but because the focus shifts. 321 puts it well: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

That is why the lesson says something very important: faith is not the absence of feelings; it is “choosing to trust God above our feelings.”

Brothers and sisters, please don’t misunderstand faith. Faith is not numbness, not pretending to be strong, not forbidding yourself to cry.

What does David say? “When I am afraid, I will put my trust in you” (Psalm 56:3).

You see, David doesn’t say “I am not afraid”; he says “when I am afraid.” The fear is still there, but in the middle of the fear he makes a choice — to put his trust in you.

And what does that father say? “I believe. Help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24).

Brothers and sisters, today you can choose to believe with trembling hands. God isn’t looking at whether your hands are shaking; God is looking at which way your hands are reaching.

Elisha’s servant got up in the morning, saw the city surrounded by horses, chariots and soldiers, and panicked. Elisha said: “Don’t be afraid; for those who are with us are more than those who are with them.” Then he prayed: “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see.” And what happened? “Yahweh opened the young man’s eyes; and he saw: and behold, the mountain was full of horses and chariots of fire around Elisha” (2 Kings 6:16–17).

Brothers and sisters, please note: Elisha did not ask God to remove the enemy army; he asked God to open his servant’s eyes.

The circumstances didn’t change one bit. The horses and chariots of fire had been there all along; the servant just couldn’t see them.

This morning, perhaps the prayer you need most is not “Lord, please change my circumstances,” but “Lord, please open my eyes.”

sections.heading: 4. Love: The Overflow of a Selfless Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we now come to the second main thread of this lesson.

“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)

Right at the outset the lesson shatters a huge misunderstanding: love is not a feeling; it is a choice.

In our culture, love is understood almost entirely as a feeling. Pop songs tell us that “love is that flutter in your heart,” so the moment a marriage runs into trouble, the first thought is: I just don’t feel anything for him any more.

But brothers and sisters, the word the New Testament uses to describe God’s love is agape. In classical Greek this word wasn’t used very often; the New Testament writers practically recast it. Agape is not eros (romantic, sensual love), not philia (the love of friendship), not storge (family affection).

The defining mark of agape is that it is a decision of the will, not a reaction of the emotions. That is why the Bible can “command” us to love. You can command someone to make a choice, but you cannot command someone to produce a feeling.

Jesus said: “A new commandment I give to you, that you love one another. Just as I have loved you, you also love one another” (John 13:34).

This is a command. And if it is a command, that means it is something we can choose.

The lesson says that the choice to love comes down to three concrete things: giving for others, sacrificing for others, and thinking of others.

Brothers and sisters, notice what these three have in common — the subject is always me, and the object is always someone else. Love means moving the centre of gravity of my life from myself to others.

This is selflessness.

How does Paul describe love? “Love is patient and is kind. Love doesn’t envy. Love doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave itself inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil” (1 Corinthians 13:4–5).

Count how many “nots” are in there. Doesn’t envy, doesn’t brag, is not proud, doesn’t behave inappropriately, doesn’t seek its own way, is not provoked, takes no account of evil.

In other words, the greatest obstacle to love has never been that I don’t give enough; it is that my “self” is standing in the way.

“Doesn’t seek its own way” — that phrase is the most precise translation of selflessness there is.

So where is the standard for love?

“Just as I have loved you, you also love one another.” Jesus put himself in the middle and became the measuring rod. The first of 321’s foundations is: Jesus is my role model.

How does the Lord love us? “By this we know love, because he laid down his life for us. And we ought to lay down our lives for the brothers” (1 John 3:16).

The lesson breaks this love down into three extremely difficult practices: choosing to love even when hurt, choosing to accept even when rejected, choosing to forgive even when wronged.

Brothers and sisters, each of these three sentences assumes one thing: that you really have been wronged.

The Bible never denies your pain. The Bible only says: inside the pain, you still have a choice.

Psychology has made an important discovery that helps us understand why these three things are so hard. In 2001 the American psychologist Roy Baumeister and his colleagues published a well-known paper in the Review of General Psychology entitled “Bad Is Stronger Than Good.” Drawing together a large body of research, they showed that in human psychology, negative events generally carry more weight than positive events of equal strength. One word of criticism does far more damage than one word of praise does good.

The research of the marriage researcher John Gottman points in the same direction. After observing couples’ interactions over many years, he proposed that marriages which stay stable over the long term keep the ratio of positive to negative interactions at about five to one.

Brothers and sisters, five to one. What does that mean? It means one hurt takes five acts of kindness to make up for.

So love cannot rely on feelings, because feelings will never keep pace with the speed of hurt. Love has to rely on choice — deliberate, repeated choice, more than five times over.

This is precisely the 321 “920 practice”: every person we have a relationship with is our “2,” and with every “2” we practise living out the “0” — the selfless life, bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

sections.heading: 5. Hate: The Natural Reaction of the Self-Centred Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, if love is the overflow of selflessness, then hate is the most direct expression of the self-centred life.

The lesson says that hate shows itself concretely in three “unwillings”: unwilling to let go, unwilling to forgive, unwilling to give way.

Hate usually isn’t because I can’t; it’s because I won’t.

And what lies hidden beneath that “won’t”? A single sentence: “Why on earth should I give way to him?”

The lesson exposes the inner logic of hate very sharply. People say, “He did it to me first,” and “Why on earth should I give way to him?”

Brothers and sisters, can you hear who the main character is in those two sentences? It’s “I.”

“He did it first” — so he’s the one in the wrong; I’m the victim; I’m entitled.

“Why on earth should I” — so I have my rights, and my rights must not be infringed.

This is the self-centred life. The self-centred life doesn’t necessarily look arrogant and overbearing; its most common form is actually “I feel I’m in the right.”

But Jesus said: “But I tell you, don’t resist him who is evil; but whoever strikes you on your right cheek, turn to him the other also” (Matthew 5:39).

Brothers and sisters, this verse is often misunderstood, so we need to be clear about it.

First, it doesn’t mean Christians should stand by and do nothing in the face of every evil. The Bible equally teaches us to uphold justice, protect the weak and resist sin. Paul himself invoked his Roman citizenship and appealed to Caesar (Acts 25:11).

Second, notice the detail of the “right cheek.” In the Jewish cultural setting, most people were right-handed. To strike someone’s right cheek with your right hand, you could only do it with the back of your hand. A backhanded slap was a grievous insult in those days, the contempt of a superior for an inferior, and the fine for it was far heavier than for an ordinary punch.

So what Jesus is talking about is not, first of all, physical pain but the humiliation of one’s dignity. He is saying: when someone humiliates you, you don’t have to repay them with humiliation.

Third, “turning the other cheek” is not weakness. As the lesson says, it is “laying down our rights and living in God’s system.”

Brothers and sisters, this takes enormous strength. Retaliation is instinct; anyone can do it. It takes real power not to retaliate.

321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

In the human system, the one who gives way is the loser; in God’s system, the one who gives way is the victor.

What makes hate so terrible is that the first person it wounds is the one doing the hating.

John says: “Whoever hates his brother is a murderer, and you know that no murderer has eternal life remaining in him” (1 John 3:15). And again: “But he who hates his brother is in the darkness, and walks in the darkness, and doesn’t know where he is going, because the darkness has blinded his eyes” (1 John 2:11).

Brothers and sisters, see the link between these two verses: hate makes people blind.

So here the two main threads of this lesson meet. Those who live by sight hate easily; those who hate become blinder still; and the blinder they become, the more they can only live by sight. It is a cycle — a cage.

Scientific research also confirms that the harm of hate is very real. In 2001 the psychologist Charlotte vanOyen Witvliet of Hope College in the United States and her colleagues published a study in the journal Psychological Science. They asked participants to recall a real experience of being wronged and then to enter two different states of mind in turn: holding a grudge, and forgiving. They found that when participants were in a grudging, vengeful frame of mind, their blood pressure, heart rate, facial muscle tension and skin conductance all rose significantly; and when they moved into empathy and forgiveness, these physiological measures fell markedly.

Brothers and sisters, this is why the concentration-camp survivor Corrie ten Boom is generally credited with saying: “To forgive is to set a prisoner free and discover that the prisoner was you.”

Corrie ten Boom’s own story is the best testimony of all. She was the daughter of a watchmaker in Haarlem in the Netherlands. During the Second World War her whole family was arrested for hiding Jews in their home, and she and her sister Betsie were sent to the Ravensbrück concentration camp, where Betsie died. After the war Corrie travelled throughout Germany preaching the message of forgiveness. One day, after she had spoken in Munich, a man came up to her and held out his hand — she recognised him as one of the guards from the camp. He told her he had become a Christian, and he asked her to forgive him.

Corrie later recalled that in that moment her whole body froze; her arm felt as heavy as lead and she could not lift it. She knew perfectly well in her heart that she ought to forgive, yet she couldn’t. So she prayed silently: Lord, I cannot forgive him; give me your forgiveness. And at the very instant she obediently thrust out her hand, a current of warmth flowed from her shoulder down her arm and filled her.

Brothers and sisters, notice the order. It isn’t that the feeling came first and then she held out her hand; she held out her hand first, and then the feeling came.

That is why Paul says: “Let all bitterness, wrath, anger, outcry, and slander be put away from you, with all malice. And be kind to one another, tender hearted, forgiving each other, just as God also in Christ forgave you” (Ephesians 4:31–32).

sections.heading: 6. Where the Power to Love Comes From
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, by now perhaps something in you is crying out: I understand all of this, but I just can’t do it.

Thank the Lord, the lesson’s sixth point was written precisely for you.

“We love him, because he first loved us.” (1 John 4:19)

Notice the word “first.” In Greek it is protos, meaning “first, foremost.”

God’s love is not a response to our love; our love is a response to God’s love.

Paul says: “But God commends his own love toward us, in that while we were yet sinners, Christ died for us” (Romans 5:8).

“While we were yet sinners” — brothers and sisters, God didn’t wait until we became lovable to love us; God loved us when we were at our most unlovable.

At the very beginning of his “Confessions,” Augustine prays to God: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. The human heart is restless because it has not yet returned to the source who first loved us.

So the lesson says: the reason we are able to love is not that we are full of love, but that we were first loved by God.

Brothers and sisters, let’s picture something. The tap in your home can give water — is that because it’s very good at producing water? Of course not. A tap can’t produce a single drop. It is simply connected to the pipe.

Our problem has never been “my love isn’t enough.” Our problem is “I’m not connected.”

“It isn’t ‘I have love, so I go and love’; it’s ‘I choose to love, and then I experience God’s love.’”

We are so often waiting — waiting until I’m not so angry with him any more, then I’ll go and make peace; waiting until I have feelings for my spouse again, then I’ll love them; waiting until I feel filled by God, then I’ll serve.

The Bible’s order is the exact opposite: first choose, then experience.

Just like Corrie ten Boom’s hand. First it reached out, and then the warmth came.

Just like the Israelites crossing the Jordan. God said: “It shall be that when the soles of the feet of the priests who bear the ark of Yahweh, the Lord of all the earth, rest in the waters of the Jordan, that the waters of the Jordan will be cut off. The waters that come down from above shall stand in one heap” (Joshua 3:13). The water didn’t part first so that the priests could go down; the priests’ feet stepped into the water first, and then the water was cut off.

Brothers and sisters, when the feet of faith step into the water first, God’s work is revealed.

The lesson says: when you choose to love, the Holy Spirit moves, and God’s love flows out.

This is entirely in keeping with the Bible’s teaching. “And hope doesn’t disappoint us, because God’s love has been poured into our hearts through the Holy Spirit who was given to us” (Romans 5:5).

The word “poured,” in Greek ekcheo, means “to pour out, to overflow.” God’s love isn’t dripped into us drop by drop; it’s emptied over us by the bucketful.

The third of 321’s foundations is: the Holy Spirit is my guide. Love is not my achievement; it is the fruit of the Spirit. Fruit isn’t wrung out of a branch by effort; fruit grows naturally when the branch is joined to the vine.

Brothers and sisters, this morning, if you feel you simply can’t go on loving, please stop forcing yourself to squeeze out more love. Go back to the source, and quietly let God love you first, once again.

sections.heading: 7. The Road Toward Perfection
sections.html:
“Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

Brothers and sisters, this verse often crushes people. Perfect? I can’t even control my tone of voice with my family this morning — how can I talk about being perfect?

The Greek word for “perfect” is teleios, from the root telos, meaning “end, goal, the purpose for which something was made.” Teleios doesn’t mean “without any flaw”; it means “having reached the purpose for which it was made,” “mature,” “complete.”

An unripe fruit isn’t a bad fruit; it just isn’t teleios yet. When it ripens, it is teleios.

So the lesson puts it very precisely: being perfect doesn’t mean having no faults; it means becoming more and more like the Father.

And notice the context. What does the “therefore” in Matthew 5:48 follow on from? It follows verses 43 to 47: “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you, love your enemies, … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you, that you may be children of your Father who is in heaven. For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.”

Brothers and sisters, so the context of “perfect” is precisely about “loving your enemies”!

The Father’s perfection, here, means concretely this: his love has no dividing line. His sun rises on the evil and the good alike.

Paul says very honestly: “Not that I have already obtained, or am already made perfect; but I press on, that I may take hold of that for which also I was taken hold of by Christ Jesus” (Philippians 3:12).

But Paul also says: “being confident of this very thing, that he who began a good work in you will complete it until the day of Jesus Christ” (Philippians 1:6).

So how do we walk this road? The lesson gives us two sentences so simple a child could remember them:

Live by faith, not by sight; choose love, not hate.

Brothers and sisters, how do we walk this road all the way to perfection? Paul says: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit” (2 Corinthians 3:18).

Look at the order: first “seeing,” then “being transformed.”

Even brain science nods in agreement here. Neuroplasticity is the consensus of neuroscience today: the brain’s neural connections genuinely change their structure according to where we keep placing our attention and what we repeatedly practise. Whatever we gaze at, over time, we are shaped into.

What we look at, we become. Look at your circumstances, and you become like your circumstances — anxious, fearful, twisted. Look at the Lord, and you become like the Lord — from glory to glory.

This is what 321 says: change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. The fivefold change is: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry.

And the destination of this road, as the lesson rightly says, is the selfless life.

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, see how this verse binds today’s two main threads perfectly together.

“I live by faith in the Son of God” — this is faith.

“Who loved me, and gave himself up for me” — this is love.

Selflessness is not becoming nothing. 321 is very clear: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

A drop of water left on a table dries up; put it into the ocean and it will never dry up. That isn’t loss; it is entering the infinite.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
First, the Three Foundations.

Jesus is my role model — just as he has loved us, we also must love one another (John 13:34). On the cross he prayed for the very people who crucified him: “Father, forgive them, for they don’t know what they are doing” (Luke 23:34). This is the highest standard of love.

The Bible is my standard — living by faith means taking God’s word as our final ground, not our circumstances, resources or feelings. “So faith comes by hearing, and hearing by the word of God” (Romans 10:17).

The Holy Spirit is my guide — the power to love isn’t something we’re born with; it is the Holy Spirit pouring God’s love into our hearts (Romans 5:5).

Second, the Two Core Values.

Let Jesus be King — at every crossroads of choice, ask: in this matter, am I King, or is Jesus King? Living by sight, I am King; living by faith, Jesus is King. In hate, I am King; in love, Jesus is King.

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when someone who has been wronged can still forgive, and someone who has been humiliated can still bless, the first reaction of those around them is not admiration for that person but the question: who on earth is living inside him? That is glory going to Jesus.

Third, the Goal: establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, from beginning to end this lesson has been about “two systems.” The self-centred system runs on sight and keeps its boundaries with hate; the selfless system runs on faith and binds people together with love.

The Babylonian system is a system of sight; the system of God’s kingdom is a system of faith.

Fourth, life first, then relationships, then ministry.

Today’s lesson is entirely a lesson in life and relationships. Living by faith is my relationship with God; choosing love is my relationship with others. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things.

Fifth, the 920 practice and 235 relationships.

The 920 practice: every person around you is your “2.” The hardest-to-love person God has measured out to you today is exactly the lesson God has given you for practising the “0.” Of the nine graces, the very first is love.

235 relationships: when we become a “2” with someone selfless, we support each other; we establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; and we go on to become a “5,” a team of spiritual comrades. Brothers and sisters, someone who lives by sight and is full of bitterness can never build relationships like these. Because the cement of relationships is faith and love.

Sixth, a shift of perspective.

From a human perspective to God’s perspective: people thought Lot had chosen well; God saw that Abraham had chosen well.

From an earthly perspective to a heavenly perspective: Lot gained the plain; Abraham gained the promise.

From a temporary perspective to an eternal perspective: “For the things which are seen are temporal, but the things which are not seen are eternal” (2 Corinthians 4:18).

From a worldly perspective to a godly perspective: the world says “an eye for an eye, a tooth for a tooth”; the Lord says “turn to him the other also.”

Brothers and sisters, this is a change in our choices. Change the mindset and you change the life.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take each one deeper using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: choose faith in your circumstances.

When you meet difficulty, don’t look at your circumstances first; first declare God’s promise, and practise seeing things through God’s eyes.

Information: first find the verse that fits your situation. If you’re worried, read Philippians 4:6–7; if you’re afraid, read Isaiah 41:10; if you’re waiting, read Isaiah 40:31. Copy the verse onto a card and put it where you’ll see it.

Revelation: quietly ask the Holy Spirit to open that verse to you. Information is your head knowing; revelation is your heart lighting up. “Yahweh, please open his eyes, that he may see” (2 Kings 6:17).

Conviction: say to God, “I believe.” Like that father, you can also honestly add: “Help my unbelief!” (Mark 9:24).

Implementation: the moment difficulty arrives, first speak the verse aloud as a declaration, and then deal with the matter. The order must not be reversed.

Evaluation: before bed, ask yourself: at what moment today did I live by sight? How did my body react in that moment?

Correction: identify the trigger that most easily trips you up — perhaps checking your bank balance, perhaps reading a certain person’s messages — and have a verse ready for that moment.

Repetition: don’t expect to succeed the first time. A hen sits on her eggs for twenty-one days.

Multiplication: share your experience with your “2.” When you say, “Last month I came through exactly this,” those words carry more power than a hundred sermons.

Practice two: deliberately choose a loving response.

When you’re offended or hurt, don’t follow your emotions; take the initiative to choose forgiveness and blessing.

Information: recognise that love is a command, not a feeling (John 13:34).

Revelation: ask God to let you see that the person who wronged you is also someone who has been hurt. Once you see this, the hate begins to loosen.

Conviction: admit that the sentence “Why on earth should I give way to him?” is the self-centred life.

Implementation: do one concrete thing. Pray for him once, speak one sentence of blessing, or send a message first. “Love your enemies, … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:44).

Evaluation: write it down — after I did it, did my heart grow tighter or looser?

Correction: if you can’t yet take an act of forgiveness, start by no longer repeating his faults to others. One sentence fewer means one brick fewer in the wall.

Repetition: forgiveness often isn’t a one-time thing. The Lord said to forgive seventy times seven (see Matthew 18:22).

Multiplication: when you truly walk through forgiveness, you become a way out for others.

Practice three: reflect on God’s love every day.

Through prayer and meditation, let yourself soak continually in God’s love, so that love becomes a natural overflow.

Information: each day read a passage about God’s love. 1 John 4, Romans 8:31–39 and Psalm 103 are all wonderful pools to soak in.

Revelation: change “God so loved the world” to “God so loved me.” Put your own name in and read it through.

Conviction: it isn’t because I behave well that God loves me; God loved me “while we were yet sinners” (Romans 5:8).

Implementation: have a quiet time each day where you ask for nothing and simply let yourself be loved.

Evaluation: this week, was there one day I got out of bed feeling, “God really delights in me today”?

Correction: if you always feel God doesn’t like you, it’s often because we are looking at God through the eyes of the law. Ask God to correct this mindset.

Repetition: soaking isn’t a one-off; it’s every day.

Multiplication: only those who are loved can love. When love overflows, it takes no effort; it simply flows onto your “2.”

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
The lesson gives us one very important sentence: you don’t live in your circumstances; you live in your “choices.”

Today’s message can be distilled into two roads and two systems.

The first road: live by sight, and fear is born; fear pushes us back into the self-centred life.

The second road: live by faith, and peace is born; peace leads us into selflessness.

And one more pair: hate brings bondage; love brings victory.

Brothers and sisters, look at the four signposts along these two roads. Those who live by sight stop at the station called fear and end at the terminus of the self-centred life; those who live by faith pass through the station called peace and end at the terminus of selflessness.

Which station are you standing at today?

At Shechem, Joshua said to the whole assembly: “If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; … but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15).

“Choose today.” Not next year, not when I’m ready — today.

Brothers and sisters, I want to invite you to make one simple yet decisive choice this very morning.

First, choose faith. Take that egg you’ve been sitting on for so long, put it back in the nest, and keep on sitting. God’s promises will not fail.

Second, choose love. Bring to mind that name, that face, that sentence. Today you can stop letting that person live on in your bitterness. Let them go, and you will be free as well.

This is letting Jesus be King: King over my eyes, so that I see as he sees; King over my emotions, so that I love with his heart.

This is letting Jesus receive all the glory. For when someone who lived by sight begins to live by faith, and when someone with hate in their heart begins to love, what people see is no longer that person, but the One who lives inside them.

Choose faith, choose love, live out selflessness, and let Jesus be everything.

keyVerses: “For we walk by faith, not by sight.” (2 Corinthians 5:7)
“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18)
practices: Reflect on God’s love every day
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Lord, I confess that I often live by sight. I look at my circumstances, my resources, my feelings, and then I grow anxious, afraid, and want to take control. Please forgive me, and just as you opened the eyes of Elisha’s servant, open my eyes too, so that I may see the mountain full of horses and chariots of fire, and see that you have been here all along.

Lord, I also confess that there are people inside me I’m unwilling to let go of, and things I’m unwilling to forgive. I often say, “He did it to me first,” and “Why on earth should I give way to him?” Lord, this is my self-centred life. Today I place it in your hands.

Lord, I choose to live by faith, not by sight; I choose to love others, and no longer to live in hate and in myself. I know I don’t have the power to do this, but I am reaching out my hand first; please pour your love into my heart.
Lord, let your life be lived out in me. May every choice I make today let you be King and let you receive all the glory.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “For we walk by faith, not by sight.” (2 Corinthians 5:7) Think back to something recent that made you anxious. In that situation, what were you mainly “looking at” — your circumstances, your resources, or God’s promises? If you looked at it again through God’s eyes, what would you say?

“My little children, let’s not love in word only, or with the tongue only, but in deed and truth.” (1 John 3:18) Whose name comes to mind right now? This week, are you willing to do one small, concrete thing for that person “in deed and truth”? Say it aloud, and let your group pray for you.
