sections.heading: Introduction: A Flight Path One Degree Off
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to Lesson 109 of 321 Morning Devotion, and our title is “Caring About Every Single Choice.”

Let me begin by asking you to picture something.

A passenger jet takes off from Taoyuan Airport bound for Los Angeles. At take-off, the nose is pointing just one degree off course. How much is one degree? Stretch your arm out straight: the width of your little finger is about one degree. On the cockpit instruments, that single degree is barely visible; the passengers in the cabin feel nothing at all.

But let’s do the sums. One degree off over a hundred kilometres puts you about 1.7 kilometres off course; over a thousand kilometres, about seventeen kilometres; and the flight from Taipei to Los Angeles is over ten thousand kilometres, so one degree off means ending up about 175 kilometres off course — not landing at the other end of the runway, but landing in another city.

Brothers and sisters, a one-degree deviation barely exists at the moment of take-off; at the moment of landing, it makes a world of difference.

We often think the direction of our life is decided by the “big decisions”: which school to attend, which job to take, whom to marry, which church to go to, whether to serve full-time. These certainly matter. But the lesson’s introduction opens with a sentence that cuts to the heart: what truly sets the course of our life is not one major choice, but the choices we make every day and every moment.

Every thought. Every reaction. Every decision.

All of these are quietly establishing a “system.”

So the lesson says: it’s not about what kind of life you’re living, but about what kind of system you’re establishing.

This sentence deserves careful thought. For “daily living” is the surface others can see, while a “system” is the structure others can’t see. Daily living is like the outer walls of a house; the system is like its foundation and its steel reinforcement. The outer walls can be repainted, but a foundation can only be poured inch by inch.

The Lord Jesus told a parable we all know well: “Everyone therefore who hears these words of mine, and does them, I will liken him to a wise man, who built his house on a rock. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it didn’t fall, for it was founded on the rock. Everyone who hears these words of mine, and doesn’t do them will be like a foolish man, who built his house on the sand. The rain came down, the floods came, and the winds blew, and beat on that house; and it fell — and great was its fall” (Matthew 7:24–27).

Notice: these two men heard the same message, met the same storm, and both built a house. There was only one difference: one “did them,” and the other “didn’t do them.” And “doing” is not one heroic feat; it is choosing, again and again.

Paul puts it even more directly: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life” (Galatians 6:7–8).

At sowing time, a single seed doesn’t look like much; at harvest time, the hills and fields are covered. Brothers and sisters, this morning you and I are both holding seeds in our hands.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Words Spoken on the Way to Gethsemane
sections.html:
Our key verse comes from John 15:19. To grasp the weight of these words, we first have to stand at the scene where they were spoken.

The author of John’s Gospel is the disciple whom the Lord loved, the apostle John, son of Zebedee. Most evangelical scholars believe this Gospel was written sometime between AD 85 and 95, very likely in Ephesus, for believers scattered in many places who were already beginning to face expulsion from the synagogue and pressure from Rome. By then the first generation of eyewitnesses was passing away one by one, and the church needed a testimony from someone who had seen the Lord with his own eyes.

And John 13 to 17 is the most concentrated passage in the whole Bible — the Lord Jesus’ “farewell discourse.” These are the last few hours the Lord spent with the eleven disciples, after the Last Supper and before the Garden of Gethsemane. He washed their feet, he promised that the Holy Spirit would come, he said he was the true vine.

Then, from John 15:18 on, the Lord’s tone suddenly shifts: “If the world hates you, you know that it has hated me before it hated you” (John 15:18). And then comes our key verse: “If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you” (John 15:19).

The word “world” here is the Greek kosmos. In John’s Gospel this word carries at least three layers of meaning: the first is the created universe and all it contains; the second is the human population of the world; and the third — which is the meaning here — is an “operating system” that is hostile to God, centred on man, and ruled from behind the scenes by Satan. Later, in his letter, John names the three pillars of this system very clearly: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s” (1 John 2:16).

Notice that the Lord did not tell his disciples to flee the world. That same night he prayed to the Father: “I pray not that you would take them from the world, but that you would keep them from the evil one. They are not of the world even as I am not of the world” (John 17:15–16).

This is our situation: in the world, yet not of the world.

Another piece of background is the book of Daniel. In 605 BC Nebuchadnezzar, king of Babylon, besieged Jerusalem for the first time (Daniel 1:1–2) and carried off young men of Judah’s royal family and nobility to Babylon. The Bible records that they were assigned to learn “the learning and the language of the Chaldeans,” ate from the king’s table and drank the king’s wine every day, underwent three years of training, and even had their names changed: Daniel was renamed Belteshazzar (Daniel 1:7).

Brothers and sisters, see how subtle Babylon’s methods were: change your language, change your diet, change your name. This wasn’t violent suppression; this was absorption into the system. It didn’t force you to give up your faith; it simply let you slowly forget who you were.

And Daniel’s response takes up just one verse: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself” (Daniel 1:8).

“Purposed,” in the Hebrew, literally means “set upon the heart” (sim al-lev). This wasn’t a passing emotional impulse; it was a decision placed in the heart and settled there. And where did he settle it? On “food and drink” — the smallest of everyday matters.

Brothers and sisters, Daniel spent some seventy years in Babylon, through Nebuchadnezzar and Belshazzar right up to Darius of Persia. The steadfastness of his whole life began not with a miracle, but with a meal.

sections.heading: 1. We Live in the World, Yet Are Not of the World
sections.html:
The lesson’s first key point begins by settling where we stand.

“If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.” (John 15:19)

There is a key verb in this verse: “I chose you out of the world.” “Chose,” in Greek eklegomai, means “to pick out from a pile, to set apart for oneself.” God didn’t move us out of the world; he “set us apart” right in the middle of the world.

So our identity is twofold: our address is in the world, but our citizenship is in heaven. Paul says: “For our citizenship is in heaven, from where we also wait for a Savior, the Lord Jesus Christ” (Philippians 3:20).

Here the lesson raises a crucial question — please write it down: are you living in the world’s “environment,” or in the world’s “system”?

The two are worlds apart. The environment is your outward situation — your company, your family, your school, your hospital ward. The system is what’s running on the inside — the standard by which you judge right and wrong, the method you use to solve problems, what you put at the centre of your life.

God has never promised to move us out of our environment; what God wants to do is move us out of the system.

Daniel is the best example: he was in Babylon, but not of Babylon.

He wore Babylonian official robes, spoke the Babylonian language, drew a Babylonian salary, and served as a chief administrator in the Babylonian court. His “environment” was entirely Babylonian. Yet by Daniel 6, when the decree came down and the lions’ den opened its mouth, the Bible says: “When Daniel knew that the writing was signed, he went into his house (now his windows were open in his room toward Jerusalem) and he kneeled on his knees three times a day, and prayed, and gave thanks before his God, as he did before” (Daniel 6:10).

Notice the last few words: “as he did before.”

Brothers and sisters, he could stay unchanged on the day of the lions’ den because he hadn’t changed on any of the days in the decades before. Steadfastness in a crisis is the fruit of choices made again and again on ordinary days. Windows open toward Jerusalem — it looked like a small, entirely unproductive habit, yet that small habit guarded his whole system.

Psychology confirms, from the other side, just how hard this is. In the early 1950s the social psychologist Solomon Asch conducted his famous conformity experiments at Swarthmore College. Participants were asked to judge which of three lines was the same length as a reference line — a task so easy it was almost impossible to get wrong. Yet when the other “participants” in the room (actually confederates planted by the researchers) all gave the same obviously wrong answer, about three-quarters of the real participants went along at least once with an answer they knew was wrong.

Three-quarters. And that was with a group of strangers, over a line on a card, in a setting that cost nothing. Brothers and sisters, if a line on a card can make people change their answer, how strong is the pull of the system where your job, your face and your future are at stake?

So the key is not “where you are” but “how you choose.”

The 321 vision says the Three Foundations are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Brothers and sisters, these Three Foundations are exactly the secret of how someone can be “in Babylon but not of Babylon.” When everyone around you measures things by the world’s standard, you have another measuring rod in your hand; when everyone relies on themselves, you have another Guide within you. Your address hasn’t changed, but your system is already different.

sections.heading: 2. A System Doesn’t Form Automatically — It Is Built Up from Choices
sections.html:
The lesson’s second key point states a very important fact: God’s system does not appear naturally.

This sentence is worth pausing over.

The world’s system forms automatically. You don’t have to do anything, and it grows — like a field: you don’t need to plant weeds; weeds grow by themselves. But wheat doesn’t grow by itself. Wheat needs someone to turn the soil, sow, water and weed.

God’s system has to be established deliberately.

How is it established? The lesson gives the answer: not by one big decision, but by every small choice.

Paul uses the language of “building” for this: “According to the grace of God which was given to me, as a wise master builder I laid a foundation, and another builds on it. But let each man be careful how he builds on it. For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ” (1 Corinthians 3:10–11).

The foundation has already been laid by the Lord — that is grace; “how he builds on it” is the responsibility we carry every day. And building is never finished in one go — it goes up brick by brick, day by day.

The lesson lists five choices we are making every day:

Whether to be humble. Whether to lay ourselves down. Whether to obey the Holy Spirit. Whether to trust God. Whether to love.

Brothers and sisters, look closely: not one of these five is a “big decision.” They happen at the breakfast table, in group chat messages, in a single sentence in a meeting room, in a thought when you wake in the middle of the night — so small you don’t even feel you’re making a choice.

Yet behavioural science tells us that these “unnoticed” choices make up the bulk of our lives. In a study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, Wendy Wood, then at Texas A&M University, and her colleagues found that about 43 per cent of people’s daily behaviour consists of habitual responses, repeated in the same settings, with almost no conscious thought.

In other words, nearly half of the content of your life isn’t something you “decided”; it’s something you “accumulated.”

And accumulation takes time. In a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, Phillippa Lally’s team at University College London followed ninety-six participants and found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a new behaviour to become automatic, with individual differences ranging from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

Sixty-six days. Brothers and sisters, that number is both discouraging and comforting. Discouraging, because there is no spiritual crash course that gets you there in one go. Comforting, because you don’t need to get a hundred things right at once; you only need to choose rightly in the same thing, again and again.

The Lord Jesus said: “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much” (Luke 16:10).

“In a very little” — so the measuring rod of the kingdom of heaven doesn’t measure how big a thing you’ve done; it measures how small a thing you’re still faithful in.

Paul says something else that lays bare the relationship between choices and systems: “Don’t you know that when you present yourselves as servants and obey someone, you are the servants of whomever you obey; whether of sin to death, or of obedience to righteousness?” (Romans 6:16).

“Obey” is an action; “being a servant” is a system. Every time you obey someone, you are handing yourself over to them, little by little.

So the lesson says: every choice is building a system.

The 321 vision speaks of “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” Why does life come first? Because life is the system. Ministry can surge ahead for a while on gifting; relationships can hold up for a while on enthusiasm; only life grows day by day. We are not piling up a record of ministry achievements; we are building a life that can carry ministry.

sections.heading: 3. Right Choices Establish God’s System
sections.html:
The lesson’s third key point turns the camera to the positive side: when you choose rightly, what happens?

The lesson lists four pairs of choices, and each pair is a fork in the road.

First, choose humility rather than insisting on your own way.

“But he gives more grace. Therefore it says, ‘God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble’” (James 4:6). The 321 vision puts it well: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — letting man be man and letting God be God. So every time you choose not to fight over that one remark, not to argue for the sake of your pride, you haven’t lost; you have returned to your originally intended position.

Second, choose to rely on the Holy Spirit rather than on yourself.

“‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies” (Zechariah 4:6). Paul also says: “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh” (Galatians 5:16).

Third, choose to live by faith rather than by sight.

“For we walk by faith, not by sight” (2 Corinthians 5:7). The twelve spies saw the same land of Canaan, the same descendants of Anak, the same cluster of grapes. Ten said, “We can’t go up”; only two, Caleb and Joshua, stood on God’s promise, and Caleb said, “Let’s go up at once, and possess it.” What they saw was the same; what they chose was different — and the outcome differed by forty years.

Fourth, choose love rather than hate.

“But I tell you, love your enemies, … and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you.” (Matthew 5:44)

The lesson says: when you choose like this, you are doing one thing — establishing God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, I want to point something out: these choices really do look small. So small that by evening you’ve forgotten them. Holding back that one remark today hasn’t turned you into a spiritual giant; you just feel a bit stifled.

But look at what the lesson says next: the result of long-term accumulation is a changed life, changed relationships, a changed spiritual condition — and in the end, Christ lived out.

There’s a piece of mathematics here that every one of us should remember. If something improves by just one per cent a day, what will it be after a year? 1.01 to the power of 365 comes to about 37.8 times. Conversely, if it declines by just one per cent a day, 0.99 to the power of 365 comes to about 0.03 — less than a thirtieth of what you started with.

The same 365 days, the same “one per cent difference a day” — and after a year, one is thirty-seven times larger, the other a thirtieth. The gap between them is more than a thousandfold.

Brothers and sisters, this is the compound interest of choice. Each choice on its own looks trivial, but added together they decide who you are.

The British apologist and man of letters C. S. Lewis wrote something in “Mere Christianity” that fills me with awe every time I read it. He said that every time you make a choice, you are turning the central part of you, the part that chooses, into something a little different from what it was before; and taking your life as a whole, with all its innumerable choices, all your life long you are slowly turning this central thing either into a heavenly creature or into a hellish creature.

No choice is neutral. Every choice is carving you.

Nature works the same way. The Colorado River cut the Grand Canyon, more than 1,600 metres deep at its deepest point; geologists generally hold that this was achieved by the river’s waters scouring, day after day, over millions of years. The water was never violent on any given day; it simply never stopped.

The 321 vision’s fivefold change says: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living. And the stretch of road from mindset to life is walked by “choice after choice.”

The lesson sums up this section in three words: Christ lived out.

Paul’s own words are: “For to me to live is Christ, and to die is gain” (Philippians 1:21). Brothers and sisters, living out Christ isn’t some spiritual plateau; it is the accumulated result of a whole chain of choices. Choose humility once today, and Christ is revealed in you a little more.

sections.heading: 4. Wrong Choices Establish the Worldly System
sections.html:
The lesson’s fourth key point is the reverse side of the same truth.

When you choose pride, choose to rely on yourself, choose to go by your feelings, choose to hold a grudge — you are also doing one thing: establishing the Worldly system.

Notice that the lesson doesn’t say “you have sinned”; it says “you are establishing a system.” That is even more frightening. A single sin can be confessed and forgiven; but a system traps you, so that you fall in the same place again and again.

James describes the process as if in slow motion: “But each one is tempted when he is drawn away by his own lust and enticed. Then the lust, when it has conceived, bears sin. The sin, when it is full grown, produces death” (James 1:14–15).

Lust, conception, sin born, sin full grown, death produced — it’s a production line. The system is that production line.

When Paul speaks about harbouring anger, he uses a very vivid word: “‘Be angry, and don’t sin.’ Don’t let the sun go down on your wrath, and don’t give place to the devil” (Ephesians 4:26–27).

“Place,” in Greek topos, means “a place, a space.” Brothers and sisters, every time we hold a grudge, we clear a little plot of ground in our heart for the enemy; clear enough of it, and he moves in to live there. Hebrews also warns: “looking carefully lest there be any man who falls short of the grace of God, lest any root of bitterness springing up trouble you, and many be defiled by it” (Hebrews 12:15). Bitterness is a “root” — roots aren’t above ground; roots are underground; the root is the system.

The lesson then names three results of this system, and these three sentences hold up a mirror to many weary servants of God:

The more you live, the more tired you get. The more you serve, the drier you become. The harder you try, the more powerless you feel.

Brothers and sisters, please ask yourself honestly: have you had days like that? You still go to the meetings, still take on the ministry, still pray — yet inside you feel as though you’ve been drained dry.

The lesson names the reason: because your life is not in the right environment.

Then the lesson gives a very precise picture: it’s like a fish out of water — however hard it tries, it cannot live.

The picture holds true biologically. A fish’s gills are made of extremely fine filaments. In water, buoyancy holds the filaments apart one by one, giving a huge surface area that can take in dissolved oxygen efficiently. But the moment the fish leaves the water, the filaments stick together and collapse, and the surface area shrinks drastically — so even though air holds twenty or thirty times as much oxygen as water, the fish still suffocates and dies.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully: there is actually more oxygen on the bank. The fish doesn’t die from a lack of oxygen; it dies from leaving the environment that allowed it to take oxygen in.

That is a portrait of many Christians. We have never had so many resources around us: sermons to listen to at any moment, devotional books at our fingertips, worship songs playing around the clock. And yet we are still dry — because we have left the water.

The Lord Jesus said: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing” (John 15:5).

Notice that this verse comes just before our key verse. The Lord first says “remain in me,” and only then says “you are not of the world.” The order can’t be reversed: it isn’t that we first strive to draw a line between ourselves and the world; it’s that we first remain in the Lord, and the line appears of its own accord.

The Lord also extends an invitation: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light” (Matthew 11:28–30).

Brothers and sisters, if your service is making you heavier and heavier, it very likely isn’t the Lord’s yoke; it’s one you’ve added yourself. The 321 vision says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and we rejoice, rely on the brain and we worry. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win.

And the compound-interest maths from earlier applies here too — only in reverse. One per cent decline a day, and after a year you’re left with a thirtieth. Brothers and sisters, the Worldly system won’t tear you down in a day; all it needs is for you to give it a little ground every day.

sections.heading: 5. Mindset Determines Choices; Choices Establish a System
sections.html:
At this point someone may say: Pastor, I know I should make the right choice, but when the moment comes, I just can’t do it.

The lesson’s fifth key point answers exactly that. It says something crucial: the starting point of revival is not behaviour but mindset.

The lesson gives us a chain: mindset → choices → system → life.

Notice where this chain begins. Not with “effort,” not with “resolve,” but with “mindset.”

Paul says: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God” (Romans 12:2).

“Transformed by the renewing of your mind” — the Greek word for “renewing” is anakainosis, meaning a renovation of the very substance; and “transformed” is metamorphoo, the root of the English word “metamorphosis,” the very word used for a caterpillar becoming a butterfly. What Paul means is this: it isn’t about training a caterpillar to be a slightly faster caterpillar; it’s about letting it become a butterfly from the inside.

And where does the transformation begin? In the “mind” — in our mindset.

The Old Testament said the same thing long ago. In the Chinese Union Version, Proverbs 23:7 reads: “For as he thinks in his heart, so is he.” And again: “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

On this point, modern psychology has simply added a footnote to the Bible. In the 1960s, while treating patients with depression, the University of Pennsylvania psychiatrist Aaron T. Beck discovered that what really shapes a person’s emotions and behaviour is often not the event itself but the “automatic thoughts” the person has about the event. The cognitive behavioural therapy that grew out of this has as its core principle: only by changing our thinking can we change our emotions and behaviour. This therapy went on to become one of the most strongly evidence-supported approaches in psychotherapy.

Brothers and sisters, psychology says “change your thinking”; the Bible says “the renewing of your mind”; 321 says “change the mindset and you change the life.” Truth is all of a piece — only the Bible said it two thousand years earlier, and gave us the One psychology cannot give: the Holy Spirit.

So which mindset needs renewing? The lesson points to two sentences.

The first: “It is no longer I who live.”

The lesson says: when you believe this, you will no longer feed the “self.”

Brothers and sisters, the “self” needs to eat. Every time you argue your own case, you feed it a mouthful; every time you feel sorry for yourself, you feed it a mouthful; every time you feed on other people’s opinions of you, you feed it a big mouthful. And what comes of all that feeding? It grows bigger, and its appetite grows bigger and bigger. The 321 vision says: the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. The most effective way to deal with the “self” is not to fight it every day, but to stop feeding it.

The second sentence: “Christ lives in me.” The Chinese Union Version’s wording is: “but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

The lesson says: when you believe this, you will naturally depend on God, obey God and live out God.

Notice the word “naturally.” Not “strive to,” but “naturally.” That is the power of a mindset. Someone who believes they’re an orphan will hoard frantically; someone who believes they’re a son will naturally trust.

Paul prays for the church in Ephesus: “that Christ may dwell in your hearts through faith, to the end that you, being rooted and grounded in love” (Ephesians 3:17). And he speaks of “Christ in you, the hope of glory” (Colossians 1:27).

So the lesson concludes: the real key isn’t effort but “what you believe.”

The 321 vision speaks of a shift of perspective: from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Brothers and sisters, when your perspective shifts, your choices shift; when your choices shift, your system shifts; when your system shifts, your life shifts.

sections.heading: 6. The Key Turn from Mindset to Life
sections.html:
The lesson’s last key point describes a phenomenon that is very real, and very heartbreaking.

Many people stop right here: they know about selflessness, yet they can’t live it out.

Brothers and sisters, does that describe you? We have heard the word “selflessness” hundreds of times in 321. We can talk about it, we can teach it, we can even lead others through it. But we get home, one remark goes wrong, and that “self” is instantly back on its feet.

Why? The lesson’s answer is a single sentence: the mindset is still stuck in the “head.”

Hebrews diagnosed this sickness long ago: “For indeed we have had good news preached to us, even as they also did, but the word they heard didn’t profit them, because it wasn’t mixed with faith by those who heard” (Hebrews 4:2).

“Mixed” is a beautiful word; in the original it carries the sense of “blended, fused into one.” The word came in, but it wasn’t mixed with faith — like oil floating on water: in the same glass, but never truly blended.

James also says: “But be doers of the word, and not only hearers, deluding your own selves” (James 1:22).

So how does real change happen? The lesson gives four steps: Information → Revelation → Conviction → Implementation.

These are exactly the first four of 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset. Let’s take them one at a time.

Step one, Information. You’ve heard it, you know it. This is a necessary starting point, but it is only at the level of the head.

Step two, Revelation. The Holy Spirit “opens up” that knowledge and lets it drop from your head into your heart. When Peter recognised Jesus as the Christ, the Lord said: “Blessed are you, Simon Bar Jonah, for flesh and blood has not revealed this to you, but my Father who is in heaven” (Matthew 16:17). Paul also prayed this for the church in Ephesus: “that the God of our Lord Jesus Christ, the Father of glory, may give to you a spirit of wisdom and revelation in the knowledge of him, having the eyes of your hearts enlightened” (Ephesians 1:17–18).

Brothers and sisters, notice “the eyes of your hearts.” Revelation isn’t your head knowing one more fact; it’s your heart seeing one more glimpse of God.

Step three, Conviction. After revelation comes, there is a moment inside you when you “yield.” No longer “I agree in principle,” but “my whole being surrenders.”

Step four, Implementation. Conviction always leads to action. If it hasn’t led to action, it isn’t yet true conviction.

The lesson says: when “I already” moves from knowledge to revelation, your choices will change and your life will change.

This “I already” is the lesson of Lesson 100, “From ‘I Can’ to ‘I Already Am’” — “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20). Not “I am going to be crucified,” not “I am able to be crucified,” but “I already have been.” It is a fact already accomplished.

And implementation, in turn, deepens revelation. Even brain science can see this. In a study published in 2000 in the Proceedings of the National Academy of Sciences, Professor Eleanor Maguire’s team at University College London found that London taxi drivers, who to pass the extremely demanding exam known as “the Knowledge” must memorise tens of thousands of the city’s streets, had markedly greater grey-matter volume in the rear part of the hippocampus than the control group — and the longer they had been driving, the more pronounced the difference.

Brothers and sisters, repeated practice really does change the structure of the brain. Human beings, as God made them, are shaped by “repetition.” That is why the eight stages have four more steps after these: Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Evaluation is facing things honestly; Correction is adjusting at once; Repetition is practising steadily; Multiplication is bringing others along with you.

From Information to Multiplication, this road is the road from the head to life.

sections.heading: 7. Integrating the 321 Vision: Every Choice Builds God’s System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the Goal of the 321 vision is to “establish God’s system.” Today’s lesson in effect takes that Goal apart and places it into the twenty-four hours of our day.

The Three Foundations are three questions we ask at every choice:

Jesus is my role model — faced with this, what would the Lord do?

The Bible is my standard — on this matter, what does God’s word say?

The Holy Spirit is my guide — right now, what is the Holy Spirit saying in my heart?

Brothers and sisters, if at just three junctures in a day you stop and ask these three questions, your system is already changing.

The Two Core Values are the criteria for every choice:

Let Jesus be King — this time, is it “I have the final say,” or “the Lord has the final say”?

Let Jesus receive all the glory — when this is done, will people see me, or him?

The Goal is the direction of every choice: establish God’s system.

When the lesson says, “it’s not about what kind of life you’re living, but about what kind of system you’re establishing,” that sentence and 321’s Goal are one and the same thing.

Next, let’s bring several main threads of 321 into today’s message.

First, the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. Every wrong choice feeds the “self”; every right choice makes the “self” step down. Humility overcomes pride; selflessness overcomes Satan. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Second, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. The lesson’s fifth key point, “mindset → choices → system → life,” describes exactly the first half of this road. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

Third, life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and finally with things. Brothers and sisters, if the order of our choices is turned upside down — tasks first, then people, and God last — what we build will not be God’s system, however much it looks like service on the outside.

Fourth, a shift of perspective: from the human to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. In fact today’s lesson is asking: from which perspective are you making your small daily decisions?

Fifth, the 920 practice. Every person we have a relationship with is our “2”; before every “2” we practise living out the selfless (0) life and bearing the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions — “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control” (Galatians 5:22–23).

Brothers and sisters, notice: not one of the nine graces grows in a vacuum. Patience only grows when someone provokes you; gentleness only shows when someone talks back to you; self-control is only trained when something tempts you. So that hardest-to-get-along-with “2” is not your enemy; they are the training ground God has given you.

Sixth, 235 relationships. Become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with someone selfless; establish the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; become a “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. A system isn’t built by one person. When one person makes right choices, that’s spiritual discipline; when a whole group makes right choices together, it becomes God’s system. This is also the final step of the eight stages — Multiplication.

Seventh, the Path of Serving: Spirit, Understanding, Life, Service, God. The Holy Spirit guides me, the Bible enlightens me, Jesus is my role model, I let him be King, and in the end all the glory goes to him. Brothers and sisters, these five are not five stages to pass through once; they are a road to be walked afresh every day, in every choice.

sections.heading: 8. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them one at a time, and drive each one deep using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice one: notice your everyday choices

The lesson says: deliberately pay attention to your reactions in daily life — are you choosing the self-centred life or selflessness?

Information: first recognise a fact — you are choosing every day, and most of those choices you don’t notice. Professor Wood’s research reminds us that nearly half of our daily behaviour is automatic.

Revelation: ask the Holy Spirit to open the eyes of your heart. You can use David’s prayer: “Search me, God, and know my heart. Try me, and know my thoughts. See if there is any wicked way in me, and lead me in the everlasting way” (Psalm 139:23–24).

Conviction: admit that you are not a victim shaped by your circumstances, but a builder shaped by your choices.

Implementation: starting today, do one very concrete thing — set three reminders on your phone, one each in the morning, at noon and in the evening. When a reminder goes off, stop for thirty seconds and ask yourself one question: “In the past hour, have I been living in the self-centred life, or in selflessness?”

Evaluation: before bed, write down one moment today when you noticed the “self.” No need to beat yourself up; just see it.

Correction: for that moment, confess to the Lord, and ask him to give you a different response next time.

Repetition: do it for twenty-one days in a row. Remember the Lally team’s research — the average is sixty-six days, so please don’t give up on day five.

Multiplication: find a companion and share what you’ve noticed with each other once a week. That is the beginning of a “2.”

Practice two: deliberately make the right choice

The lesson says: in conflict, under pressure and amid strong emotions, practise choosing humility, faith and love rather than reacting on instinct.

Information: an instinctive reaction is the fastest, but often the oldest. It is a path the old self left behind.

Revelation: see the Lord Jesus’ own choice — “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men. And being found in human form, he humbled himself, becoming obedient to the point of death, yes, the death of the cross” (Philippians 2:6–8).

Conviction: acknowledge “I have the right not to react this way.” In Christ, I am not a slave to my emotions.

Implementation: learn a very simple practice called “six seconds.” The moment your emotions rise, don’t open your mouth straight away; first say silently in your heart, “Lord, in this matter I let you be King.” Then respond.

Evaluation: review once a week — how many times this week did you manage to stop? How many times didn’t you?

Correction: identify the situation where you are most likely to lose your guard — is it a particular person? A particular time of day? A particular kind of tiredness? Then prepare a prayer and a verse in advance for that situation.

Repetition: practise that one sentence until it becomes like Daniel’s “as he did before.”

Multiplication: when people around you ask, “How come you’ve changed?” you have the chance to introduce them to the Lord.

Practice three: let mindset become action

The lesson says: don’t stop at “I know”; live out “I already” in practice every day, and let faith enter daily living.

Information: be clear on the difference between three sentences — “I will” means I haven’t done it yet; “I can” means I do it in my own strength; “I already” means Christ has already accomplished it.

Revelation: let the Holy Spirit turn “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20) from a verse into an assurance within you.

Conviction: stop negotiating with your old self, because it has already been crucified.

Implementation: every morning when you get up, stand in front of the mirror and speak the lesson’s declaration of faith aloud once; every night before bed, write down one different choice you made today because of this mindset.

Evaluation: look back at that notebook after a month, and you’ll be amazed to find that your system really is changing.

Correction: if you find yourself slipping back into “I will” or “I can,” return at once to “I already.”

Repetition: keep it up for a whole year. 1.01 to the power of 365 is thirty-seven times.

Multiplication: bring one person along to do these three practices with you. When your practice has a companion, it moves from a habit to a system.

sections.heading: 9. Closing and Call
sections.html:
The lesson’s closing words say: life isn’t changed overnight; it is shaped through countless choices.

One choice — you can’t see the difference. A hundred choices — they decide your direction.

Brothers and sisters, let’s go back to that plane from the beginning. One degree off at take-off, and you feel nothing; 175 kilometres off at landing, and it’s too late to change. So the best time to correct your course is always now — always at take-off.

There is a famous saying often attributed to Aristotle: “We are what we repeatedly do.” In fact the sentence comes from the American historian Will Durant’s summary of Aristotle’s thought in “The Story of Philosophy.” Whoever said it, it bears witness to today’s lesson: what you repeatedly do is becoming who you are.

But, brothers and sisters, the Christian faith holds out more hope than that sentence does. For our repetition isn’t held up by sheer willpower; our repetition is the natural fruit of a branch that remains on the vine. “He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit” (John 15:5).

So this morning I want to issue a call.

Not a call to make some earth-shaking big decision. A call for you to come back to today.

Back to your very first thought this morning: will you choose to complain, or choose to give thanks?

Back to that phone call at noon today: will you choose to argue, or choose humility?

Back to that message tonight that never got a reply: will you choose to hold a grudge, or choose to love?

Back to every moment no one else sees: will you choose to rely on yourself, or choose to obey the Holy Spirit?

The lesson says: starting today, choose Jesus in every small choice, and you are walking toward the selfless life, and walking into the end time revival.

Brothers and sisters, the great revival won’t suddenly drop out of the sky. The great revival grows out of thousands upon thousands of early mornings and thousands upon thousands of small choices. Every choice that lets Jesus be King lays another brick toward that day.

Let Jesus be King, starting with your first choice this morning.

Let Jesus receive all the glory, starting with that moment today that no one sees.

keyVerses: “If you were of the world, the world would love its own. But because you are not of the world, since I chose you out of the world, therefore the world hates you.” (John 15:19)

“But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.” (Daniel 1:8)

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)
declarations: The lesson leaves us a short but weighty reminder:
You are not shaped by your circumstances; you are shaped by your “choices.”

Brothers and sisters, take this sentence to heart. Most of our circumstances we cannot change: a pandemic, the economy, a family member’s temper, the weakness of our body, that colleague who always gives you a hard time. But the choice is always in our hands. Daniel couldn’t change Babylon, but he could decide what he ate; he couldn’t change that decree, but he could decide which way his window faced.

At the end of the wilderness journey, Moses likewise placed the same authority back in the Israelites’ hands: “I call heaven and earth to witness against you today that I have set before you life and death, the blessing and the curse. Therefore choose life, that you may live, you and your descendants” (Deuteronomy 30:19).
At Shechem, Joshua set the same words before the people: “But as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh” (Joshua 24:15).
Brothers and sisters, God has never made this choice for us. He sets it before us, he calls us, he gives us strength — and then he waits for us to reach out our own hand.
So let’s speak the lesson’s declaration of faith together, out loud:
Lord, in every choice I am willing to choose you, to establish God’s system, and to let Christ live out his life in me!
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

You did not move us out of the world, yet you chose us out of the world. Lord, we confess that we often live in the world’s environment, and without realising it we have also slipped into the world’s system.

Lord, please forgive us. Forgive us for comforting ourselves with big decisions while indulging ourselves in the small choices of every day; forgive us for knowing about selflessness while still feeding the “self” every day.
Give us the spirit of wisdom and revelation, enlighten the eyes of our hearts, so that “I have been crucified with Christ” is no longer just a verse but becomes a real assurance within us.
Lord, help us to choose you in every thought, choose you in every reaction, choose you in every decision. Let us choose humility in conflict, faith under pressure, and love when we are hurt.
Make us like Daniel, in Babylon yet not of Babylon; make us like branches joined to the vine, no longer dry, but bearing much fruit.
Lord, we are willing to establish God’s system in every choice. Reign as King in our lives, and receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: “But Daniel purposed in his heart that he would not defile himself with the king’s dainties, nor with the wine which he drank. Therefore he requested of the prince of the eunuchs that he might not defile himself.” (Daniel 1:8) Daniel’s “purpose” settled on a very small everyday matter. In your present circumstances, what “small thing” does God want you to purpose in your heart to hold fast? Why is that small thing especially hard for you?

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2) Looking back on this week, what self-centred reaction did you fall into most often? What old mindset lies hidden behind that reaction? Which word of God will you use this week to renew it?

l109.subtitle: A Change of Choices (Part 7): Establishing a System Begins with Every Small Choice
l109.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: You Are Not Just Living Your Life — You Are Establishing a System
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we come to today’s lesson, I’d like you to picture a very ordinary scene.

On a mountainside there is a slope covered in wild grass. The first person walks across it, and the grass is pressed down only a little; the next day it springs back up, and there is no trace left at all. A second person crosses the same way, then a third, a tenth, a hundredth. Six months later a faint pale line appears on the slope; a year later that pale line has become a firm little path; three years later, whoever comes that way doesn’t have to think at all — their feet simply take them onto that path.

Brothers and sisters, let me ask you: on what day was that path made?

On no day at all. Nobody held a meeting and decided to build a path there. Nobody drew up plans. Nobody turned a single spadeful of earth. That path was made by countless footsteps passing over it.

That is the first thing today’s lesson wants to say to us.

We often think of a “system” as something very large, as though only churches, nations and institutions deserve to be called systems. A system sounds remote — someone else’s business, the business of the people on the platform, the kind of thing that only comes about through endless meetings and pages of regulations.

But the lesson takes that misunderstanding apart right at the start. It says that, in fact, the way you live each day, your habits in making decisions, your attitude in responding to things — these are establishing a system.

Listen carefully to those three phrases.

First, the way you live each day. What is the first thing you do when you wake up in the morning? Where do you put your time? Where does your money flow?

Second, your habits in making decisions. When you stand at a fork in the road, do you first ask, “Do I like it?” or do you first ask, “Lord, what do you want me to do?”

Third, your attitude in responding to things. When someone bumps into you, what is the very first reaction that comes out of you?

Brothers and sisters, these three are the feet that cross that grassy slope, one pair after another. Every time you walk it, you press the path a little deeper. Walk it long enough and the path is no longer only your path; it becomes the path of the people in your home, the path of the people you serve, even the path of the next generation.

So the lesson says: this system affects not only you; it affects your family, your church, even a whole generation.

That is why today’s lesson is called “Care About Every Choice.” Not only the few big choices — whether to change jobs, whether to buy a house, whether to emigrate — but every choice: including the sentence you said to your spouse this morning, including the message you just sent in the group chat, including how you are going to respond in a moment to that person who makes you uncomfortable.

Because the kingdom of God has never been established from the big things down; it is established from the small things up. The Lord Jesus said, “He who is faithful in a very little is faithful also in much. He who is dishonest in a very little is also dishonest in much.” (Luke 16:10)

Today we are going to walk six stretches of road with the lesson. First, a system begins with the individual, but it doesn’t stop with the individual. Second, a wrong choice brings the fall of a whole system. Third, two kinds of wisdom establish two kinds of system. Fourth, the way you lead determines the system you establish. Fifth, don’t bring the world’s system into God’s kingdom. Sixth, the key to establishing God’s system is 321.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background
sections.html:
Today’s lesson draws on two key passages: one is a negative warning, the other a positive standard. Let’s first get the background of these two passages clear, so that the rest of the road is firm underfoot.

(1) 1 Samuel 8: The Day a Nation Changed Its System

First and 2 Samuel were originally a single book, called “Samuel” in the Hebrew Bible. Jewish tradition holds that its material came from the hands of the prophet Samuel, the prophet Nathan and the seer Gad (see 1 Chronicles 29:29). The book records Israel’s crucial turning point, from the age of the judges into the age of the kingdom, roughly between 1100 and 1010 BC; the events of chapter 8 are generally dated around 1050 BC, at Ramah, Samuel’s home town.

Before that, Israel was a theocracy. They had no king, because Yahweh was their King. When the people fell into danger, God raised up judges to rescue them. This system had something very distinctive about it: it had no visible centre of power. All its reliance rested on the God who could not be seen, yet was truly present.

But Samuel had grown old. He appointed his two sons as judges in Beersheba, yet they “didn’t walk in his ways, but turned away after dishonest gain, took bribes, and perverted justice” (1 Samuel 8:3). So the elders of Israel gathered, came to Samuel at Ramah, and made a request. That request is the verse our lesson quotes today.

(2) James 3: Two Kinds of Wisdom in One Church

The James who wrote the letter of James is not either of the two Jameses among the twelve apostles, but the Lord Jesus’ brother in the flesh (Matthew 13:55; Galatians 1:19). The risen Lord appeared to him (1 Corinthians 15:7), and he later became a leader of the church in Jerusalem, one of those Paul calls the “pillars” of the church (Galatians 2:9).

The letter was written roughly between AD 45 and 49, and may well be the earliest book of the New Testament. It is addressed to “the twelve tribes which are in the Dispersion” (James 1:1) — Jewish Christians scattered abroad by persecution.

The first half of James 3 is about the tongue; the second half is about wisdom. Why put the two together? Because the church of that day had problems: some were jostling to be teachers (James 3:1), some were biting one another with their tongues, and there were even “wars and fightings” in the church (James 4:1). James did not begin by revising the structure; he went first to the source of wisdom. He asks, “Who is wise and understanding among you? Let him show by his good conduct that his deeds are done in gentleness of wisdom.” (James 3:13)

Brothers and sisters, notice that order. Whatever wisdom people use, that is the system they establish. First Samuel 8 shows us how one wrong choice can tear down a system; James 3 shows us how two kinds of wisdom grow two utterly different environments.

sections.heading: 3. A System Begins with the Individual, but Doesn’t Stop There
sections.html:
The lesson says that systems exist on different levels: the individual, the family, the church, the nation.

These four levels are really like four concentric circles, one ring enclosing the next. The psychologist Urie Bronfenbrenner, in The Ecology of Human Development, published in 1979, put forward his well-known “ecological systems theory.” He pointed out that a person’s growth never happens in a vacuum; it is shaped by environment upon environment, layer upon layer — innermost the family and close relationships, further out school and community, further out still culture and institutions. His conclusion was this: if you want to understand a person, you have to understand the layers of systems that person lives in.

The Bible said this thousands of years before the theory. When God saves a person, he never thinks only of that one person. God said to Abraham, “All the families of the earth will be blessed through you.” (Genesis 12:3) When God spoke to Noah, he saved Noah “with all of your household” (Genesis 7:1). In the New Testament, the Philippian jailer asked Paul in the middle of the night, “Sirs, what must I do to be saved?” And the answer was, “Believe in the Lord Jesus Christ, and you will be saved, you and your household.” (Acts 16:30-31)

The lesson goes on to state a principle of influence: the larger the system, the greater the influence.

It uses a lovely comparison: a fish in a fish tank, and a fish in the ocean.

This comparison is not just a literary flourish; there is something behind it. In ichthyology there is a class of fish known as “indeterminate growers” — goldfish and koi, for example. They keep growing all their lives, and how fast and how far they grow is heavily affected by the size of the body of water, its quality and its dissolved oxygen. The very same koi, kept in a small tank in the living room, may spend its whole life at little more than ten centimetres; put it in a spacious pond and it can grow to sixty or seventy centimetres.

The same water, the same fish — but a different environment, and a different scale of life.

Brothers and sisters, please take this to heart: the size of the system you place yourself in is the size your life will grow to. Some people’s spiritual horizon, all their lives, is no bigger than their own little fish tank — my needs, my grievances, my plans, my face. Others live in the ocean of God’s kingdom — God’s heart, God’s household, God’s kingdom. They are equally born again and saved, yet the scale of their lives is worlds apart.

Yet the lesson immediately pulls us back to the most crucial point: everything begins with “the individual.”

This is what 321 means by “life first, then relationships, then ministry.” It is true that the larger the system, the greater its influence; but a system is not built from the large down to the small; it grows from the small up to the large. The kingdom of God is not an organisation dropped from the sky. The Lord Jesus said it is like a mustard seed, “which indeed is smaller than all seeds. But when it is grown, it is greater than the herbs” (Matthew 13:32).

So the lesson puts it very directly: if individuals have not established God’s system, families cannot be healthy, churches cannot be united, and the kingdom cannot be revived.

The psalmist said it long ago: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain. Unless Yahweh watches over the city, the watchman guards it in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Notice the words “in vain.” They don’t mean “builds more slowly,” nor “builds less well”; they mean “labours for nothing.” A person can be extremely hard-working, extremely self-sacrificing, extremely gifted — and yet be building a house God never asked them to build. Brothers and sisters, how much that deserves our quiet reflection.

In pastoral ministry I often meet brothers and sisters like this. There was one sister who had a part in every ministry in the church, large or small — Sunday school, welcoming, visitation, the kitchen; she never missed a thing. But one day she said to me through her tears, “Pastor, at church I’m the busiest person there; at home I’m the biggest stranger. My children have to book an appointment to talk to me.”

It wasn’t that she didn’t love the Lord; she loved him dearly. She had simply got the order of the system the wrong way round — she started building from the outermost ring and never built the innermost one first.

The Lord Jesus said, “But seek first God’s Kingdom, and his righteousness; and all these things will be given to you as well.” (Matthew 6:33) Those words “seek first” are precisely about order.

Brothers and sisters, please don’t get the order wrong. It is not “once the church is healthy, I’ll be healthy,” but “once I am healthy, the church can become healthy.” It is not “wait for my family to change first,” but “I change first, and then my family will change.” The Goal of 321 is to establish God’s system, and in that Goal, the first brick is always laid on you yourself.

sections.heading: 4. A Wrong Choice Brings the Fall of a Whole System
sections.html:
“They said to him, ‘Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.’” (1 Samuel 8:5)

Brothers and sisters, notice that on the surface this sounds entirely reasonable. Samuel was old — that was a fact. His sons were corrupt — that too was a fact. What the elders put forward was a proposal grounded in reality, one that looked very responsible.

But how did God see it?

“Yahweh said to Samuel, ‘Listen to the voice of the people in all that they tell you; for they have not rejected you, but they have rejected me as the king over them.’” (1 Samuel 8:7)

With a single sentence God peels away the outward reasons and exposes the real problem underneath. The word “rejected” is the Hebrew מָאַס (ma’as), meaning to refuse, to cast away, to regard as useless. The people were not adjusting a structure; they were casting away their King.

So the lesson rightly asks: what was Israel’s problem?

First, they were not content to have God as King. Second, they wanted to be like the world.

“Like all the nations” — that short phrase is the key to the whole passage. Later the people said it again, even more bluntly: “No; but we will have a king over us, that we also may be like all the nations, and that our king may judge us, and go out before us, and fight our battles.” (1 Samuel 8:19-20)

What they wanted was not a better leader; what they wanted was “something visible to lean on.” What they wanted was not justice; what they wanted was “to be like everyone else.”

Psychology calls this force conformity. In 1951 the psychologist Solomon Asch ran a famous series of experiments at Swarthmore College. Participants were asked to judge which of three lines was the same length as a standard line. The answer was obvious; a person answering alone almost never got it wrong. But when everyone else in the room — all of them, in fact, the experimenter’s confederates — unanimously gave a plainly wrong answer, about three-quarters of the real participants conformed at least once; overall, in roughly a third of the critical trials, participants went along with the wrong answer.

Brothers and sisters, think about it: if people will give an answer against their own judgement about something as simple as the length of a line, just because of other people — how much more about something invisible like “shall we let God be King?”

The pressure to be “like all the nations” has been blowing from 1050 BC right down to today.

The lesson says this was a “choice.” But the result of that choice was a shift from the rule of God to the rule of man, from God’s system to the Worldly system.

This is exactly the change of perspective 321 speaks of — only running in reverse. 321 calls us to turn from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. What Israel did that day was those four turns in the opposite direction: they exchanged God’s for man’s, the heavenly for the earthly, the eternal for the temporary, the godly for the worldly.

Samuel spelled out the consequences to them one by one: the king would take their sons for his chariots and to be his horsemen; he would take their daughters to be perfumers, cooks and bakers; he would take the best of their fields, vineyards and olive groves; he would take a tenth of their grain and of their vineyards; and in the end, “you will be his servants” (1 Samuel 8:11-17).

Did the people hear? They heard. Did the people change? They did not. “But the people refused to listen to the voice of Samuel” (1 Samuel 8:19).

And so the three results the lesson names came true, one after another.

First, the nation was divided. After Solomon died, his son Rehoboam chose to rule the people with a heavier yoke, and ten tribes abandoned the house of David, saying, “To your tents, Israel!” (1 Kings 12:16) One kingdom split into two, north and south.

Second, spiritual corruption. The northern kingdom of Israel had nineteen kings in all, and Scripture’s verdict on every one of them is the same: none was good; all did what was evil in Yahweh’s sight.

Third, the road to destruction. In 722 BC the northern kingdom was destroyed by Assyria; in 586 BC Jerusalem, in the southern kingdom, fell to Babylon, and the temple was burned.

Brothers and sisters, between that phrase “like all the nations” in 1 Samuel 8 and the fall of Jerusalem’s walls lie more than four hundred years. One wrong choice affected a whole generation.

That is why the lesson is called “Care About Every Choice.” Because at the moment of choosing, you often cannot see where it ends.

sections.heading: 5. Two Kinds of Wisdom Establish Two Kinds of System
sections.html:
At this point the lesson quotes James 3:14-18. Let’s read the whole passage through once:

“But if you have bitter jealousy and selfish ambition in your heart, don’t boast and don’t lie against the truth. This wisdom is not that which comes down from above, but is earthly, sensual, and demonic. For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed. But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” (James 3:14-18)

Scripture tells us plainly here: there are two kinds of wisdom.

(1) Worldly wisdom is the wisdom of the self-centred life

James says this wisdom “is earthly, sensual, and demonic.” The three words in the original descend in stages. “Earthly” is ἐπίγειος (epigeios): its vision reaches no further than the horizon. “Sensual” is ψυχικός (psychikos), literally “of the soul,” driven by human emotion, will and desire. “Demonic” is δαιμονιώδης (daimoniōdēs): its source, astonishingly, is the power of darkness. Brothers and sisters, this is a staircase going down: first the vision grows short, then the soul takes charge, and finally Satan makes use of it.

The lesson lists four fruits of this wisdom: jealousy, selfish ambition, selfishness and confusion.

“Jealousy” is ζῆλος (zēlos) in the original. The word is neutral in itself — “zeal” — but once it centres on “self,” zeal turns into being unable to bear seeing others do well. “Selfish ambition” is ἐριθεία (eritheia), a word that originally described the mindset of a hired hand working for his wages, and came to mean “forming factions for one’s own advantage.” Notice that there is nothing in this word about “contending for the truth”; there is only “I want to win.”

And the result? James says, “For where jealousy and selfish ambition are, there is confusion and every evil deed.” (James 3:16) “Confusion” is ἀκαταστασία (akatastasia) in the original: turmoil, disorder, an inability to settle.

Brothers and sisters, isn’t this exactly what 321 says: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose. When a self-centred person meets a self-centred person, it is like two stones striking each other — what comes off is not sparks, but chips.

Professor John Gottman of the University of Washington, a leading authority on marriage research, found in a longitudinal study carried out with Robert Levenson in 1992 that the most accurate predictor of whether a couple would divorce was not whether they argued but how they argued. He called criticism, contempt, defensiveness and stonewalling the “Four Horsemen” of marriage, and the most destructive of them is contempt. In his long-term samples, by watching just a few minutes of a couple’s interaction, he could predict with roughly ninety per cent accuracy whether they would later divorce.

What is contempt? Contempt is “I am above you.” Contempt is the self-centred life at its most naked.

(2) The wisdom from above is the wisdom of selflessness

“But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.” (James 3:17)

The lesson lists the qualities of this wisdom as purity, peace, gentleness, yieldedness, mercy and abundant fruit. Here we need to match the wording precisely. Where the Chinese Union Version has a single phrase for “gentle and yielding,” the original has two words: ἐπιεικής (epieikēs), meaning forbearing, not insisting on one’s own rights; and εὐπειθής (eupeithēs), meaning easily persuaded, willing to listen to counsel. And where the Chinese Union Version says “abundant in good fruit,” it is not a vague “bearing much fruit” but bearing fruit that is good.

Notice James’s order: “first pure, then peaceful.” Purity comes first, peace after. Because peace without purity is only compromise, only papering over the cracks. Only when we are first pure before God can there be true peace with others.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? “Not insisting on one’s own rights” and “willing to listen to counsel” — these two are exactly what 321 calls selflessness. 321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. ἐπιεικής is laying down our rights; εὐπειθής is returning to our originally intended position.

And the result? The lesson says: peace, the fruit of righteousness, growth in life. James says, “Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” (James 3:18)

This is a farmer’s picture. The fruit of righteousness is not argued into being; it is sown and grown. And the seed that is sown has a name: peace. Whatever seed you scatter in a home or in a church, that is what you will reap.

So the lesson sums it up in one sentence: whichever wisdom you use, that is the system you establish.

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly where 321’s 920 practice comes in. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the “0,” the selfless life; and what grows from it is the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions: “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

You see, the list in James 3:17 and the list in Galatians 5:22 are scenery along the same road. For the wisdom from above is, in the end, the wisdom of the Holy Spirit.

sections.heading: 6. The Way You Lead Determines the System You Establish
sections.html:
Here the lesson asks three very concrete and very piercing questions:

In the family — is it control, or love?

In the church — is it power, or service?

In relationships — is it demanding, or building others up?

Brothers and sisters, please don’t rush to answer. First, think back to last night.

The Lord Jesus himself laid out these two roads with perfect clarity: “But Jesus summoned them, and said, ‘You know that the rulers of the nations lord it over them, and their great ones exercise authority over them. It shall not be so among you, but whoever desires to become great among you shall be your servant. Whoever desires to be first among you shall be your bondservant, even as the Son of Man came not to be served, but to serve, and to give his life as a ransom for many.’” (Matthew 20:25-28)

“It shall not be so among you.” Those few words are the watershed between the two systems.

Peter learned this lesson too. In his old age he wrote to the elders: “Shepherd the flock of God which is among you, exercising the oversight, not under compulsion, but voluntarily, not for dishonest gain, but willingly; not as lording it over those entrusted to you, but making yourselves examples to the flock.” (1 Peter 5:2-3)

Not lording it over them, but being an example. This is the first of 321’s Three Foundations: Jesus is my role model. And we ourselves are to become a role model for others.

The lesson says: every choice is establishing an environment.

Kurt Lewin, the father of social psychology, carried out a classic study in 1939 with Ronald Lippitt and Ralph White. They divided boys of about ten years old into several groups doing handicrafts, and gave them adult leaders of three different styles: autocratic, democratic and laissez-faire. The results were very clear. The autocratic groups’ output was not low, but the groups were full of hostility and aggression, and as soon as the leader left the room, work stopped at once. The democratic groups were friendly and cooperative, and even when the leader was absent the boys kept on working.

Brothers and sisters, pay special attention to that detail: what happens once the leader leaves the room.

That is the system you have really established.

Control establishes an environment where people “only move when someone is watching”; love establishes an environment where people “are willing even when no one is watching.” Power establishes a church that “is afraid of you”; service establishes a church that “becomes like you.” Demanding establishes a group of people who “don’t dare make a mistake”; building others up establishes a group of people who “dare to grow up.”

The organisational psychologist Edgar Schein, in Organizational Culture and Leadership (first edition 1985), wrote a much-quoted line: culture and leadership are two sides of the same coin. In his view, the most important work of leaders is to create and manage culture.

The lesson says that over time this forms a culture, an atmosphere, a system.

Brothers and sisters, culture is not a slogan on the wall; culture is “the way we usually do things around here.” When someone in your family makes a mistake, do they usually hide first, or come to you first? When someone in your small group is struggling, do they usually put on a mask, or tell the truth? That “usually” is the system you have established.

And how was it established? Not through one special conference, but through your choices, made again and again. Just like that path on the mountainside.

321 says: people matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things; life first, then relationships, then ministry. When we lead by control, power and demands, we are putting tasks ahead of people; only when we lead by love, service and building others up are we putting people ahead of tasks.

Paul says, “doing nothing through rivalry or through conceit, but in humility, each counting others better than himself” (Philippians 2:3). Brothers and sisters, if this one verse were truly lived out in a home, that home would become God’s system.

Let’s turn the lesson’s three questions into three very concrete scenes for you to take home.

The first scene is at home. Your child brings home a report card, and it isn’t good. The controlling response is: “See? I told you so, and you wouldn’t listen.” The loving response is: “Let’s look at it together and see where you got stuck.” Both are concern, both are for the child’s good; but the first response establishes a home of “I don’t dare let you know,” and the second establishes a home of “when something happens, I’ll tell you first.” Ten years from now, how far apart will those two homes be?

The second scene is at church. A young co-worker has made a mess of a task. The response of power is: “Don’t give him this job again.” The response of service is: “I’ll go through it with him one more time.” Both are being responsible; but the first response establishes a team where “only a handful of people dare to lift a finger,” and the second establishes a team where “new people keep growing up.”

The third scene is in relationships. Your spiritual companion has a gift that is stronger than yours. The demanding response is: “Why isn’t he helping more?” The response that builds up is: “I want to find a way to give his gift a stage.” In Ephesians 4:11-12 Paul says that the fivefold ministry the Lord gave is “for the perfecting of the saints, to the work of serving, to the building up of the body of Christ.” Building people up is the very purpose for which God established those ministries.

sections.heading: 7. Don’t Bring the World’s System into God’s Kingdom
sections.html:
Here the lesson says something that cuts deep: very often the problem is not that we aren’t serving, but that we are serving in “the world’s way.”

Brothers and sisters, listen to that once more. The problem is not that there is no service; the problem is the way we serve.

The lesson gives three examples: competition in place of building others up, control in place of leading, performance in place of life.

None of these three substitutions involves not working; on the contrary, they often involve working very hard. The most dangerous thing in a church has never been laziness; it is doing God’s work with worldly drive.

Paul puts it with absolute firmness: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

The word “world” in Greek is κόσμος (kosmos). Its original meaning is “an ordered arrangement, a system,” the opposite of chaos. Brothers and sisters, do you see it? The very word Scripture uses for “the world” means “a system.” The world is not a heap of loose sand; the world is a system that runs with great precision and great allure.

The apostle John names the three pillars of this system: “For all that is in the world, the lust of the flesh, the lust of the eyes, and the pride of life, isn’t the Father’s, but is the world’s.” (1 John 2:16)

The lust of the flesh is “I want to feel good”; the lust of the eyes is “I want to possess”; the pride of life is “I want to be seen.”

Brothers and sisters, “I want to be seen” is precisely the root of “performance in place of life.”

Psychology has observed this very clearly. In 1971 the psychologist Edward Deci found that when people are doing something out of their own interest, once they start doing it for an external reward, the reward actually erodes their inner motivation. In 1973 Mark Lepper, David Greene and Richard Nisbett ran a well-known experiment at Stanford University. They took young children who already liked drawing, and told one group in advance, “When you finish your drawing you’ll get a certificate.” The result: the group that expected a reward spent noticeably less time drawing of their own accord during later free play. This phenomenon came to be known as the “overjustification effect.”

Brothers and sisters, this gives us a sober warning: when service begins to be for applause, the heart of service begins to die. The busier things are on the outside, the drier they are within.

The lesson says: this is bringing Babylon into the church.

In Scripture, Babylon has never been just a city. From the Tower of Babel in Genesis 11 — “Come, let’s build ourselves a city, and a tower whose top reaches to the sky, and let’s make a name for ourselves, lest we be scattered abroad on the surface of the whole earth” (Genesis 11:4) — the spirit of Babylon was set: man climbing upward by his own strength, man making a name for himself. By the time we reach Revelation, God issues a call to his people: “Come out of her, my people, that you have no participation in her sins, and that you don’t receive of her plagues” (Revelation 18:4).

The lesson says the result is: busy on the outside, dry within.

Scripture really does describe such a church. The Lord said to the church in Sardis, “I know your works, that you have a reputation of being alive, but you are dead.” (Revelation 3:1)

A reputation of being alive, but dead. Brothers and sisters, what a fearful sentence that is.

321 says: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled. 321 also says: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When we shift our focus from Jesus to what people think of us, we are already building God’s temple the Babylonian way.

Paul reminds us, “But let each man be careful how he builds on it.” (1 Corinthians 3:10) He does not say “whether to build”; he says “how to build.” Because “if anyone builds on the foundation with gold, silver, costly stones, wood, hay, or stubble, each man’s work will be revealed. For the Day will declare it, because it is revealed in fire; and the fire itself will test what sort of work each man’s work is” (1 Corinthians 3:12-13).
