sections.heading: 8. The Key to Establishing God’s System: 321
sections.html:
The lesson puts it beautifully: establishing God’s system does not depend on methods; it means going back to the foundation.

Paul says, “For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” (1 Corinthians 3:11)

The foundation is not ours to lay; the foundation has already been laid. What we have to do is go back and build on that foundation.

The lesson divides this foundation into five practical realities.

The Three Foundations

First, Jesus is my role model. When I don’t know what to do, I ask: what would Jesus do? On the night of his greatest authority, what he picked up was a towel for washing feet — he “arose from supper, and laid aside his outer garments. He took a towel and wrapped a towel around his waist. Then he poured water into the basin, and began to wash the disciples’ feet” (John 13:4-5).

Second, the Bible is my standard. Not my feelings, not majority opinion, not the way the wind of this age is blowing. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105)

Third, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Not cleverness, not experience. “‘Not by might, nor by power, but by my Spirit,’ says Yahweh of Armies.” (Zechariah 4:6)

The Two Core Values

First, let Jesus be King. This is the very opposite of 1 Samuel 8. Israel said, “We want a king, like all the nations”; we are to say, “Lord, you are my King.”

Second, let Jesus receive the glory. Not me receiving the glory, not my ministry receiving the glory, not my family or my church receiving the glory. “For of him, and through him, and to him are all things. To him be the glory for ever! Amen.” (Romans 11:36)

The lesson says: when these five realities are lived out, God’s system is being established.

Brothers and sisters, notice the words “lived out.” The lesson’s last sentence carries great weight: not slogans, but every choice.

Slogans hang on the wall; choices are walked out underfoot.

We can also see it along 321’s Path of Serving: Spirit — the Holy Spirit is my guide; Understanding — the Bible is my standard; Life — Jesus is my role model; Service — let Jesus be King; God — let Jesus receive all the glory. The end of that path is exactly the Goal of 321: establish God’s system.

Brothers and sisters, have you noticed? The Goal of 321 is exactly the subject of today’s lesson. The Three Foundations plus the Two Core Values are not five nice-sounding sentences; they are five realities that must be cashed out in every single choice.

There is a little mathematical calculation that shows the weight of “every choice” very well. If a person improves by just one per cent a day, after three hundred and sixty-five days they are at 1.01 to the power of 365 — about 37.8 times where they began. Conversely, if they slip back one per cent a day, after a year they are left with 0.99 to the power of 365 — about 0.03, almost nothing. The same one per cent, in different directions, and after a year the difference is more than a thousandfold.

This is not motivational talk; this is the truth about “every choice.” A system grows exactly like this, one day at a time.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s walk today’s road once more and string the 321 vision together.

First, the Goal: establish God’s system. This is where all of 321’s practice is headed, and it is the theme of today’s lesson. We do not pursue selflessness to make ourselves better; we pursue it so that God’s kingdom may be established on earth. The Lord taught us to pray, “Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.” (Matthew 6:10)

Second, the self-centred life and selflessness. “Like all the nations” in 1 Samuel 8 is the self-centred life; the “gentle, reasonable” of James 3 is selflessness. The self-centred life builds Babylon; selflessness builds Jerusalem. Selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus, and living it out — “it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me” (Galatians 2:20).

Third, humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. When Israel wanted a king, they were reaching to seize a visible power; when Rehoboam chose the heavier yoke, he too was seizing power. “God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6) Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win.

Fourth, the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. This is exactly the order of the lesson’s conclusion. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; change relationships and you change ministry. A system is what these five changes add up to.

Fifth, life first, then relationships, then ministry. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. What points four and five of the lesson expose is that we so often turn this order upside down — grabbing at ministry first, managing relationships second, and only thinking of life last. Turn the order upside down, and the system is bent out of shape.

Sixth, the change of perspective: from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. First Samuel 8 is those four turns in reverse; today we are to turn each of them back again.

Seventh, the 920 practice and 235 relationships. In the family, in the small group, at work — everyone you have a relationship with is your “2”; before them you live out the “0” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions, and this is the smallest and truest unit of God’s system. Going further, you become a “2,” a spiritual companion, with a selfless person; you form the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children; you become part of the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades — and so God’s system grows, ring by ring.

sections.heading: 10. Practice for Daily Living
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s take them deeper one at a time, using 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

Practice 1: Examine the system I am establishing

Ask yourself honestly: my present daily living, my family, my service — are they God’s system or the Worldly system?

Information: Today you have heard the two lists of the two kinds of wisdom. Copy out James 3:17 and stick it somewhere you’ll see it every day.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light. Don’t ask, “Have I committed any big sins?” Ask, “What atmosphere is growing in my home and in my service?”

Conviction: Admit that I really am building something. If I don’t admit it, I will never check whether I am building it right.

Implementation: Tonight, take a sheet of paper and draw two columns. On the left, write “the three moods that come up most often in my home”; on the right, write the qualities listed in James 3:17; then compare them.

Evaluation: This week, on which day did I respond to someone in an earthly, soulish way?

Correction: Say to the person I affected: “I’m sorry; my attitude that day was wrong.”

Repetition: Examine yourself regularly, every Sunday evening; don’t do it just once and call it done.

Multiplication: Take this self-examination into your small group, and bring one person to do it with you.

Practice 2: Choose the wisdom that comes from heaven

In conflicts and decisions, don’t follow emotion and instinct; choose a response of peace, gentleness and humility.

Information: Remember James’s order — first pure, then peaceful. That order cannot be reversed.

Revelation: In the moment of conflict, ask the Holy Spirit to remind you: what is stirring in me right now — jealousy, or peace?

Conviction: Believe that the Lord Jesus’ way really is right, even when in the moment it looks like losing out.

Implementation: Set a concrete rule, for example: when emotions rise, stay quiet for sixty seconds before you speak.

Evaluation: Was there anything I said today that my emotions said, not the Holy Spirit?

Correction: Turn back straight away, take those words back, and say it more gently than the first time.

Repetition: Once a day, seven times a week, three hundred and sixty-five times a year. Remember that 1.01 calculation.

Multiplication: When someone at home asks you, “Why have you changed?”, tell them about the wisdom from above.

Practice 3: Change your environment, starting with yourself

Don’t wait for your environment to change; start by living out 321 yourself, so that God’s system spreads outward from you.

Information: “Unless Yahweh builds the house, they who build it labor in vain.” (Psalm 127:1)

Revelation: See that God has already placed a “seed of God’s system” within you.

Conviction: From today on, stop saying, “Let the others change first.”

Implementation: This week, choose one of your “2”s — a family member, a co-worker — and in a concrete way live out one of the nine graces towards that person.

Evaluation: This week, did I slip back again into the mindset of “waiting for my environment to change”?

Correction: Change every sentence that runs “He ought to do this and that” into “Lord, change me first.”

Repetition: Keep it up for four weeks; don’t do it only once.

Multiplication: Bring one person to walk with you and become your spiritual companion — this is the beginning of a 235 relationship.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, the lesson’s conclusion says: a system is not established in a day; it is the result of countless choices added together.

Then it gives us a very clear road: when one person changes, a family changes; when a family changes, a church changes; when a church changes, a generation changes.

Look where that road begins — with “one person.”

And that one person is sitting right here this morning, listening to this lesson.

Let’s go back to the grassy slope where we started. You don’t have to wait for someone to come and build a highway; you only have to walk it once more today. Walk in the right direction, walk across, and walk it again tomorrow. A year from now, the path will be there; ten years from now, your children will be walking that path; a hundred years from now, perhaps someone you have never met will walk the path your feet wore down, and it will bring them into the presence of God.

At the end of his life Joshua stood at Shechem and said to all Israel, “If it seems evil to you to serve Yahweh, choose today whom you will serve; whether the gods which your fathers served that were beyond the River, or the gods of the Amorites, in whose land you dwell; but as for me and my house, we will serve Yahweh.” (Joshua 24:15)

“As for me and my house” — Joshua didn’t wait for anyone else. He began with himself, with his own household.

Brothers and sisters, starting today: in every choice, let Jesus be King, and let God’s system be established on earth.

Not for our name, but for his name. Not that I receive the glory, but that Jesus receives all the glory.

keyVerses: James 3:17-18

“But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy. Now the fruit of righteousness is sown in peace by those who make peace.” (James 3:17-18)
1 Samuel 8:5
“They said to him, ‘Behold, you are old, and your sons don’t walk in your ways. Now make us a king to judge us like all the nations.’” (1 Samuel 8:5)
1 Corinthians 3:11
“For no one can lay any other foundation than that which has been laid, which is Jesus Christ.” (1 Corinthians 3:11)
declarations: The lesson leaves us with a short but powerful sentence:
You are not just “living your life”; you are “establishing a system.”

Brothers and sisters, keep this sentence in your heart. The glass of water you poured this morning, the sentence you spoke today, the message you held back from answering today — they look like nothing more than daily life, but in fact they are bricks.
Then let us make this declaration of faith together:
Lord, I am willing to begin with myself, to bring every choice back into you, to establish God’s system, and to let your kingdom reign in my life!
practices: Examine the system I am establishing
Choose the wisdom that comes from heaven
Change my environment, starting with myself
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

This morning you have shown us that we are not just living our lives; we are establishing a system. The way we live each day, our habits every time we make a decision, our attitude every time we respond to something — all of these are wearing a path in our families, our churches and our generation.

Lord, forgive us. So often, like Israel, we want to be “like all the nations”; so often we handle relationships with earthly, soulish wisdom — competition in place of building others up, control in place of leading, performance in place of life — and we bring Babylon into your house.

Lord, wash us clean with your precious blood, and give us the wisdom that is from above — first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.

Help us, starting with the very first choice of today: to let Jesus be my role model, to let the Bible be my standard, to let the Holy Spirit be my guide, to let Jesus be King, and to let Jesus receive all the glory.
Let your Kingdom come. Let your will be done on earth as it is in heaven.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Think back to one small choice you made this week (a sentence, a message, an attitude). If that choice were repeated for a year, what kind of culture would it establish in your home? Compare it with James 3:17: “But the wisdom that is from above is first pure, then peaceful, gentle, reasonable, full of mercy and good fruits, without partiality, and without hypocrisy.”

In your present service, is there anything that you are “doing,” but doing in the world’s way? Compare it with Romans 12:2: “Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” How do you plan to hand it back to the Lord and let Jesus be King?
l110.title: Caring About Every Choice
l110.subtitle: A Change of Choices (Part 8): Establishing a System
l110.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: 1. Introduction: It’s Not That You Can’t — You’re Just Not Used to It Yet
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Before we come to today’s lesson, let me ask you a very homely question.

The stairs in your home — how many thousands of times have you walked them? Each morning as you come down, do you have to look down and count the steps? Do you have to decide in advance, “Left foot first, or right foot first?” No, you don’t. You can come down the stairs while thinking about what groceries to buy today, or about the phone call you have to make in a moment.

But suppose today you were put on an unfamiliar spiral staircase, with steps that are narrow and high and open in between — how would you walk it? You’d grip the handrail, look down, take it one step at a time with total concentration, and breathe a sigh of relief when you got to the bottom.

Brothers and sisters, both are stairs — so why is one as easy as breathing, and the other as hard as an exam? Notice: walking down stairs hasn’t suddenly become difficult; you just aren’t used to that staircase yet.

That is what today’s lesson is about.

In Kingdom 321 Online Fellowship we often talk about “selflessness.” Brothers and sisters have all heard the word, and everyone nods. But the lesson is very honest right at the start: many people have a wrong mindset about selflessness — it sounds wonderful, but it’s very hard to do.

Because it feels hard, selflessness ends up stuck in three places: stuck in the vision, as a beautiful piece of doctrine; stuck in the slogans, as a resounding line in our meetings; stuck in our hopes, as a longing for “some day, I hope.”

But it never gets into three other places: it never gets into our life, never gets into our habits, never gets into our actual daily living.

In pastoral ministry I often see this picture. A sister, during morning devotions, says through her tears, “Lord, I am willing to be selfless.” She means it. But less than five minutes after she gets home, her husband kicks his shoes off anywhere, and that “self” inside her climbs straight back onto the throne. She is frustrated, and even wonders: maybe I’m just not cut out for this?

Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson wants to dismantle that misunderstanding and tell us a truth that sets us wonderfully free —

Selflessness is not hard at all; in fact it is the lightest road there is.

This is not a pep talk; these are the Lord’s own words. The Lord Jesus said, “Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:29-30)

Listen carefully: the Lord did not say, “My yoke is heavy; grit your teeth and hold on.” The Lord said his yoke is easy and his burden is light. What is truly heavy has never been selflessness; it is the self-centred life.

Today we will walk six stretches of road with the lesson:

First, selflessness is not a slogan; it is the cultivation of life.

Second, why we find selflessness hard.

Third, selflessness is actually the easiest road.

Fourth, the power of habit: from unnatural to natural.

Fifth, you already have the selfless life.

Sixth, the more you practise, the lighter it gets.

May the Holy Spirit, this morning, remove this misunderstanding from our hearts, so that we no longer stand at the foot of the mountain gazing up at selflessness, but lift our feet and walk in.

sections.heading: 2. Scripture Background: The Good Shepherd and the Abundant Life
sections.html:
To understand today’s message, let’s first stand at the historical scene of our theme verse.

The author of John’s Gospel is John, the son of Zebedee, the disciple whom the Lord Jesus loved. This Gospel is generally thought to have been written around AD 80 to 90, very probably in Ephesus in Asia Minor. At that time the generation who had seen the Lord with their own eyes was passing away, and distorted teaching about the person of Christ was beginning to appear in the church. So John carefully selected seven signs and seven “I am” sayings, all pointing to one purpose. He says so himself: “but these are written, that you may believe that Jesus is the Christ, the Son of God, and that believing you may have life in his name.” (John 20:31)

Chapter 10, where our theme verse is found, follows on from chapter 9. Chapter 9 records the Lord healing a man born blind. His healing should have been a joy for the whole city; instead the Pharisees interrogated him, intimidated his parents, and finally “threw him out” (John 9:34). Far from feeding the sheep, the shepherds drove a sheep out of the fold.

It was against this background that the Lord Jesus told the parable of the sheepfold. He said, “Most certainly, I tell you, I am the sheep’s door.” (John 10:7) And then comes our theme verse for today.

“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

This verse sets out two forces that come among the flock, in the sharpest possible contrast.

The Greek for “thief” is kleptēs, a sneak-thief who strikes when no one is looking; the English word kleptomania comes from it. He doesn’t rob openly; he steals in secret. Brothers and sisters, that is exactly Satan’s method. He rarely announces loudly, “I’m coming to destroy your life.” He just whispers softly in your ear, “You need to think of yourself, you know.”

His aims go three levels deep, each deeper than the last. To steal is to take what is in your hands; to kill is to rob you of the life within; to destroy carries the sense in the original of “laying utterly waste” — trampling the whole pasture to ruin.

The Lord Jesus comes in the completely opposite direction. He says, “I came that they may have life.” The word “life” here is zōē, a word especially characteristic of John’s Gospel, meaning the eternal, heavenly life of God — not bios, mere being alive.

And “abundantly” is perissos in the original, meaning “beyond, exceeding, overflowing.” It is not “just enough”; it is “spilling over.” Like a glass of water filled to the top and still being poured, running down the rim onto the table. The psalmist says, “My cup runs over” (Psalm 23:5) — that is the picture.

Brothers and sisters, fix this firmly in your mind: the selfless life is not a diminished life; it is an overflowing life. Satan lies to us that if you deny yourself you’ll have less; the Lord says that only when you deny yourself will you be full.

Read one verse further and the Lord explains how he will give it: “I am the good shepherd. The good shepherd lays down his life for the sheep.” (John 10:11) Abundant life doesn’t come from nowhere; the Shepherd bought it with his life. He also says, “No one takes it away from me, but I lay it down by myself. I have power to lay it down, and I have power to take it again.” (John 10:18)

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the foundation of today’s third point. “Lay it down” — that is the cross, which dealt with the self-centred life; “take it again” — that is the resurrection, which gives us the selfless life. The hard part, the Lord has already done himself.

Now look at the second passage, Matthew 5:48. It comes from the Sermon on the Mount, as the conclusion of the whole section on “loving your enemies.” The Lord first says, “You have heard that it was said, ‘You shall love your neighbor and hate your enemy.’ But I tell you, love your enemies, bless those who curse you, do good to those who hate you, and pray for those who mistreat you and persecute you” (Matthew 5:43-44). Then he points to the Father’s heart: “For he makes his sun to rise on the evil and the good, and sends rain on the just and the unjust.” (Matthew 5:45) Only then does this sentence land: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

The Greek for “perfect” is teleios, from the root telos, “purpose, end, goal.” So teleios does not mean “without the slightest flaw”; it means “having reached the purpose one was made for, grown into what one should be, whole and mature.” A green, unripe fruit is not “bad”; it simply isn’t teleios yet. When it has ripened and grown sweet and can feed people, then it is teleios.

So the lesson puts it with great precision: this verse is less an unreachable demand than a revelation of an identity already given. How does the Father love? His love makes no distinction; his sun shines on the good and the evil alike. And you are his child; his life is already in you — so you can.

Brothers and sisters, with the background in place, we can step into the lesson.

sections.heading: 3. Selflessness Is Not a Slogan but the Cultivation of Life
sections.html:
The lesson’s first point says: selflessness is not an instant change; it is a process of cultivation.

This is very important. Because many people are disappointed not because the teaching is wrong but because their expectation is wrong. We think selflessness is a switch: flick it, and from then on all is peace. Then we press it for ages with no response, and conclude that the switch is broken — or that we are.

No. Selflessness is not a switch; it is a seedling. Paul says it very clearly: “that you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit, and that you be renewed in the spirit of your mind, and put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:22-24)

Notice the two actions, “put away” and “put on.” Putting on clothes is not something you do once and never have to do again; it is something you do every morning. The old self “grows corrupt” gradually, and the new self is put on gradually too.

The lesson tells us that this process of cultivation has three levels.

The first level: a change of mindset — “I have already.”

“I have already” is a very precious phrase in 321, and its basis is in Galatians. Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

“I have been crucified with Christ” — the verb here in Greek is synestauromai, a perfect passive. The perfect tense means something was completed in the past and its effect continues right up to the present. It is not “I am trying hard to be crucified,” nor “I hope one day I’ll be crucified,” but — it has been done, and it still stands today.

Brothers and sisters, this is a change of mindset. You are not trying to “become” a selfless person; you are to “believe” that you already are.

The second level: a change of choice — denying of self.

The Lord Jesus said, “If anyone desires to come after me, let him deny himself, take up his cross, and follow me.” (Luke 9:23)

The Greek for “deny himself” is aparneomai, and this word has a startling use elsewhere. The Lord said to Peter, “tonight, before the rooster crows, you will deny me three times.” (Matthew 26:34) That word “deny” is the very same word.

So “denying of self” literally means: disowning yourself. When the old self comes knocking and raises its voice — “This is my right, my face, my point of view” — I need to be able to say: I don’t know him.

And Luke adds one word — “daily” (it stands in the Chinese Union Version and in most Greek manuscripts: “take up his cross daily”). Mark 8:34 and Matthew 16:24 do not have it; only Luke adds it. Brothers and sisters, that one word is the key to this whole lesson. Denying of self is not one heroic act in a lifetime; it is a choice made once a day, many times a day.

The third level: a change of habit — living out selflessness.

The lesson puts it very directly: having the mindset isn’t enough; making the choice isn’t enough either. The choice must be repeated, become a habit, and finally become life.

Let me use an example from daily life. When someone learns a foreign language, first they memorise the grammar rules — that is mindset. Then they pluck up the courage to say their first sentence — that is choice. But when do we say that they really “know” the language? When they no longer have to translate in their head first, and the words simply come out by themselves. By then the language is no longer a tool they “use”; it is part of who they “are.”

Neuroscience offers a fascinating confirmation. Professor Ann Graybiel of the Massachusetts Institute of Technology, in a series of studies published from 1998 onward, showed that when a sequence of actions is performed over and over, the brain “packages” it into a single unit — what is called chunking — and hands it over to the basal ganglia to run automatically. At that point, activity in the prefrontal cortex, which is responsible for thinking and judgement, drops markedly. In other words, the essence of a habit is that the brain transfers something from “I have to think hard about it” to “I can do it without thinking.”

Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the road the lesson describes: mindset, choice, habit, and finally life.

In 321’s teaching we call this the fivefold change: mindset, life, daily living, relationships, ministry. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living; change daily living and you change relationships; and only when relationships change is there real ministry. Note that this order cannot be reversed — life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people have a very large ministry, but their life hasn’t kept up, and the ministry ends up as just another stage for “self.”

And the lesson’s three levels are exactly the bridge that leads from “mindset” to “life.” There is only one way across that bridge: step by step, walking it again and again.

sections.heading: 4. Why We Find Selflessness Hard
sections.html:
The lesson’s second point asks a very good question: why do we find selflessness hard?

The answer comes down to one thing: because we are used to the self-centred life.

The lesson lists three habits, each more piercing than the last: the habit of thinking of ourselves, the habit of fighting for ourselves, the habit of living by our own feelings.

Brothers and sisters, please be still for three seconds and honestly ask yourself: from this morning until now, how many of the thoughts that have passed through your heart have circled around “me”? Did I sleep well? Am I tired today? Am I valued? Have I been short-changed?

Paul describes this predicament with great honesty: “For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good. For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:18-19)

Notice: it isn’t that Paul was unwilling; he “desired” it. The problem was not in the will but in the inertia.

Science offers a very apt analogy: static friction and kinetic friction. When you push a very heavy wooden crate, when is it hardest? At the moment the crate goes from standing still to starting to slide. That is because the coefficient of static friction is usually greater than the coefficient of kinetic friction. Once the crate is moving, you find it much easier to push.

Brothers and sisters, most of the difficulty we feel in selflessness is “the difficulty of starting,” not “the difficulty along the way.”

Psychology also provides solid data. Professor Wendy Wood of the University of Southern California and her colleagues, in a study published in 2002 in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology, found that about forty-three per cent of people’s everyday behaviour is habitual behaviour repeated in the same settings — in other words, nearly half of our lives each day is not “decided”; it is “on autoplay.”

So here is the question: if nearly half of life is on autoplay, who recorded what’s playing? We did — slowly, over decades, every time we thought of ourselves, fought for ourselves, lived by our own feelings.

A very natural picture comes to mind: a riverbed. When the rain falls, at first the water spreads everywhere; it could go anywhere. But as water keeps flowing, it cuts a channel in the ground; the deeper the channel, the more naturally the next rain runs into it. In the end the water has no choice left — not because it wants to go there, but because that is now the way.

Brothers and sisters, the self-centred life is that deep, smooth riverbed in our hearts. So when the Holy Spirit asks us to be selfless, it feels like telling water to flow up the bank — unnatural, uncomfortable.

But the lesson reminds us of one crucial sentence: the problem is not that “selflessness is hard” but that “we’re not used to it yet.”

The difference between those two sentences is the difference between heaven and earth. “Selflessness is hard” describes the nature of the thing; once you define it like that, all that’s left is to give up. “I’m not used to it yet” describes the stage I’m at — and stages pass.

Let me give you an experiment everyone has tried. If you’re right-handed, pick up a pen now and write your name with your left hand. The letters will be crooked, slow and ugly, and a voice inside you will say, “I can’t.” But can’t you really? Your left hand has bones, muscles and nerves — everything it needs. It’s not that you “can’t”; it’s just that you’re “not used to it.”

Brothers and sisters, that is selflessness exactly. It’s not that you don’t have that life; it’s that you don’t yet have that habit.

On the power of habit there is an often-quoted saying: “We are what we repeatedly do. Excellence, then, is not an act, but a habit.” It is usually attributed to Aristotle, but on investigation the actual words come from the American historian Will Durant, in The Story of Philosophy (1926), as his summary of Aristotle’s Nicomachean Ethics. When we quote it we should be honest about where it comes from — but the truth it states does agree with Scripture.

From 321’s point of view, the self-centred life is not merely a bad habit; it is the shape pride takes in everyday life. We say: pride is leaving our originally intended position, seizing rights and wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God.

“The habit of thinking of ourselves” is putting ourselves at the centre — and that is God’s place.

“The habit of fighting for ourselves” is seizing rights, afraid of being short-changed.

“The habit of living by our own feelings” is letting our feelings be king, instead of letting Jesus be King.

We have also said: pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility inspires humility, and both sides win. The most hurtful quarrels at home are often not about big things; they are about who backs down first. When two self-centred lives collide, it’s like two stones smashing together — a great deal of noise, and both sides lose.

Brothers and sisters, what you are to lay down today is not your worth; it is your old riverbed.

sections.heading: 5. Selflessness Is Actually the Easiest Road
sections.html:
The lesson’s third point is the turning point of the whole lesson. It says: selflessness is actually the easiest road.

At first hearing this seems the exact opposite of our experience. But look at the verse the lesson quotes —

“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

Brothers and sisters, let me ask: giving the sheep life — is that something the sheep do, or the shepherd? The sheep only have to follow; the life is given by the shepherd.

The lesson then states the key: selflessness is not achieved by effort; it comes through the grace of Jesus.

Jesus has already done two crucial things.

The first: the cross — dealing with the self-centred life.

Paul says, “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him, that the body of sin might be done away with, so that we would no longer be in bondage to sin.” (Romans 6:6)

Notice the phrase “old man,” the old self. The old self is not “bad behaviour”; it is the very life that has itself at the centre. And God’s way of dealing with the old self is not repair; it is execution. Because the old self cannot be fixed — you can polish the leaves of a bitter tree one by one, and the fruit will still be bitter.

The second: the resurrection — giving you the selfless life.

“We were buried therefore with him through baptism into death, that just as Christ was raised from the dead through the glory of the Father, so we also might walk in newness of life.” (Romans 6:4)

And again: “But if the Spirit of him who raised up Jesus from the dead dwells in you, he who raised up Christ Jesus from the dead will also give life to your mortal bodies through his Spirit who dwells in you.” (Romans 8:11)

Brothers and sisters, what good news this is. God did not give us an “improved version of the old self”; he gave us a brand-new life. “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

So the lesson draws out a wonderfully liberating principle: Jesus does the hard part; we do the simple part.

I often use a lift as an illustration. A building has twenty floors, and you want to get to the top. You can take the stairs — panting, gripping the handrail, climbing floor by floor; that’s “effort.” Or you can step into the lift, stand steady, and press the button. Tell me: lifting your whole self, body weight and all, sixty metres straight up — who did that “hard thing”? The steel cables, the motor, the counterweight. All you did were three “simple things”: step in, stand steady, press the button.

Brothers and sisters, that is how salvation works. “For by grace you have been saved through faith, and that not of yourselves; it is the gift of God, not of works, that no one would boast.” (Ephesians 2:8-9) And sanctification works the same way: “For it is God who works in you both to will and to work, for his good pleasure.” (Philippians 2:13) Even the “willing” is God at work within us.

So what is our part? The lesson names three things: believe, choose, practise.

Interestingly, these three correspond exactly to three verbs in Romans 6.

Believe — “knowing this, that our old man was crucified with him” (Romans 6:6). First know it; first believe it.

Choose — “Thus consider yourselves also to be dead to sin, but alive to God in Christ Jesus our Lord.” (Romans 6:11) “Consider” is logizesthe in the original, a bookkeeping term meaning “enter it into the account.” This is a choice of the mind.

Practise — “present yourselves to God as alive from the dead, and your members as instruments of righteousness to God.” (Romans 6:13) Presenting is action, with hands and feet.

Knowing, counting it so, presenting — that is believing, choosing, practising.

So the lesson sums it up in one sentence: it is not “striving to become selfless”; it is “living out the life you have already been given.”

Brothers and sisters, the difference between those two is the difference between religion and the gospel. Religion says: you must strive, until you are good enough. The gospel says: you have already been accepted; now live out of that identity.

James Hudson Taylor, the nineteenth-century missionary to China, long struggled with a sense of spiritual powerlessness. In 1869, in a letter to his sister, he described his breakthrough. In essence: he had always been striving to “work up faith,” and later he understood that true rest lies not in how great one’s own faith is, but in looking to the Lord who is utterly trustworthy. The most flourishing years of the China Inland Mission began after that breakthrough.

From 321’s point of view, this is the first of the Three Foundations — Jesus is my role model. He is not only the one we imitate; he is the source and substance of our life. He walked the road of denying of self, and opened for us a new and living way.

It is also the first of the Two Core Values — let Jesus be King. Selflessness is not erasing the “I” into a blank; selflessness is handing the throne back to the true King.

sections.heading: 6. The Power of Habit: From Unnatural to Natural
sections.html:
The lesson’s fourth point uses an example we have all lived through yet none of us remembers — learning to walk.

The lesson says: at first it is hard; we fall often; we are very unsteady. So why does it become easy later? Because it becomes a habit.

How true is this example? Professor Karen Adolph of New York University and her colleagues, in a study published in 2012 in the journal Psychological Science, followed toddlers who had just learned to walk. They found that these children, aged twelve to nineteen months, took on average about 2,368 steps and fell about seventeen times every hour.

Brothers and sisters, picture it. A child who falls seventeen times an hour, more than a hundred times a day. If he thought with our adult logic, he would have given up long ago: “I’ve tried; I’m not suited to walking; I’ll stick to crawling — crawling is safer.”

But the child doesn’t think like that. He falls, cries for a moment, grabs the coffee table and stands up again.

And us? We choose selflessness, fail three times, and start drawing conclusions: “I can’t do it.”

How well the lesson puts it: when you first begin choosing selflessness, you won’t be used to it, and you will fail. But as long as you get up whenever you fall, choose again.

Scripture said it long ago: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.” (Proverbs 24:16)

Notice that this verse does not say the righteous “don’t fall”; it says the righteous fall and “rise up again.” The difference between the righteous and the wicked lies not in whether they fall, but in whether they get up.

The psalmist also says, “Though he stumble, he shall not fall, for Yahweh holds him up with his hand.” (Psalm 37:24)

Brothers and sisters, you think you’re practising getting up; in fact, there has been a hand under your arm all along.

So what does repetition actually do in us?

Neuroscience has a beautiful answer, called myelination. When nerve fibres in our brain are used again and again, surrounding cells wrap them in layer upon layer of myelin, like putting insulation on an electric wire. Research by Dr R. Douglas Fields of the US National Institutes of Health and other scholars shows that this sheath greatly increases the efficiency of signal transmission — unmyelinated nerve fibres conduct at roughly one metre per second, while well-myelinated fibres can reach more than a hundred metres per second.

Brothers and sisters, this is the physiological basis of “the more you practise, the more natural it becomes.” You don’t turn into a different person; that road gets paved into a motorway.

So how long does it take?

Dr Phillippa Lally of University College London and her colleagues, in a study published in 2010 in the European Journal of Social Psychology, followed ninety-six participants as they formed a new daily behaviour. They found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become “automatic,” with great individual variation — anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days.

But one finding in this study matters especially for us today: missing the occasional day had “no significant effect” on the whole process of forming the habit.

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Missing one day won’t ruin everything. Falling once doesn’t mean you’ve lost it all. What really ruins everything is lying on the ground after you fall, refusing to get up, and berating yourself all the while.

The word Scripture uses means exactly this. Hebrews says, “But solid food is for those who are full grown, who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14) That word “exercised” is a participle of the Greek gymnazō, the root of the English word gymnasium; it means to strip off one’s outer garment and get into training. Paul uses the same word to Timothy: “Exercise yourself toward godliness. For bodily exercise has some value, but godliness has value in all things, having the promise of the life which is now, and of that which is to come.” (1 Timothy 4:7-8)

So the way God grows spiritual life is not by “infusion” but by “training.” He puts us into a spiritual gym — not to wear us out, but so that we grow muscle.

So the lesson says: you will find it becoming more and more natural, easier and easier. Selflessness is not pressure; it is freedom.

“Stand firm therefore in the liberty by which Christ has made us free, and don’t be entangled again with a yoke of bondage.” (Galatians 5:1)

Brothers and sisters, learn to tell these two yokes apart. One is the yoke of bondage, which “self” puts on you: you must win, you must be seen, you must prove you’re right. The other is the Lord’s yoke, of which the Lord says, “For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:30)

In 321 we speak of the eight stages of changing our mindset: Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication. Notice the seventh stage — Repetition. It is the least conspicuous stage, yet it is the only passage by which a “choice” becomes a “habit.” Without repetition, the six stages before it are only a one-off moment of being moved.

sections.heading: 7. You Already Have the Selfless Life
sections.html:
The lesson’s fifth point takes us somewhere deeper. It says: you already have the selfless life.

The verse is: “Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)

The lesson says: this verse is not a demand but a revelation.

We looked earlier at the word teleios — not “without flaw,” but “having reached its purpose, grown into what it should be.” The Lord said this right after the section on loving our enemies. The Father’s love makes no distinction; it shines on the good and the evil alike. He wants us to be like him — to love wholly, to love without gaps.

So why can we be perfect? The lesson’s answer is: because the life of Christ is in you.

Paul says, “to whom God was pleased to make known what are the riches of the glory of this mystery among the Gentiles, which is Christ in you, the hope of glory.” (Colossians 1:27)

Peter says, “by which he has granted to us his precious and exceedingly great promises; that through these you may become partakers of the divine nature, having escaped from the corruption that is in the world by lust.” (2 Peter 1:4)

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to what these two verses are saying. It is not that God gives you an operating manual and tells you to imitate him by following it; it is that God puts his own nature inside you.

So the lesson says: it is not that you become perfect; it is that Christ in you lives out perfection.

I think of an acorn. Hold one in your palm — small, unremarkable. Yet that acorn doesn’t need to “strive to become an oak tree”; it already contains the complete blueprint of the whole oak. It has only two things to do: put down roots, and reach up to the light. It doesn’t become an oak by struggle; it lets the life within it grow out.

The Lord Jesus himself says it most clearly: “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

Notice that the Lord does not require the branches to “try hard to produce grapes.” He requires only one thing — remain in him. Fruit is the natural overflow of life, not the result of a branch gritting its teeth.

So the lesson swaps the whole question out. It says the key is not “Can I do it?” but “Am I willing to let him live?”

Brothers and sisters, notice the difference between those two questions.

“Can I do it?” — the focus is on me, on my ability, on my track record of past failures. That question only makes you smaller the more you ask it.

“Am I willing to let him live?” — the focus is on him, on his power, on his promises. That question brings you to a place where you can answer, because “willing or not” is something you can decide.

Psychology confirms the importance of this shift. The self-determination theory developed from 1985 onward by Edward Deci and Richard Ryan of the University of Rochester shows that behaviour change driven by autonomous motivation lasts longer and goes deeper than change driven by outside pressure or fear. Only when a person does something because “I am willing,” not because “I have to,” does the change last.

Brothers and sisters, this is the secret of selflessness. God never forces us. He asks just one question: are you willing?

321 says: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the fullness and victory of Jesus and living it out; “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

Think carefully about that sentence. A drop of water in the palm of your hand soon dries up; but if that drop falls into the ocean, it no longer has a shape of its own — yet from then on it possesses the vastness of the whole ocean. Selflessness is not the drop disappearing; it is the drop entering into fullness without limit.

This is also the second of the Three Foundations — the Bible is my standard. We do not judge by our feelings whether we have the selfless life; we judge by God’s word. If God’s word says you already have it, then you already have it.

sections.heading: 8. The More You Practise, the Lighter It Gets
sections.html:
The lesson’s sixth point is the peak of the whole lesson, and its sweetest promise. It says: when you begin to cultivate the habit of selflessness, you will become more and more at ease, more and more joyful, more and more free.

Why? The lesson’s answer is a single sentence: because you no longer live under the heavy burden of “self.”

Brothers and sisters, we often think “self” is our asset; in fact “self” is our luggage. The lesson lists the three heaviest pieces of luggage.

The first: no longer needing to prove yourself.

How exhausting is proving yourself? You have to keep comparing, keep calculating what others think of you, keep fearing being outdone. Paul says, “For am I now seeking the favor of men, or of God? Or am I striving to please men? For if I were still pleasing men, I wouldn’t be a servant of Christ.” (Galatians 1:10) When a person no longer has to prove himself, he is instantly half as heavy.

The second: no longer needing to hold on to your rights.

The role model here is the Lord himself. “who, existing in the form of God, didn’t consider equality with God a thing to be grasped, but emptied himself, taking the form of a servant, being made in the likeness of men.” (Philippians 2:6-7)

“Emptied himself” is ekenōsen in Greek, literally “poured himself out.” This is the most important verse on selflessness in the whole Bible. Notice: what the Lord emptied was not his deity but his claim to exercise his rights. He had the right; he chose not to grasp it.

Brothers and sisters, those who cling to their rights think they have gained something, but in fact they are bound by the very thing they are clinging to. When your hand is gripping something, it can’t do anything else.

The third: no longer needing to control everything.

Peter says, “casting all your worries on him, because he cares for you.” (1 Peter 5:7) “Casting” in the original carries the sense of “throwing with force” — like heaving the bundle off your shoulders onto someone else’s back. It is an action, not a feeling.

Paul also says, “In nothing be anxious, but in everything, by prayer and petition with thanksgiving, let your requests be made known to God. And the peace of God, which surpasses all understanding, will guard your hearts and your thoughts in Christ Jesus.” (Philippians 4:6-7)

Finally the lesson says: you simply let Jesus live. This is the lightest life, the most abundant life.

Let me use a boat as an illustration. You have to cross the same stretch of sea. You can sit in a rowing boat and pull with both hands for all you’re worth, until your palms blister and you can’t straighten your back, and make ten kilometres a day. Or you can raise a sail and let the wind drive you; all you have to do is hold the tiller, and you can make a hundred kilometres a day.

Brothers and sisters, the self-centred life is rowing for all you’re worth; selflessness is spreading the sail. The sail itself produces not one ounce of power; it does only one thing — it doesn’t block the wind, and it lets itself be filled by the wind.

And that wind is the Holy Spirit. This is the third of the Three Foundations — the Holy Spirit is my guide. 321 puts it well: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you are glad, rely on the brain and you are troubled. For “out of it is the wellspring of life” (Proverbs 4:23).

When the sail is spread, what happens? The fruit of the Spirit grows naturally. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22-23)

Notice that Scripture says “fruit,” not “product.” Products are churned out in factories; fruit grows out of life.

This is exactly 321’s 920 practice: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; before them we practise living out the selfless “0,” and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions. The person beside you today is the training ground God has given you.

Brothers and sisters, read the theme verse once more: “I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)

Selflessness does not make you less; it makes you overflow.

sections.heading: 9. Integrating the 321 Vision: Selflessness Is the Road Home
sections.html:
Having come this far, let’s place today’s message within the whole picture of 321, and we’ll see it more clearly.

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide.

Today’s lesson uses every one of the Three Foundations. Jesus is my role model — he emptied himself, he laid down his life, he went ahead of us, so we are not walking a road no one has walked before. The Bible is my standard — when my feelings say “I can’t do it,” the Bible says “I have been crucified with Christ” (Galatians 2:20), and I do my reckoning by the Bible, not by my feelings. The Holy Spirit is my guide — it is not me gritting my teeth and squeezing out fruit; it is the Holy Spirit bearing fruit within me.

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory.

The lesson’s question, “Am I willing to let him live?”, is precisely about letting Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, there is only one throne. Either Jesus sits on it, or “self” does. Every act of selflessness is a small but real coronation. And when Christ is lived out in us, what people see is no longer our good temper or our self-discipline but his beauty — and that is letting Jesus receive all the glory.

The Goal of 321 is: establish God’s system.

God’s system is not piled up out of structures; it is put together by a company of selfless people. If everyone has to prove themselves, cling to their rights and control everything, then however big that system is, it is a Tower of Babel; if everyone has learned selflessness, then however small that system is, it is God’s temple.

Now look at a few of 321’s core sayings; today they shine especially bright.

The first: the old self is self-centred; the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall; pride is the root of the problem. The temptation in Eden — “you will be like God, knowing good and evil” (Genesis 3:5) — was enlarging “self” into God’s place. From that day on, the riverbed in the human heart has been cut in that direction.

The second: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Brothers and sisters, notice that we do not overcome Satan by willpower; we overcome him by having “nothing he can get a grip on.” The Lord Jesus said, “the prince of the world comes, and he has nothing in me.” (John 14:30) The devil could not find a trace of “self” in the Lord, so he had nowhere to lay hold.

The third: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks, and relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Today’s lesson sits entirely on the level of “life.” When life is right, relationships naturally loosen; when life is wrong, the more ministry there is, the more friction there is.

The fourth: the change of perspective — from man’s to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. From man’s perspective, selflessness is loss; from God’s perspective, selflessness is abundance. From a temporary perspective, swallowing your pride is hard; from an eternal perspective, that pride was never worth keeping.

The fifth: Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances. When you fail, don’t stare at yourself; that is self-pity. And don’t stare at the other person; that is resentment. Lift your eyes to Jesus, and you will be able to stand up again.

Last of all, 235 relationships. The road of selflessness is not walked alone. Become a “2” with a selfless person, supporting and reminding each other; have the “3” of spiritual parents and spiritual children, passing life on; and finally come together into the “5,” a fivefold-ministry team of comrades, building together. Brothers and sisters, when a habit is hardest to form, what’s usually lacking is not willpower but companionship. If today you can find a “2,” and each week ask each other, “In what small thing were you selfless this week?”, your sixty-six days will be far steadier.

sections.heading: 10. Putting It into Practice: Walking the Whole Way with the Eight Stages of Changing Our Mindset
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices for daily living. Let’s look at them one by one, and walk them out solidly with 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication.

The first practice: begin practising selflessness in small things.

The lesson says: in daily life, deliberately set yourself aside in small things — for example, setting aside your opinions, setting aside your face, setting aside your insistence.

Brothers and sisters, notice the words “small things.” Many people talk straight away about laying down their lives for the Lord, yet go red in the face at the dinner table over a single remark. Habits are never formed in the big things; they are formed in the small things.

Make it one concrete thing. For example: today when the family eats out, someone else chooses the restaurant, and I don’t offer an opinion. Or: in today’s meeting there’s a suggestion I really want to make; I let others finish first — I even let someone else say it and get the credit. Or: today my wife says something that isn’t very pleasant to hear; I don’t answer back; I go and pour her a glass of water.

The second practice: when you fall, choose again at once.

The lesson says: when you find you’ve slipped back into the self-centred life, don’t blame yourself; turn back at once and choose selflessness again.

Notice the words “don’t blame yourself.” Self-reproach looks very spiritual, but it is still the self-centred life — the focus is still on me. “God is light, and in him is no darkness at all” (1 John 1:5); his light exposes our sin in order to forgive, not to humiliate. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

So practise a “ten-second turnaround”: notice it, confess it, receive forgiveness, and choose again straight away. Don’t spend ten minutes stewing over it; ten minutes is long enough to do it three more times.

The third practice: declare every day, “Christ lives in me.”

The lesson says: through prayer and declaration, let “I have already” move from mindset into life, so that selflessness becomes something lived out naturally.

Declaring is not shouting slogans; declaring is putting God’s word back into your own heart. Every morning, say this once to your own heart: “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Now let’s use the eight stages to walk these three practices out solidly.

Stage one, Information. Today you have received a whole new set of information: selflessness is not hard, you’re just not used to it yet; Jesus does the hard part, we do the simple part. Write those two sentences down and put them where you can see them.

Stage two, Revelation. Information goes into the head; revelation goes into the heart. Ask the Holy Spirit today to shine his light on you in one specific situation: at that moment, how did your “self” climb onto the throne? Without revelation, information is just notes.

Stage three, Conviction. Conviction is your heart truly yielding, saying: Lord, you are right. Not a grudging admission, but a willing surrender.

Stage four, Implementation. Choose one small thing today; don’t wait. Settle it in your heart: today I will be selfless in this one thing.

Stage five, Evaluation. Tonight, spend three minutes looking back: at what moment was I selfless? At what moment was I self-centred again? Just record it; don’t condemn.

Stage six, Correction. For the moment you failed, think of a better way. For example: next time she says that, I’ll take a deep breath for three seconds before I speak.

Stage seven, Repetition. This is the most crucial stage, and the one nobody loves. Remember Dr Lally’s research — an average of sixty-six days, and missing one day won’t ruin everything. Give yourself sixty-six days, not six.

Stage eight, Multiplication. When this habit has grown, pass it on. Find a spiritual companion, tell them your experience, and walk alongside them for a while. The mark of mature life is that it can reproduce. “The things which you have heard from me among many witnesses, commit the same things to faithful men, who will be able to teach others also.” (2 Timothy 2:2)

Brothers and sisters, the lesson ends by giving us a gentle reminder; please take it home with you:

It’s not that you can’t — it’s that you’re not used to it yet.

sections.heading: 11. Closing and Call: Let Every Choice Become an Opportunity to Cultivate the Life of Christ
sections.html:
The lesson’s conclusion is beautifully put: selflessness is not some unattainable plane; it is a choice you can live out every day.

One choice shows no change; choices sustained become life.

Brothers and sisters, this is a great comfort, and also a great challenge.

The comfort is this: today you don’t have to become a completely selfless person. Today God only asks you to choose once, in one small thing.

The challenge is this: you can’t choose only once. A single choice is like one footstep on the grass — by the next day the grass has sprung back up; but a thousand choices wear a path.

So today I want to issue this call to you, brothers and sisters.

First, let Jesus be King. Not your feelings as king, not your face as king, not your arguments as king. This morning, in your heart, hand the throne back to him and say: Lord Jesus, come and be King.

Second, let Jesus receive all the glory. When you have been selfless in some small thing, and the relationship has eased, and the matter has passed, don’t quietly make a note in your heart: “That was my self-discipline.” Give it back to him: Lord, that was you living it out in me.

Brothers and sisters, starting today, let every choice become an opportunity to cultivate the life of Christ.

Your first thought in the morning is an opportunity.

The words you say before you leave the house are an opportunity.

That unfairness at the office is an opportunity.

That silence at the dinner table is an opportunity.

Time after time, the Lord’s likeness will show in you. And one day you will suddenly find that the thing you once had to grit your teeth to do now comes as naturally as walking down the stairs in your own home.

Then you will understand — selflessness really isn’t hard after all.

keyVerses: John 10:10
“The thief only comes to steal, kill, and destroy. I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10)
Matthew 5:48
“Therefore you shall be perfect, just as your Father in heaven is perfect.” (Matthew 5:48)
practices: Remind yourself each day: I no longer need to prove myself; I simply let Jesus live.
When your rights are infringed, choose not to grasp them; follow the Lord who emptied himself.
Cast today’s worries firmly onto God, and stop trying to control everything.
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus,

We thank you. You said you came that the sheep may have life, and may have it abundantly. This morning we place a long-held misunderstanding in your hands: we always thought selflessness was hard, when really we just weren’t used to it yet.

Lord, thank you that you have already done the hard part. The cross dealt with our self-centred life; the resurrection gave us the selfless life. We are not striving to become selfless people; we are living out the life you have already given us.

Forgive us; we are in the habit of thinking of ourselves, fighting for ourselves and living by our own feelings. May your Spirit shine on us today, so that we see that moment, that remark, that thought.

Lord, we are willing. We are willing to begin with small things — setting aside our opinions, setting aside our face, setting aside our insistence. When we fall, help us not to blame ourselves, but to turn back at once and choose again. We are willing to declare every day: I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.
Lord Jesus, come and be King. Be King over my tongue, King over my emotions, King in my home. May all the goodness that shows in us bring glory to you, and not to us.
In the name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: The lesson says, “The problem is not that selflessness is hard, but that we’re not used to it yet.” Share something you have gone through “from not being used to it to being used to it” (for example, learning to drive, learning a language, getting up early). What does that experience remind you of as you practise selflessness today? “who by reason of use have their senses exercised to discern good and evil.” (Hebrews 5:14)

The lesson says, “The key is not ‘Can I do it?’ but ‘Am I willing to let him live?’” Say specifically: in what small thing will you practise selflessness this coming week? Which spiritual companion do you need to walk these sixty-six days with you? “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me.” (Galatians 2:20)

sections.heading: Introduction: Why Does Trying Harder Only Make Us Fail More?
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we’re going to face together a struggle that almost everyone who earnestly loves the Lord has been through.

There was a sister who had believed in the Lord for more than ten years. She loved the Lord, she served, she gave — in every way she kept up with the best of them. But she carried a deep pain: her temper. Every time she finished shouting at her children at home, she would hide in her room and weep. Again and again she resolved: “Next time I will never lose my temper.” She wrote “I WILL BE GENTLE” in big letters in a notebook and stuck it on the fridge, on her dressing-table mirror, beside the steering wheel of her car. And the result? She told me, “Pastor, the more I remind myself not to lose my temper, the more easily I lose it. I stare at those words, and all the while my heart keeps saying: I’ve failed again.”

Her predicament isn’t hers alone. It’s a dead end that countless Christians walk down every single day: straining to “deal with themselves” without ever “cultivating life”. The result is that the harder they try, the more they fail; the more they struggle, the more they hurt.

Psychology, in fact, discovered this phenomenon long ago. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner, then at Trinity University in San Antonio (he later moved to Harvard), and his team carried out a famous experiment, published in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. He sat his participants down and gave them just one instruction: “For the next five minutes, please don’t think of a white bear.” Every single participant failed. What’s more, once the experiment was over, this group thought of white bears more often than the group that had never been asked to suppress the thought at all. Wegner called it the “rebound effect”, and it later grew into his “ironic process theory”.

That experiment tells us something that cuts close to the bone: the harder you push “don’t”, the more your heart fills up with “that very thing”. Because when you say “don’t think of a white bear”, your mind first has to summon the white bear in order to know what it’s fighting. And so the white bear moves in.

Brothers and sisters, that is exactly why so many people’s spiritual lives stay stuck. We pour all our strength into staring at our sins, staring at our weaknesses, staring at our self-centred life; and because we call that self-centred life out to look at it every day and feed it our attention every day, it just keeps growing bigger.

But God’s way is not like that. God doesn’t want you to combat the self-centred life; he wants you to cultivate selflessness. That is the heart of today’s lesson. In the last lesson we saw that changing a habit is a matter of life; in this lesson we will see that habits are changed not by combating, but by cultivating.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Letters, Two Angles, One Truth
sections.html:
Today’s key passages come from two apostles and two letters written into very different situations, yet they point to the same truth.

Second Corinthians is the letter the apostle Paul wrote from Macedonia to the church in Corinth, somewhere between AD 55 and 57. Corinth was then the capital of the province of Achaia, a great port city — commercially booming, ideologically mixed and morally loose. The Corinthian church was one Paul had planted with his own hands, and yet it was the church that grieved him most: they split into factions, tolerated sexual immorality and looked down on Paul’s apostleship. Second Corinthians is the most personal and emotionally intense of all Paul’s letters; in it he defends his ministry and also lays his own weakness open before them.

The context of 2 Corinthians 5:17 matters enormously. Verse 14 says, “For the love of Christ constrains us; because we judge thus, that one died for all, therefore all died.” Verse 15 says, “He died for all, that those who live should no longer live to themselves, but to him who for their sakes died and rose again.” Notice the logic of these two verses: one died for all, therefore all died — that is the end of the self-centred life; no longer living to themselves but to the Lord — that is the beginning of selflessness. So the “new creation” of verse 17 is not a motivational slogan. Paul is speaking of a fact that has already happened, a fact legally accomplished.

“New creation” in the original is kainē ktisis. Greek has two words for “new”: neos means new in time, brand new off the production line; kainos means new in kind, never seen before. Paul uses kainos. In other words, when you believed, it wasn’t that the old you was repaired, refurbished and polished up; an “essentially brand-new creature” came into being. The twentieth-century apologist C. S. Lewis put it very clearly in Mere Christianity: God became man not to turn the old kind of man into a better man, but to produce a new kind of man.

First John, for its part, was written by the apostle John somewhere between AD 80 and 95, from the region around Ephesus, to the churches of Asia Minor. At the time an early form of Gnosticism was beginning to seep into the church, with some claiming that spiritual people could sin freely and that whatever the body did made no difference. Against this error John lists, one by one, the marks of true believers in a string of statements about “whoever is born of God”. The “doesn’t commit sin” of 3:9 is in the Greek present tense: it expresses an ongoing state, a habitual way of life. It isn’t saying that a believer will never stumble even once — because the same letter says in 1:8, “If we say that we have no sin, we deceive ourselves, and the truth is not in us.” What John means is this: the life that is born of God does not by nature make sin its normal state, because God’s word abides in him.

Notice that word “word”. The Chinese Union Version has very honestly added a small-print note: in the original it is “seed” — Greek sperma, a seed. What does a seed do? A seed grows. So John’s point is not “You must strain with all your might not to sin”, but “A seed of God has already been placed inside you — let it grow.”

Two letters, two apostles, two situations — yet with one voice they proclaim one thing: a Christian’s victory comes not by repairing the old, but by cultivating the new.

sections.heading: 1. You Are Already a New Creation
sections.html:
“Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)

Brothers and sisters, notice the tense of this verse. Paul didn’t say, “You will become a new creation”, nor did he say, “If you try hard enough you’ll become a new creation.” He said: he is a new creation. Already.

The moment you believed, two things happened at once: your identity was changed, and your life was renewed. You are no longer a person in Adam; you are a person in Christ. Colossians 1:13 says that God is the one “who delivered us out of the power of darkness, and translated us into the Kingdom of the Son of his love”. The word “translated” in the original was the term used when ancient empires moved whole populations — your household registration has been transferred. You are not a temporary resident; your registration has been moved.

So in the language of 321 we can put it like this: selflessness has already been accomplished in our standing. It is an established fact, not a goal. In Galatians 2:20 Paul says, “I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” “I have been crucified with Christ” is in the perfect tense — the thing has been done and settled.

So where is the problem? The problem is this: our daily living hasn’t caught up yet.

And so an awkward situation appears in us: our identity is new, but our habits are old.

I often use an illustration. A man moves from the countryside into a new house in the city. The house is new, the address is new, the keys are new; but the habits he built up over twenty years are still there — he doesn’t take his shoes off at the door, he drops rubbish wherever he is, and at three in the morning he’s still out in the yard talking at the top of his voice. The house has changed; his living hasn’t. It isn’t that he’s “not the owner” — he is the owner. He just hasn’t yet learned how to live in his new house.

Brothers and sisters, your struggle doesn’t mean you aren’t a new creation. Your struggle is precisely the proof that you are. A fish on the bank thrashes in agony, because it belongs in the water; put a stone on the bank and it feels nothing at all. You grieve over your sin because there is already a new life inside you, protesting. People who haven’t been saved don’t feel heartache over sin; they only feel heartache over getting caught.

That is where the struggle comes from — and it is also a sign of hope.

From the 321 perspective, this is exactly the starting point of the “fivefold change”: mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry. Many people want to jump straight to “daily living”, to get rid of some bad habit right away; but God’s order is to change the mindset first. If you still believe “I’m a terrible, failing person who keeps on sinning”, your daily living will never turn around, because daily living flows out of life, and life is steered by mindset. Change the mindset and you change the life; change the life and you change daily living.

This morning, the first mindset that has to go is this one: I am not “a sinner trying hard to be better”. I am “a child who has already been made new and is learning to grow up”.

sections.heading: 2. Two Lives at Work Within
sections.html:
In Romans 7 Paul describes this war in vivid, unsparing detail:

“For I don’t know what I am doing. For I don’t practice what I desire to do; but what I hate, that I do.” (Romans 7:15)

“For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:19)

“I find then the law that, to me, while I desire to do good, evil is present.” (Romans 7:21)

“But I see a different law in my members, warring against the law of my mind, and bringing me into captivity under the law of sin which is in my members. What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:23–24)

Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? These are the words of the apostle Paul. Not a new believer, not a Christian in name only — this is Paul, who wrote the greater part of the New Testament. If even Paul could say “What a wretched man I am!”, then your struggle this morning is nothing strange.

Paul uses a key word: “law”, Greek nomos. Here it doesn’t mean the written commandments of Moses; it means a principle that operates consistently, an inevitable regularity — like gravity. There are two “laws” at work within us; that is, two lives at work within us.

The first is the self-centred life, the old life. Its traits are these: it sins, it likes to have its own way, it is pulled along by sin. This isn’t an occasional slip; it is its nature. Paul says, “For I know that in me, that is, in my flesh, dwells no good thing. For desire is present with me, but I don’t find it doing that which is good.” (Romans 7:18) Notice: the resolving you can manage; the doing you can’t. That is the limit of the old life.

The second is the selfless life, the new life. Its traits are these: it comes from God, it does not sin, it delights in God’s will. Paul says, “For I delight in God’s law after the inward man.” (Romans 7:22)

When two lives exist at the same time, there is a tug of war. Galatians 5:17 puts it even more bluntly: “For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.”

Here I want to point out something very important: the tug of war is not itself sin; the tug of war is the battlefield. A nation without an army has no wars; a person without new life has no struggle. When you hear that voice inside you saying “Don’t do this”, that isn’t your own self-reproach — that is the Holy Spirit.

Physiology offers a fascinating parallel. In the human heart there is a cluster of special cells called the sinoatrial node. It generates its own electrical signal, sixty to a hundred times a minute, and for your whole life it never needs reminding and never needs your effort — it simply beats. That is what we call “the nature of life”. You don’t have to get up every morning and resolve, “Today I will make my heart beat.” In the same way, the new life has the nature of the new life: of itself it longs for God, it loves people, it hates sin. Your task is not to beat for it, but not to strangle it.

Here the 321 vision gives us a crucial sentence: selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me. So selflessness is not hollowing yourself out into a zero; it is letting the infinite Lord take first place within you.

sections.heading: 3. The Wrong Method: Combating the Self-Centred Life
sections.html:
Once they know there are two lives inside, many people immediately adopt a method that looks very spiritual but leads absolutely nowhere: combating the self-centred life.

Their approach is this: suppress hard, restrain with all their might, and try to make themselves stop sinning.
