And so come all kinds of spiritual effort: resolution charts, fasting charts, check-in charts, confession lists, self-punishment, berating themselves a hundred times over in their hearts. On the surface it looks very devout; the result is more exhaustion, more failure, more discouragement.

Why? The answer is so simple it’s hard to believe: because the life of sin sins by nature.

The lesson uses a wonderfully vivid picture: a duck swims naturally; a chicken swimming is pure misery. Throw a chicken into the water and it isn’t that it doesn’t try — it flaps for all it’s worth — but it isn’t built for water. A duck has waterproof feathers, webbed feet and a thick layer of fat; a chicken has none of these. The problem isn’t effort; the problem is nature.

So listen carefully: you cannot turn the self-centred life into selflessness. You can train a chicken to run faster and crow louder, but you can never train it to become a duck. That road goes nowhere.

In Colossians 2:23 Paul passes a very stern verdict on this kind of religious effort: “These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.” Those words, “not of any value”, wipe out thousands of years of human moral effort at a stroke.

Go back to Wegner’s white bear experiment from the introduction. When that sister stuck “I WILL BE GENTLE” on her fridge, she thought she was cultivating gentleness; in fact, twenty times a day she was reminding herself, “I lose my temper easily.” What she was feeding wasn’t the new life; it was the old life’s sense of its own presence. That is the rebound effect of suppression: the harder you press down, the harder it springs back; the more it springs back, the more worn out you get.

Ancient China has a saying, “pulling up the sprouts to help them grow”, from the Mencius (Gongsun Chou, Part One). A farmer in the state of Song thought his rice shoots were growing too slowly, so he pulled each one up a little higher, then went home and said, “I’m worn out today — I’ve helped the shoots grow taller.” His son ran out to the field to look, and every shoot had withered. Brothers and sisters, the spiritual life is the same — life can only be cultivated; it cannot be yanked. The harder you combat, the faster the shoots die.

321 says: pride is leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place; humility is laying down our rights and returning to our originally intended position — let man be man and let God be God. The deepest problem with “combating the self-centred life” isn’t the method; it’s the position. It is me snatching God’s work away from him and setting myself up as the lord who changes lives. And there has only ever been One who can change a life.

sections.heading: 4. The Key to the Truth: Not Combating, but Cultivating
sections.html:
“Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God.” (1 John 3:9)

Brothers and sisters, the key is not making the self-centred life better; it is letting selflessness grow up.

John uses an agricultural picture: a seed. A seed doesn’t need to be persuaded, doesn’t need to be whipped along, doesn’t need a pep talk. A seed needs only three things: soil, water and light. Give it those three and it grows by itself. That is the law of life.

The Lord Jesus himself used the same picture. Mark 4:26–28: “God’s Kingdom is as if a man should cast seed on the earth, and should sleep and rise night and day, and the seed should spring up and grow, though he doesn’t know how. For the earth bears fruit: first the blade, then the ear, then the full grain in the ear.” Look: “though he doesn’t know how.” The farmer doesn’t know how the seed grows, and he doesn’t need to know. His job is to sow, to water, to clear away whatever blocks the light; the growing is God’s work. First Corinthians 3:6 says, “I planted. Apollos watered. But God gave the increase.”

So God’s method can be said in a single sentence: not getting rid of the darkness, but turning on the light.

That is a physical fact and a spiritual truth. Darkness isn’t a substance; darkness is the absence of light. You can’t pour darkness into a bucket and carry it out, you can’t chase it away with a stick, you can’t suck it up with a vacuum cleaner. The strongest man in the world can’t shift a single cubic centimetre of darkness. But a candle, a torch — one click, and the darkness leaves the stage at once. The sun’s light travels a hundred and fifty million kilometres, taking about eight minutes and twenty seconds to reach the earth, and the moment it arrives, the night is over for half the planet. When the light comes, darkness simply leaves.

John 1:5 says, “The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.” The Lord Jesus said, “I am the light of the world. He who follows me will not walk in the darkness, but will have the light of life.” (John 8:12)

The nineteenth-century Scottish minister Thomas Chalmers (1780–1847) preached a famous sermon called “The Expulsive Power of a New Affection”. He said that an old love in the human heart is not driven out by “not loving it”; it is pushed out by a new love that is greater, more beautiful and more true. If you want a child to let go of the toy in his hand, the most effective way isn’t to snatch it — it’s to give him something better.

Every parent understands this. A toddler grips a pair of scissors and won’t let go: the more you grab, the tighter he holds, screaming as he does. But put an ice cream in front of him, and his hand loosens all by itself. Brothers and sisters, this isn’t a technique; it’s the law of life.

Nature gives us a very beautiful example too. Oaks and beeches show a phenomenon called “marcescence”: their dead leaves don’t fall in late autumn but hang on the branches all winter, through wind and rain. When do they finally fall? Not until spring, at the moment the new bud pushes out from beneath the leaf stalk — then the old leaf drops to the ground. Brothers and sisters, those old habits you’ve been fighting for ten years and still can’t pull out — perhaps you aren’t meant to pull harder one more time, but to wait for the new life to grow and push them off.

So God’s method is: don’t combat the old life; cultivate the new life.

This is the very heart of 321: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Notice, it isn’t “I overcome Satan”; it’s “selflessness overcomes Satan”. If you take on Satan with the self-centred life, you’re playing on his home ground; if you let Christ reign as King within you, it’s his ground of defeat.

sections.heading: 5. Why Is Combating the Self-Centred Life a Lie?
sections.html:
“As it is written, ‘There is no one righteous; no, not one.’” (Romans 3:10)

“Because by the works of the law, no flesh will be justified in his sight; for through the law comes the knowledge of sin.” (Romans 3:20)

Brothers and sisters, think about it with the simplest logic: if people could overcome sin by effort, Jesus wouldn’t have needed to come.

If moral self-cultivation could save people, the cross would be the greatest waste in history; if dealing with ourselves could make us holy, the sweat like great drops of blood in Gethsemane would mean nothing; if people could become good by themselves, then Paul’s words in Galatians 2:21 would hold: “I don’t reject the grace of God. For if righteousness is through the law, then Christ died for nothing!”

So we have to say something very weighty: “combating the self-centred life” is relying on ourselves; and relying on ourselves is going back to the self-centred life. That is precisely Satan’s trap.

See how cunning Satan’s trap is. He doesn’t need to tempt you into some great sin — that would be too obvious. All he needs is to get you doing something that looks very spiritual: working hard at dealing with yourself. And so you enter a loop: keep trying, keep failing, and finally give up. In the first stage you’re full of ambition; in the second you start to doubt; in the third you conclude, “This is just who I am. I can’t change.” The moment you say that sentence, Satan’s work is done. He hasn’t made you worse; he has made you despair.

Revelation 12:10 calls Satan the one “who accuses them before our God day and night”. His main weapon isn’t temptation; it’s accusation. Temptation makes you fall once; accusation keeps you lying on the ground and never getting up.

In Galatians 3:3 Paul fires a deafening question at the Galatians: “Are you so foolish? Having begun in the Spirit, are you now completed in the flesh?” When you were saved, it was by grace — and now that you’re being made holy, you want to rely on yourself? Logically, it makes no sense.

At the opening of Book One of his Confessions, Augustine wrote the prayer that has been repeated for sixteen hundred years: you have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you. The emptiness inside a person can’t be filled by patching ourselves up; only God himself can fill it.

From the 321 perspective there is a crucial shift here: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly to the heavenly, from the temporary to the eternal, from the worldly to the godly. Man’s perspective says, “I must try harder”; God’s perspective says, “I have already accomplished it for you; all you need to do is remain in me.” Man’s perspective sees my record of failure; God’s perspective sees Christ’s perfect record. Jesus is the focal point — not ourselves, not other people, not our circumstances.

321 has another very down-to-earth saying: rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the heart and you’ll be glad, rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled. Dealing with ourselves is the textbook case of “relying on the brain and ourselves” — analysing, reviewing, calculating, regretting, and the more we calculate, the more troubled we get. Cultivating Christ is “relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit” — looking up, obeying, drawing on his supply, giving thanks, and the further we go, the gladder we become.

sections.heading: 6. The Right Way: Cultivating the Selfless Life
sections.html:
So how exactly do we cultivate it?

The answer isn’t mysterious; it’s even a little ordinary: every time, choose selflessness; every time, obey the Holy Spirit; every time, live out Christ.

Not one earth-shattering act of consecration, but small choices, day by day, one at a time. Each time you choose selflessness once more, you live for yourself once less; and slowly selflessness grows stronger and the self-centred life grows weaker.

Remember this sentence: you don’t defeat it — you starve it.

There’s a widely told fable: an old man tells his grandson that two wolves are fighting inside every human heart, one evil and one good. The grandson asks, “Which one wins?” The old man says, “The one you feed.” Accounts of where the fable comes from vary widely, and we needn’t trace its origins, but it states a truth: whatever you feed grows.

Physiology gives us very reliable supporting evidence. A team led by Phillippa Lally at University College London published a study in the European Journal of Social Psychology in 2010 that followed ninety-six participants as they formed a new daily behaviour. They found that it took an average of sixty-six days for a behaviour to become automatic, with large individual differences, anywhere from eighteen to two hundred and fifty-four days. Even more important was another finding: missing a day now and then did not wreck the overall curve of habit formation. Brothers and sisters, did you hear that? Missing the odd day won’t ruin you. What really ruins you is giving up after you’ve missed one.

Brain science says the same thing. The principle the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb set out in 1949 in his book The Organization of Behavior is usually summed up in one catchy line: neurons that fire together wire together. Every time you choose to obey, you walk that spiritual path one more time; walk it often enough and the grass is trampled flat and a path appears. Every time you choose to indulge, you also tread out a path — down the other way. Your life will grow into the shape of the path you walk every day.

So there are three very concrete channels for cultivating selflessness:

The first is prayer. Prayer isn’t persuading God; it’s handing ourselves over. The Lord Jesus’ prayer in Gethsemane is the supreme example: “nevertheless, not what I desire, but what you desire.” (Matthew 26:39) Every time we pray like that, selflessness grows another inch.

The second is reading the Bible. “Your word is a lamp to my feet, and a light for my path.” (Psalm 119:105) The Bible is my standard. Not my feelings, not other people’s opinions, not the mood of the times. First Peter 2:2 says, “as newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow.” A baby doesn’t drink milk to combat thinness; it drinks to grow.

The third is obeying the Holy Spirit. “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” (Galatians 5:16) Notice the order of cause and effect in this verse: first walk by the Spirit, and then you won’t fulfil the lust of the flesh. It is not that you must first clean the lusts out completely before you can walk by the Spirit. Reverse that order and you’ll never get on the road in your whole life.

Here 321’s “920 practice” finds its footing: everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”; as we practise living out the selfless (0) life before them, we bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine (9) of its expressions. “But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control. Against such things there is no law.” (Galatians 5:22–23) Notice: it’s “fruit”, not “product”. Products are manufactured; fruit grows. You have never seen an apple tree gritting its teeth in the night, straining to produce apples.

That sister who suffered over her temper later did something. She tore the words “I WILL BE GENTLE” off the fridge and put up a small card instead, which read: “Lord, right now I hand this child to you. Please let your gentleness flow through me.” She said, “Pastor, I still fail, but I no longer despair, because I know I’m not repairing myself; I’m inviting the Lord in.” Six months later her child said to her, “Mum, you’ve changed.” She hadn’t combated her temper away; she had cultivated Christ.

sections.heading: 7. The Real Key to Growth in Life
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s last point gathers the six before it into one sentence: you are not “repairing yourself”; you are “cultivating Christ”.

The difference between the two is the difference between heaven and earth. In repairing yourself, the main character is me, the tool is my willpower, and success or failure depends on my performance. In cultivating Christ, the main character is him, the tool is his grace, and success or failure depends on his faithfulness.

The Lord Jesus said, “I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5) A branch’s job isn’t to bear fruit; a branch’s job is to “remain”. Fruit is the by-product of being connected.

As Christ grows more and more within you, three things happen: sin naturally loses its influence, the struggle naturally lessens, and life naturally overcomes.

Notice that word “naturally”. It doesn’t mean easily, or without cost; it means no longer twisted, no longer forced. It’s like a tree: once it grows tall, the weeds beneath it naturally thin out — not because you squat there pulling weeds every day, but because the canopy blocks the sunlight and the weeds can’t grow. In gardening this is called “shade suppression”, and it is a real ecological phenomenon. Your task isn’t to pull weeds; it’s to let the tree grow tall.

So victory is not the result of effort; it is the result of life.

Right after crying out “What a wretched man I am!” in Romans 7, Paul says at once in 7:25, “I thank God through Jesus Christ, our Lord!” And then 8:1–2 goes on: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus … For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.”

Look at the logic here: the law of sin and of death hasn’t been abolished; it still exists. But a higher law — the law of the Spirit of life — has overcome it. It’s like gravity: gravity hasn’t been abolished, but once the lift of aerodynamics is at work, a four-hundred-tonne aeroplane can fly. The aeroplane doesn’t fly by “combating gravity”; it flies by a higher law. Cut the engines and it drops at once; start the engines and it rises naturally into the sky.

In 2001 the American psychologist Barbara Fredrickson put forward her “broaden-and-build theory” in the journal American Psychologist. Her research showed that negative emotions narrow a person’s attention, while positive emotions broaden the range of thoughts and actions open to us and, over time, build up resources such as psychological resilience. From a side angle, this confirms the Bible’s order exactly: condemnation narrows us; grace enlarges us. Condemn yourself every day and your life grows narrower and narrower; look to Christ every day and your life grows wider and wider.

Second Corinthians 3:18 describes the beauty of this process: “But we all, with unveiled face seeing the glory of the Lord as in a mirror, are transformed into the same image from glory to glory, even as from the Lord, the Spirit.” Just keep looking at him, and you will become like him. This is the gentlest way of sanctification in the whole Bible.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision: One Road from Combating to Cultivating
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s lesson is really an exercise in the very core of the 321 vision.

The Three Foundations of 321 are: Jesus is my role model, the Bible is my standard, the Holy Spirit is my guide. Notice that none of these three foundations is called “my willpower is my strength”. The three channels for cultivating selflessness — obedience, Bible reading and prayer — correspond exactly to these three foundations: Jesus is my role model, so in Gethsemane I follow him in saying “not what I desire”; the Bible is my standard, so I don’t live by feelings but by God’s word; the Holy Spirit is my guide, so I don’t rely on the brain and myself — I rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values of 321 are: let Jesus be King, and let Jesus receive all the glory. The deadliest thing about “combating the self-centred life” is that it puts “me” on the throne, judging myself with one hand and saving myself with the other. “Cultivating selflessness” hands the throne back to the Lord. There’s a very simple test here: if you succeeded by combating, who gets the glory? Your perseverance. If you overcame by cultivating, who gets the glory? The Christ who lives within you. The Goal is to establish God’s system — not to build my record, but to build his Kingdom.

321 says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless; the self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. Go back to Eden: what did the serpent say to Eve? “You will be like God, knowing good and evil.” (Genesis 3:5) Humanity’s first sin was leaving our originally intended position and seizing rights, wanting to take God’s place. And today, when we grit our teeth and say, “I will beat this sin by myself if it kills me”, we are really doing the same thing in a more hidden way: taking God’s place. Pride has two faces. One says, “I’m so capable”; the other says, “How can I be so useless?” — and at the centre of both faces is “I”.

So 321 says: humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan. Pride provokes pride, and both sides lose; humility draws out humility, and both sides win. When you stop wrestling with your own sin and humbly hand yourself over to Christ, the battle you’ve fought for ten years and could never win is lifted off your shoulders.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. Many people fail at changing their habits because they have the order upside down. They want to get the ministry right first, to prove their life is fine; or to fix their relationships first, to make themselves feel a little better inside. God’s order is always life first. When life is right, relationships naturally come right; when relationships are right, ministry naturally bears fruit. The priority of relationships works the same way: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. If you’re still at war with yourself, how could you possibly get on well with other people?

Here 321’s “235 relationships” are an extremely practical help: becoming a “2” with a selfless person means a spiritual companion; establishing the “3” means spiritual parents and spiritual children; becoming a “5” means a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades. Changing a habit is almost impossible to do alone. Ecclesiastes 4:9–10 says, “Two are better than one, because they have a good reward for their labor. For if they fall, the one will lift up his fellow; but woe to him who is alone when he falls, and doesn’t have another to lift him up.” You need a “2” — not to police you or catch you out, but to remind you, when you fall, that you are a new creation.

Finally, 321’s shift of perspective is especially crucial in this lesson: from man’s to God’s — don’t look at what I can do; look at what God has already done; from the earthly to the heavenly — don’t look at my performance today; look at my standing in Christ; from the temporary to the eternal — don’t look at this one fall; look at the direction of a whole life; from the worldly to the godly — don’t pursue “being a better person”; pursue “letting Christ be lived out”.

The Path of Serving is the same road: Spirit (the Holy Spirit is my guide) → Understanding (the Bible is my standard) → Life (Jesus is my role model) → Service (let Jesus be King) → God (let Jesus receive all the glory). You’ll find that from beginning to end not one step of this road is “combating”; every step is “cultivating”.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to drive them deep and make them solid.

Practice 1: Stop Combating Yourself; Start Cultivating Life

When you discover your own weakness, don’t condemn or suppress it any more; turn to Jesus instead and let his life work within you.

Information: Copy today’s four key verses onto the first page of your notebook — 2 Corinthians 5:17, 1 John 3:9, Romans 8:1 and Colossians 2:23.

Revelation: Be still for three minutes and ask the Holy Spirit to show you how you have been “dealing with yourself” all these years. Not to add one more item of self-blame, but so that you can see where that road ends.

Conviction: Confess to God: “Lord, I’ve kept doing what you never asked me to do. I thought dealing with myself was godliness; in fact it was unbelief.”

Implementation: This week, whenever the voice of condemnation speaks up, change your words immediately — swap “How could I do this again?” for “Lord, I hand this over to you; please live it out in me.”

Evaluation: Every night before you sleep, ask one question: today, was I repairing myself, or cultivating Christ?

Correction: If you find you’ve slipped back into dealing with yourself, there’s no need to be upset; just come straight back to the cross. “If we confess our sins, he is faithful and righteous to forgive us the sins, and to cleanse us from all unrighteousness.” (1 John 1:9)

Repetition: For forty days in a row, let this new response become a reflex. Lally’s team reminds us that a new behaviour takes an average of sixty-six days to become automatic, so don’t judge yourself a failure on day ten.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister who is suffering over some habit, and share today’s lesson with them.

Practice 2: Deliberately Feed the Selfless Life

Through prayer, Bible reading and obeying the Holy Spirit, make one selfless choice every day, so that the new life is cultivated.

Information: Set one concrete, tiny, doable “selfless choice”. Don’t make it “I will love people more”; make it “Every day I will pray for one minute for the person I least want to pray for.”

Revelation: Ask God to show you which “2” in your life he wants you to love in a special way this season.

Conviction: Believe that this one minute of prayer has more power than a whole year of self-examination.

Implementation: A fixed time, a fixed place, a fixed scripture. Habits need anchors.

Evaluation: After a week, check: have my feelings towards that person changed? Which of the nine graces of the fruit of the Spirit is starting to put out a tender shoot?

Correction: If this practice is too big to manage, shrink it until you can definitely do it. Better small and steady than big and broken off.

Repetition: Feed it, time after time, until the new response shows up faster than the old one.

Multiplication: Invite a spiritual companion to do it with you, so you become each other’s “2”.

Practice 3: Value Direction, Not Failure

When you fall, don’t lose heart; turn back at once, choose selflessness once more, and keep walking the road of growth in life.

Information: Memorise Proverbs 24:16: “for a righteous man falls seven times and rises up again; but the wicked are overthrown by calamity.”

Revelation: See that the difference between the righteous and the wicked isn’t whether they fall, but whether they get up.

Conviction: Accept a new measure — not “Was I perfect today?” but “Which way was my face turned today?”

Implementation: After a fall, give yourself a “sixty-second rule”: confess, give thanks, get up and move forward — no lying on the ground chewing it over and over.

Evaluation: This month, after I fell, how long on average did it take me to turn back?

Correction: Shorten the time it takes to turn back. The mark of maturity is turning back faster and faster.

Repetition: Until “turning back at once” becomes your instinct.

Multiplication: Tell the true story of how you fell and got up again; it will help people far more than a perfect image. “Forgetting the things which are behind, and stretching forward to the things which are before, I press on toward the goal.” (Philippians 3:13–14)

A Gentle Reminder

You don’t become good by trying hard; you let Christ be lived out.

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, today’s closing word is just two sentences: combating yourself is a heavy burden; cultivating Christ is light.

The more you combat, the more you fail; the more you cultivate, the more you overcome.

The Lord Jesus told us long ago all there is to say about the difference between these two roads: “Come to me, all you who labor and are heavily burdened, and I will give you rest. Take my yoke upon you, and learn from me, for I am gentle and humble in heart; and you will find rest for your souls. For my yoke is easy, and my burden is light.” (Matthew 11:28–30)

Notice that the Lord didn’t say, “You don’t need to carry a yoke.” He said, “Take my yoke.” Christians aren’t people without responsibilities; they are people who have changed yokes. The old yoke is “I must make myself good”, and that yoke rubs your shoulders raw; the new yoke is “I will let Christ live in me”, and that yoke is made to measure for you — it is light.

This morning I want to invite you to make a decision. Not another resolution, not signing another contract you can’t keep. Rather, take that list in your hands, filled with “I absolutely must”, lay it quietly at the Lord’s feet, and say to him: Lord, I’m done combating; I want to cultivate you.

No more combating the self-centred life; give yourself to cultivating selflessness; let Jesus live out his life within you.

May you live this day not to prove yourself, but so that Jesus may reign as King; and may all the glory for every bit of growth in your life go to him alone.

keyVerses: “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” (2 Corinthians 5:17)
“Whoever is born of God doesn’t commit sin, because his seed remains in him, and he can’t sin, because he is born of God.” (1 John 3:9)
declarations: Lord, I will no longer rely on myself to combat sin. I will cultivate your life within me, and let Christ live in me, living out a victorious, free and abundant life!
practices: Stop combating yourself; start cultivating life
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

Thank you that while we were still straining to deal with ourselves, you had long since accomplished everything for us on the cross. Thank you that we are not sinners trying hard to be better; we are new creations you have already made.

Lord, we confess to you: for far too many years we have walked a road you never asked us to walk. We thought gritting our teeth was godliness, self-blame was repentance and suppression was holiness. Please forgive us, and please set us free.

Turn our eyes from our own failures to your perfection; turn our strength from combating the old life to cultivating the new. May the Holy Spirit remind us every day to choose selflessness once more and live for ourselves once less.
Lord, grow within us. As you increase more and more within us, may our sin naturally lose its influence, our struggle naturally lessen, and our life naturally overcome.
Let Jesus reign as King within us; let Jesus receive all the glory.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Second Corinthians 5:17 says, “Therefore if anyone is in Christ, he is a new creation. The old things have passed away. Behold, all things have become new.” Looking back over this year, in what area have you kept on “dealing with yourself”? When you hear the words “You are already a new creation”, what is your heart’s honest reaction — comfort, or doubt? Why?

Galatians 5:16 says, “But I say, walk by the Spirit, and you won’t fulfill the lust of the flesh.” This week, what concrete, tiny choice that you can make every day will you use to “feed” the new life? Whom are you willing to invite to be your “2”, to practise alongside you and support each other?
l112.title: Not Combating, but Cultivating
l112.subtitle: A Change of Habits (Part 2)
l112.partTitle: Unit 7 · The Journey to Selflessness — Denying of Self

sections.heading: Introduction: Two Men Quit Smoking
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, good morning. Today we come together to lesson 113 of 321 Morning Devotion, entitled “Not Combating, but Cultivating”. This is the third lesson in our series on “changing habits”.

Let me begin with two scenes that are common in real life.

Two brothers made up their minds to quit smoking in the same month.

The first brother’s method was “combating”. He threw out every cigarette in the house, smashed his lighter and put up a big poster on the wall: “NO SMOKING!” The first thing he did every morning when he got up was to tell himself, “Today I absolutely must not smoke.” And the result? All day long his mind was full of cigarettes. He thought about them in meetings, he thought about them in traffic jams, and lying in bed at night he was still thinking about them. On day eleven he stood outside a convenience store for three minutes, then bought a packet. He went home, sat down on the sofa, slumped, and said to himself, “Just as I thought — I can’t do it.”

The second brother’s method was different. He didn’t put the focus on “not smoking”; he put the focus on other things. He signed up for the neighbourhood morning running group and every day at six o’clock ran three kilometres with a crowd of people. He started learning the harmonica, and whenever his hands were free he picked it up. He joined the church prayer group and every evening prayed for twenty minutes with two other brothers. Three months later someone asked him, “How’s quitting smoking going?” He paused for a moment and said, “Oh — I don’t think I’ve thought about that for a long time.”

Brothers and sisters, both of them were quitting smoking. One poured all his strength into “combating”; the other quietly set about “cultivating”. In the end, the one who strained failed, and the one who didn’t strain overcame.

This isn’t just a story about quitting smoking. It’s a portrait of the spiritual life of many Christians.

So many of us want to overcome sin. We combat it with all our strength, we suppress it with all our might, we struggle without end. We weep and wail in prayer, we write resolutions in our notebooks, we make vows before the pulpit on Sunday. And then?

The harder we try, the weaker we get. The more we combat, the more we fail.

Why? Because we’re using the wrong method. We have turned God’s work into our own construction project. We have taken the road of grace and walked it as the hard labour of the law.

Brothers and sisters, God’s way is not “combating”. God’s way is — cultivating life.

Today’s lesson will show us a great spiritual principle: victory is not straining; victory is letting a stronger life grow within us.

sections.heading: Scripture Background: Two Letters, One Answer
sections.html: Our key passages today come from two places, one in Romans and one in Colossians. One speaks of a “law”, the other of “putting to death”; together they answer exactly the question of this lesson.

sections.heading: 1. The Background to Romans 8:2
sections.html:
The apostle Paul wrote Romans in the city of Corinth around AD 56 to 57, towards the end of his third missionary journey. The church in Rome that received it was one Paul had neither planted nor ever visited. It had Jewish believers and Gentile believers, and the two groups were sometimes in tension over the question of the law. So Paul used a full sixteen chapters to set out the gospel completely — from sin, to justification, to sanctification, to God’s plan.

To understand Romans 8:2, you must first read Romans 7. Chapter 7 records the most honest and most painful cry of a believer:

“For the good which I desire, I don’t do; but the evil which I don’t desire, that I practice.” (Romans 7:19)

“What a wretched man I am! Who will deliver me out of the body of this death?” (Romans 7:24)

Brothers and sisters, notice the word that appears most in chapter 7: “I”. I desire, I can’t, I resolve, I can’t carry it out. The main character of the whole chapter is “I”, and the whole chapter ends in failure. Chapter 7 describes precisely a person who is trying to overcome sin by the method of “combating”. It isn’t that he doesn’t try; he tries too hard. It isn’t that he lacks resolve; resolve is all he has.

Then 8:1 turns the corner: “There is therefore now no condemnation to those who are in Christ Jesus.” And verse 2 follows straight on with the real secret of overcoming sin: not that “I” am stronger, but that another “law” has come in.

sections.heading: 2. The Background to Colossians 3:5
sections.html:
Paul wrote Colossians from prison, generally thought to be during his first Roman imprisonment, around AD 60 to 62. Colossae was a city in the Lycus Valley in Asia Minor. Its church wasn’t planted by Paul himself but through the preaching of his co-worker Epaphras (Colossians 1:7).

At the time the church was facing a hybrid heresy: on one side it mixed in the regulations of the Jewish law, on the other the asceticism of the East and early Gnostic thought. What did these false teachers teach? They taught “Don’t handle, don’t taste, don’t touch”, using harsh prohibitions to suppress the flesh.

What was Paul’s verdict on the whole package? He put it very bluntly:

“These things indeed appear like wisdom in self-imposed worship, humility, and severity to the body; but aren’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh.” (Colossians 2:23)

Brothers and sisters, this verse is the key to today’s lesson. Severity to the body, combating with all your strength — it looks very spiritual and sounds very devout, but it “isn’t of any value against the indulgence of the flesh”. God himself says this method doesn’t work.

So what is Paul’s method? He gives the answer at the very start of chapter 3: “If then you were raised together with Christ, seek the things that are above, where Christ is, seated on the right hand of God. Set your mind on the things that are above, not on the things that are on the earth.” (Colossians 3:1–2)

First seek the things above, first set your mind on the things above, and only then — in verse 5 — does he say, “Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth.” The order can’t be reversed. First comes looking upward, then comes putting to death downward; first comes cultivating life, then comes the withering of the flesh.

That is what this lesson is about: not combating, but cultivating.

sections.heading: Key Point 1: The Key to Overcoming Sin Is the Law of Life
sections.html:
“For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)

In this verse, the word “law” in Greek is nomos. Its original sense is not only a written law of rules but also “a law, a principle, an ongoing operating principle”. Like a law of physics, it doesn’t need your agreement; it simply operates.

In this verse Paul sets out two laws:

The first law is called “the law of sin and of death”. The way this law operates is automatic and downward. No one has to teach a small child to lie; he’ll do it on his own. No one has to remind the human heart to be jealous, to compare, to be greedy; it does it on its own. This law is like gravity: you don’t have to do anything, and it pulls you down.

The second law is called “the law of the Spirit of life”. This law is one God has placed within us. It too operates automatically, only in the opposite direction — upward, towards life.

Brothers and sisters, listen carefully to what this verse does not say. It doesn’t say, “Because I tried harder, I was freed from the law of sin and of death.” What it says is: “The law of the Spirit of life … made me free.” The word “made free” in Greek is eleutheroō, meaning to buy a slave out of his master’s hand and take off his chains. The subject isn’t me; the subject is that law.

So the key has never been “you try harder”; the key is “which law is operating within you”.

Let me give an illustration. Put a piece of iron on a table: gravity holds it down firmly, and you have to make an effort to lift it. But what happens if you hold a powerful magnet above it? The iron rises by itself. Has gravity disappeared? No. Gravity is still there; it hasn’t stopped working for one second. It’s just that a stronger force has come in and overcome it.

Brothers and sisters, since you believed in the Lord, has the pull of sin disappeared? No. It’s still there. But God has placed a “magnet” in your life — the Holy Spirit, the life of Christ. When the law of life is at work, the law of sin naturally loses its power.

From the 321 mindset, this is exactly the starting point of the “fivefold change”: change the mindset and you change the life. Many brothers and sisters have been spiritually stagnant for years, not because they haven’t tried hard enough, but because their mindset is wrong. With the wrong mindset, the harder you try, the further off course you go; with the right mindset, one step gets you there.

321 says: “Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad.” Romans 7 is relying on the brain and ourselves, so that man’s conclusion is “What a wretched man I am!” Romans 8 is relying on the heart and the Holy Spirit, so that man’s conclusion is “no condemnation”. The same Paul, two mindsets, two lives.

The third of the Three Foundations is: “The Holy Spirit is my guide.” Brothers and sisters, the Holy Spirit is not the backup plan of our spiritual life; the Holy Spirit is the power source of our spiritual life. When we let the Holy Spirit be our guide, the law of life begins to work.

sections.heading: Key Point 2: The Parable of the Leaf and the Fish
sections.html:
At this point the lesson asks two fascinating questions. Brothers and sisters, think them through with me.

The first question: why don’t all the leaves fall off the trees?

If gravity were the only thing operating in this world, every leaf ought to be lying on the ground. Yet when you walk into the park in the morning and look up, the trees are full of leaves growing happily on their branches. Why?

The answer is: because there is life.

This isn’t just a spiritual metaphor; it’s verifiable plant physiology. Where the leaf joins the twig there is a layer of cells called the “abscission layer”. While the leaf is alive and still growing, it keeps producing a plant hormone called “auxin”, so the abscission layer doesn’t form and the leaf stays firmly attached to the tree. Only in autumn, when the days shorten and the temperature drops, does the auxin decrease while another hormone, “ethylene”, rises; then the abscission layer forms and the leaf falls.

Brothers and sisters, notice: the leaf isn’t “clinging” to the tree. The leaf isn’t straining, isn’t struggling, isn’t wrestling with gravity. The leaf is simply “alive”, simply joined to the tree, simply going on receiving supply from the trunk.

Isn’t that exactly what the Lord Jesus said?

“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

The Lord didn’t say, “Hold on to me tightly”; he said, “Remain in me.” Holding on is straining; remaining is rest.

The second question: why doesn’t a fish in salt water become salt fish?

Seawater has a salinity of about thirty-five parts per thousand — that is, three and a half per cent. A fish spends its whole life soaking in salt water like that, so why is its flesh fresh and not salty?

The answer is: because it is alive.

In biology this is called “osmoregulation”. The body fluids of a marine bony fish are only about one third as salty as seawater, so by rights water should be constantly draining out of the fish’s body and salt constantly seeping in. So what does it do? It keeps drinking seawater, then uses special cells on its gills to actively pump the excess salt out of its body, while passing only a very small amount of concentrated urine. It is a continuous, energy-consuming activity of life.

A living fish is doing this every second, so it isn’t salty. And a dead fish? Put a dead fish in brine and in two days it’s salt fish.

Brothers and sisters, a living fish isn’t changed by its environment; only a dead fish is shaped by its surroundings.

This gives us a vitally important reminder: the key isn’t the environment; the key is life.

We often blame our environment. We say, “My workplace is so dark.” “No one in my family believes.” “Everyone on my course mocks faith.” Brothers and sisters, Daniel in the palace of Babylon, Joseph in the house of the captain of the guard in Egypt, Paul in prison in Rome — their environments were far saltier than ours. Why didn’t they become salt fish? Because they were alive.

“Don’t be conformed to this world, but be transformed by the renewing of your mind, so that you may prove what is the good, well-pleasing, and perfect will of God.” (Romans 12:2)

In this verse “be conformed” and “be transformed” carry the sense of the passive voice — if you don’t actively let your mind be renewed, you will passively be shaped by the world. Just like that dead fish: it doesn’t have to do anything, and its surroundings will pickle it into salt fish all by themselves.

This is where 321’s shift of perspective shows itself: from man’s perspective to God’s, from the earthly perspective to the heavenly. From man’s perspective, environment decides everything; from God’s perspective, life overcomes environment. From the earthly perspective, I’m pickled in salt water; from the heavenly perspective, there are rivers of living water within me.

sections.heading: Key Point 3: The Two Lives Within You
sections.html:
There are two lives within us. That is the clear teaching of the Bible, and it is the real experience of every true believer.

The first is the self-centred life — the old life

The marks of this life are: it sins easily, it is easily lured, it is easily weak.

“That you put away, as concerning your former way of life, the old man that grows corrupt after the lusts of deceit.” (Ephesians 4:22)

Notice the words “grows corrupt”. The old man doesn’t need you to cultivate him; he goes bad all by himself. He slides downhill; he decays automatically.

The second is the life of Jesus — the new life

The marks of this life are: holiness, victory, freedom.

“And put on the new man, who in the likeness of God has been created in righteousness and holiness of truth.” (Ephesians 4:24)

“I have been crucified with Christ, and it is no longer I who live, but Christ lives in me. That life which I now live in the flesh, I live by faith in the Son of God, who loved me, and gave himself up for me.” (Galatians 2:20)

Brothers and sisters, these two lives within us are in competition. Paul says it very clearly:

“For the flesh lusts against the Spirit, and the Spirit against the flesh; and these are contrary to one another, that you may not do the things that you desire.” (Galatians 5:17)

So please stop being shocked and condemning yourself over “Why are there still such ugly thoughts inside me?” Having those thoughts shows precisely that the war is still going on; and the fact that the war is still going on shows precisely that there is a new life inside you that refuses to surrender. A person who is wholly of the flesh has no war inside, because there is no opponent.

But, brothers and sisters, here comes a crucial turn.

The question isn’t which life exists. Both exist.

The question is which one you feed.

On this point psychology gives us very powerful corroboration. In 1987 the American psychologist Daniel Wegner and his colleagues published the famous “white bear experiment” in the Journal of Personality and Social Psychology. He sat his participants in a room and gave them just one instruction: “For the next five minutes, please don’t think of a white bear.” What happened? Those who were told “Don’t think of a white bear” had a white bear pop into their minds far more often than those who were given no such instruction. And when the experiment ended and the ban was lifted, the number of times they thought of white bears rebounded even higher. Wegner called this the “rebound effect”.

Brothers and sisters, that is why “combating with all your strength” is doomed to fail. When you spend all day telling yourself, “I mustn’t lose my temper”, “I mustn’t look at that”, “I mustn’t think about that thing”, you are in effect keeping that thing at the very centre of your thoughts all day long. You think you’re combating it; in fact you’re feeding it.

There is a vivid saying commonly attributed to Martin Luther: “You cannot stop the birds from flying over your head, but you can stop them from building a nest in your hair.” Brothers and sisters, you don’t have to chase the birds across the sky; you just don’t give them twigs to build a nest.

321 says: the old self is self-centred, the new self is selfless. The self-centred life is the root of humanity’s fall, and pride is the root of the problem. And selflessness is not having nothing; it is entering into the infinite and living out the infinite — “I” no longer live, but Christ lives in me.

So, dear brothers and sisters, today’s question isn’t “Is there any self-centred life in me?” but “Whom did I feed today?”

sections.heading: Key Point 4: The Story of the Black Dog and the White Dog
sections.html:
At this point the lesson tells a story. It is very widely told and is generally thought to come from a Native North American legend; its true origin can no longer be traced, but it puts a spiritual truth with remarkable vividness.

There was a farmer who kept two dogs. One was a black dog and one was a white dog.

The black dog stands for the self-centred life; the white dog stands for selflessness.

At first the farmer had a hard time of it. The black dog kept eating and kept growing, becoming fiercer and fiercer; the white dog ate very little and grew thinner and weaker. Every time the two dogs fought, the black dog won. The farmer beat the black dog with a stick, and it grew fiercer still; the farmer locked the black dog up, and it barked in its cage all night so that no one could sleep. The farmer tried every way he could think of to combat the black dog, yet his household grew more and more chaotic.

Later the farmer changed his strategy. He ignored the black dog — he didn’t beat it, didn’t scold it, and didn’t feed it. He put all his heart and energy into feeding the white dog. He fed it every morning and every evening, took it for walks and played with it.

And the result? The white dog grew stronger and stronger, and the black dog grew thinner and weaker.

One day the two dogs faced off again. This time the white dog simply stood there, and the black dog backed away.

In the end, the white dog won.

Brothers and sisters, remember the point of this story: the key isn’t “defeating the black dog”; the key is “feeding the white dog”.

Modern habit science confirms this principle too. In 2012 the American journalist Charles Duhigg, in his book The Power of Habit, gathered up the academic research on the habit loop and pointed out that a habit is made up of three parts: the cue, the routine and the reward. He put forward what he called the “Golden Rule of Habit Change”: you can almost never pull an old habit out by the roots; what you can do is keep the same cue and the same reward and swap out the routine in the middle. In other words, not “delete” but “replace”; not “destroy” but “substitute”.

In addition, research published in 2002 by the psychologist Wendy Wood and her colleagues showed that a considerable proportion of people’s everyday behaviour — about forty-three per cent in her study — consists of habitual actions repeated in the same settings. Brothers and sisters, what does that mean? It means that nearly half of our life isn’t decided by “resolve” but by “feeding”. Resolve governs a single moment; feeding governs a whole life.

Let me bring this story back to 321.

321 says: “Humility overcomes pride, and selflessness overcomes Satan.” Notice how the overcoming happens. It isn’t pride fighting pride, because “pride provokes pride, and both sides lose”; it is humility stepping in — “humility draws out humility, and both sides win”.

The farmer beating the black dog is using pride to combat pride, and both sides lose. The farmer feeding the white dog is letting humility step in, and quietly overcoming.

“God resists the proud, but gives grace to the humble.” (James 4:6b)

The next verse goes on: “Be subject therefore to God. Resist the devil, and he will flee from you.” (James 4:7) Brothers and sisters, see the order: first submit to God, then resist the devil. First feed the white dog, then the black dog runs away. How many people turn the order upside down, resisting the devil all day long but not submitting to God — and end up both exhausted and defeated.

sections.heading: Key Point 5: What the Bible Really Means by “Put to Death”
sections.html:
“Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth: sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” (Colossians 3:5)

When many people read this verse, they assume the Bible is telling us to “combat sin with all our might”. So some begin treating themselves harshly, some tie themselves up in all kinds of rules, and some even live in years of self-reproach.

But brothers and sisters, we need to go back to the original language and the context.

The word “put to death” in Greek is nekroō. Its root is nekros, meaning “a corpse”. The verb doesn’t mean “to kill something that is alive”; it means “to treat it as a corpse”.

Look at what Paul has just said in the preceding passage: “For you died, and your life is hidden with Christ in God.” (Colossians 3:3)

And look at what Galatians says: “Those who belong to Christ have crucified the flesh with its passions and lusts.” (Galatians 5:24)

Brothers and sisters, this is a completed action. Already crucified. Already dead. So “put to death” doesn’t tell you to finish a job that hasn’t been finished; it tells you to live in line with a fact that has already been accomplished — to stop supplying an old life that has already been ended on the cross.

So the true meaning of “put to death” is: don’t feed it.

Give it no opportunity. Give it no room. Give it no resources.

Let it wither on its own.

That is what the Bible means by “putting to death”.

Let me give another example from daily life. There is a clump of weeds in your garden. You can go out every day with shears and cut it back; you cut it and it grows, it grows and you cut it, and after three hundred cuttings in a year you still haven’t finished. But move the hosepipe away so it gets no more water, and in a month it will wither by itself. Cutting the weeds is “combating”; cutting off the water is “putting to death”.

The Lord Jesus himself told a more sobering parable. He said that when an unclean spirit leaves a person, it passes through waterless places looking for rest and finds none, and so it says it will return to the house it came from. “When he has come back, he finds it empty, swept, and put in order. Then he goes, and takes with himself seven other spirits more evil than he is, and they enter in and dwell there. The last state of that man becomes worse than the first.” (Matthew 12:44–45)

Brothers and sisters, notice the state of that house: “empty, swept, and put in order”. This is a house where the combating has been a great success! The sin has been driven out, the floor has been mopped clean, it has even been put in order. So where’s the problem? The problem is that it is “empty”. No new master has moved in.

That is why Paul says, “Don’t be drunken with wine, in which is dissipation, but be filled with the Spirit.” (Ephesians 5:18) He doesn’t stop at “Don’t be drunken with wine”; it must be followed by “but be filled with the Spirit”. Emptying isn’t enough; there must also be filling. Combating isn’t enough; there must also be cultivating.

And the true order is stated most completely in Romans 8:13: “For if you live after the flesh, you must die; but if by the Spirit you put to death the deeds of the body, you will live.” (Romans 8:13)

Look at those words: “by the Spirit”. There is a putting to death, but it is not by me; it is by the Spirit.

The Three Foundations of 321 say: “The Holy Spirit is my guide.” Brothers and sisters, even putting sin to death isn’t our own construction project; it is the work of the Holy Spirit. Our responsibility is to give the old life no resources; our privilege is to let the Holy Spirit be our guide.

sections.heading: Key Point 6: Every Day You Are Feeding One Life or the Other
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, now we need to bring this truth down to the most practical level.

Every one of your choices feeds a life. If it isn’t feeding selflessness, it’s feeding the self-centred life. There is no neutral ground.

When you choose humility, you feed selflessness; when you choose pride, you feed the self-centred life.

When you choose faith, you feed selflessness; when you choose fear, you feed the self-centred life.

When you choose love, you feed selflessness; when you choose hatred, you feed the self-centred life.

You are feeding every day; you just haven’t noticed.

Paul uses “sowing” to say the same thing: “Don’t be deceived. God is not mocked, for whatever a man sows, that he will also reap. For he who sows to his own flesh will from the flesh reap corruption. But he who sows to the Spirit will from the Spirit reap eternal life.” (Galatians 6:7–8)

Notice the words “Don’t be deceived”. What is self-deception? Self-deception is thinking that one bite doesn’t count, that one remark doesn’t matter, that no one saw those thirty minutes. Brothers and sisters, every bite counts. The soil doesn’t forget the seed you sow in it.

Neuroscience offers a very beautiful confirmation here too. In 1949 the Canadian psychologist Donald Hebb set out a principle in his book The Organization of Behavior: when one nerve cell repeatedly takes part in firing another, the connection between the two is strengthened. People since have often summed it up in one sentence: “Neurons that fire together wire together.” This is the basis of “neuroplasticity”.

Brothers and sisters, what does that mean? It means that every time you choose to lose your temper, you haven’t just lost your temper once; you have walked the “temper” path in your brain one more time, treading it wider, flatter and easier to walk. Next time you’ll get onto it faster. And the other way round: every time you choose patience, you also tread one more step on the “patience” path in your brain.

God has made us so wonderfully — our very bodies bear witness to the truth of “feeding”.

So the Bible says, “Keep your heart with all diligence, for out of it is the wellspring of life.” (Proverbs 4:23)

321 puts it well: “Rely on the heart and the Holy Spirit, not on the brain and ourselves; rely on the brain and you’ll be troubled, rely on the heart and you’ll be glad. Out of the heart is the wellspring of life.”

Here we come to 321’s “920 practice”. Everyone we have a relationship with is our “2”. That person may be your spouse, your children, or the hardest colleague to get along with in your office. When that “2” is standing in front of you, you have two choices: one is to bring out the “self” — to haggle with them, compare yourself with them, compete with them; the other is to live out the “0” — the selfless life — and bear the fruit of the Spirit in all nine of its expressions towards them.

“But the fruit of the Spirit is love, joy, peace, patience, kindness, goodness, faith, gentleness, and self-control.” (Galatians 5:22–23a)

Brothers and sisters, look at that word: “fruit”. Fruit is borne, not made. You have never seen an apple tree gritting its teeth to produce apples. Fruit is the natural overflow of life. The 920 practice isn’t nine targets you must strive to hit; it’s what a well-fed life naturally grows into.

sections.heading: Key Point 7: The Real Road to Victory
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, we come to the conclusion of this lesson.

Victory isn’t “I try harder”; victory isn’t “I get stronger”.

Victory is “the life of Jesus grows stronger in me”.

Listen to this verse: “Therefore we don’t faint, but though our outward man is decaying, yet our inward man is renewed day by day.” (2 Corinthians 4:16)

“Renewed day by day” — that is cultivating. Not one great struggle, but a small supply each day.

When you give yourself to cultivating the life of Christ, three things happen:

First, the pull of sin naturally declines. Not because sin has grown ugly, but because Christ has grown beautiful.

Second, the struggle naturally lessens. Not because the battlefield has disappeared, but because the outcome of the war has already been settled by what you feed.

Third, victory naturally happens. One day you’ll suddenly realise, “Hm? I don’t think I’ve thought about that thing for a long time.”

It’s just like the brother who quit smoking that we spoke about at the start. He didn’t beat the cigarettes; he lived out a different kind of life, and the cigarettes left the stage on their own.

In his Confessions Augustine wrote a prayer repeated through the ages: “You have made us for yourself, and our heart is restless until it rests in you.” Brothers and sisters, only God can fill the emptiness of the human heart. If you don’t give it God, it will go looking for something else to fill it. That is why “giving up without filling up” never works.

So the conclusion of this lesson is just one sentence:

Not combating sin, but living out life.

“I came that they may have life, and may have it abundantly.” (John 10:10b)

The Lord Jesus didn’t come to give us a list of prohibitions; he came to give us a more abundant life.

sections.heading: Integrating the 321 Vision
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, let’s look at today’s truth again, set within the framework of 321.

The Three Foundations

Jesus is my role model. When the Lord Jesus was tempted in the wilderness, how did he overcome Satan? Not by arguing with the devil, but by saying three times, “It is written.” He didn’t combat the temptation; he lived in the Father’s word. Though he existed in the form of God, he “emptied himself, taking the form of a servant” (Philippians 2:7a) — emptying himself is the supreme role model of selflessness.

The Bible is my standard. Today we put the word “put to death” back into the original language and back into its context, and saw that it doesn’t mean “combat with all your strength” but “stop supplying”. Brothers and sisters, our feelings can deceive us, our traditions can mislead us; only the Bible is our standard.

The Holy Spirit is my guide. Romans 8:2 says it was “the law of the Spirit of life” that made me free; 8:13 says it is “by the Spirit” that we “put to death the deeds of the body”. From beginning to end, the power comes from the Holy Spirit.

The Two Core Values

Let Jesus be King. Brothers and sisters, whomever you feed, you let reign as king. Feed the self-centred life and you keep yourself sitting on the throne; feed selflessness and you give up the throne to Jesus. The essence of victory is really a change of who sits on the throne.

Let Jesus receive all the glory. If victory came from my straining, then after the victory I would be sure to feel a secret pride. But if victory comes because the life of Christ has grown within me, then all the glory naturally goes to him. One very deep reason God doesn’t let us overcome by the method of “combating” is that he will not give his glory to another.

The Goal

Establish God’s system. A life that has been fed until it is strong won’t stop at itself. It becomes a blessing to others; it passes this principle of life on to the next person; and so God’s system is established, one person at a time.

The Fivefold Change

Mindset → life → daily living → relationships → ministry.

The central change in this lesson is in the very first link — mindset. Exchange the mindset “I must combat sin” for the mindset “I will cultivate life”. Change the mindset and the life changes; change the life and daily living changes; change daily living and relationships change; change relationships and ministry changes.

321 says: life first, then relationships, then ministry. People matter more than tasks; relationships matter more than things. The priority of relationships is: first with God, then with ourselves, then with others, and last with things. Brothers and sisters, this is exactly the order of “feeding”. If you aren’t first fed in your relationship with God, sooner or later your ministry will dry up.

The Shift of Perspective

From man’s perspective to God’s: man says, “Try harder”; God says, “Remain in me.”

From the earthly perspective to the heavenly: the earth sees how fierce the black dog is; heaven sees who is feeding the white dog.

From the temporary perspective to the eternal: combating is about getting through today; cultivating is about bearing fruit for a lifetime.

From the worldly perspective to the godly: the world tells you, “Conquer yourself”; the Bible tells you, “Let Christ live in you.”

The 235 Relationships

Brothers and sisters, feeding life is hard to do alone. 321’s “235 relationships” tell us: first become a “2” with a selfless person, spiritual companions who support each other; then establish the “3”, the passing-on between spiritual parents and spiritual children; and finally build together in the “5” — a fivefold-ministry team of spiritual comrades.

One person feeding the white dog easily grows slack; two people feeding it together find it hard to stop. That is God’s wisdom.

sections.heading: Putting It into Practice: Three Practices, Eight Stages
sections.html:
The lesson gives us three practices. Let’s use 321’s eight stages of changing our mindset — Information, Revelation, Conviction, Implementation, Evaluation, Correction, Repetition, Multiplication — to take them deeper.

Practice 1: Recognise What You Are Feeding

Reflect every day: are today’s choices feeding the self-centred life, or selflessness?

Information: Today you’ve already received the information — there are two lives within you, and every day you feed one of them.

Revelation: Ask the Holy Spirit to shine his light on you so that you can see specifically what you fed today. You might pray like this: “Lord, please point out the bite I gave the self-centred life today.”

Conviction: Not “I agree with this teaching”, but “I believe this is really at work in me.”

Implementation: Tonight before you sleep, spend three minutes on a “two-column reflection”. In the left column write three choices you made today that fed selflessness; in the right column write three choices that fed the self-centred life. Just write — no condemnation.

Evaluation: After a week, look back: which column is longer? In what situation are you most likely to feed the black dog?

Correction: For that most dangerous situation, set a counter-measure in advance.

Repetition: Do it for thirty days in a row. Habits aren’t changed in a day.

Multiplication: Find a brother or sister and teach them the “two-column reflection”.

Practice 2: Deliberately Feed the Life of Jesus

Through prayer, Bible reading and obeying the Holy Spirit, actively let the life of Christ be nourished within you.

Information: “As newborn babies, long for the pure milk of the Word, that with it you may grow.” (1 Peter 2:2)

Revelation: Ask the Lord to show you whether your spirit is hungry or well fed. A person who is spiritually hungry is especially easily drawn to sin.

Conviction: Believe that “feeding” is more powerful than “combating”, because it is God’s own method.

Implementation: Set a portion so small you can certainly manage it. For example: read three verses of the Bible early each morning, pray for five minutes, memorise one verse. Don’t set a grand plan you’ll abandon after three days.

Evaluation: After a month, ask yourself: is my heart hungrier for the Lord’s word, or more numb to it?

Correction: If it’s numb, change the way you feed — read aloud, copy it out by hand, share it with someone.

Repetition: “He will be like a tree planted by the streams of water, that produces its fruit in its season, whose leaf also does not wither.” (Psalm 1:3a) A tree doesn’t grow up in a day; a tree puts down roots day after day.

Multiplication: Bring someone to do the morning devotion with you. Your feeding becomes their feeding.

Practice 3: Stop Feeding Self-Centred Habits

Cut down on the choices that make the flesh strong — complaining, comparing, judging — and let the old life gradually wither.

Information: “But put on the Lord Jesus Christ, and make no provision for the flesh, for its lusts.” (Romans 13:14)

Revelation: “Make no provision for the flesh” — ask the Holy Spirit to point out which “provision” in your daily living is really preparing the black dog’s dinner. Is it that time of day? That chat group? That app on your phone?

Conviction: Believe that what isn’t fed will wither. You don’t need to cut it down; cut off the supply and it will die by itself.

Implementation: This week, pick one “provision” and remove it. Don’t leave a blank where it was; fill the gap with something that feeds selflessness. Emptying must always be followed by filling.

Evaluation: Once it’s gone, how do you react? Restless, empty, or lighter? That reaction will tell you how tightly it had you bound.

Correction: If it’s too hard, first shorten the time, change the place, or find a companion to go through it with you.

Repetition: “Whatever things are true, whatever things are honorable, whatever things are just, whatever things are pure, whatever things are lovely, whatever things are of good report: if there is any virtue and if there is any praise, think about these things.” (Philippians 4:8) Whatever you think about, you feed.

Multiplication: Once you’ve tasted freedom yourself, go and help the brother or sister who is still struggling. Don’t teach them to strain; teach them to feed.

A Gentle Reminder

You don’t have to defeat the darkness; you only need to turn on the light.

Brothers and sisters, have you ever tried fighting the darkness? No one can do it. Darkness has no substance; you can’t hit it and you can’t push it. But strike just one match, and the darkness retreats.

“God is light, and in him is no darkness at all.” (1 John 1:5b)

“The light shines in the darkness, and the darkness hasn’t overcome it.” (John 1:5)

It isn’t that the light attacks the darkness; it’s that the moment the light comes, the darkness is no longer darkness.

“You are the light of the world. A city located on a hill can’t be hidden.” (Matthew 5:14)

sections.heading: Closing and Call
sections.html:
Brothers and sisters, there is a war going on inside you.

But the key to who wins is simple: whom you feed.

Feed the self-centred life, and you lose more and more. Feed selflessness, and you win more and more.

This morning I’m not asking you to make a bigger vow or to grit your teeth harder. I’m asking you to do something simpler and deeper — give your first bite of today to Christ.

Hand your first thought to him. Offer your first word to him. Yield your first choice to him.

Let Jesus reign as King in your heart. Let Jesus receive all the glory.

Because as Jesus grows greater and greater within you, you will find that you no longer have to fight every day; you only have to feed every day.

“I am the vine. You are the branches. He who remains in me and I in him bears much fruit, for apart from me you can do nothing.” (John 15:5)

From today on, give yourself to cultivating the life of Christ, and you will experience a truly victorious life.

keyVerses: “For the law of the Spirit of life in Christ Jesus made me free from the law of sin and of death.” (Romans 8:2)
“Put to death therefore your members which are on the earth: sexual immorality, uncleanness, depraved passion, evil desire, and covetousness, which is idolatry.” (Colossians 3:5)
declarations: Lord, I choose to feed your life within me and no longer feed the self-centred life. Let Christ grow within me, so that I live out a victorious, free and glorious life!
practices: Deliberately feed the life of Jesus
prayer: Dear Lord Jesus, we thank you.

We confess that for far too many years we have spent our strength combating ourselves, and the more we combated, the weaker we became. Today you have shown us that victory is not my being stronger; it is your life growing stronger in me.
Lord, forgive us our past self-deception. We thought that one bite didn’t count, but every bite counts. Shine your light on us, and let us see whom we have fed today.
May the law of the Spirit of life work mightily within us, and set us free from the law of sin and of death.
Teach us to stop treating ourselves harshly, and instead to look to you, set our minds on the things above, and feed the new life within us with your word every day.
Let our black dog wither because its supply has been cut off, and let our white dog grow strong because it is fed every day.
Lord, reign as King in our hearts; may all the glory be yours.
In the holy name of the Lord Jesus Christ we pray. Amen.
discussion: Read Romans 7:19 and 8:2. Think of something you have long “combated with all your strength yet kept failing at”. If you changed your method from “combating” to “cultivating”, what would you do? Name one specific small action you could start tomorrow.

Read Colossians 3:1–5. Paul first says “seek the things that are above” and then says “put to death your members which are on the earth”. What does this order remind you of? This week, what will you stop feeding, and what will you deliberately feed?
